articles/formats/ani.html.title: ANI | Egami
articles/formats/ani.html.summary: ANI Egami reads and writes Windows animated cursors (.ani), written from Microsoft's description of the RIFF ACON form. AniFormat.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default. An animated cursor stores a set of frames, each a whole cursor or icon, and a list of steps that says which frame shows and for how long; Egami's ICO and CUR reader decodes the frames, so a frame loads exactly as the same cursor would, and its CUR writer stores the frames when Egami writes one. Reading animated cursors Raster.Load returns one animated raster with a frame per step: the seq list is played out, so a frame it shows twice is in the raster twice, and each frame's Delay is its step's rate in jiffies (1/60 s), or the header's default rate. Animated cursors always loop, so LoopCount is 0. Every frame replaces the one before it (FrameDisposal.ClearToBackground, FrameBlend.Source), so the frames save straight to GIF, APNG or WebP. Each frame's hotspot is in its IcoDetails, and can move from frame to frame. All frames of a raster share one size, but a frame's cursor can hold several. Load picks one for the whole animation the way it picks an icon's entry: the largest, or with ReaderOptions.MinimumSize the smallest size at least that big. A frame without that size is resized from its nearest larger image, hotspot and all, with the Ani.SizeMissing warning. Raster.LoadAll returns the animation once for every size, largest first. // One frame per step of the animation, all at one size: the largest, as for an icon. using Raster<Rgba8> busy = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("busy.ani"); foreach (Frame<Rgba8> frame in busy.Frames) { Point? hotspot = ((IcoDetails)frame.Metadata.FormatDetails!).Hotspot; Console.WriteLine($"{frame.Metadata.Delay.TotalMilliseconds:F0} ms, hotspot {hotspot}"); } // MinimumSize picks the smallest size at least that big; LoadAll gives the animation at every size, largest first. using Raster<Rgba8> small = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("busy.ani", options: new ReaderOptions { MinimumSize = new Size(32, 32) }); using RasterList sizes = Raster.LoadAll("busy.ani"); Raster.Probe reads the chunks and each frame's directory without decoding a pixel: RasterInfo.FrameCount is the number of steps and ImageCount the number of sizes. AniDetails, the raster's format details, gives the title and artist from the file's INFO list (also added to the raster's text entries as Title and Author, the keys PNG and TGA use), the default delay, how many frames the file stores, the frame each step shows and every size. // Probe reads the chunks and each frame's directory without decoding a pixel. RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("busy.ani"); Console.WriteLine($"{info.FrameCount} steps; {info.ImageCount} sizes; Load gives {info.Width}×{info.Height}"); // The steps replay the stored frames in the file's order; a frame can show more than once. using Raster busy = Raster.Load("busy.ani"); AniDetails details = (AniDetails)busy.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"\"{details.Title}\" by {details.Artist}: {details.StoredFrames} frames stored, steps {string.Join(", ", details.Steps)}"); Old files sometimes store raw bitmaps instead of cursors (the header's icon flag is clear): whole BMP files, BMP data without the file header, or bare 24 or 32-bit rows at the header's size. Egami reads all three; their frames have no hotspot, and AniDetails.RawBitmaps is true. A frame that is a cursor in a file that says otherwise is read as a cursor, with the Ani.IconInRawFile warning. Writing animated cursors Raster.Save with a .ani path, or AniFormat.Info, writes an animated raster as a cursor: each frame is a step. A frame with the same pixels and hotspot as an earlier one is stored once, and a seq list says which stored frame each step shows, so a spinner that comes back to its first picture costs nothing extra. Every stored frame is a cursor written by Egami's CUR writer, 32-bit BMP entries below 256 × 256 and PNG at 256, which is what Windows expects. AniWriterOptions has the same words as IcoWriterOptions. Sizes gives every stored frame each size, from the frame resized with Filter; AniWriterOptions.CursorSizes (32, 48, 64, 96 and 128) are the sizes Windows draws cursors at as the display scale grows. Without Sizes the frames keep the raster's size, fitted down to 256 with the Save.IcoFitted warning when larger. With several sizes and no Encoding, every entry of every frame has one encoding: 32-bit BMP while each entry starts within the frame's first 64 KiB, else PNG, as for the five cursor sizes. Windows loads no animated cursor with an entry past that point, and given BMP and PNG entries in one frame it may draw a BMP entry of another size. Encoding = IcoEntryEncoding.Bmp at sizes that cannot fit is written as asked, with the Save.AniTooLarge warning. Hotspot sets every frame's hotspot at the raster's size, scaled to each entry; without it each frame keeps its own IcoDetails.Hotspot, so a cursor loaded from ANI or CUR saves with its hotspots. Title and Artist go into the INFO list, or come from a loaded cursor's AniDetails, else from the raster's Title and Author text entries, unless StripMetadata is set; so a PNG's title carries into the cursor. // Every frame is a step; frames that repeat are stored once. Each stored frame holds every size Windows may draw. spin.Save("spin.ani", new AniWriterOptions { Sizes = AniWriterOptions.CursorSizes, Hotspot = new Point(32, 32), Title = "Spinning duck", }); Delays are rounded to the nearest jiffy. A frame shown for less than 20 ms is written as 100 ms, as browsers play such GIF frames, with the Save.AniDelayRaised warning. The most common delay becomes the header's default rate, and a rate list is written only when the delays differ. Animated cursors always loop, so a LoopCount other than 0 is not written, with the Save.AniLoops warning. Raw-bitmap frames are read but never written. The same raster and options give the same bytes, and egami convert spinner.gif spinner.ani --set ani.sizes=32,48 turns a GIF into a cursor from the command line. Damaged and hostile data Every count, index and size is checked before it is used; CVE-2007-0038 came from a reader that trusted the anih header's size. The steps are checked against SafetyLimits.MaxFrames and every frame's size against the other limits before its pixels are allocated, and each stored frame is decoded once however often it shows. In lenient mode, the default, damage becomes a warning and the parts that can be used load: an anih chunk that is not 36 bytes is read for its first 36 (Ani.HeaderSize), a step that names a frame the file does not store is left out (Ani.SequenceIndex), a rate of 0 uses the default rate (Ani.ZeroRate), and a frame that cannot be read is left out with the steps that show it (Ani.FrameDamaged), as is the cut-off end of a truncated file. In strict mode each of these throws CorruptDataException; a file with no step left to show throws in both. Odd-sized chunks without RIFF's pad byte, which some writers leave out, are followed. The reader is fuzzed through whole files.

articles/formats/av1.html.title: AV1 video frames | Egami
articles/formats/av1.html.summary: AV1 video frames Av1StreamDecoder decodes AV1 video a temporal unit at a time and Av1StreamEncoder encodes it; both work on frames, and Egami.Video uses them for its containers. Decoding Av1StreamDecoder decodes AV1 video a temporal unit at a time: key, inter, intra-only and switch frames with every inter tool of the Main, High and Professional profiles (single and compound references, OBMC, local and global warps, wedge, difference-weighted and distance-weighted compound, inter-intra), 8, 10 and 12 bits, 4:0:0 to 4:4:4, film grain, frame size changes with scaled references, superres and scalable streams. Every frame equals libaom's sample for sample, on libaom's test vectors and on clips made with its encoder for each tool. It reads temporal units, not files: WebM, Matroska, MP4 and IVF are read by Egami.Video, which uses this decoder, and units from any other source decode the same way. // AV1 temporal units in stream order, here from an IVF file (Egami.Video reads WebM, Matroska, MP4 and IVF for you). using Av1StreamDecoder decoder = new(new Av1DecoderOptions { ApplyFilmGrain = true }); foreach (byte[] temporalUnit in IvfFrames("clip-av1.ivf")) { decoder.Send(temporalUnit); while (decoder.NextFrame is Av1FrameInfo next) { // A unit can show no frame (a hidden reference), one, or one per spatial layer. using YuvRaster picture = next.BitDepth == 8 ? YuvRaster.Create(next.Width, next.Height, next.Chroma, YuvColor.Bt601Limited) : YuvRaster.Create(next.Width, next.Height, next.Chroma, next.BitDepth, YuvColor.Bt601Limited); decoder.TryReceiveFrame(picture, out Av1FrameInfo info); // the picture is the caller's: change it or keep it shown++; } } Send takes one temporal unit: the low-overhead OBUs a container sample holds, each with its size. A unit can show no frame (a hidden frame, kept only as a reference), one frame, or with OutputAllLayers one per spatial layer. NextFrame gives the size, bit depth and chroma format of the next frame, and TryReceiveFrame copies it into a YuvRaster of that shape: 8-bit samples for an 8-bit stream, 16-bit samples holding 10 or 12 bits otherwise. The copy belongs to the caller, so it can be changed or kept while later units decode. A frame shown again with show_existing_frame comes out without decoding. Av1FrameInfo says what the frame was: its type (Av1FrameKind), whether it is a key frame shown in its own unit (a point a player can start from), its size and render size, bit depth, chroma format, temporal and spatial layer, and the sequence header's color code points. LastHeaders lists the fields of the last unit's sequence and frame headers under the specification's names. Options Av1DecoderOptions chooses what comes out. ApplyFilmGrain (on by default) adds the stream's film grain to the frames; the references keep the frames without grain either way. OperatingPoint picks the layers of a scalable stream that decode (0 by default), and OutputAllLayers gives every spatial layer of a unit instead of only the highest. Broken data and limits Decoding starts at a key frame. A broken unit, or one that refers to a frame the decoder does not have, throws CorruptDataException, and the decoder carries on from the next unit it is given; Reset drops the references so the next unit must start a sequence again. A frame larger than the context's SafetyLimits throws LimitExceededException. Memory and threads The decoder keeps the eight reference frames and the frame being decoded. A frame's tiles decode on up to EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads, and its loop filter, CDEF and loop restoration run in rows on the same threads; the result does not depend on the thread count. Encoding Av1StreamEncoder encodes YuvRaster pictures of one size into AV1 frames: key frames and intra-only frames with the AVIF encoder's intra search, and inter frames that predict each block from up to seven references. The motion search starts from the vectors the neighbours and the reference frames give, searches whole pixels and then refines to a quarter or an eighth of a pixel, and every block weighs NEARESTMV, NEARMV, GLOBALMV and NEWMV, the compound pairs and the intra modes by rate and distortion. Higher efforts add distance-weighted, wedge and difference-weighted compounds, inter-intra, overlapped and locally warped motion, dual interpolation filters and each reference's global motion. libaom and dav1d decode every frame exactly as Av1StreamDecoder does. // Pictures of one size, here decoded from a clip; Egami.Video writes WebM, MP4 and IVF and plans the frames for you. using Av1StreamEncoder encoder = new(new Av1SequenceOptions { Width = pictures[0].Width, Height = pictures[0].Height }); units.Add(encoder.Encode(pictures[0], new Av1FramePlan { Kind = Av1FrameKind.Key, Quality = 60 }).Data.ToArray()); // A hidden frame from four pictures ahead goes into slot 1; the three pictures between read it as ALTREF (from the future) // and the frame before as LAST, then the hidden frame is shown when its time comes. Av1FramePlan between = new() { Quality = 60, ReferenceSlots = [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1] }; encoder.Encode(pictures[4], new Av1FramePlan { Quality = 55, Show = false, OrderHint = 4, RefreshSlots = 0b10 }); for (int i = 1; i < 4; i++) { Av1EncodedFrame frame = encoder.Encode(pictures[i], between); // the first unit also holds the hidden frame units.Add(frame.Data.ToArray()); // an MP4 sample or a Matroska block; frame.LumaPsnr says how close it came } units.Add(encoder.ShowExisting(1).Data.ToArray()); Av1SequenceOptions describes the stream: its size, bit depth (8, 10 or 12), chroma format, color code points, chroma siting and level; the encoder picks the Main, High or Professional profile they need. Av1SequenceOptions.FromSequenceHeader takes the sequence header of an existing stream instead, and the encoder then writes that header byte for byte, so its frames can join the stream, as a frame-exact cut needs. SequenceHeader is the OBU an MP4 or Matroska av1C box holds. Each call takes an Av1FramePlan, so the caller decides what the stream looks like: Kind makes a key frame, an intra-only frame or an inter frame; the first frame is always a key frame. Quality (0 to 100, AVIF's scale) or QIndex (base_q_idx, 0 to 255, for rate control; 0 is lossless) sets the frame's quantizer, and Effort (0 to 10, default 4) how hard the encoder searches. ReferenceSlots names the slot each of LAST to ALTREF reads, References (an Av1References) which of them blocks may use, and RefreshSlots which slots the frame replaces. References that read the same frame are searched once. Show = false codes a hidden frame, such as an alternate reference from frames to come; OrderHint says where it shows, and ShowExisting shows it later with show_existing_frame. Tune is Av1Tune.Video (the default: one quantizer for luma and chroma, no quantization matrices, rate-distortion weights by frame type) or Av1Tune.Image, the still-picture tools AVIF uses. Layer is the frame's layer in its group's pyramid: the deeper it is, the fewer frames predict from it and the fewer bits it spends. Referenced says whether any later frame does. ErrorResilient makes a frame that decodes without the probabilities and vectors of the frames before it, PrimaryReference picks the reference a frame takes them from, DeltaQuantizers turns the per-superblock quantizers off, VarianceBoost gives flat superblocks finer ones, and ScreenContent the palettes on or off. Encode returns an Av1EncodedFrame with the temporal unit's OBUs, without temporal delimiters, as MP4 samples and Matroska blocks store them; a key frame's unit starts with the sequence header. A hidden frame's data is empty: its OBUs lead the next shown frame's unit, so every unit has one shown frame. The result also gives the frame's bits, quantizer, order hint and the squared error of the decoded frame against the picture (LumaPsnr from it), what rate control needs to plan the next frame. The encoder keeps the eight reference slots as a decoder does, and decides a frame's tiles on up to EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads; its output does not depend on the thread count. AVIF stills are not affected: they encode as before, byte for byte. Temporal analysis Before coding a group, Analyze can look at its frames and the group after it in coding order, each naming the frames it will predict from. For every 16x16 block it measures what predicting from the references saves against coding the block alone, and carries that back from the last frame to the first: a block the frames after it reuse a lot carries much. Importance sums it over the frame, so a group's key frame and alternate reference can take finer quantizers the more they are reused, and a plan's Analysis gives a referenced layer-0 frame finer quantizers in the superblocks that matter most and the other frames lower rate-distortion weights there. The analysis reads the pictures only and is the same at any thread count. // The frames ahead in coding order: a key frame, a hidden frame four pictures on, then the three between, each predicting // from the frames on both sides of it (their places in this list). IReadOnlyList<Av1FrameAnalysis> analysis = encoder.Analyze( [ new Av1AnalysisFrame { Picture = pictures[0] }, new Av1AnalysisFrame { Picture = pictures[4], References = [0] }, new Av1AnalysisFrame { Picture = pictures[1], References = [0, 1] }, new Av1AnalysisFrame { Picture = pictures[2], References = [0, 1] }, new Av1AnalysisFrame { Picture = pictures[3], References = [0, 1] }, ]); // The more the frames after them reuse the key and hidden frames, the finer their steps; each plan carries its analysis. int keyQ = (int)Math.Round(100 / Math.Sqrt(analysis[0].Importance)); encoder.Encode(pictures[0], new Av1FramePlan { Kind = Av1FrameKind.Key, QIndex = keyQ, Analysis = analysis[0] }); encoder.Encode(pictures[4], new Av1FramePlan { QIndex = 110, Show = false, OrderHint = 4, RefreshSlots = 0b10, Analysis = analysis[1] }); for (int i = 1; i < 4; i++) { encoder.Encode(pictures[i], new Av1FramePlan { QIndex = 140, Layer = 1, ReferenceSlots = [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1], RefreshSlots = 0, Analysis = analysis[i + 1] }); } encoder.ShowExisting(1);

articles/formats/avif.html.title: AVIF | Egami
articles/formats/avif.html.summary: AVIF Egami reads and writes AVIF still images, written from the AV1 and HEIF specifications with no native code: the HEIF container, a managed AV1 intra decoder and a managed AV1 intra encoder. AvifFormat.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default, so Raster.Load recognizes an ftyp box with the avif or avis brand and Save writes a file whose name ends in .avif. Raster.Probe reads the container alone: size, natural pixel type and orientation, without decoding any AV1. // The container alone: size, natural pixel type and orientation, without decoding any AV1. RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("duck.avif"); bool isAvif = info.Format == AvifFormat.Info; long bytes = info.EstimatedBytes; // what a full load would allocate Reading AV1 intra frames decode with every coding tool, in-loop filter and film grain, equal to dav1d's decode, and are converted to RGB as libavif converts them, so Raster.Load equals avifdec's output. Alpha (straight or premultiplied), grids, overlays, the clean aperture (cropped), irot and imir (as the orientation), ICC, CICP, HDR metadata, Exif and XMP are all read. // AVIF loads like any format, in its natural pixel type: Rgb8 or Rgba8 for 8-bit files, Rgb16 or Rgba16 for 10 and 12 bits. using Raster duck = Raster.Load("duck.avif"); duck.Save("duck.png"); The natural pixel type follows the bit depth: Rgb8 or Rgba8 for 8-bit files, Rgb16 or Rgba16 for 10 and 12 bits, and Gray8 or Gray16 (with alpha, GrayAlpha8 or GrayAlpha16) for monochrome. AvifReaderOptions.FilmGrain set to false leaves out the grain the AV1 stream asks the decoder to add, giving the image as coded; the grain's parameters are in AvifDetails.FilmGrain as an AvifFilmGrain either way. // Load decodes the AV1 image, converts it to RGB the way libavif does, and crops the clean aperture. using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.avif"); // The image as coded, without the film grain its AV1 stream asks the decoder to add. using Raster clean = Raster.Load("duck.avif", options: new AvifReaderOptions { FilmGrain = false }); AvifFilmGrain? grain = ((AvifDetails)clean.Metadata.FormatDetails!).FilmGrain; // null when there is none YuvRaster.Load gives the AV1 planes themselves, without the conversion to RGB (see Planar YUV): // The AV1 planes themselves, without the conversion to RGB: luma, then chroma at the file's subsampling. using YuvRaster planes = YuvRaster.Load("duck.avif"); ChromaFormat chroma = planes.ChromaFormat; // Yuv420 for most AVIF files Writing Save codes the image with Egami's own AV1 encoder. Lossy images use avifenc's quality scale, so AvifWriterOptions.Quality gives about the same file as avifenc -q with the same number; the default is 60. Lossless keeps every sample: the image is written as 4:4:4 RGB with the identity matrix, at its own bit depth. A file read from a lossless AVIF is written lossless again unless the options say otherwise (AvifDetails.Lossless). // Save picks AVIF from the extension; the defaults are lossy at quality 60 on avifenc's scale, effort 4. duck.Save("duck-q60.avif"); // Smaller and softer, or every sample exact (4:4:4 RGB with the identity matrix). duck.Save("duck-q35.avif", new AvifWriterOptions { Quality = 35 }); duck.Save("duck-lossless.avif", new AvifWriterOptions { Lossless = true }); Lossy color is 4:2:0 below Quality 90 and 4:4:4 from 90, or the Chroma you choose; gray images are written 4:0:0. 8-bit pixels are written at 8 bits and deeper pixels at 10, or at the BitDepth you choose (8, 10 or 12). Transparency goes in an alpha item, a second AV1 image, kept exactly unless AlphaQuality is below 100. Effort, 0 to 10, trades encoding time for size: it is 10 minus avifenc's speed, and the default 4 works like avifenc's default speed 6. The encoder weighs partitions, prediction modes and transforms by the bits they cost and the error they leave, spends finer quantizer steps on flat areas, where banding shows, and picks the deblocking and CDEF filters. Screenshots, text and graphics are recognized: their few colors are coded as palettes, and repeated content as copies of what came before (intra block copy). // A transparent image keeps its alpha as a second AV1 image; AlphaQuality below 100 codes it lossy too. using Raster<Rgba8> logo = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(64, 64); logo.Save("logo.avif", new AvifWriterOptions { Quality = 80, AlphaQuality = 100 }); From effort 5, 8-bit 4:2:0 images are converted with sharp RGB to YUV, as libavif does: luma and chroma are refined together so sharp colored edges keep their color. A YuvRaster is written as its planes are, at 8, 10 or 12 bits, with no conversion or chroma resampling; its matrix, range and chroma siting go into the file, and Lossless keeps every sample of the planes. // YUV planes are written as they are: no conversion or resampling, their matrix, range and siting in the file. using YuvRaster planes = YuvRaster.Load("duck.avif"); planes.Save("duck-planes.avif", new AvifWriterOptions { Lossless = true }); Metadata goes with the image: EXIF and XMP as items, the EXIF orientation as irot and imir (which readers apply), PQ and HLG code points with the HDR luminances as clli and mdcv, and a gain map as a tmap item that readers without gain maps skip. The ICC profile is written only when the colors have no code points and it is not plain sRGB, which the nclx box always says. StripMetadata leaves EXIF, XMP, the profile and the gain map out. An image up to 8192 x 4352 is one AV1 frame, split into tiles every 4096 samples across that are coded in parallel; a larger image is written as a grid of equal cells, or of the GridTileSize you choose, coded in parallel too. The file is the same whatever the number of threads. Every file Egami writes decodes in dav1d and libavif to the same pixels as in Egami; tools/check-avif-interop.py checks this. Animated AVIF A raster with more than one frame saves as an image sequence (the avis brand), as libavif writes one: the frames as one AV1 stream of a key frame and inter frames in a track, each with its delay, and the loop count in the edit list. When any frame has transparency the alpha goes into a second, monochrome track; it is exact unless AlphaQuality is below 100. The first frame is also the file's primary image, so readers of stills show it. Quality, Effort, Lossless, Chroma and BitDepth apply to every frame; gain maps and grids are for stills only. avifdec decodes every frame exactly as Egami does. // A raster with several frames saves as an animated AVIF: one AV1 stream of a key frame and inter frames, each frame's // delay, the loop count (0 plays forever) and, when any frame is transparent, an alpha track. using Raster<Rgba8> pan = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("pan.gif"); pan.Metadata.LoopCount = 0; pan.Save("pan.avif", new AvifWriterOptions { Quality = 70 }); HDR PQ and HLG files keep their curve; converting to sRGB as they load tone maps them, the peak taken from the file's clli box: // An HDR (PQ or HLG) AVIF, tone mapped into sRGB as it loads; the peak comes from the file's clli box when it has one. using Raster<Rgb8> sdr = Raster.Load<Rgb8>("hdr.avif", options: new ReaderOptions { ConvertColorTo = Egami.Colors.ColorProfile.Srgb }); sdr.Save("hdr-as-sdr.jpg"); Gain maps (tmap) load into RasterMetadata.GainMap, and ReaderOptions.Hdr renders the HDR rendition from them, as for Ultra HDR JPEGs (see the HDR guide): // An AVIF with a gain map loads as its base image, the map in Metadata.GainMap; ReaderOptions.Hdr renders the HDR // rendition for a display with the given headroom (its peak over SDR white), as linear RgbaF16. using Raster sdr = Raster.Load("gainmap.avif"); bool hasMap = sdr.Metadata.GainMap is not null; using Raster hdr = Raster.Load("gainmap.avif", options: new ReaderOptions { Hdr = new HdrDecode { Headroom = 4 } }); Items AvifDetails describes the AV1 configuration, color, alpha, grid and brands, and lists every item of the file as an AvifItem with its AvifItemRole to the image Load gives: the primary image, alpha, thumbnails, depth maps, gain maps, grid cells and metadata. AvifImage.ReadItem decodes any image item on its own. // Every item of the file, with what it is to the image Load gives: alpha, thumbnails, depth maps, grid cells, metadata. using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.avif"); IReadOnlyList<AvifItem> items = ((AvifDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!).Items; AvifItem primary = items.First(i => i.Role == AvifItemRole.Primary); // Any image item decodes on its own, with its own color, such as a depth map or a thumbnail. using Raster item = AvifImage.ReadItem("duck.avif", primary.Id); // The file's other images: thumbnails, depth maps and auxiliary images, each read on its own. AvifDetails details = (AvifDetails)sdr.Metadata.FormatDetails!; foreach (AvifItem item in details.Items.Where(i => i.IsImage && i.Role is AvifItemRole.Thumbnail or AvifItemRole.Depth or AvifItemRole.GainMap)) { using Raster image = AvifImage.ReadItem("gainmap.avif", item.Id); image.Save($"item-{item.Id}-{item.Role}.png"); } Sequences and layers Image sequences (avis) load every frame, inter frames included, each with its duration from the sample table, and the loop count from the edit list; an alpha track gives each frame its alpha. Every frame equals avifdec's. A range of frames (ReaderOptions.Frames) decodes from the key frame before its first. Layered images load their base layer. // An image sequence whose frames are all key frames loads as an animation; save it as an animated WebP. using Raster<Rgba8> frames = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("sequence.avif"); TimeSpan firstDelay = frames.Frames[0].Metadata.Delay; frames.Save("sequence.webp");

articles/formats/bmp.html.title: BMP | Egami
articles/formats/bmp.html.summary: BMP Egami reads Windows bitmaps with core, info, V2 to V5 and OS/2 2.x headers at 1 to 32 bits, RLE4, RLE8 and RLE24, bit fields, embedded PNG and JPEG and V5 ICC profiles. It writes 24-bit, 32-bit with alpha, 16-bit 5-5-5, 5-6-5 and 1-5-5-5, and 1, 2, 4 or 8-bit palettes, with resolution and ICC. A BMP loads as Bgr8, or Bgra8 with alpha. // Auto (the default): 24-bit when every pixel is opaque, 32-bit with alpha otherwise. image.Save("duck.bmp"); // A 16-color palette, built from the image and dithered. image.Save("duck-16.bmp", new BmpWriterOptions { PixelFormat = BmpPixelFormat.Indexed4 }); A plain 32-bit BMP's fourth byte is used as alpha unless it is 0 in every pixel, in which case the image loads opaque; an alpha mask in the header is always used. Pixels that an RLE delta skips are black. BmpPixelFormat.Indexed2 writes Windows CE 2-bit files, which many desktop readers cannot open, so Auto never picks it. Bgr555 writes the default 16-bit layout with no bit fields; Bgr565 and Bgra5551 write a V4 header with bit-field masks. Loading a 16-bit file as Bgr555, Bgr565 or Bgra5551 copies its rows when the masks match the type. Resolution is written in pixels per meter, and an ICC profile switches the header to V5 with the profile embedded.

articles/formats/ccitt.html.title: CCITT fax | Egami
articles/formats/ccitt.html.summary: CCITT fax Egami decodes raw CCITT fax data: modified Huffman and Group 3 (ITU-T T.4, one- and two-dimensional) and Group 4 (ITU-T T.6), the bi-level coding of fax machines, of many scanned PDFs and of TIFF compressions 2, 3 and 4. Raw data has no header, so its parameters come from outside: in a PDF they are the CCITTFaxDecode filter's DecodeParms dictionary, and CcittFaxParameters holds the same eight values with the same defaults. CcittFax.Encode writes Group 4 and one-dimensional Group 3 for PDF images; inside TIFF CCITT data is read and written by the TIFF format. Every CCITT stream of a 4,000-file PDF corpus, byte-aligned Group 4 among them, and of a matrix of every parameter combination decodes bit for bit as PDFium and pdf.js decode it. As a PDF filter CcittFax.Decode gives what the filter gives: one bit a pixel, most significant first, each row padded to whole bytes, black 0 and white 1 unless BlackIs1 is set. The PDF library then applies the image's /Decode array, /ImageMask and color space, as it does after every other filter. // A PDF image with /Filter /CCITTFaxDecode: its DecodeParms become the parameters, and the result is the filter's // output, packed rows with black 0 and white 1, ready for the image's /Decode array and color space. CcittFaxParameters parameters = new() { K = -1, EncodedByteAlign = true, Columns = 301, Rows = 48 }; byte[] rows = CcittFax.Decode(stream, parameters, out int rowCount); Parameter Default Meaning K 0 Below 0 Group 4; 0 one-dimensional Group 3; above 0 mixed Group 3, a bit after each EOL picking the next row's coding EndOfLine false EOLs are required before each row; they are accepted where present either way EncodedByteAlign false Group 4 rows start on byte boundaries; Group 3 EOLs end on one, after fill bits Columns 1728 Row width in pixels Rows 0 Row count; 0 decodes until the data or its end-of-block code ends EndOfBlock true The data ends with RTC (Group 3) or EOFB (Group 4); decoding stops there either way BlackIs1 false The output's bit sense: 1 for black instead of 0 DamagedRowsBeforeError 0 With EOLs and K 0 or above, how many damaged rows are skipped to the next EOL Writing CcittFax.Encode is the filter's inverse: it takes packed rows in the same form Decode gives (black 0 unless BlackIs1) and writes them with the parameters' coding. K below 0 writes Group 4, which is usually the smallest coding for scanned text, often half of Flate's size; K 0 writes one-dimensional Group 3. EndOfLine puts an EOL before each Group 3 row and EndOfBlock ends the data with RTC or EOFB. Mixed Group 3 (K above 0) and EncodedByteAlign are not written. The same parameters then go in the image's DecodeParms, and Decode gives back the rows exactly. // A bi-level scan as a PDF image with /Filter /CCITTFaxDecode: pack its rows (0 black, 1 white), then write Group 4. int rowBytes = (scan.Width + 7) / 8; byte[] rows = new byte[rowBytes * scan.Height]; for (int y = 0; y < scan.Height; y++) { Span<Gray8> row = scan.Row(y); for (int x = 0; x < scan.Width; x++) { if (row[x].L >= 128) { rows[(y * rowBytes) + (x >> 3)] |= (byte)(0x80 >> (x & 7)); } } } // These parameters are the image's DecodeParms: << /K -1 /Columns 301 /Rows 48 >>. CcittFaxParameters parameters = new() { K = -1, Columns = scan.Width, Rows = scan.Height }; byte[] g4 = CcittFax.Encode(rows, parameters); As an image CcittFormat loads the data as Gray8, black 0 and white 255, as 1-bit TIFF and JBIG2 load, whatever BlackIs1 says. The parameters go in CcittReaderOptions. With Rows given, Raster.Probe reads nothing and RasterDecoder decodes a row at a time, holding only the current row and the one above it. The format has no signature, so detection never picks it. // The same data as an image: Gray8, black 0 and white 255. The data has no header, so name the format. CcittReaderOptions options = new() { Parameters = new CcittFaxParameters { K = -1, EncodedByteAlign = true, Columns = 301, Rows = 48 } }; using Raster image = Raster.Load(stream, CcittFormat.Info, options: options); Damaged data A row that does not decode ends decoding: the rows before it are kept, the rest are white, and the warning Ccitt.Damaged goes to EgamiContext.Diagnostics (or to RasterMetadata.Warnings for a load). With EOLs and K 0 or above, up to DamagedRowsBeforeError damaged rows are first skipped to the next EOL, each repeating the row before it (Ccitt.RowsSkipped). Data that ends before Rows rows warns Ccitt.Truncated. Only data in which not one row decodes throws CorruptDataException; a strict load throws on any of these. PDFium and pdf.js carry on decoding after damage instead, so the later rows of a damaged stream differ from theirs. Columns and Rows are checked against SafetyLimits before memory is taken, and with Rows 0 the output grows only up to MaxPixels, so a stream of EOLs cannot use up memory. Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Decode a PDF's CCITT image // An image XObject with /Filter /CCITTFaxDecode: DecodeParms keys not given keep PDF's defaults. The image's /Height // stands in for a missing Rows, so the decoder stops where the image does. CcittFaxParameters parameters = new() { K = k, EncodedByteAlign = aligned, Columns = columns, Rows = rows > 0 ? rows : height }; byte[] bits = CcittFax.Decode(data, parameters, out int decoded); // The filter's samples: 0 black, 1 white. /Decode [1 0] inverts them, and an /ImageMask paints where a sample is 0. bool invert = decode is [> 0.5, ..]; int rowBytes = (columns + 7) / 8; using Raster<Gray8> image = Raster.Create<Gray8>(width, decoded); for (int y = 0; y < decoded; y++) { Span<Gray8> row = image.Row(y); for (int x = 0; x < Math.Min(width, columns); x++) { bool sample = ((bits[(y * rowBytes) + (x >> 3)] >> (7 - (x & 7))) & 1) != 0; row[x] = new Gray8(sample != invert ? (byte)255 : (byte)0); } } CcittFax.Decode gives what the CCITTFaxDecode filter gives, byte-aligned Group 4 included; the image's /Decode, /ImageMask and color space then apply as after any filter. To load the data straight to Gray8, use CcittFormat.

articles/formats/custom.html.title: Your own format | Egami
articles/formats/custom.html.summary: Your own format Egami's formats are plug-ins like any other: a format you write loads, probes, streams and saves through the same calls as PNG or JPEG, and stays inside the same safety limits. Register it on an EgamiContext and every Load, Probe and Save with that context can use it. A format is a FormatInfo: a name, extensions, a signature check, a reader and a writer. /// <summary>A minimal format: "RAW8", width and height as big-endian numbers, then RGBA rows.</summary> public static class Raw8Format { public static FormatInfo Info { get; } = new() { Name = "RAW8", Extensions = ["raw8"], SignatureLength = 4, Matches = header => header.StartsWith("RAW8"u8), Reader = new Reader(), Writer = new Writer(), }; private sealed class Reader : IFormatReader { public RasterInfo ReadInfo(EgamiInput input, ReaderOptions options) { (int width, int height) = Header(input); return new RasterInfo { Format = Info, Width = width, Height = height, Layout = Rgba8.Layout, FrameCount = 1, EstimatedBytes = 4L * width * height }; } public Raster<TPixel> Read<TPixel>(EgamiInput input, ReaderOptions options) where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> { (int width, int height) = Header(input); // CreateRaster checks the size against the safety limits before allocating. Raster<TPixel> raster = input.CreateRaster<TPixel>(width, height); using IMemoryOwner<byte> row = input.RentScratch(width * 4); for (int y = 0; y < height; y++) { input.ReadExactly(row.Memory.Span[..(width * 4)]); PixelConvert.Convert<Rgba8, TPixel>(MemoryMarshal.Cast<byte, Rgba8>(row.Memory.Span[..(width * 4)]), raster.Row(y)); } return raster; } public Raster Read(EgamiInput input, ReaderOptions options) => Read<Rgba8>(input, options); private static (int Width, int Height) Header(EgamiInput input) { input.Skip(4); return ((int)input.ReadUInt32BigEndian(), (int)input.ReadUInt32BigEndian()); } } private sealed class Writer : IFormatWriter { public void Write<TPixel>(Raster<TPixel> raster, Stream output, WriterOptions options) where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> { Span<byte> header = stackalloc byte[12]; "RAW8"u8.CopyTo(header); BinaryPrimitives.WriteUInt32BigEndian(header[4..], (uint)raster.Width); BinaryPrimitives.WriteUInt32BigEndian(header[8..], (uint)raster.Height); output.Write(header); Rgba8[] row = new Rgba8[raster.Width]; for (int y = 0; y < raster.Height; y++) { PixelConvert.Convert<TPixel, Rgba8>(raster.Row(y), row); output.Write(MemoryMarshal.AsBytes(row.AsSpan())); } } } } // Register it in a context... EgamiContext context = EgamiContext.Default.WithFormat(Raw8Format.Info); using (FileStream output = File.Create("duck.raw8")) { image.Save(output, Raw8Format.Info); } using Raster back = Raster.Load("duck.raw8", context); // ...or, once at startup before any other Egami call, make it part of the default context: // EgamiContext.SetDefault(new EgamiContext().WithFormat(Raw8Format.Info)); Readers read only through EgamiInput, which keeps them inside the safety limits: Member Use Peek, Read, ReadExactly, Skip, ReadByte, ReadUInt16/32… Read the data; a short read throws CorruptDataException CreateRaster<TPixel>(width, height) The raster you decode into, size-checked before any allocation AddFrame(raster) Another frame for animated formats, counted against MaxFrames and the memory budget RentScratch(bytes) Working memory counted against the same budget CheckFrameSize, CheckMemory, CheckFrameCount, CheckMetadataBytes Check a number from the header before acting on it Warn(raster, id, text) Note something a lenient read recovered from, with a stable id such as Pcx.PaletteMissing; Warn(metadata, id, text) does the same for an open RowReader's metadata Corrupt(offset, problem) The exception to throw for data that breaks the format's rules Respect ReaderOptions.Recovery: in Lenient mode keep what decoded and warn; in Strict mode throw. The writer gets the raster and a stream; options come as your own WriterOptions subclass. Streaming Two optional interfaces let a format stream. A reader that also implements IRowFormatReader returns a RowReader<TNatural> from Open: the open image hands out rows as RasterDecoder asks for them (top-down, never going back within a frame) and moves through frames with NextFrame. The decoder applies Region, MinimumSize and the pixel conversion after it. A writer that also implements IRowFormatWriter returns a RowEncoder<TPixel> from Start, which takes rows (or frames, for an animation) one at a time; Save, SaveAsync, RasterEncoder and Transcode then all write through it. When streaming, EncodeStart.Whole is null: an option that needs every pixel before the first byte should call EncodeStart.Refuse. An open image checks the header's size with CheckFrameSize before it rents its row buffers, since it creates no raster. An encoder calls EncodeStart.ReportLosses with the SaveKeeps flags for what it writes, so a save that drops alpha, depth, frames or metadata says so in the Warnings, as Egami's own writers do. /// <summary>The same RAW8 format, streaming: rows go in and out one at a time, so RasterDecoder, RasterEncoder and Transcode stream it.</summary> public static class StreamingRaw8Format { public static FormatInfo Info { get; } = Raw8Format.Info with { Reader = new Reader(), Writer = new Writer() }; private sealed class Reader : IFormatReader, IRowFormatReader { private static readonly IFormatReader Whole = Raw8Format.Info.Reader!; public RasterInfo ReadInfo(EgamiInput input, ReaderOptions options) => Whole.ReadInfo(input, options) with { Access = RasterAccess.Streamed }; public Raster<TPixel> Read<TPixel>(EgamiInput input, ReaderOptions options) where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> => Whole.Read<TPixel>(input, options); public Raster Read(EgamiInput input, ReaderOptions options) => Whole.Read(input, options); // The open image reads each row when it is asked for; the decoder crops, reduces and converts after it. public RowReader Open(EgamiInput input, ReaderOptions options) { input.Skip(4); int width = (int)input.ReadUInt32BigEndian(); int height = (int)input.ReadUInt32BigEndian(); // No raster checks the size here, so check it before the row buffer is allocated. input.CheckFrameSize(width, height); return new Rows(input, width, height); } } private sealed class Rows(EgamiInput input, int width, int height) : RowReader<Rgba8> { private readonly Rgba8[] _row = new Rgba8[width]; private int _next; private bool _started; public override int Width => width; public override int Height => height; public override Metadata.RasterMetadata Metadata { get; } = new(); public override Metadata.FrameMetadata? NextFrame() { if (_started) { return null; } _started = true; return new Metadata.FrameMetadata(); } public override void ReadRow<TPixel>(int y, int x, Span<TPixel> destination) { for (; _next <= y; _next++) { input.ReadExactly(MemoryMarshal.AsBytes(_row.AsSpan())); } PixelConvert.Convert<Rgba8, TPixel>(_row.AsSpan(x, destination.Length), destination); } } private sealed class Writer : IFormatWriter, IRowFormatWriter { public void Write<TPixel>(Raster<TPixel> raster, Stream output, WriterOptions options) where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> => Raw8Format.Info.Writer!.Write(raster, output, options); // Save, SaveAsync, RasterEncoder and Transcode all write through the encoder. public RowEncoder<TPixel> Start<TPixel>(Stream output, EncodeStart<TPixel> start) where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> { // RAW8 keeps 8-bit RGBA and nothing else: deeper samples or metadata are reported as lost. start.ReportLosses("RAW8", SaveKeeps.Alpha); return new Encoder<TPixel>(output, start.Width, start.Height); } } private sealed class Encoder<TPixel> : RowEncoder<TPixel> where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> { private readonly Stream _output; private readonly Rgba8[] _row; public Encoder(Stream output, int width, int height) { _output = output; _row = new Rgba8[width]; Span<byte> header = stackalloc byte[12]; "RAW8"u8.CopyTo(header); BinaryPrimitives.WriteUInt32BigEndian(header[4..], (uint)width); BinaryPrimitives.WriteUInt32BigEndian(header[8..], (uint)height); output.Write(header); } public override void WriteRow(ReadOnlySpan<TPixel> row) { PixelConvert.Convert<TPixel, Rgba8>(row, _row); _output.Write(MemoryMarshal.AsBytes(_row.AsSpan())); } public override void Complete() { } } } A format without them still works everywhere: the decoder reads the whole image with Read and serves rows from it, and the encoder gathers the image and calls Write at the end. Writing your own operation or pixel type is covered in Custom operations and formats.

articles/formats/extended.html.title: Extended formats | Egami
articles/formats/extended.html.summary: Extended formats Egami.Formats.Extended reads and writes image formats that most apps never meet but some still need: PCX, SGI, Sun raster, XBM, XPM, WBMP and Farbfeld. They are plugins on core Egami's public format API, the one your own format uses, so they load, probe, stream and save as the core formats do, inside the same safety limits. The package depends on core Egami only and ships with every Egami release. Registering the formats Nothing registers them on their own. WithExtendedFormats(), an extension method in ExtendedContextExtensions, returns a context with every stable format of the package, detected after core Egami's own; pass it to the calls, or make it the default once at startup with EgamiContext.SetDefault(new EgamiContext().WithExtendedFormats()). // Every stable format of Egami.Formats.Extended, once at startup before any other Egami call: // EgamiContext.SetDefault(new EgamiContext().WithExtendedFormats()); // ...or in a context of its own. EgamiContext context = EgamiContext.Default.WithExtendedFormats(); using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.png", context); // A raster saves to a path through the context it was loaded with, so the extension picks PCX. image.Save("duck.pcx"); using Raster back = Raster.Load("duck.pcx", context); string format = back.Metadata.FormatName!; // "PCX" Each format also has its own method and its own FormatInfo, for an app that wants only one: // One format at a time: each has its own method and its own FormatInfo. EgamiContext context = EgamiContext.Default.WithSgi().WithSunRaster(); using (FileStream output = File.Create("duck.sgi")) { image.Save(output, SgiFormat.Info); } RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("duck.sgi", context); Console.WriteLine($"{info.Format.Name} {info.Width}×{info.Height} {info.Layout.ChannelOrder}"); The formats Format FormatInfo Reads Writes PCX PcxFormat 1, 2, 4 and 8-bit indexed, 1-bit EGA planes, 24-bit and 32-bit, run-length coded or not 8-bit gray with a gray palette, or 24-bit RGB, run-length coded SGI SgiFormat 1 to 4 channels of 8 or 16 bits, plain or run-length coded the raster's channels and depth, run-length coded unless SgiWriterOptions.Rle is off Sun raster SunRasterFormat 1, 8, 24 and 32 bits, with or without a colormap, plain or run-length coded 8-bit gray or 24-bit, run-length coded when SunRasterWriterOptions.Rle is set XBM XbmFormat X11 files of bytes and X10 files of 16-bit words X11, black where gray is below half XPM XpmFormat version 3, any number of characters a pixel, None, hex colors and X11 color names every color of the raster, None below half alpha WBMP WbmpFormat type 0, extension headers skipped type 0, white where gray is at least half Farbfeld FarbfeldFormat 16-bit RGBA 16-bit RGBA SGI and Farbfeld keep 16-bit samples and alpha. PCX, Sun raster and WBMP have no alpha, XPM only on or off, and a save that loses something the raster has says so in the Warnings, as Egami's own writers do. The formats with a run-length option take it from their writer options: // SGI codes its rows by default; Sun raster writes them plain unless asked. using (FileStream sgi = File.Create("duck.rgb")) { image.Save(sgi, SgiFormat.Info, new SgiWriterOptions { Rle = false }); } using (FileStream sun = File.Create("duck.ras")) { image.Save(sun, SunRasterFormat.Info, new SunRasterWriterOptions { Rle = true }); } What a header says that the pixels do not is kept in RasterMetadata.FormatDetails: PcxDetails (version, planes, palette), SgiDetails (image name, channels, depth), SunRasterDetails (depth, colormap, coding), XbmDetails and XpmDetails (the C name and the cursor hotspot). The SGI, XBM and XPM writers take the name and hotspot back from them. // What the header said that the pixels do not: PcxDetails, SgiDetails, SunRasterDetails, XbmDetails and XpmDetails. using Raster image = Raster.Load("arrow.xbm", context); if (image.Metadata.FormatDetails is XbmDetails xbm) { Console.WriteLine($"{xbm.Name}, hotspot {xbm.Hotspot}"); } // Writers take the name and hotspot back from the details. image.Metadata.FormatDetails = new XbmDetails { Name = "pointer", Hotspot = new Point(0, 0) }; image.Save("pointer.xbm"); Streaming and damaged files PCX, Sun raster, WBMP and Farbfeld decode their rows from the input as RasterDecoder asks for them; an 8-bit PCX first reads to its end, where its palette is. SGI stores each channel as its own plane of bottom-up rows, and XBM and XPM are C source, so those three read the file whole. A lenient read of a file that ends early keeps the rows it has and leaves the rest transparent black, with a RowsMissing warning such as Pcx.RowsMissing; a strict read throws CorruptDataException. Formats in preview The package also holds formats still in development, as previews. A preview is never part of WithExtendedFormats(): its own With<Format>() method and its FormatInfo carry .NET's [Experimental] attribute with a diagnostic id of its own, so a call to it does not compile until the app suppresses that id, which is the opt-in. A preview may change, change its output or be removed in any minor release; it becomes stable after an API review, comparison gates and fuzzing, and the attribute comes off. The ids are EGAMIX and three digits, one per format, given out in order from EGAMIX001 and never reused. Suppress one in the project file (<NoWarn>$(NoWarn);EGAMIX001</NoWarn>) or around the call (#pragma warning disable EGAMIX001). There are no formats in preview in this release. The egami command reads and writes them only with --preview-formats.

articles/formats/farbfeld.html.title: Farbfeld | Egami
articles/formats/farbfeld.html.summary: Farbfeld Farbfeld is suckless.org's lossless format: the word farbfeld, the width and height as big-endian 32-bit numbers, then 16-bit big-endian RGBA pixels, row by row. It reads and writes through the Egami.Formats.Extended package: register it with WithFarbfeld() or WithExtendedFormats() (Extended formats). Reads The whole format Writes Every raster as 16-bit RGBA, so nothing but metadata is lost Natural pixel type Rgba16 FormatInfo FarbfeldFormat.Info: name Farbfeld, extension .ff, MIME type image/x-farbfeld Rows stream from the input as they are asked for. Farbfeld files are often compressed with a general-purpose tool such as bzip2; Egami reads and writes the uncompressed file only.

articles/formats/gif.html.title: GIF | Egami
articles/formats/gif.html.summary: GIF Egami reads GIF 87a and 89a files, with every disposal method, interlaced images, transparency, the loop count, comments, XMP and ICC profiles, and writes GIF 89a. Reading A GIF loads as Rgba8, every frame composited to full size as a browser shows it. Damaged files load as far as they can, with the warnings the Diagnostics page lists under Gif.. GIF files keep their palettes, version and application extensions in GifDetails, and each frame's in GifFrameDetails: using Raster<Rgba8> clip = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("pan.gif"); GifDetails details = (GifDetails)clip.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"GIF{details.Version}, {details.GlobalPalette.Length} global colors, repeats {details.RepetitionCount}"); foreach (GifApplicationExtension extension in details.OtherExtensions) { Console.WriteLine($"Kept extension {extension.Identifier}: {extension.Data.Length} bytes"); } foreach (Frame<Rgba8> frame in clip.Frames) { if (frame.Metadata.FormatDetails is GifFrameDetails frameDetails) { Console.WriteLine($"Frame: {frameDetails.LocalPalette.Length} local colors, transparent index {frameDetails.TransparentIndex}"); } } Writing using FileStream output = File.Create("duck.gif"); photo.Save(output, GifFormat.Info, new GifWriterOptions { Palette = new PaletteOptions { MaxColors = 128, Dither = DitherMode.Ordered }, // FloydSteinberg (default), Ordered or None PaletteScope = GifPaletteScope.PerFrame, // Auto (default): one table when all frames fit, else one per frame }); GIF holds at most 256 colors per frame. Frames with few enough colors keep them exactly. Others get a palette from Wu's quantizer, dithered with Floyd–Steinberg by default. GIF transparency is on or off, so pixels below PaletteOptions.AlphaThreshold (128 by default) become transparent. Option Default Does Palette 256 colors, Floyd–Steinberg How a palette is built when a frame has more colors than fit; see Palettes and dithering PaletteScope Auto One global table when all frames fit in it, else one per frame; Global and PerFrame choose OptimizeFrames true Each frame after the first stores only the rectangle that changed; false writes every frame whole Saving a raster with more than one frame writes an animation; see the animation guide.

articles/formats/heic.html.title: HEIC | Egami
articles/formats/heic.html.summary: HEIC HEIC is the format iPhones and most Android phones save photos in: HEIF files whose images are coded with HEVC (H.265). HEVC is covered by patents, so Egami reads HEIC through a separate package, Egami.Heic, that an app opts in to. The core Egami package contains no HEVC code and never depends on Egami.Heic. Egami.Heic decodes HEIC images with a managed HEVC decoder: the intra pictures of the Main, Main 10, Main Still Picture and format range extensions profiles, up to 12 bits and from 4:0:0 to 4:4:4. Gain maps, the photo's other images (thumbnails, depth maps, mattes) and image sequences whose frames are all intra are read too. Without Egami.Heic Core Egami recognizes HEIC by its brands (heic, heix, hevc and the other HEVC brands) and reads the container, so Raster.Probe gives the size, the natural pixel type and the orientation. Raster.Load throws an UnsupportedFormatException that names the package. // Core Egami detects HEIC and reads its container: size, natural pixel type and orientation. RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("photo.heic"); string name = info.Format.Name; // "HEIC" // Loading needs the Egami.Heic package: the exception says so. try { using Raster image = Raster.Load("photo.heic"); } catch (UnsupportedFormatException e) { Console.WriteLine(e.Message); } The size is the image's after its clean aperture (clap) crop; its rotation and mirroring (irot and imir) are given as RasterInfo.Orientation, as for AVIF. The natural pixel type follows the bit depth: Rgb8 for 8-bit files, Rgb16 for 10 and 12 bits, with alpha when the file has an alpha image, and gray for monochrome. Registering Egami.Heic Nothing registers Egami.Heic on its own. WithHeic(), an extension method in HeicContextExtensions, returns a context with Egami.Heic's HeicFormat.Info in place of core Egami's HEIC entry; pass it to the calls, or make it the default once at startup with EgamiContext.SetDefault(new EgamiContext().WithHeic()). // Opt in to HEVC once: register Egami.Heic in a context (at startup, EgamiContext.SetDefault(new EgamiContext().WithHeic()) // makes it the default for every call). EgamiContext heic = new EgamiContext().WithHeic(); RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("photo.heic", heic); bool fromPackage = info.Format == HeicFormat.Info; Egami.Heic ships with every Egami release, at the same version, and depends on exactly that version of Egami. Loading With Egami.Heic registered, HEIC loads like any format, in its natural pixel type. // An iPhone photo: a grid of HEVC tiles, decoded in parallel and converted to RGB as heif-dec converts them. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("photo.heic", heic); photo.Apply(ops => ops.AutoOrient()); // irot and imir come as the orientation photo.Save("photo.jpg"); Grids. Phone photos are grids of tiles (an iPhone photo has 48 or more). The tiles decode in parallel, on up to EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads, and a ReaderOptions.Region decodes only the tiles it touches. Tiles and wavefront rows inside one HEVC picture decode in parallel too. The pixels are the same at any number of threads. Color. The planes are converted to RGB as libheif's heif-dec converts them, so Raster.Load gives the same samples. The phone photos and HEVC-coded files of Egami's test corpus equal heif-dec's output sample for sample, except a clean aperture at half-sample offsets, which Egami crops at whole samples. The colors come from the colr property, or else from the HEVC stream's own color description. An ICC profile is kept in RasterMetadata.IccProfile. Geometry and alpha. The clean aperture (clap) is cropped; rotation and mirroring (irot and imir) are kept as the orientation, which AutoOrient applies. An alpha image loads as straight alpha. Overlays (iovl) are composed. Metadata. Exif and XMP items are read into RasterMetadata.Exif and RasterMetadata.Xmp. The decoded HEVC planes are available without the conversion to RGB, as for AVIF and JPEG (see Planar YUV): // The HEVC planes themselves, without the conversion to RGB: luma, then chroma at the file's subsampling. using YuvRaster planes = YuvRaster.Load("photo.heic", heic); ChromaFormat chroma = planes.ChromaFormat; // Yuv420 for phone photos int depth = planes.BitDepth; // 8, or 10 for HDR photos Every intra picture of the HEVC conformance streams in these profiles decodes bit-exact to HM, the reference decoder. HDR photos iPhones store an HDR photo as an SDR image with a gain map: Apple's HDRGainMap auxiliary image (its headroom in the maker note or the map's XMP), and on newer iPhones an ISO 21496-1 tone-map item as well, which is preferred. Load gives the SDR image with the map in RasterMetadata.GainMap; ReaderOptions.Hdr gives the HDR rendition for a display's headroom, as for Ultra HDR JPEGs. // An iPhone photo's gain map (Apple's HDRGainMap, or ISO 21496-1 on newer iPhones) comes with the SDR image; ask for the HDR // rendition for a display with 2 stops of headroom. using Raster sdr = Raster.Load("portrait.heic", heic); bool hasGainMap = sdr.Metadata.GainMap is not null; using Raster hdr = Raster.Load("portrait.heic", heic, new ReaderOptions { Hdr = new HdrDecode { Headroom = 2 } }); A gain map that cannot be read (Apple's without a headroom, a damaged tone-map item) never fails the load: the image loads as SDR with a Heic.GainMapDropped warning. Thumbnails, depth maps and mattes HeicDetails.Items lists every item of the file with its HeicItemRole, what it is to the photo: the primary image, thumbnails, the gain map, depth maps and other auxiliary images (an iPhone's portrait, skin and sky mattes), Exif and XMP. HeicImage.ReadItem reads an image item on its own, with its own color and crop, and its own rotation as the orientation. // The other images a photo holds: thumbnails, gain maps, depth maps and mattes (portrait, skin, sky). HeicDetails details = (HeicDetails)sdr.Metadata.FormatDetails!; HeicItem sky = details.Items.First(i => i.AuxiliaryType == "urn:com:apple:photo:2020:aux:semanticskymatte"); using Raster matte = HeicImage.ReadItem("portrait.heic", sky.Id, context: heic); matte.Apply(ops => ops.AutoOrient()); matte.Save("sky-matte.png"); Image sequences A HEIC image sequence (the hevc and hevx brands) whose frames are all intra loads every frame, as an animation; Egami.Heic does not decode inter frames. A sequence with inter frames gives its still image when the file has one, and otherwise its first frame with a Heic.SequenceFirstFrame warning. Patents Egami.Heic decodes HEVC (H.265), a format covered by patents. Egami's authors grant no patent rights and are not lawyers. Whether you need a patent licence depends on your country and on how you use and distribute this package; commercial products may need one from the HEVC patent pools or holders. The core Egami package contains no HEVC code and does not depend on this package.

articles/formats/ico.html.title: ICO and CUR | Egami
articles/formats/ico.html.summary: ICO and CUR Egami reads and writes Windows icons (.ico) and cursors (.cur), written from Microsoft's documentation of the icon directory. IcoFormat.Info and CurFormat.Info are registered in EgamiContext.Default. An icon holds several images, its entries, each a whole PNG file or a BMP without its file header; Egami's own PNG and BMP readers decode them, so an entry loads exactly as the same PNG or BMP would. Every entry of the test corpus decodes as ImageMagick and Pillow decode it, and the icons Egami writes open in ImageMagick, Pillow, SkiaSharp and Windows' own decoder (WIC) with the same pixels. Reading icons Raster.Load returns the best entry: the largest, then the deepest (a PNG entry counts as 32 bits), then the first. SkiaSharp picks the same entry, except that among entries of the largest size it takes the first where Egami takes the deepest, as Windows prefers. Raster.LoadAll returns every entry at its own size, in the file's order, and Raster.Probe lists them from the directory without decoding a pixel: RasterInfo.ImageCount, and IcoDetails.Entries on a loaded raster. // Load gives the best entry: the largest, then the deepest. LoadAll gives every entry at its own size. using Raster best = Raster.Load("app.ico"); using RasterList entries = Raster.LoadAll("app.ico"); // MinimumSize picks the smallest entry at least that big, so a 32 × 32 toolbar icon decodes only the 32 × 32 entry. using Raster small = Raster.Load("app.ico", options: new ReaderOptions { MinimumSize = new Size(32, 32) }); ReaderOptions.MinimumSize picks the smallest entry at least that big before the reduction rule applies to it, so a 32 × 32 request from a 16, 32, 48 and 256 icon decodes only the 32 × 32 entry. IcoReaderOptions.Entry names an entry by its index in the directory. // Pick an entry by its place in the file's directory. using Raster second = Raster.Load("app.ico", options: new IcoReaderOptions { Entry = 1 }); // Probe reads only the directory: the sizes an icon holds, without decoding a pixel. RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("app.ico"); Console.WriteLine($"{info.ImageCount} entries; Load gives {info.Width}×{info.Height}"); using Raster best = Raster.Load("app.ico"); foreach (IcoEntry entry in ((IcoDetails)best.Metadata.FormatDetails!).Entries) { Console.WriteLine($"{entry.Width}×{entry.Height}, {entry.BitsPerPixel} bits, {entry.Encoding}"); } Every entry loads as Rgba8. BMP entries at 1, 4, 8, 16, 24 and 32 bits are read, with palettes and bit fields; the 1-bit AND mask after the color rows makes pixels transparent. At 32 bits the alpha channel wins, as in Windows, except that an alpha channel of 0 everywhere, which old writers left, falls back to the mask; ImageMagick, Pillow and SkiaSharp keep such an entry fully transparent instead. The directory's sizes and depths are hints: the entry's own header wins, with the Ico.DirectoryMismatch warning. A cursor's entries carry IcoDetails.Hotspot. Writing icons Saving one raster writes one entry at its own size; a raster larger than 256 is fitted to 256 with the Save.IcoFitted warning. IcoWriterOptions.Sizes writes a set instead, each size resized from the largest raster given with Filter, or taken as drawn from a raster of exactly that size; FaviconSizes (16, 32, 48) and WindowsSizes (16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 256) are ready-made. A raster that is not square is fitted inside each square and centred on transparency. // A favicon: 16, 32 and 48 resized from one raster. A raster that is not square is centred on transparency. logo.Save("favicon.ico", new IcoWriterOptions { Sizes = IcoWriterOptions.FaviconSizes }); // Windows' set: 16 to 256, the 256 entry as PNG and the rest as 32-bit BMP, as Microsoft's guidance asks. logo.Save("app.ico", new IcoWriterOptions { Sizes = IcoWriterOptions.WindowsSizes, Filter = Egami.Operations.ResampleFilter.Lanczos3 }); // Hand-drawn small sizes: each raster is written at its own size; the 48 comes from the largest raster. using Raster<Rgba8> drawn16 = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Fit(16, 16)); Raster.SaveAll([logo, drawn16], "drawn.ico", new IcoWriterOptions { Sizes = [16, 48] }); FaviconSizes writes 16, 32 and 48; every browser and Windows read the file. IcoWriterOptions.Encoding, an IcoEntryEncoding, forces every entry to PNG or BMP. Left null, the default, it writes 256 × 256 entries as PNG and smaller ones as 32-bit BMP with an AND mask built from alpha, as Microsoft's guidance asks; a raster loaded from an icon and written at its own size keeps its entry's kind. A wholly transparent BMP entry gets black colors: Windows ignores an alpha channel that is 0 everywhere and draws the colors through the mask, and black draws nothing. PNG entries are always 8-bit RGBA, the only kind Windows lists. Entries are sorted smallest first, two entries of one size throw ArgumentException, and the same rasters and options give the same bytes. Pixels are written at 8 bits; an ICC profile goes into PNG entries, while EXIF, XMP and IPTC are not written and a warning says so. Cursors are icons with a hotspot: IcoWriterOptions.Hotspot gives it at the raster's own size, scaled to each entry and kept inside it; without it, a raster loaded from a cursor keeps its hotspot. // A cursor is an icon with a hotspot, given at the raster's own size and scaled to each entry. arrow.Save("pointer.cur", new IcoWriterOptions { Sizes = [32, 48], Hotspot = new Point(0, 0) }); using RasterList cursor = Raster.LoadAll("pointer.cur"); Point? hotspot = ((IcoDetails)cursor[0].Metadata.FormatDetails!).Hotspot; Speed An icon is read whole, since its directory points anywhere in it. On the 256 × 256 PNG entry Egami decodes faster than SkiaSharp, and 24 and 32-bit BMP entries go straight into place, twice as fast as SkiaSharp; writing Windows' six sizes from a 256 × 256 image takes half the time ImageMagick (Magick.NET) does. Damaged and hostile data The entry count is checked against SafetyLimits.MaxFrames and every entry's size against the other limits before its pixels are allocated; every offset and size is checked against the file. In strict mode an entry that lies outside the file, overlaps another or is neither PNG nor BMP throws CorruptDataException; in lenient mode it is skipped with the Ico.EntrySkipped warning, and the load fails only when no entry is left. A BMP entry that ends before its mask loads with the missing rows opaque (Ico.MaskMissing). The reader is fuzzed with AFL++ through whole files and through single entries.

articles/formats/index.html.title: Formats | Egami
articles/formats/index.html.summary: Formats Egami reads and writes PNG, APNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, TGA, QOI and the Netpbm formats (PBM, PGM, PPM, PAM and the PFM float map), TIFF, Radiance .hdr, OpenEXR, JPEG XL, AVIF, and Windows icons and cursors, and reads JBIG2, raw CCITT fax data, JPEG 2000, Windows animated cursors (ANI) and Photoshop's PSD and PSB. HEIC phone photos load through the separate, opt-in Egami.Heic package; core Egami detects and probes them. SVG and Windows metafiles (WMF, EMF) load through the separate Egami.Svg and Egami.Metafiles packages, and PCX, SGI, Sun raster, XBM, XPM, WBMP and Farbfeld through Egami.Formats.Extended. The Package column says which package holds each format. Every reader checks sizes against the safety limits before it allocates, and every reader has been fuzzed. Each format has its own page with its options and what it keeps from the file; the table below links them. VP8 and AV1 video frames decode through Vp8StreamDecoder and Av1StreamDecoder, VP8 and AV1 frames encode through Vp8StreamEncoder and Av1StreamEncoder, and the boxes of MP4, QuickTime and HEIF files can be walked with IsoBoxReader. This page covers what all formats share: natural pixel types, detection, files with several images, and what writers drop. At a glance Format Reads Writes Natural pixel type Package PNG Every color type and bit depth, interlaced, transparency, text, EXIF, XMP, ICC Every color type and bit depth, adaptive filtering, built palettes, Adam7 interlacing, compression on several cores The file's own: Gray8, Gray16, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8, Rgba8 or Rgba16 Egami APNG Every PNG color type and depth, every disposal and blend Any raster with more than one frame, changed rectangles only Rgba8, or Rgba16 for 16-bit Egami JPEG Baseline, extended and progressive, Huffman or arithmetic, 8 and 12-bit, lossless at 2 to 16 bits, any subsampling, gray, CMYK, YCCK, scaled decode, EXIF, XMP, ICC Baseline or progressive, 8 or 12-bit, quality 1 to 100, 4:4:4, 4:2:2, 4:2:0, gray, CMYK or YCCK, optimized Huffman tables Gray8 or Rgb8; Gray16, Rgb16 or Cmyk16 above 8 bits Egami GIF 87a and 89a, every disposal, interlaced, transparency, loop count, comments, XMP, ICC 89a, exact or quantized palettes, global or per frame, dithering, frame optimization Rgba8 Egami WebP Lossless (VP8L) with every transform; lossy (VP8) with alpha, as RGB or as YUV planes; ICC, EXIF, XMP Lossless at effort 0 to 6, exact transparent colors; ICC, EXIF with resolution, XMP Rgb8, or Rgba8 with alpha Egami BMP Core, info, V2 to V5 and OS/2 2.x headers; 1 to 32 bits; RLE4, RLE8, RLE24; bit fields; embedded PNG and JPEG; V5 ICC 24-bit, 32-bit with alpha, 1, 2, 4 or 8-bit palettes; resolution and ICC Bgr8, or Bgra8 with alpha Egami TGA Color-mapped, true-color and gray, raw and RLE, 8 to 32 bits, all origins, TGA 2.0 footer and extension area 8-bit gray, 24 and 32-bit, 8-bit palette, raw or RLE, TGA 2.0 footer Bgr8, Bgra8, Gray8 or GrayAlpha8 Egami QOI The whole format, 3 or 4 channels, both colorspaces 3 or 4 channels, byte-identical to the reference encoder Rgb8 or Rgba8 Egami TIFF Every page, strips and tiles, chunky and planar, classic and BigTIFF; PF and Pf Gray8, Gray16, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8, Rgba8 or Rgba16; RgbF32 or GrayF32 for PFM Egami PCX 1 to 8-bit indexed, EGA planes, 24 and 32-bit, coded or not 8-bit gray or 24-bit, run-length coded Gray8, Rgb8 or Rgba8 Egami.Formats.Extended SGI 1 to 4 channels of 8 or 16 bits, plain or run-length coded The raster's channels and depth, coded or not Gray8, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8, Rgba8 or their 16-bit forms Egami.Formats.Extended Sun raster 1, 8, 24 and 32 bits, colormaps, byte-encoded 8-bit gray or 24-bit, plain or byte-encoded Gray8 or Rgb8 Egami.Formats.Extended XBM X11 and X10 bitmaps X11 bitmaps Gray8, black 0 and white 255 Egami.Formats.Extended XPM Version 3, any color keys, None, hex colors and X11 names Version 3 with every color of the raster Rgba8 Egami.Formats.Extended WBMP Type 0 Type 0 Gray8, black 0 and white 255 Egami.Formats.Extended Farbfeld The whole format 16-bit RGBA Rgba16 Egami.Formats.Extended Raster.Load returns the natural type; Raster.Load<TPixel> decodes straight into the type you ask for, converting row by row. using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.png"); switch (image) { case Raster<Rgb8> rgb: Console.WriteLine($"8-bit color, {rgb.Width} × {rgb.Height}"); break; case Raster<Rgba8> rgba: Console.WriteLine($"8-bit color with alpha, {rgba.Width} × {rgba.Height}"); break; default: Console.WriteLine($"{image.Layout.ChannelOrder}, {image.Layout.ChannelType}"); break; } Detection Loading never trusts the file extension: the format comes from the first bytes, in the order PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, QOI, PNM, TIFF, JBIG2, JPEG 2000, ICO, CUR, ANI, PSD, Radiance, OpenEXR, JPEG XL (FF 0A or its signature box), AVIF (an ftyp box with the avif or avis brand), HEIC (an ftyp box with a HEVC brand such as heic or heix), then TGA, then the formats a plugin package registers, such as Egami.Formats.Extended's. TGA has no signature, so it is matched only when its whole 18-byte header is consistent. No file of another format in Egami's test corpora is taken for TGA, and neither is any of a million random headers. When you know the format, register only that one: // TGA has no signature, so it is detected last. When you know a file is TGA, register only that format. EgamiContext tgaOnly = EgamiContext.Default with { Formats = [TgaFormat.Info] }; using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.tga", tgaOnly); Data without a signature of its own, such as the JBIG2 or CCITT stream of a PDF image, loads with its format named, which skips detection. Load, LoadAll, Probe and RasterDecoder.Open all take the format this way; naming the wrong one throws CorruptDataException, as damaged data of that format would. // Data without a signature of its own (a TGA here; a JBIG2 stream from a PDF) loads with its format named, // which skips detection. Probe, LoadAll and RasterDecoder.Open take the format the same way. using Raster image = Raster.Load(data, TgaFormat.Info); RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe(data, TgaFormat.Info); Saving to a path picks the writer from the extension; an animated raster saved as .png writes an APNG. Saving to a stream takes the format's Info. Several images in one file Frames are animation and share one size. A TIFF's pages are separate images, each with its own size and pixel type, so they come as a RasterList from Raster.LoadAll, which owns them; RasterInfo.ImageCount says how many there are. Every other format gives its one image, so LoadAll works on any file. Raster.SaveAll writes several rasters to a format that holds several, and one raster to any format. // Every page at its own size and pixel type. The list owns the rasters. using RasterList pages = Raster.LoadAll("scan.tif"); foreach (Raster page in pages) { Console.WriteLine($"{page.Width} × {page.Height}"); } // Keep one page after the list is gone. using Raster first = pages.Detach(0); What each writer drops Writers never change the raster. When a format cannot hold something, it is left out: Alpha: JPEG (unless JpegWriterOptions.Background blends it onto a color), BMP and TGA with Bgr24, PPM, QOI with IncludeAlpha = false. Frames after the first: JPEG, BMP, TGA, QOI and PNM. Metadata: every writer keeps what its format can carry; StripMetadata = true on any writer options drops it all. See the API reference for every option. What the file said Every reader fills RasterMetadata.FormatDetails with the header's own terms: PngDetails, JpegDetails, GifDetails, BmpDetails, TgaDetails, QoiDetails or PnmDetails. A writer of the same format uses them to keep what it can, and ignores another format's details. // Each reader fills in what the file's header says, in the format's own terms. using Raster png = Raster.Load("duck.png"); if (png.Metadata.FormatDetails is PngDetails pngDetails) { Console.WriteLine($"PNG {pngDetails.ColorType}, {pngDetails.BitDepth}-bit, interlaced: {pngDetails.Interlaced}"); foreach (PngTextSource source in pngDetails.TextSources) { Console.WriteLine($"Text from a {source.ChunkType} chunk, compressed: {source.Compressed}"); } } using Raster bmp = Raster.Load("duck.bmp"); BmpDetails bmpDetails = (BmpDetails)bmp.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"BMP {bmpDetails.BitsPerPixel}-bit, {bmpDetails.Compression}, {bmpDetails.HeaderSize}-byte header"); using Raster tga = Raster.Load("duck.tga"); TgaDetails tgaDetails = (TgaDetails)tga.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"TGA type {tgaDetails.ImageType}, origin {tgaDetails.Origin}, alpha {tgaDetails.AlphaType}"); using Raster qoi = Raster.Load("duck.qoi"); QoiDetails qoiDetails = (QoiDetails)qoi.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"QOI {qoiDetails.Channels} channels, linear: {qoiDetails.Linear}"); using Raster pgm = Raster.Load("duck.pgm"); PnmDetails pnmDetails = (PnmDetails)pgm.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"PNM {pnmDetails.Kind}, maxval {pnmDetails.MaxValue}, plain text: {pnmDetails.PlainText}"); Each format is described by a FormatInfo: its name, extensions, MIME types, and how to recognize it from its first bytes. // Every built-in format, with its name, extensions and MIME types; Raster.Save picks one by extension. foreach (FormatInfo format in new[] { PngFormat.Info, JpegFormat.Info, GifFormat.Info, BmpFormat.Info, TgaFormat.Info, QoiFormat.Info, PnmFormat.Info }) { Console.WriteLine($"{format.Name}: {string.Join(", ", format.Extensions)} ({string.Join(", ", format.MimeTypes)})"); } // A SignatureMatcher decides from the first SignatureLength bytes whether a file is in the format. SignatureMatcher isPng = PngFormat.Info.Matches; bool png = isPng(File.ReadAllBytes("duck.png").AsSpan(0, PngFormat.Info.SignatureLength)); Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Batch convert a folder // Convert a folder of images to QOI, a few at a time. Each image runs on one thread, so the files run side by side. EgamiContext oneThread = EgamiContext.Default with { MaxParallelism = 1 }; Directory.CreateDirectory("out"); Parallel.ForEach(Directory.GetFiles("in"), new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 4 }, path => { try { using Raster image = Raster.Load(path, oneThread); image.Save(Path.Combine("out", Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(path) + ".qoi")); } catch (EgamiException e) { Console.WriteLine($"{path}: {e.Message}"); } }); Read the size without decoding RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("sideways.jpg"); bool sideways = info.Orientation is >= Egami.Metadata.ImageOrientation.Transpose; (int width, int height) = sideways ? (info.Height, info.Width) : (info.Width, info.Height); Console.WriteLine($"{info.Format.Name}, shown as {width} × {height}, about {info.EstimatedBytes:N0} bytes to load"); Probe reads only the header, and reports the EXIF orientation, so you know how the image will be shown. Run it samples/Formats is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Formats writes its results to ./output.

articles/formats/iso-boxes.html.title: ISO BMFF boxes | Egami
articles/formats/iso-boxes.html.summary: ISO BMFF boxes MP4, QuickTime, HEIF, HEIC and AVIF files are made of boxes (ISO/IEC 14496-12). Egami reads AVIF and HEIC itself; for other work on these files, such as reading an MP4's tracks or a tag Egami does not keep, IsoBoxReader walks the boxes for you. It reads one level at a time from bytes in memory, allocates nothing, and checks every size: a box that runs past its parent, or one too small for its header, raises a CorruptDataException that names the format you gave and the box's offset. // List an AVIF, HEIC or MP4 file's top-level boxes and the boxes inside meta. IsoBoxReader top = new(avif, "AVIF"); while (top.Next(out IsoBox box)) { found.Add($"{box.Type} {box.Size}"); if (box.Type == FourCC.Parse("meta")) { // meta is a full box: its version and flags (4 bytes) come before its children. IsoBoxReader children = top.Children(box, skip: 4); while (children.Next(out IsoBox child)) { found.Add($" {child.Type} at {child.Start}"); } } } IsoBox gives each box's type, where it starts, where its contents start and where it ends. Box types are FourCC values: FourCC.Parse("moov") makes one, and ToString prints it, with bytes outside printable ASCII escaped (\xa9nam). Children(box, skip) walks the boxes inside one; skip passes the fields a box has before its children, such as a full box's version and flags (4 bytes) or a sample description's entry count (8 bytes). Content(box) gives a box's bytes. Large sizes, size 0 (to the end of the parent) and uuid boxes, whose extended type is IsoBox.UserType, are read too. Large files A file too large to read into memory is walked from a stream: IsoBoxReader.ReadHeader reads a box header from its first IsoBoxReader.MaxHeaderSize bytes, so you can skip over media data and load only the boxes you need. A reader made with an offset reports file offsets for the boxes inside the part you loaded. // Walk a large file's top-level boxes without reading it into memory, then load only moov. using FileStream stream = File.OpenRead("duck.avif"); byte[] header = new byte[IsoBoxReader.MaxHeaderSize]; for (long at = 0; at < stream.Length;) { stream.Position = at; int read = stream.ReadAtLeast(header, (int)Math.Min(header.Length, stream.Length - at), throwOnEndOfStream: false); IsoBox box = IsoBoxReader.ReadHeader(header.AsSpan(0, read), at, stream.Length, "MP4"); types.Add(box.Type); if (box.Type == FourCC.Parse("moov")) { byte[] moov = new byte[box.ContentLength]; stream.Position = box.ContentStart; stream.ReadExactly(moov); IsoBoxReader inside = new(moov, "MP4", offset: box.ContentStart); // the boxes inside report file offsets while (inside.Next(out IsoBox track)) { types.Add(track.Type); } } at = box.End; } Egami.Video reads MP4 and QuickTime files this way.

articles/formats/jbig2.html.title: JBIG2 | Egami
articles/formats/jbig2.html.summary: JBIG2 Egami reads JBIG2 (ITU-T T.88 | ISO/IEC 14492), the bi-level format of scanned documents and of the JBIG2Decode images in PDF, written from the 2018 edition of T.88 and the PDF specification. Jbig2Format.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default. JBIG2 is never written.
