Every page of Egami's corpus (made with jbig2enc in each of its modes), of PDFBox's JBIG2 test streams and of the T.88 Annex H datastream decodes bit for bit as PDFium and jbig2dec decode it. Reading files A standalone file starts with the T.88 file header, so Raster.Load recognizes it. Each page loads as Gray8: black 0, white 255, as 1-bit TIFF does. Load reads the first page, or the one Jbig2ReaderOptions.Page names; LoadAll reads every page at its own size, and RasterInfo.ImageCount says how many there are without decoding any. // A standalone .jb2 file is detected like any other format; each page loads as Gray8, black 0 and white 255. using Raster first = Raster.Load("book.jb2"); using RasterList pages = Raster.LoadAll("book.jb2"); using Raster third = Raster.Load("book.jb2", options: new Jbig2ReaderOptions { Page = 2 }); Images from a PDF A PDF holds JBIG2 in T.88's embedded form: segments without a file header, and often a separate JBIG2Globals stream with the symbol dictionaries several images share. The embedded form has no signature, so load it with the format named. Jbig2Globals.Parse decodes the globals once; the object is immutable and can be shared by every image of the document, on any thread. // A PDF's JBIG2Decode image has no file header, so name the format. Parse the JBIG2Globals stream once and share it: // every image of the document that refers to it reuses its decoded symbols. Jbig2Globals globals = Jbig2Globals.Parse(globalsStream); using Raster image = Raster.Load(imageStream, Jbig2Format.Info, options: new Jbig2ReaderOptions { Globals = globals }); A PDF image's /Decode array and its color space stay the PDF library's business: Egami returns the page as T.88 defines it. What is decoded Segment Read Generic regions Templates 0 to 3 and the extended template, adaptive pixels anywhere, typical prediction, skipped pixels; MMR through Egami's CCITT Group 4 decoder Refinement regions Templates 0 and 1, typical prediction, against the page or an intermediate region Symbol dictionaries, text regions Arithmetic and Huffman, refinement and aggregation, every reference corner and transposition, standard tables B.1 to B.15 and code table segments Pattern dictionaries, halftone regions Arithmetic and MMR gray-scale planes, any grid, skipping Pages Known and unknown height, striped, every combination operator, intermediate regions; end of file and random-access files Extensions Comments into Jbig2Details.Comments; others skipped unless marked necessary, which throws NotSupportedException Colour palettes (T.88 Amendment 3) Skipped with a warning; the page decodes as bilevel Jbig2Details reports, per page, the stream's Jbig2Organization, whether the page used the globals, its striping, default pixel and Jbig2CombinationOperator, the Jbig2RegionKinds it is made of and whether it is eventually lossless. The page information's resolution goes to RasterMetadata.Resolution. using Raster page = Raster.Load("book.jb2"); var details = (Jbig2Details)page.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"Page {details.PageIndex}, {details.Organization}, regions {details.Regions}"); Console.WriteLine($"Default pixel {details.DefaultPixel}, combined by {details.CombinationOperator}, lossless {details.Lossless}"); Damaged and hostile data JBIG2 decoders are a long-standing attack surface (FORCEDENTRY, in 2021, was an integer overflow in one), so every size is checked arithmetic and counted against SafetyLimits before memory is taken: page and region sizes against MaxWidth, MaxHeight and MaxPixels; symbols, patterns, tables and every bitmap together against MaxTotalBytes. A segment that refers to a segment that is not before it, in the stream or in the globals, always throws. In lenient mode a damaged region is skipped with a warning and the rest of the page decodes; strict mode throws CorruptDataException. The ITU's own conformance streams for T.88 mostly break the Recommendation (their text regions refer to no symbol dictionary), and PDFium and jbig2dec reject them as Egami does; the two that follow it, and the Annex H datastream, decode exactly.

articles/formats/jpeg.html.title: JPEG | Egami
articles/formats/jpeg.html.summary: JPEG JPEG files load like any other: baseline, extended and progressive, Huffman or arithmetic-coded, gray, YCbCr, RGB, CMYK and YCCK, any chroma subsampling. The decoded pixels match libjpeg-turbo's djpeg exactly. Arithmetic, 12-bit and lossless files Arithmetic-coded files load like Huffman-coded ones. 12-bit files load in their natural 16-bit types (Gray16, Rgb16, or Cmyk16 for four components), each sample scaled so 4095 becomes 65535; ask for an 8-bit type and they are rounded to it. Lossless JPEG, the kind inside DNG tiles and many DICOM files, decodes to its exact samples at 2 to 16 bits: up to 8 bits as Gray8 or Rgb8, deeper as Gray16 or Rgb16. Three-component lossless files are RGB unless a JFIF segment or Adobe transform says YCbCr. Lossless files have no DCT, so MinimumSize reduces them after a full decode. JpegDetails.Precision, Arithmetic and Lossless say what a file is. Hierarchical files are refused with UnsupportedFormatException. Browsers show none of these modes. Egami writes 12-bit files on request (below), but no arithmetic or lossless ones. Threads A large file decodes on up to MaxParallelism threads with the same pixels as one thread. A file with restart markers is split at the markers already in it; a progressive file's scans run as a pipeline, each refinement scan a few rows behind the scan before it, and the last pass is split by rows. A sequential file without markers overlaps its entropy decoding with the rest on a second thread. Damaged data falls back to one thread, so warnings and recovery are as before. Scaled decode // At least 100 × 75 from the stored JPEG, decoded at 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 scale straight from the DCT. using Raster preview = Raster.Load("duck.jpg", options: new ReaderOptions { MinimumSize = new Size(100, 75) }); ReaderOptions.MinimumSize picks the smallest of 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 scale that still covers the size you need, and decodes at that scale straight from the DCT. For a thumbnail from a 12-megapixel photo it is many times faster than decoding in full and resizing. Other formats ignore it. Orientation Cameras and phones store pixels as the sensor saw them and say in EXIF how to turn them. Raster.Probe reports the orientation, and AutoOrient applies it; see resizing and geometry. To turn the file itself upright without re-encoding it, use JpegTransform with AutoOrient (see lossless rotation). Writing using FileStream output = File.Create("duck-q85.jpg"); image.Save(output, JpegFormat.Info, new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 85, // 75 by default, on libjpeg's scale Subsampling = ChromaSubsampling.Subsample444, // 4:2:0 by default OptimizeHuffman = true, // a few percent smaller, a little slower }); Option Default Does Quality 75 1 to 100, the same scale as libjpeg's cjpeg Subsampling Subsample420 Subsample422 or Subsample444 keep more color detail OptimizeHuffman false Tables built for the image: a few percent smaller ColorType Auto Gray writes one gray component whatever the pixel type; Cmyk and Ycck write four (Auto picks Cmyk for CMYK pixels) Progressive false Scans that show a coarse image first and refine it, with tables optimized per scan Precision 8 12 keeps more of 16-bit and float pixels RestartInterval 0 Restart markers every so many blocks, for damaged-stream recovery Background none Composites alpha onto this color first; without it alpha is ignored Progressive // Shows coarse first and sharpens as it loads; usually a few percent smaller, and decodes to the same pixels. image.Save("duck-progressive.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Progressive = true }); Progressive writes the scan script libjpeg's cjpeg -progressive writes: ten scans for color, six for gray, spectral selection and successive approximation, each scan with its own optimized Huffman tables. The file decodes to exactly the pixels the baseline file at the same quality gives, and is the same file cjpeg -progressive writes. The encoder holds every quantized coefficient until the last scan, about 2 bytes per sample (72 MB for a 24-megapixel 4:2:0 photo), counted against SafetyLimits.MaxTotalBytes; a streamed encode buffers them. Re-saving a progressive file writes baseline unless you set it. CMYK and YCCK // CMYK pixels save as CMYK, inverted behind an Adobe marker as Photoshop writes; YCCK is usually smaller. using Raster<Cmyk8> inks = image.As<Cmyk8>(); inks.Save("duck-cmyk-out.jpg", JpegWriterOptions.Default); inks.Save("duck-ycck.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { ColorType = JpegColorType.Ycck }); Cmyk8 and Cmyk16 pixels save as four CMYK components with an Adobe marker, the values inverted as Photoshop writes them and every reader expects, and no JFIF segment (JFIF covers gray and YCbCr only). Ycck converts cyan, magenta and yellow to YCbCr as libjpeg does and subsamples their chroma by Subsampling, keeping black at full size; it is usually smaller. Other pixel types written as Cmyk or Ycck are converted with the plain formula. djpeg, ImageMagick and Pillow read the files to the same inks. 12-bit // 16-bit and float pixels keep more than 8 bits in a 12-bit file; it loads back as Rgb16. No browser shows it. using Raster<Rgb16> deep = image.As<Rgb16>(); deep.Save("duck-12bit.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Precision = 12, Quality = 95 }); Precision = 12 writes 12-bit samples (an extended, SOF1 file, or SOF2 when progressive) from any pixel type, narrowing 16-bit samples to 12 bits; it is worth it for 16-bit and float pixels. The Huffman tables are always optimized, as libjpeg-turbo does at 12 bits, and quantization tables pass 255 at low quality, in 16-bit entries. libjpeg-turbo's djpeg reads them; browsers, Pillow and many ImageMagick builds do not. Lossless rotation, flips and crops // Turns the photo upright by its EXIF orientation without re-encoding: no quality is lost, and the tag is reset. JpegTransform.Apply("sideways.jpg", "upright.jpg", new JpegTransformOptions { Operation = JpegTransformOperation.AutoOrient }); // Rotates, crops and drops the color in one pass; a file can be transformed in place. JpegTransformResult result = JpegTransform.Apply("upright.jpg", "upright.jpg", new JpegTransformOptions { Operation = JpegTransformOperation.Rotate90, Crop = new Rect(0, 0, 200, 120), Grayscale = true, }); Console.WriteLine($"{result.Width} × {result.Height}"); JpegTransform turns, mirrors, crops and drops the color of a JPEG without decoding it to pixels, as jpegtran does: the quantized DCT coefficients move and change sign block by block, and are coded again, so the result has exactly the quality the file had. Quantization tables and chroma subsampling stay as they were. It takes every mode the reader takes except lossless JPEG: baseline, progressive, arithmetic (written back with Huffman coding), 12-bit, gray, CMYK and YCCK. The result decodes to the same pixels as the file jpegtran makes with the same switches, on every subsampling and edge case. Option Default Does Operation None FlipHorizontal, FlipVertical, Rotate90, Rotate180, Rotate270, Transpose, Transverse, or AutoOrient: what the EXIF orientation needs, then the tag is reset to normal Crop none The area to keep, after the operation; its top-left corner moves to the MCU grid (8 or 16 pixels), as jpegtran -crop does Grayscale false Keeps only luma: a gray file with no loss. YCbCr files only Edges Trim What happens at a mirrored edge that is not a whole number of MCUs (below) Progressive false Writes progressive scans, as JpegWriterOptions.Progressive does OptimizeHuffman true Tables built for the result, a few percent smaller than the standard ones CopyMetadata true Copies EXIF, ICC, XMP, IPTC, comments and other segments A block of 8 × 8 pixels moves as a whole, so an edge that is not a whole number of MCUs (8 pixels, or 16 with subsampled chroma) cannot be mirrored to the other side intact. JpegTransformEdges.Trim drops that partial MCU from each mirrored edge, so the image loses up to 15 pixels there, as jpegtran -trim does; Strict throws instead, as -perfect does; Keep leaves it in place unmirrored, as jpegtran does by default. Edges that are not mirrored keep every pixel, and Transpose never loses any. EXIF's pixel dimensions follow the result, and its thumbnail gets the same rotation, flip and gray conversion; after a crop the thumbnail is dropped, since it would still show the whole picture. An MPF index (the extra images some cameras append) is dropped too. Other segments are copied byte for byte. The result's size and any warnings about a damaged source are in the returned JpegTransformResult. The whole image's coefficients are held while it runs, about 2 bytes per sample, counted against SafetyLimits.MaxTotalBytes. A 12-megapixel photo turns in 170 ms with optimized tables (jpegtran -optimize: 305 ms), 130 ms with the standard ones (jpegtran: 246 ms) and 260 ms written progressive (jpegtran: 458 ms). What the file says using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.jpg"); if (image.Metadata.FormatDetails is JpegDetails jpeg) { Console.WriteLine($"Progressive: {jpeg.Progressive}, saved at about quality {jpeg.EstimatedQuality}"); } EXIF, XMP (including extended XMP) and ICC profiles are read and written back. A JPEG saved again is re-encoded: pixels lose a little each time, so keep a lossless master if you edit repeatedly, or use JpegTransform for rotations, flips and crops. Details The components, color space and estimated quality are in JpegDetails. JpegReaderOptions.FastUpsampling trades a little chroma sharpness for speed; JpegColorType.Gray writes one channel. CMYK and YCCK files load as RGB by the plain formula, R = (1 − C)(1 − K). Raster.Load<Cmyk8> returns the file's ink amounts instead, without the RGB step; print-accurate color needs the embedded ICC profile, which Egami keeps but does not apply yet. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.jpg", options: new JpegReaderOptions { FastUpsampling = true }); JpegDetails details = (JpegDetails)photo.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"{details.ColorSpace}, progressive: {details.Progressive}, quality about {details.EstimatedQuality}"); foreach (JpegComponent component in details.Components) { Console.WriteLine($"Component {component.Id}: sampled {component.HorizontalSampling} × {component.VerticalSampling}"); } // Gray output, and 4:4:4 (no chroma subsampling) for sharp colored edges. photo.Save("gray.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { ColorType = JpegColorType.Gray }); photo.Save("sharp.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90, Subsampling = ChromaSubsampling.Subsample444 }); Multi-Picture JPEG files Phones store more than one image in a JPEG: a gain map for HDR, large previews, the second view of a stereo pair. The CIPA Multi-Picture Format (MPF) lists them in an APP2 segment. JpegDetails.MultiPicture gives that index as MpfData: an MpfImage for each image with its MpfImageType, flags, length, and offset from the start of the file (the same numbers ExifTool prints). Raster.Probe counts them in RasterInfo.ImageCount, and Raster.LoadAll loads each JPEG one, the primary first. A damaged index never fails a load: the primary loads with a Jpeg.MpfDamaged warning. // A JPEG's Multi-Picture index lists the images stored after the primary: previews, stereo views, a gain map. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("ultrahdr.jpg"); MpfData? index = ((JpegDetails)photo.Metadata.FormatDetails!).MultiPicture; foreach (MpfImage image in index?.Images ?? []) { Console.WriteLine($"{image.Type}: {image.Length:N0} bytes at {image.Offset:N0}"); } // LoadAll gives every JPEG image the index lists, the primary first; a plain JPEG gives one. using RasterList all = Raster.LoadAll("ultrahdr.jpg"); The gain maps of Ultra HDR photos are in the HDR guide. Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Read a CMYK JPEG's inks // A CMYK JPEG loads as RGB by the plain formula, as before; ask for Cmyk8 to get the file's ink amounts instead. using Raster<Cmyk8> inks = Raster.Load<Cmyk8>("duck-cmyk.jpg"); Cmyk8 corner = inks.Row(0)[0]; Console.WriteLine($"Cyan {corner.C}, magenta {corner.M}, yellow {corner.Y}, black {corner.K} (0 = no ink)"); // Resizing filters the four inks, so black stays in the black channel; color adjustments go through RGB instead. inks.Apply(ops => ops.Fit(160, 160)); Run it samples/Jpeg is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Jpeg writes its results to ./output.

articles/formats/jpeg2000.html.title: JPEG 2000 | Egami
articles/formats/jpeg2000.html.summary: JPEG 2000 Egami reads JPEG 2000 (ITU-T T.800 | ISO/IEC 15444-1, all of Part 1), written from the 2019 edition of T.800, T.801's JPX boxes and the PDF specification's JPXDecode filter. Jpeg2000Format.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default; JPEG 2000 is never written. Every ISO/IEC 15444-4 conformance codestream decodes within its tolerances: the reversible ones to OpenJPEG 2.5.4's samples exactly, the irreversible ones within one level, at full resolution and with levels dropped. Reading files JP2 and JPX files start with the JP2 signature box and raw codestreams (J2K, J2C, a PDF's JPXDecode stream) with SOC and SIZ, so Raster.Load recognizes both. MinimumSize drops whole wavelet levels, JPEG 2000's own reduction (a quarter of the levels' work for each level dropped), and Region decodes only the tiles and code-blocks the rectangle needs, so a thumbnail of a large scan or a viewport into a map costs a fraction of the whole decode. Rows stream a row of tiles at a time. // JP2, JPX and raw codestreams are detected like any other format, so is a PDF's JPXDecode stream. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("photo.jp2"); // A thumbnail drops whole wavelet levels instead of decoding at full size, and a region decodes only the code-blocks // it needs. using Raster thumbnail = Raster.Load("photo.jp2", options: new ReaderOptions { MinimumSize = new Size(24, 18) }); using Raster corner = Raster.Load("photo.jp2", options: new ReaderOptions { Region = new Rect(0, 0, 32, 32) }); What it loads as Jpeg2000ReaderOptions.Components chooses between two readings of the same samples. Jpeg2000Components Pixels Color (default) Palettes applied, channels placed by the channel definitions, sYCC and CIELab converted to sRGB; gray, RGB or CMYK, with alpha when a channel is opacity Raw The codestream's components after its own component transform: 1 as gray, 2 as gray and alpha, 3 as RGB, 4 as CMYK, for a PDF that names its own color space Depths widen to the next Egami type by bit replication, so the stored value is recoverable by a shift: 1 to 8 bits load as Gray8, Rgb8, Rgba8 or Cmyk8, 9 to 16 bits as their 16-bit forms, deeper ones as float types. Signed samples are offset by half their range, with the Jpeg2000.SignedSamples warning. Premultiplied alpha loads straight. ICC profiles go to RasterMetadata.IccProfile and the pixels stay as stored, as for every format; XMP, the resolution box and COM markers are read. Subsampled sYCC (4:2:0 and 4:2:2) is upsampled with the YUV kernels at JPEG 2000's chroma siting, or loads straight into a YuvRaster without upsampling; FastUpsampling repeats chroma as OpenJPEG does instead. MaxQualityLayers decodes only the first layers of a layered file, for a quick preview. // A PDF that names its own color space wants the codestream's components as stored. using Raster components = Raster.Load(jpxStream, options: new Jpeg2000ReaderOptions { Components = Jpeg2000Components.Raw }); // A quick preview of a layered file: only its first quality layer, chroma repeated as OpenJPEG does. using Raster preview = Raster.Load("photo.jp2", options: new Jpeg2000ReaderOptions { MaxQualityLayers = 1, FastUpsampling = true }); What is decoded Part Read Codestream SIZ, COD, COC, QCD, QCC, RGN, POC, PPM, PPT and COM; TLM, PLM, PLT and CRG read past; SOP and EPH; tiles and tile-parts in any order Tier 2 Packet headers with tag trees, all five progression orders, progression order changes, precincts of any size, packed packet headers Tier 1 The three coding passes and every code-block style: arithmetic bypass, context reset, termination on each pass, vertically causal contexts, predictable termination, segmentation symbols; ROI by max-shift Reconstruction Reversible 5/3 and irreversible 9/7 wavelets at any number of levels, odd sizes and offsets; RCT and ICT; subsampled and signed components JP2 and JPX ihdr, colr (enumerated, restricted and any ICC), pclr, cmap, cdef, res, XMP uuid; JPX's several colr boxes and rreq; the first codestream Refused Part 2 coding tools and High-Throughput (Part 15) code-blocks throw NotSupportedException naming the feature Jpeg2000Details describes what was decoded: the Jpeg2000Container, the profile, each Jpeg2000Component's precision, sign and sampling, the wavelet, levels, layers and Jpeg2000ProgressionOrder, the tiling, the Jpeg2000ColorSpace, whether there is a palette, the Jpeg2000Channel definitions with their Jpeg2000ChannelType, and the comments. using Raster image = Raster.Load("photo.jp2"); var details = (Jpeg2000Details)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"{details.Container}, {(details.Reversible ? "lossless 5/3" : "lossy 9/7")}, {details.DecompositionLevels} levels"); Console.WriteLine($"{details.QualityLayers} layers in {details.ProgressionOrder} order, {details.TileCount} tiles, {details.ColorSpace}"); foreach (Jpeg2000Component component in details.Components) { Console.WriteLine($"{component.Precision} bits{(component.IsSigned ? " signed" : "")}, sampled every {component.SubsamplingX}×{component.SubsamplingY}"); } foreach (Jpeg2000Channel channel in details.Channels) { Console.WriteLine($"Channel {channel.Channel}: {channel.Type} for color {channel.Association}"); } Speed and threads Code-blocks are independent, so tier 1 runs across cores by EgamiContext.MaxParallelism, with the same output at any thread count; the wavelets and color conversions are vectorized. On a 10-megapixel photo Egami decodes lossy files faster than OpenJPEG on one thread and every file two to four times faster on all cores. Damaged and hostile data Every size in SIZ is checked against SafetyLimits before a tile is read; the number of tiles, components, levels, passes and packet lengths are bounded by the standard and by the data; the samples held count against MaxTotalBytes, and a codestream whose tiles and components would build far more structure than its samples fill is refused. A codestream that ends early decodes what it holds with the Jpeg2000.Truncated warning, and throws CorruptDataException in strict mode.

articles/formats/jxl.html.title: JPEG XL | Egami
articles/formats/jxl.html.summary: JPEG XL Egami reads and writes JPEG XL (ISO/IEC 18181), written from the specification with no native code. JxlFormat.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default, so Raster.Load recognizes a bare codestream (FF 0A) or the box format from the first bytes, and Save("x.jxl") picks the writer. JxlDetails describes the container. Raster.Probe reads the headers alone: size, sample format, channels, orientation and frame count. // The headers alone: size, natural pixel type, orientation and frame count, without decoding any pixels. RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("duck.jxl"); bool isJxl = info.Format == JxlFormat.Info; long bytes = info.EstimatedBytes; // what a full load would allocate Reading Every kind of still decodes: Lossless Modular: every predictor, RCT, palette and squeeze, 1 to 31-bit and float samples, alpha. Lossy VarDCT or Modular in XYB: every transform size, Gaborish, the edge-preserving filter, LF frames, upsampling, patches, splines and noise. // JPEG XL loads like any format: lossless, lossy, animated or recompressed from a JPEG, in its natural pixel type. using Raster duck = Raster.Load("duck.jxl"); duck.Save("duck.png"); The natural pixel type follows the bit depth: Rgb8, Rgba8 or Gray8, their 16-bit forms, RgbaF16 for 16-bit float, and RgbF32, RgbaF32 or GrayF32 beyond. CMYK loads as Cmyk8 or Cmyk16. Color: lossy (XYB) files come out in the file's own color space, enumerated (as djxl gives it) or from its ICC profile through Egami's color pipeline, and that space goes on the raster. PQ and HLG files keep their curve, named by H.273 code points, with intensity_target as HdrMetadata.MaxContentLightLevel; converting to sRGB as they load tone maps them: // An HDR (PQ or HLG) file, tone mapped into sRGB as it loads; the peak comes from the file's intensity_target. using Raster<Rgb8> sdr = Raster.Load<Rgb8>("hdr.jxl", options: new ReaderOptions { ConvertColorTo = Egami.Colors.ColorProfile.Srgb }); sdr.Save("hdr-as-sdr.jpg"); A jhgm gain map loads into RasterMetadata.GainMap, and ReaderOptions.Hdr renders HDR from it as for Ultra HDR JPEGs (see the HDR guide). Groups decode on several threads (EgamiContext.MaxParallelism), and ReaderOptions.Region on a still decodes only the groups it touches. JxlReaderOptions adds three choices on top of the general reader options: Option Default Does MaxDownscale 1 8 or more decodes only a lossy still's LF image, an eighth of the size each way and far faster RenderSpotColors true Mixes spot color channels into the color as djxl does; false leaves the color as coded LinearOutput false Gives linear light in float, in the file's own primaries, instead of its encoded color space Animations, layers and previews Animations load as their blended frames with delays and loop count. JxlImage.ReadLayers gives the frames before blending, each a JxlLayer with its offset, duration and JxlLayerBlend mode, for an editor; JxlImage.ReadPreview gives the preview a file may carry. // An animation loads as its frames, blended onto the canvas, each with its delay. using Raster animation = Raster.Load("sprite.jxl"); int frames = animation.FrameCount; // The layers before blending, for an editor: each at its own size and place. IReadOnlyList<JxlLayer> layers = JxlImage.ReadLayers("sprite.jxl"); foreach (JxlLayer layer in layers) { Console.WriteLine($"{layer.Raster.Width}x{layer.Raster.Height} at {layer.X},{layer.Y}: {layer.Blend}, {layer.Duration.TotalMilliseconds} ms"); layer.Dispose(); } // The preview some files carry for quick display, or null. using Raster? preview = JxlImage.ReadPreview("duck.jxl"); // A lossy still at an eighth of its size, from its LF image alone. using Raster thumbnail = Raster.Load("duck.jxl", options: new JxlReaderOptions { MaxDownscale = 8 }); Extra channels Alpha loads straight (premultiplied color is divided out). JxlDetails.ExtraChannels lists every channel as a JxlExtraChannel with its JxlExtraChannelKind (alpha, depth, spot color, selection mask and others), and JxlImage.ReadExtraChannel reads any one alone as gray floats. // Alpha joins the pixels (straight, even when the file premultiplies); other extra channels are listed in the details. using Raster image = Raster.Load("sprite.jxl"); JxlDetails details = (JxlDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!; foreach (JxlExtraChannel channel in details.ExtraChannels) { Console.WriteLine($"{channel.Kind} '{channel.Name}', {channel.BitsPerSample} bits"); } // Any one of them alone, such as depth or a selection mask, as gray floats. using Raster<GrayF32> alpha = JxlImage.ReadExtraChannel("sprite.jxl", 0); // Spot colors are mixed into the color as djxl does, unless turned off. using Raster plain = Raster.Load("sprite.jxl", options: new JxlReaderOptions { RenderSpotColors = false }); Recompressed JPEGs JPEG XL can hold a JPEG losslessly, about a fifth smaller. JxlImage.RecompressJpeg makes such a file from a JPEG, and JxlImage.ReconstructJpeg gives the original back byte for byte. JxlDetails.HasJpegReconstruction says which files can. // A JPEG becomes a JPEG XL file about a fifth smaller with the same pixels, and comes back byte for byte. JxlImage.RecompressJpeg("duck.jpg", "duck.jxl"); JxlImage.ReconstructJpeg("duck.jxl", "duck-again.jpg"); Baseline and progressive JPEGs with any Huffman tables, restart markers, ICC, Exif and XMP are taken; arithmetic-coded, lossless, hierarchical, 12-bit and CMYK JPEGs, and 4:1:1 sampling, are refused. Such files also load as pixels like any other: // A JPEG recompressed into JPEG XL loads as pixels like any other file, and gives its JPEG back byte for byte. using Raster image = Raster.Load("recompressed.jxl"); if (((JxlDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!).HasJpegReconstruction) { JxlImage.ReconstructJpeg("recompressed.jxl", "original.jpg"); } Writing The writer makes lossless Modular files in the raster's own precision, or lossy VarDCT files in XYB, with ICC, EXIF, XMP and orientation. JxlWriterOptions follows cjxl's own knobs, so the same numbers give about the same files: Option Default Does Lossless null true writes Modular, false VarDCT; null keeps the kind of the JPEG XL file the raster came from and writes lossy otherwise Effort 5 1 (fastest) to 7 (smallest), cjxl's -e, for both kinds Quality 90 Lossy quality, 0 to 100, cjxl's -q scale; 90 is distance 1.0, visually lossless Distance null A distance as cjxl's -d instead of a quality, 0.1 to 25 AlphaDistance 0 Lossy files: 0 keeps alpha exact, larger values code it lossy KeepTransparentColors true Lossy files keep the color under fully transparent pixels; false gives smaller files Progressive false Lossy files as cjxl -p makes them: a coarse image first that sharpens PhotonNoiseIso null Film-like noise the decoder adds, as cjxl's --photon_noise_iso // Lossless JPEG XL, about the size cjxl -d 0 makes at the same effort (1 fastest to 7 smallest, 5 by default). using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.png"); photo.Save("duck-lossless.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = true, Effort = 7 }); Lossless files give back every pixel exactly, in the raster's own precision: 8 or 16-bit, half or single float, gray or RGB, with alpha when it is not opaque everywhere. The effort follows cjxl's: 1 is its fast path, 7 learns a context tree and tries palettes and color transforms, for files within a few bytes of cjxl's. The ICC profile (or an enumerated sRGB, linear or HDR space), EXIF, XMP and orientation are kept. // Lossy JPEG XL at cjxl's default: quality 90, which is distance 1.0 (visually lossless). using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.png"); photo.Save("duck-lossy.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = false }); // A distance as cjxl -d takes it instead of a quality, and more effort for a smaller file. photo.Save("duck-small.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = false, Distance = 2.5f, Effort = 7 }); Lossy files are VarDCT in XYB, as cjxl writes them for PNG input, and come out within 5% of cjxl's size and Butteraugli score at the same settings (libjxl 0.12.0). Pick either a quality or a distance: Quality is cjxl's -q (90 by default, 100 lossless) and Distance its -d, where 1.0 is visually lossless and each step up gives a smaller file with more visible loss; a distance, when set, wins. Effort 6 adds the full block-size search and a per-block edge-preserving filter strength, 7 patches for repeated shapes such as text. Large images are coded in 2048-pixel chunks, as cjxl does, so memory stays bounded. A JPEG source is better recompressed than re-encoded: recompressing keeps its pixels exactly and the original file recoverable, where lossy encoding its decoded pixels loses detail a second time. // Alpha stays exact in lossy files by default, and fully transparent pixels keep their color. using Raster<Rgba8> logo = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("duck.png"); logo.Save("logo.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = false, Quality = 85 }); // Smaller: alpha coded lossy too, and the color under transparent pixels left to the encoder (as cjxl does). logo.Save("logo-small.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = false, AlphaDistance = 1, KeepTransparentColors = false }); Alpha is an extra channel coded apart from the color, exact by default, so cut-outs keep their edges (below distance 10; from there cjxl and Egami code the whole image at half size). AlphaDistance above 0 codes it lossy as cjxl's --alpha_distance does. Fully transparent pixels keep their color unless KeepTransparentColors is false, which lets the encoder replace it, as libjxl does by default, for a smaller file.

articles/formats/openexr.html.title: OpenEXR | Egami
articles/formats/openexr.html.summary: OpenEXR ExrFormat reads scanline and tiled files, single and multi-part (ExrPartKind), with every compression of OpenEXR 3 (ExrCompression: NONE, RLE, ZIPS, ZIP, PIZ, PXR24, B44, B44A, DWAA and DWAB; HTJ2K is refused), half, float and uint channels (ExrPixelType), and luminance-chroma images. Pixels match OpenEXR's own decode bit for bit, DWA within one half-float step. A load gives the first part's R, G, B and A (or Y, YA or the luminance-chroma channels) as linear light; a tiled part loads its full-resolution level (ExrLevelMode says which levels it has). Deep parts throw UnsupportedFormatException. ExrDetails lists every part as an ExrPart: its name, channels (ExrChannel), layers, data and display windows, tile size, chromaticities and every header attribute as an ExrHeaderEntry. ExrReaderOptions picks the Part, a Layer (such as diffuse for diffuse.R, diffuse.G and diffuse.B) and the ExrWindow to load: the data window, the pixels the file stores (the default), or the display window, padded with transparent black where there is no data. ExrImage.ReadChannel loads any one channel, such as depth or an object id, as 32-bit float. // The first part's RGBA channels as linear light, 1.0 reference white; other layers by name. using Raster<RgbaF32> beauty = Raster.Load<RgbaF32>("render.exr"); var details = (ExrDetails)beauty.Metadata.FormatDetails!; IReadOnlyList<string> layers = details.Parts[details.Part].Layers; // "diffuse", "specular" using Raster<RgbaF32> diffuse = Raster.Load<RgbaF32>("render.exr", options: new ExrReaderOptions { Layer = "diffuse" }); // Any one channel, such as depth or an object id, as 32-bit float. using Raster<GrayF32> depth = ExrImage.ReadChannel("aov.exr", "Z"); The writer writes one scanline part with R, G, B and A when the raster has alpha (ExrWriterOptions): ZIP by default, or NONE, RLE, ZIPS or PIZ, in half or float (ExrWriterOptions.PixelType; by default float for float rasters other than RgbaF16, half otherwise). A non-linear raster, such as sRGB, is converted to linear light first, and primaries other than Rec. 709 are written as chromaticities. OpenEXR reads every file Egami writes to the same values. // Half-float RGBA, ZIP-compressed, by default; a sRGB or other non-linear raster is linearized first. beauty.Save("copy.exr"); beauty.Save("float.exr", new ExrWriterOptions { Compression = ExrCompression.Piz, PixelType = ExrPixelType.Float }); Pixels are linear light with 1.0 as reference white; the HDR guide explains the scale, and ToneMap in color management turns them into SDR. Recipes A render pass from OpenEXR as JPEG // One render pass of a multi-layer OpenEXR file, tone mapped for the web. using Raster<RgbaF32> diffuse = Raster.Load<RgbaF32>("render.exr", options: new ExrReaderOptions { Layer = "diffuse" }); diffuse.Apply(ops => ops.ToneMap(ToneMapping.Bt2390)); diffuse.Save("diffuse.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90 }); ExrReaderOptions.Layer picks a pass by name; ExrDetails lists the parts and layers a file has. ToneMap rolls off what is brighter than white instead of clipping it.

articles/formats/pcx.html.title: PCX | Egami
articles/formats/pcx.html.summary: PCX PCX is ZSoft's PC Paintbrush format: a 128-byte header, then scanlines of one to four color planes, nearly always run-length coded. It reads and writes through the Egami.Formats.Extended package: register it with WithPcx() or WithExtendedFormats() (Extended formats). Reads 1, 2, 4 and 8-bit images of one plane; 1-bit images of 2 to 4 planes (EGA, 16 colors); 24-bit (three planes) and 32-bit (four planes, the fourth as alpha); coded or not; runs that carry on into the next scanline Writes Version 5, run-length coded: gray rasters as one 8-bit plane with a gray palette, everything else as 24-bit RGB; the resolution in dots per inch (72 when the raster has none) Natural pixel type Gray8 for 1-bit and for 8-bit images the header calls gray, Rgba8 for four planes, Rgb8 otherwise FormatInfo PcxFormat.Info: name PCX, extension .pcx, MIME types image/vnd.zbrush.pcx and image/x-pcx Palettes come from the header (16 colors) or, for 8-bit images, from the 769 bytes after the pixels, so an 8-bit file is read to its end before its first row. A 1-bit image of one plane is black where a bit is clear and white where it is set, as its palette says; ImageMagick writes and reads such files the other way round, so its 1-bit PCX files load inverted. A file whose 256-color palette is missing reads as gray levels with the warning Pcx.PaletteMissing. PcxDetails keeps the version, the bits per pixel, the plane count and the palette. // What the header said that the pixels do not: PcxDetails, SgiDetails, SunRasterDetails, XbmDetails and XpmDetails. using Raster image = Raster.Load("arrow.xbm", context); if (image.Metadata.FormatDetails is XbmDetails xbm) { Console.WriteLine($"{xbm.Name}, hotspot {xbm.Hotspot}"); } // Writers take the name and hotspot back from the details. image.Metadata.FormatDetails = new XbmDetails { Name = "pointer", Hotspot = new Point(0, 0) }; image.Save("pointer.xbm"); The files Egami writes have no alpha and no metadata but the resolution; a save that drops alpha or deeper samples says so in the Warnings. Images are at most 65,534 pixels wide and 65,536 high.

articles/formats/png.html.title: PNG and APNG | Egami
articles/formats/png.html.summary: PNG and APNG Egami reads and writes PNG and its animated form, APNG: every color type and bit depth, interlaced files, transparency, text, EXIF, XMP and ICC profiles. Reading A PNG loads in its own layout: Gray8, Gray16, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8, Rgba8 or Rgba16. An APNG loads as Rgba8, or Rgba16 for 16-bit files, with every frame composited to full size through every disposal and blend, as a browser shows it. Damage is handled as the Diagnostics page lists under Png.: ancillary chunks with a bad checksum are ignored, and when the image data ends early the rows not decoded are transparent black. Writing using FileStream output = File.Create("duck-small.png"); image.Save(output, PngFormat.Info, new PngWriterOptions { Reduce = true, // the smallest exact form: no alpha if all opaque, gray or a palette when nothing is lost CompressionLevel = 9, // 0 (fastest) to 9 (smallest); 5 by default }); Option Default Does ColorType, BitDepth The pixel type's own Force a layout, such as PngColorType.Palette Reduce false Scan the image and write the smallest exact form Palette 256 colors, Floyd–Steinberg How a palette is built when ColorType is Palette and the image has more colors CompressionLevel 5 zlib level, 0 to 9 Filter Adaptive Row filter, or one fixed filter FirstFrameOnly false Write a still PNG from an animation Interlace false Write Adam7, so a viewer can show a coarse image early; files are usually larger ParallelCompression false Compress images with more than 4 MiB of image data on several cores Interlace is never taken from the source: an interlaced PNG is written plain unless you set it. With ParallelCompression, the image data is cut into fixed bands of 1 MiB that compress on up to EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads. The file is the same on any machine and at any thread count, and in Egami's tests it was 0.1% to 0.3% larger; a 24-megapixel photo saved 8 times as fast on 12 cores. Smaller images are written exactly as with the option off. image.Save("duck-large.png", new PngWriterOptions { ParallelCompression = true, // big images compress on several cores; the same file at any thread count Interlace = true, // Adam7: a coarse image shows before the whole file has arrived }); Kept for round trips in PngDetails: gamma, chromaticities, sRGB intent, cICP, the ICC profile name, and every chunk Egami does not read itself. The writer also takes a palette you force, a fixed filter and a zlib strategy, and writes chunks you add to PngDetails: // Force a palette, choose a filter and a zlib strategy, and keep a private chunk. ((PngDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!).OtherChunks.Add( new PngChunk("prVt", "hello"u8.ToArray(), PngChunkPosition.AfterImageData)); image.Save("duck-palette.png", new PngWriterOptions { ColorType = PngColorType.Palette, Filter = PngFilterMode.Paeth, CompressionStrategy = PngCompressionStrategy.Filtered, }); APNG Saving a raster with more than one frame as PNG writes an APNG. APNG keeps full color and partial alpha, so nothing is quantized. Each frame stores only the rectangle that changed, and blends with Over when that stores less. Set PngWriterOptions.FirstFrameOnly to write a still PNG from an animation. The animation guide covers frames, delays and loops.

articles/formats/pnm.html.title: Netpbm (PBM, PGM, PPM, PAM, PFM) | Egami
articles/formats/pnm.html.summary: Netpbm (PBM, PGM, PPM, PAM, PFM) Egami reads and writes the Netpbm formats: P1 to P6, plain and binary, at maxval 1 to 65,535, P7 PAM with alpha, and the PF and Pf float maps. A file loads as Gray8, Gray16, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8, Rgba8 or Rgba16, and a float map as RgbF32 or GrayF32. // Auto: P5 (PGM) for gray, P6 (PPM) for color, P7 (PAM) when the pixel type has alpha. image.Save("duck.ppm"); // The plain-text forms, for tools that read them; lines are at most 70 characters. image.Save("duck-plain.ppm", new PnmWriterOptions { PlainText = true }); // A 1-bit bitmap, thresholded at 50% gray. image.Save("duck.pbm", new PnmWriterOptions { Kind = PnmKind.Bitmap }); Maxvals other than 255 and 65,535 are scaled exactly, as round(v × 255 / maxval). A PAM with an unknown tuple type is read by its depth, with a warning. A stream with several images reads the first and warns. # comments become Comment text entries and are written back. Saving to a .pbm, .pgm, .ppm, .pam or .pfm path writes that variant unless PnmWriterOptions.Kind names one; .pnm chooses from the pixel type. PFM float maps load as RgbF32 (PF) or GrayF32 (Pf), marked as linear light, with their scale and byte order in PnmDetails; values outside 0..1 are kept. Writing uses PFM for float types without alpha, or when PnmKind.FloatMap is asked for: little-endian, scale −1, as Netpbm and ImageMagick write it.

articles/formats/psd.html.title: PSD and PSB | Egami
articles/formats/psd.html.summary: PSD and PSB Egami reads Adobe Photoshop documents (.psd) and large documents (.psb), written from Adobe's Photoshop File Format Specification. PsdFormat.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default; PSD is never written. Egami reads the flattened image Photoshop stores after the layers, in every color mode and depth, and lists the layers as metadata without their pixels. Reading files // Load gives the flattened image Photoshop stores after the layers, in the type that fits the file: Rgb8 here, Rgba16 for // a 16-bit file with transparency, Cmyk8 for CMYK. Save it as anything. using Raster flat = Raster.Load("layered.psd"); flat.Save("layered.png"); // The ICC profile, resolution, EXIF, XMP and IPTC are in the metadata as for every format. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("photo.psd"); ReadOnlyMemory<byte> icc = photo.Metadata.IccProfile; Resolution? dpi = photo.Metadata.Resolution; A file saved without Maximize Compatibility holds only a placeholder; PsdDetails.HasRealComposite says so. Color mode 1-bit 8-bit 16-bit 32-bit Bitmap Gray8, 1 black Grayscale, duotone Gray8, GrayAlpha8 Gray16, GrayAlpha16 GrayF32; RgbaF32 with alpha Indexed Rgb8; Rgba8 with a transparent index RGB Rgb8, Rgba8 Rgb16, Rgba16 RgbF32, RgbaF32 CMYK Cmyk8; Rgba8 with alpha Cmyk16; Rgba16 with alpha Lab Rgb8, Rgba8, converted to sRGB Rgb16, Rgba16 Multichannel Gray8 of the first channel Gray16 CMYK loads as ink amounts, with the file's ICC profile, so ConvertColorTo and ConvertColor turn it into RGB through the profile as for a CMYK JPEG; with transparency it loads as RGBA by the plain formula. Lab is converted to sRGB from D50 by Bradford, as for TIFF's CIELab. 32-bit files are linear light and say so in RasterMetadata.ColorSpace, or carry the file's profile. A duotone file loads as its gray channel, its inks kept in PsdDetails.ColorModeData; a multichannel file has no color model, so its first channel loads as gray with the Psd.ChannelsDropped warning. Transparency is the channel after the color ones when the layer count is negative, as Photoshop marks it; Photoshop stores the flattened image flattened onto white, and the white is divided back out, so colors under partial transparency come out as painted. ImageMagick does the same for RGB files only, and Pillow not at all. Other extra channels (alpha and spot channels) are not loaded; their names are in PsdDetails.ExtraChannels. PsdDetails says what the file is: PSD or PSB (Version), its PsdColorMode, bits a channel, channel count and the PsdCompression of the flattened image. The image resources map to metadata: the ICC profile (1039), resolution (1005), EXIF (1058, whose orientation reaches RasterInfo.Orientation), XMP (1060) and IPTC (1028). Every other resource, the thumbnail (1036) among them, is kept as it was read in PsdDetails.OtherResources. using Raster image = Raster.Load("photo.psd"); var details = (PsdDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"{(details.Version == 2 ? "PSB" : "PSD")}, {details.ColorMode} at {details.BitsPerChannel} bits, {details.ChannelCount} channels, {details.Compression}"); if (!details.HasRealComposite) { // Saved without Maximize Compatibility: what loaded is Photoshop's placeholder, and a warning says so. Console.WriteLine("Save the file again with Maximize Compatibility on."); } foreach (PsdResource resource in details.OtherResources) { Console.WriteLine($"Resource {resource.Id}, {resource.Data.Length} bytes"); } No real composite A file saved without Photoshop's Maximize Compatibility holds no real flattened image, only a placeholder. Egami loads it with the Psd.NoComposite warning and PsdDetails.HasRealComposite false; it does not composite the layers itself, which would need Photoshop's blend modes, adjustment layers, effects and text. ImageMagick flattens the layers instead. Layers PsdDetails.Layers lists the layer records bottom to top as the file does: name (the Unicode name when there is one), bounds, opacity (0 to 1, as DrawImage takes it), blend mode (Photoshop's key and Egami's BlendMode where there is one), visibility, clipping, and whether the record is a layer or one end of a group, with its nesting level. Their pixels are not loaded; LoadAll returns the flattened image only. // Layer records come as metadata, bottom to top as the file lists them; their pixels are not loaded. using Raster image = Raster.Load("layered.psd"); foreach (PsdLayer layer in ((PsdDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!).Layers) { if (layer.Kind == PsdLayerKind.GroupEnd) { continue; } string kind = layer.Kind == PsdLayerKind.Layer ? "layer" : "group"; Console.WriteLine($"{new string(' ', 2 * layer.Level)}{layer.Name} ({kind}, {layer.BlendModeKey}, opacity {layer.Opacity:P0}{(layer.IsVisible ? "" : ", hidden")})"); } Streaming and speed Rows come from the channel planes as they are asked for: raw rows at computed offsets and PackBits rows through their byte counts, read where they lie on a seekable stream, so Region reads only the rows it needs and the layer data is skipped without being read. A stream that cannot seek is read to its end first, and Deflate data is inflated whole. On 12-megapixel files Egami decodes three to ten times faster than ImageMagick (Magick.NET). Damaged and hostile data The header's size is checked against SafetyLimits before anything else; PSB's sides of up to 300,000 pixels stay behind the default limits unless the caller raises them. Every section length is checked against the data that remains, the layer section is skipped by its length, the image resources and layer records count against MaxMetadataBytes, and the PackBits row table is bounded by the header before it is read. Damaged layer records or resources are warnings (Psd.LayersDamaged, Psd.ResourcesDamaged), since the flattened image does not depend on them. Image data that ends early loads with the missing pixels 0 and the Psd.DataTruncated warning, and throws CorruptDataException in strict mode. The reader is fuzzed with AFL++ through whole files and through the image data alone.

articles/formats/qoi.html.title: QOI | Egami
articles/formats/qoi.html.summary: QOI Egami reads and writes the whole Quite OK Image format, with 3 or 4 channels and both colorspaces. Files it writes are byte for byte what the reference encoder writes. A QOI loads as Rgb8 or Rgba8. // 3 channels when every pixel is opaque, 4 otherwise. The bytes match the reference encoder's. image.Save("duck.qoi"); image.Save("duck-rgba.qoi", new QoiWriterOptions { IncludeAlpha = true }); QOI's colorspace byte maps to RasterMetadata.ColorSpace (sRGB or linear) and back.

articles/formats/radiance.html.title: Radiance | Egami
articles/formats/radiance.html.summary: Radiance Radiance pictures hold three 8-bit mantissas and a shared exponent per pixel (RGBE), or CIE X, Y and Z the same way (XYZE). RadianceFormat reads both, every scan order a resolution line can name (-Y 512 +X 768 and the other seven), and flat, old-style repeat-pixel and per-channel run-length scanlines. Pixels load as RgbF32, bit for bit what stb_image decodes; XYZE converts to RGB in Radiance's standard primaries, which RasterMetadata.Primaries then names. A PRIMARIES line sets the primaries of an RGBE file the same way; without one, Rec. 709 is assumed. RadianceDetails keeps the header: the RadiancePixelFormat, Exposure, ColorCorrection, Primaries, Software, View, PixelAspectRatio, the scan order as stored and every header line. The reader also measures the brightest value and stores it as HdrMetadata.MaxContentLightLevel, so ToneMap fits the image rather than a fixed 1,000 cd/m² peak. // Linear light, unclamped: 1.0 is reference white. The brightest value is measured as the light level ToneMap fits. using Raster<RgbF32> hdr = Raster.Load<RgbF32>("desk.hdr"); var details = (RadianceDetails)hdr.Metadata.FormatDetails!; double? exposure = details.Exposure; // the header's EXPOSURE lines; the pixels are kept as stored // To SDR: tone map, then save. Saving the HDR raster to PNG or JPEG as it is would clip the highlights. using Raster<RgbF32> mapped = hdr.Derive(ops => ops.ToneMap(ToneMapping.Bt2390)); mapped.Save("desk.jpg"); // RGBE with per-channel run-length scanlines, as Radiance writes them; EXPOSURE only when asked for. hdr.Save("copy.hdr"); hdr.Save("labeled.hdr", new RadianceWriterOptions { Exposure = 1.5 }); The writer writes RGBE, top row first, with per-channel run-length scanlines (RadianceWriterOptions.Compress = false writes them flat) and an EXPOSURE line only when RadianceWriterOptions.Exposure is set. Reading a file and writing it again gives the same floats, and the same bytes once written by Egami. Pixels are linear light with 1.0 as reference white; the HDR guide explains the scale, and ToneMap in color management turns them into SDR.

articles/formats/sgi.html.title: SGI | Egami
articles/formats/sgi.html.summary: SGI SGI is Silicon Graphics' image format (.rgb, .rgba, .bw, .sgi): a 512-byte header, then one to four channels of 8 or 16-bit samples, each channel a plane of bottom-up rows, plain or run-length coded. It reads and writes through the Egami.Formats.Extended package: register it with WithSgi() or WithExtendedFormats() (Extended formats). Reads 1 to 4 channels (gray, gray and alpha, RGB, RGBA) of 8 or 16 bits, plain or coded, dimension 1, 2 or 3; coded rows in any order in the file; further channels are skipped with a Sgi.ChannelsSkipped warning Writes The raster's own channels (gray, gray and alpha, RGB or RGBA) and depth (16-bit above 8 bits a channel), coded unless SgiWriterOptions.Rle is off, with the image name from SgiDetails Natural pixel type Gray8, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8 or Rgba8, or their 16-bit forms FormatInfo SgiFormat.Info: name SGI, extensions .sgi, .rgb, .rgba, .bw, .int, .inta, MIME types image/sgi and image/x-rgb // SGI codes its rows by default; Sun raster writes them plain unless asked. using (FileStream sgi = File.Create("duck.rgb")) { image.Save(sgi, SgiFormat.Info, new SgiWriterOptions { Rle = false }); } using (FileStream sun = File.Create("duck.ras")) { image.Save(sun, SunRasterFormat.Info, new SunRasterWriterOptions { Rle = true }); } The planes are stored bottom-up and the coded rows may lie anywhere, so a decode reads the file whole and then hands out rows, and the writer keeps the coded rows in memory until the last one. A file that ends early leaves the rows it lacks transparent black with the warning Sgi.RowsMissing, and a damaged coded row is cut short with Sgi.RowDamaged. SGI keeps alpha and 16-bit samples but no metadata. Images are at most 65,535 pixels on a side.

articles/formats/sun-raster.html.title: Sun raster | Egami
articles/formats/sun-raster.html.summary: Sun raster Sun raster is the rasterfile format of SunOS: a 32-byte big-endian header, an optional colormap, then rows of 1, 8, 24 or 32 bits, plain or byte-encoded. It reads and writes through the Egami.Formats.Extended package: register it with WithSunRaster() or WithExtendedFormats() (Extended formats). Reads Types 0 (old), 1 (standard), 2 (byte-encoded) and 3 (RGB order); 1, 8, 24 and 32 bits; colormaps of equal red, green and blue planes, and raw colormaps skipped Writes Gray rasters as 8-bit gray levels without a colormap, everything else as 24-bit pixels, blue first (type 1), or byte-encoded (type 2) when SunRasterWriterOptions.Rle is set Natural pixel type Gray8 for 1-bit and 8-bit images without a colormap or with a gray one, Rgb8 otherwise FormatInfo SunRasterFormat.Info: name Sun raster, extensions .ras and .sun, MIME type image/x-sun-raster Without a colormap, 1-bit pixels are black where set and 8-bit pixels are gray levels. The pad byte of 32-bit pixels is not read as alpha. SunRasterDetails keeps the depth, the colormap, the coding and the byte order. // SGI codes its rows by default; Sun raster writes them plain unless asked. using (FileStream sgi = File.Create("duck.rgb")) { image.Save(sgi, SgiFormat.Info, new SgiWriterOptions { Rle = false }); } using (FileStream sun = File.Create("duck.ras")) { image.Save(sun, SunRasterFormat.Info, new SunRasterWriterOptions { Rle = true }); } Rows stream from the input as they are asked for. Sun raster has no alpha and no metadata: a save that drops them says so in the Warnings.

articles/formats/tga.html.title: TGA | Egami
articles/formats/tga.html.summary: TGA Egami reads Truevision TGA files: color-mapped, true-color and gray, raw and RLE, 8 to 32 bits, every origin, and the TGA 2.0 footer and extension area. It writes 8-bit gray, 16-bit 5-5-5 with or without a 1-bit alpha, 24 and 32-bit, and 8-bit palettes, raw or RLE, with a TGA 2.0 footer. A TGA loads as Bgr8, Bgra8, Gray8 or GrayAlpha8. TGA has no signature, so detection takes a file as TGA only when its whole 18-byte header is consistent; see Detection. // Run-length encoded by default, bottom-left origin, with a TGA 2.0 footer that states the alpha type. image.Save("duck.tga"); image.Save("duck-raw.tga", new TgaWriterOptions { Rle = false }); The descriptor's attribute bits say whether the extra bits are alpha, and a TGA 2.0 alpha type of "none" overrides them; premultiplied alpha is divided out on load. The extension area's author and comments become Author and Comment text entries, and the writer stores them back. TgaPixelFormat.Bgr24 and Bgr555 drop alpha rather than blending it onto a background. 15 and 16-bit files load straight into Bgr555 and Bgra5551. The writer's pixel format and run-length coding, and the origin and alpha type a file states, read back through TgaDetails: image.Save("duck-gray.tga", new TgaWriterOptions { PixelFormat = TgaPixelFormat.Gray8, Rle = false }); using Raster back = Raster.Load("duck-gray.tga"); TgaDetails details = (TgaDetails)back.Metadata.FormatDetails!; bool upsideDown = details.Origin is TgaOrigin.BottomLeft or TgaOrigin.BottomRight; bool hasAlpha = details.AlphaType is TgaAlphaType.Straight or TgaAlphaType.Premultiplied;

articles/formats/tiff.html.title: TIFF | Egami
articles/formats/tiff.html.summary: TIFF Egami reads and writes TIFF and BigTIFF, written from the TIFF 6.0 specification, Adobe's technical notes and supplements and the BigTIFF design note, starting from the reader in Lars's ClassicMac. TiffFormat.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default, so Raster.Load recognizes TIFF from its first bytes and Save("x.tif") picks the writer. Every page of libtiff's own sample images and of Egami's corpus decodes to the samples libtiff gives. Reading // Load reads the first full-resolution page in the pixel type that fits it: Rgb16 for 16-bit color, Cmyk8 for CMYK. using Raster page = Raster.Load("scan.tif"); Console.WriteLine($"{page.Width} × {page.Height}, {page.Layout.ChannelOrder} {page.Layout.ChannelType}"); // Probe says how many pages LoadAll would return, without decoding any. Console.WriteLine($"{Raster.Probe("scan.tif").ImageCount} pages"); Load reads one page: the first full-resolution page, or the one TiffReaderOptions.Page names. Reduced-resolution pages, SubIFD previews and transparency masks are never counted as pages. // Pick another page by its index among the full-resolution pages. using Raster<Rgba8> third = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("scan.tif", options: new TiffReaderOptions { Page = 2 }); LoadAll returns every full-resolution page, each at its own size and pixel type; with IncludeReducedPages the reduced-resolution pages and SubIFDs come too, each after the page it belongs to. // Every page at its own size and pixel type. The list owns the rasters. using RasterList pages = Raster.LoadAll("scan.tif"); foreach (Raster page in pages) { Console.WriteLine($"{page.Width} × {page.Height}"); } // Keep one page after the list is gone. using Raster first = pages.Detach(0); Compression Read None, LZW (and TIFF 5.0's bit-reversed LZW), Deflate, PackBits Yes, with the horizontal and floating-point predictors CCITT modified Huffman, Group 3 (1-D and 2-D), Group 4 1-bit pages JPEG, old-style JPEG 8-bit pages, through Egami's JPEG decoder; old-style JPEG is best effort ThunderScan 4-bit gray SGILog, SGILog24 LogL and LogLuv pages, as linear GrayF32 or RgbF32 WebP Lossless and lossy, through Egami's WebP decoder JPEG XL (50002, and DNG 1.7's 52546) Chunky gray, RGB and YCbCr pages of 8 or 16-bit or float samples, lossless and lossy, through Egami's JPEG XL decoder; each strip or tile as its codestream decodes alone. DNG's camera RAW pages (CFA, LinearRaw) are not read ZSTD, LZMA, LERC Not yet: NotSupportedException names the code. Added on real demand Each page loads in the pixel type that fits it. Depths Egami has no type for widen to the next: 2 and 4 bits to 8, 10 to 14 bits to 16, scaled so the maximum stays the maximum; 24 and 32-bit integers and 16 to 64-bit floats load as float types. Photometric 1 to 8 bits 9 to 16 bits Wider or float Gray (either polarity) Gray8, GrayAlpha8 Gray16, GrayAlpha16 GrayF32; RgbaF32 with alpha RGB Rgb8, Rgba8 Rgb16, Rgba16 RgbF32, RgbaF32; RgbaF16 for 16-bit float Palette Rgb8, or Rgb16 when the color map needs 16 bits CMYK Cmyk8; Rgba8 with alpha Cmyk16; Rgba16 with alpha RgbaF32 YCbCr, at any subsampling Rgb8 Rgb16 CIE Lab, ICC Lab, ITU Lab Rgb8 Rgb16 RgbF32 Associated (premultiplied) alpha loads as straight alpha, and TiffDetails.ExtraSamples says which kind the file had; extra samples that are not alpha are dropped with a warning. Signed samples are offset so 0 becomes the middle value. Lab is relative to the page's white point, D50 when the file gives none (as Adobe's note and libtiff have it), and converted to sRGB with Bradford adaptation, as ICC does. Float pages are linear light. CMYK pages keep their ICC profile, so ConvertColorTo converts them through it. Writing // Each pixel type is written at its own depth: 16-bit color stays 16-bit. Deflate with the predictor is the default. photo.Save("duck.tif"); // Tiles, LZW, BigTIFF, or the smallest exact form the pixels allow. photo.Save("tiled.tif", new TiffWriterOptions { Compression = TiffCompression.Lzw, TileSize = 256, Layout = TiffLayout.Auto }); photo.Save("small.tif", new TiffWriterOptions { Reduce = true }); // JPEG inside TIFF: RGB is written as YCbCr 4:2:0 with the tables shared by every strip. photo.Save("photo.tif", new TiffWriterOptions { Compression = TiffCompression.Jpeg, Quality = 90 }); Option Default Does Compression the TIFF source's, else Deflate None, Lzw, Deflate, PackBits, CcittGroup3 and CcittGroup4 (1-bit), Jpeg (8-bit gray, RGB and CMYK), Webp (lossless at Quality 100, else lossy) CompressionLevel 5 Deflate level, 0 to 9 Predictor the source's, else Horizontal for integers and FloatingPoint for floats For LZW and Deflate; None turns it off Quality 75 JPEG and lossy WebP quality TileSize the source's, else strips of about 64 KB A multiple of 16 writes square tiles; 0 forces strips Layout Classic Big writes BigTIFF; Auto switches when the pixels pass 4 GB; Classic throws before writing when they would Reduce false Writes the smallest exact form: 1 bit, gray, a palette of up to 256 colors, or 8 bits from 16 AssociatedAlpha false Writes straight alpha premultiplied (ExtraSamples 1) ParallelCompression false Compresses strips and tiles on several threads; the file is the same Every pixel type is written at its own depth: gray and RGB at 8 and 16 bits with or without alpha, GrayF32, RgbF32, RgbaF32 and RgbaF16 as floats, Cmyk8 and Cmyk16 as separated, premultiplied types as associated alpha; packed types widen to 8 or 16 bits. The writer is deterministic and little-endian, except that re-saving a big-endian TIFF keeps its byte order, as it keeps the source's compression, predictor and tiling. A JPEG, WebP or CCITT source keeps its compression only while no operation has changed the pixels, so a lossy file is never compressed twice by accident. Raster.SaveAll writes several rasters as pages. // A page where every pixel is black or white saves as a 1-bit CCITT Group 4 fax. page.Save("fax.tif", new TiffWriterOptions { Compression = TiffCompression.CcittGroup4 }); Group 4 is the usual choice for scanned text; it takes 1-bit pages only, so threshold first or set Reduce. Files are checked against libtiff (no tiffinfo warnings, identical samples), ImageMagick and Pillow, and open in Windows' WIC except for BigTIFF and tiled gray-with-alpha or 16-bit CMYK, which WIC does not read from any writer. Format details and metadata The tags EXIF defines (ImageDescription, Make, Model, Orientation, Software, DateTime, Artist, Copyright and the rest) and the EXIF, GPS and Interoperability sub-IFDs become RasterMetadata.Exif, so converting a TIFF to JPEG keeps them. ICC profiles, XMP, IPTC (or the IPTC in Photoshop's resources) and the resolution are read too. TiffDetails describes each page: its TiffCompression, TiffPredictor, TiffPhotometric, TiffSampleFormat, TiffByteOrder and TiffLayout, strips or tiles, and TiffExtraSample kinds. Tags Egami does not map, such as GeoTIFF's and private ones, are kept as TiffTag values in OtherTags and written back by the TIFF writer, except tags that hold offsets to structures Egami cannot move. using Raster page = Raster.Load("scan.tif"); TiffDetails tiff = (TiffDetails)page.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"page {tiff.PageIndex}: {tiff.Photometric}, {tiff.BitsPerSample}-bit, {tiff.Compression}, {tiff.ByteOrder}, {tiff.Layout}"); Console.WriteLine(tiff.TileWidth is int tile ? $"tiles of {tile}" : $"{tiff.RowsPerStrip} rows a strip"); // Tags Egami does not map are kept as they were read. foreach (TiffTag tag in tiff.OtherTags) { Console.WriteLine($"tag {tag.Id}: {tag.Count} × {tag.Type}"); } Memory and damaged files Only the strips or tiles a read touches are decoded, a band at a time, and rows are converted from the band as they are asked for, so a region or a reduced decode of a large tiled file reads only the tiles it needs. Uncompressed strips in memory are read where they lie. A stream that cannot seek is read whole first, since a TIFF's index often comes last; the bytes count against SafetyLimits.MaxTotalBytes. Every IFD offset is checked against the file and against loops, and a strip or tile that decodes short is padded with zero samples and noted in one warning per page (RecoveryMode.Strict throws instead). Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Split a multi-page scan into PNGs using RasterList pages = Raster.LoadAll("scan.tif"); for (int i = 0; i < pages.Count; i++) { pages[i].Save($"page-{i + 1}.png"); } Each page keeps its own size and pixel type; see Reading. Combine pages into one TIFF using RasterList pages = Raster.LoadAll("scan.tif"); // Several rasters make a multi-page TIFF; one raster saves to any format. Raster.SaveAll(pages, "copy.tif"); Raster.SaveAll([pages[1]], "second.png");

articles/formats/vp8.html.title: VP8 video frames | Egami
articles/formats/vp8.html.summary: VP8 video frames Vp8StreamDecoder decodes VP8 video frame by frame and Vp8StreamEncoder encodes it; both work on frames, and Egami.Video uses them for WebM, Matroska and IVF files. Decoding Vp8StreamDecoder decodes VP8 video (RFC 6386) a frame at a time: key frames and inter frames, motion vectors, the last, golden and alternate references and hidden frames. Every frame equals libvpx's sample for sample, on libvpx's own test vectors and on clips made with its encoder, across the four versions, one to eight token partitions, segmentation and odd sizes. It reads frames, not files: WebM and IVF are read by Egami.Video, which uses this decoder, and frames from any other source decode the same way. // VP8 frames in stream order, here from an IVF file (Egami.Video reads WebM and IVF for you). using Vp8StreamDecoder decoder = new() { ConcealErrors = false }; YuvRaster<byte>? picture = null; foreach (byte[] packet in IvfFrames("clip.ivf")) { Vp8FrameInfo info = decoder.Decode(packet); if (!info.IsShown) { continue; // a hidden frame, typically an alternate reference: it only updates the references } picture ??= YuvRaster.Create(info.Width, info.Height, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Bt601Limited); decoder.CopyFrameTo(picture); // the picture is the caller's: change it or keep it shown++; } picture?.Dispose(); Decode takes the frames in stream order and returns a Vp8FrameInfo: whether the frame is a key frame and whether it is shown, the frame size from the last key frame, and the VP8 version. A hidden frame, typically an alternate reference, only updates the references and has no picture. CopyFrameTo copies a shown frame's planes into a 4:2:0 8-bit YuvRaster of the frame's size; the copy belongs to the caller, so it can be changed or kept while later frames decode. VP8 pictures are BT.601, limited range. Broken data Decoding starts at a key frame. By default a broken frame (data that runs out, a header that cannot be read) or an inter frame with no key frame before it throws CorruptDataException, and the decoder carries on from the next frame it is given; Reset drops the references so the next frame must be a key frame again. With ConcealErrors set nothing throws for broken data: the macroblocks a frame could not read are copied from the previous frame (mid-gray when there is none), a frame whose header cannot be read shows the previous frame again, and an inter frame with no key frame before it predicts from mid-gray. Vp8FrameInfo.IsConcealed says which frames were concealed. A key frame larger than the context's SafetyLimits throws LimitExceededException either way. Memory and threads The decoder keeps four frame buffers, which the references and the frame being decoded share as libvpx shares them, so a stream holds four frames however long it is. They come from the context's IPixelMemorySource and go back when the decoder is disposed. A frame's macroblock rows decode in a wavefront on up to EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads, as many as the frame's token partitions allow (one partition decodes on one thread, as in libvpx); the result does not depend on the thread count. Decoding takes at most 1.5 times libvpx's time at 720p and 1080p, on one thread and on all cores. Encoding Vp8StreamEncoder encodes 4:2:0 8-bit YuvRaster pictures of one size into VP8 frames. Key frames use the lossy WebP encoder; inter frames search the last, golden and alternate references for motion (whole pixels, then half and quarter pixels with the six-tap filter), weigh every VP8 vector mode (ZERO, NEAREST, NEAR, NEW and the four SPLIT layouts) against the intra modes by rate and distortion, and send only the probability updates that save bits. The frames decode in libvpx exactly as in Vp8StreamDecoder. // 4:2:0 pictures of one size, here decoded from a clip; Egami.Video writes WebM and IVF and plans the frames for you. using Vp8StreamEncoder encoder = new(pictures[0].Width, pictures[0].Height); for (int i = 0; i < pictures.Count; i++) { Vp8FramePlan plan = new() { KeyFrame = i % 30 == 0, // a key frame a second at 30 frames a second RefreshGolden = i % 10 == 0, // and a golden frame to fall back on every tenth Quality = 70, }; Vp8EncodedFrame frame = encoder.Encode(pictures[i], plan); packets.Add(frame.Data.ToArray()); // a WebM block or an IVF frame; frame.LumaPsnr says how close it came } Each call takes a Vp8FramePlan, so the caller decides what the stream looks like: KeyFrame starts a frame that decodes on its own; the first frame is always one. Quality (0 to 100, the scale of lossy WebP) or Quantizer (VP8's index, 0 to 127, for rate control) sets the frame's quantizer, and Effort (0 to 10, default 4) how hard the encoder searches: how far it looks for motion, how many candidates it codes in full, which split layouts it tries, where it tries the intra modes and the golden and alternate frames, and how many loop filter levels it tries. References (a Vp8References) says which references an inter frame may predict from, and RefreshLast, RefreshGolden, RefreshAlternate, CopyToGolden and CopyToAlternate (a Vp8ReferenceCopy) what becomes of them. GoldenSignBias and AlternateSignBias mark a reference that lies in the future, as a hidden alternate frame does. Show = false codes a hidden frame, typically an alternate reference built from frames to come, which only updates the references. RefreshEntropy = false keeps the frame's probability updates from the frames after it, so a lost frame does not spoil the next, and Partitions splits the coefficients into 2, 4 or 8 parts that decoders can read in parallel: what real-time streams use. FilterLevel fixes the loop filter level instead of letting the encoder choose. Encode returns a Vp8EncodedFrame with the frame's data, its size in bits, its quantizer and filter level, the squared error of the decoded frame against the picture (LumaPsnr from it), and how many macroblocks were intra or had nothing to code: what rate control needs to plan the next frame. At the default effort the frames are about as small as libvpx's at --good --cpu-used=1 for the same luma PSNR, within a few percent on natural pictures and up to about 10% larger on synthetic test patterns, and higher efforts come out smaller still. The encoder codes a frame's macroblock rows on the context's MaxParallelism threads, each row a little behind the one above it; its output does not depend on the thread count. It keeps the stream's four frame buffers from the context's memory source. Lossy WebP stills are not affected: they encode as before.

articles/formats/wbmp.html.title: WBMP | Egami
articles/formats/wbmp.html.summary: WBMP WBMP is the Wireless Application Protocol's one-bit bitmap: a type and a header byte, the width and height as multi-byte integers, then rows of bits, white where set. It reads and writes type 0 through the Egami.Formats.Extended package: register it with WithWbmp() or WithExtendedFormats() (Extended formats). Reads Type 0, with extension headers skipped Writes Type 0, a pixel white when its gray value is at least half Natural pixel type Gray8, black 0 and white 255 FormatInfo WbmpFormat.Info: name WBMP, extension .wbmp, MIME type image/vnd.wap.wbmp WBMP has no real signature: a file is taken for WBMP only when it starts with type 0, no extension headers and a size above zero, and only after every other registered format has declined it. Rows stream from the input.

articles/formats/webp.html.title: WebP | Egami
articles/formats/webp.html.summary: WebP Egami reads and writes WebP: lossless (VP8L), lossy (VP8) with or without alpha, and animated, written from RFC 9649 and RFC 6386 with no native code. WebpFormat.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default, so Raster.Load recognizes WebP from its first bytes and Save("x.webp") picks the writer. Writing // Lossy, the default for rasters not read from WebP: quality 0 to 100 and effort 0 to 6 on cwebp's scales. photo.Save("small.webp", new WebpWriterOptions { Quality = 80 }); // Lossless: every pixel exact, colors under full transparency included. Effort 0 (fastest) to 6 (smallest). photo.Save("duck.webp", new WebpWriterOptions { Lossless = true, Effort = 6 }); // A raster read from a WebP file keeps its kind when saved with the defaults. using Raster again = Raster.Load("duck.webp"); again.Save("copy.webp"); WebpWriterOptions follows libwebp's own knobs, so the same numbers give about the same files as cwebp: Option Default Does Lossless null true writes VP8L, false VP8; null keeps the kind of the WebP file the raster came from (WebpDetails.Lossless) and writes lossy otherwise Quality 75 Lossy quality, 0 to 100, cwebp's -q scale Effort 4 0 (fastest) to 6 (smallest), cwebp's -m, for both kinds AlphaQuality 100 Lossy files with transparency: 100 keeps alpha exact KeepTransparentColors true Colors under fully transparent pixels are kept (exactly in lossless files); false lets the encoder change them for smaller files SharpYuv false Lossy: a slower color conversion that keeps sharp colored edges NearLossless 100 Lossless: below 100 pixel values may move a little before coding MixedFrames false Animations: each frame is encoded both ways and the smaller kept FirstFrameOnly false Writes only the first frame, as a still Lossy files with transparency carry the alpha in an ALPH chunk: compressed losslessly with the filter that gives the smallest result (all four tried at effort 5 and 6), and with fewer levels when AlphaQuality is below 100, fully transparent and fully opaque pixels always kept exact. Lossless WebP holds sides up to 16,384 pixels and lossy up to 16,383; larger rasters throw before any work. Every pixel type can be saved: it is converted to 8-bit RGBA first. Reading Raster.Load gives Rgba8 when the file says it has alpha (the VP8X flag, the VP8L hint or an ALPH chunk) and Rgb8 otherwise. Lossless files decode to exactly libwebp's pixels. Lossy files decode to libwebp's YUV planes sample for sample, and to RGB within one level of libwebp's: chroma is brought to full resolution exactly as libwebp's default upsampler does, then converted with the BT.601 kernel of the planar YUV guide. YuvRaster.Load returns a lossy file's planes untouched (4:2:0, BT.601, limited range, chroma in the centre), with the alpha as a fourth plane. Every kind streams through RasterDecoder, with regions, reductions and incremental decode. The same VP8 decoder reads video frames too, inter frames included: see VP8 video frames. WebpReaderOptions adds two choices on top of the general reader options: using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.webp", options: new WebpReaderOptions { UseBackgroundColor = true, // animations: start from the ANIM background color instead of transparent FastUpsampling = true, // lossy files: repeat chroma samples instead of interpolating }); Format details and metadata ICC profiles, EXIF and XMP are read into RasterMetadata and written back unchanged. WebP has no resolution field, so the resolution is read from the EXIF block and written into it, in a minimal EXIF block when the raster has none. IPTC has no place in WebP and is not written. WebpDetails says what kind of file it was and keeps chunks Egami does not read, each a WebpChunk with its WebpChunkPosition; animation frames carry WebpFrameDetails. using Raster<Rgba8> image = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("duck.webp"); WebpDetails webp = (WebpDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"{(webp.Lossless ? "lossless" : "lossy")}, extended: {webp.Extended}, alpha: {webp.HasAlpha}"); // Chunks Egami does not read are kept and written back where they were. foreach (WebpChunk chunk in webp.OtherChunks) { Console.WriteLine($"{chunk.Type}: {chunk.Data.Length} bytes, {chunk.Position}"); } // An animation's frames say whether each was stored lossless. foreach (Frame<Rgba8> frame in image.Frames) { Console.WriteLine(frame.Metadata.FormatDetails is WebpFrameDetails { Lossless: true } ? "lossless frame" : "lossy frame"); } Animation Animated WebP reads and writes through the same frames as GIF and APNG. Reading composes every frame on a canvas exactly as libwebp's animation decoder does (its blending and key frames included), starting transparent unless WebpReaderOptions.UseBackgroundColor asks for the ANIM background color; ReaderOptions.Frames and streaming through RasterDecoder work as for GIF, holding one canvas whatever the frame count. Writing stores each frame's changed rectangle at even offsets, blended over the canvas when its new pixels are opaque and replacing them otherwise, with delays rounded to whole milliseconds and capped at 16,777,215. // A GIF (or APNG) becomes an animated WebP in one Load and one Save: frames, delays and loop count carry over. Each frame // stores only what changed; lossless frames are exact, MixedFrames keeps whichever kind is smaller per frame. using Raster gif = Raster.Load("pan.gif"); gif.Save("pan.webp", new WebpWriterOptions { Lossless = false, MixedFrames = true }); // Read back, every frame is the composed canvas, as with GIF and APNG. using Raster<Rgba8> webp = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("pan.webp"); foreach (Frame<Rgba8> frame in webp.Frames) { Console.WriteLine($"{frame.Metadata.Delay.TotalMilliseconds} ms, changed {frame.Metadata.Bounds}, blend {frame.Metadata.Blend}"); } Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Convert images to WebP for the web // Photos as lossy WebP, graphics with few colors as lossless: Probe reads only the header to tell them apart. foreach (string path in new[] { "duck.png", "egret.png" }) { using Raster image = Raster.Load(path); bool photo = image.Width * image.Height > 100_000; image.Save(Path.ChangeExtension(path, ".webp"), photo ? new WebpWriterOptions { Quality = 80, Effort = 4 } : new WebpWriterOptions { Lossless = true, Effort = 6 }); } Quality and Effort mean what cwebp's -q and -m mean; lossless keeps every pixel.

articles/formats/xbm.html.title: XBM | Egami
articles/formats/xbm.html.summary: XBM XBM is the X Window System's one-bit bitmap, written as C source: the width and height as #define lines, an optional hotspot, and the bits as an array, black where a bit is set. It reads and writes through the Egami.Formats.Extended package: register it with WithXbm() or WithExtendedFormats() (Extended formats).
