Reads X11 files of bytes and X10 files of 16-bit words, the leftmost pixel in the lowest bit; comments anywhere Writes X11, a pixel black when its gray value is below half, with the name and hotspot from XbmDetails Natural pixel type Gray8, black 0 and white 255 FormatInfo XbmFormat.Info: name XBM, extension .xbm, MIME type image/x-xbitmap XbmDetails keeps the name the C identifiers start with (cursor for cursor_width) and the hotspot. // What the header said that the pixels do not: PcxDetails, SgiDetails, SunRasterDetails, XbmDetails and XpmDetails. using Raster image = Raster.Load("arrow.xbm", context); if (image.Metadata.FormatDetails is XbmDetails xbm) { Console.WriteLine($"{xbm.Name}, hotspot {xbm.Hotspot}"); } // Writers take the name and hotspot back from the details. image.Metadata.FormatDetails = new XbmDetails { Name = "pointer", Hotspot = new Point(0, 0) }; image.Save("pointer.xbm"); The file is read whole; a probe reads only the #define lines. A file that ends early keeps the rows it has, with the warning Xbm.RowsMissing.

articles/formats/xpm.html.title: XPM | Egami
articles/formats/xpm.html.summary: XPM XPM, the X PixMap format, is C source holding an array of strings: the size and color count, a color table keyed by one or more characters, then one string of characters per row. It reads and writes version 3 through the Egami.Formats.Extended package: register it with WithXpm() or WithExtendedFormats() (Extended formats). Reads Up to 8 characters a pixel; of each color's keys the color (c), else gray (g, g4) or mono (m); None, #RGB to #RRRRGGGGBBBB and X11 color names, such as light blue and gray50 Writes Every color of the raster, as many characters a pixel as the count needs; a pixel below half alpha is None; the name and hotspot from XpmDetails Natural pixel type Rgba8 FormatInfo XpmFormat.Info: name XPM, extension .xpm, MIME type image/x-xpixmap A color name Egami does not know reads as black with the warning Xpm.ColorUnknown, and a pixel that names no color in the table reads as transparent with Xpm.PixelUnknown; a strict read throws for either. The writer needs every pixel before its color table, so the rows wait in memory until the last one. XpmDetails keeps the array's name, the hotspot and the characters a pixel.

articles/getting-started.html.title: Getting started | Egami
articles/getting-started.html.summary: Getting started Egami loads, edits and saves images in .NET 10, in fully managed code. This page takes you from install to a saved file. Install dotnet add package Egami One package holds everything: every format, operation and pixel type. It has no dependencies and works with trimming and Native AOT. Load, edit, save // Load in the pixel type that best fits the file (here Rgba8: this PNG stores alpha). using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.png"); Console.WriteLine($"{image.Width} × {image.Height}, {image.Layout.ChannelOrder}"); // Make a thumbnail that fits 200 × 200, keeping the aspect ratio, and save it as JPEG. image.Apply(ops => ops.Fit(200, 200)); image.Save("duck-small.jpg"); Raster.Load detects the format from the file's first bytes and returns a Raster in the pixel type that holds the file without loss. Apply runs a chain of operations in place. Save picks the writer from the file extension. Pixel types A raster is a grid of one pixel type, such as Rgba8 (8-bit red, green, blue and alpha) or Gray16. Ask for the type you want to work in, and rows come back as spans of it. // Decode straight into the type you want to work in. using Raster<Rgba8> rgba = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("duck.png"); // Pixels are a row at a time: each row is a Span<Rgba8>. for (int y = 0; y < rgba.Height; y++) { Span<Rgba8> row = rgba.Row(y); for (int x = 0; x < row.Length; x++) { row[x].A = 128; } } // Convert a whole raster; the result is a new raster you dispose too. using Raster<Gray8> gray = rgba.As<Gray8>(); gray.Save("duck-gray.png"); Type Channels Typical use Rgba8, Bgra8 8-bit color with alpha The default working type; interop with Windows and GPU buffers Rgb8, Bgr8 8-bit color Photos without alpha Argb8, Abgr8 8-bit color with alpha first Interop with alpha-first buffers Alpha8 Alpha only Masks and glyph coverage Gray8, Gray16, GrayAlpha8, GrayAlpha16 Gray Grayscale images and masks Rgba16, Rgb16 16-bit color, with or without alpha 16-bit PNG and PPM RgbaF32, RgbF32, GrayF32 32-bit float color or gray High-precision processing, PFM, depth maps RgbaF16 16-bit half-float color with alpha HDR and GPU textures Bgr565, Bgra4444, Rgb10A2 Packed 16 and 32-bit color Embedded displays, legacy textures, 10-bit displays Bgr555, Bgra5551 Packed 5-5-5 color, with a 1-bit alpha 16-bit BMP and TGA, GDI+ 16-bit bitmaps Cmyk8, Cmyk16 Cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink CMYK JPEG, TIFF and PSD PremulRgba8, PremulBgra8, PremulRgbaF32 Color premultiplied by alpha Compositing; Windows and GPU surfaces Values are sRGB-encoded with straight (not premultiplied) alpha, except in the Premul types, which store color multiplied by alpha; their conversions still take and return straight colors, and resize, blur, rotation and DrawImage run on them without multiplying first. raster.As<TPixel>() converts a whole raster; PixelConvert.Convert converts a span. Disposal // Every raster owns its pixel memory: dispose it when done, best with a using declaration. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.png"); // Copy, As and Derive return new rasters, which you dispose as well. Everything else works in place. using Raster copy = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Resize(100, 0)); photo.Apply(ops => ops.Grayscale()); Pixel memory comes from a pool, not the garbage-collected heap, so a raster you forget to dispose holds its memory until the next collection. Methods that return a new raster say so in their name: Copy, As and Derive. Sync and async // Every Load, Probe and Save has an async twin. Async reads the stream into a pooled buffer first, // then decodes (decoding is CPU work, so it is synchronous either way). await using FileStream stream = File.OpenRead("duck.png"); using Raster image = await Raster.LoadAsync(stream, cancellationToken: cancellationToken); await image.SaveAsync("duck-copy.png", cancellationToken: cancellationToken); Choosing a format // Save(path) picks the writer from the file extension... image.Save("duck-copy.qoi"); // ...or name the format, with its options. using FileStream output = File.Create("duck-q90.jpg"); image.Save(output, Egami.Formats.Jpeg.JpegFormat.Info, new Egami.Formats.Jpeg.JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90 }); // Loading never looks at the extension: the format is detected from the first bytes. RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("duck.png"); Console.WriteLine(info.Format.Name); // PNG Use Format Photos for the web JPEG (or PNG when you need alpha) Screenshots, diagrams, anything with sharp edges or alpha PNG Short animations GIF for reach, APNG for full color and alpha Fast lossless storage QOI Interchange with older tools BMP, TGA, PNM Next: the guides explain each area in order, starting with pixel types and formats, many ending with recipes for common tasks.

articles/guides/analysis.html.title: Comparing and measuring images | Egami
articles/guides/analysis.html.summary: Comparing and measuring images Calls that look at images rather than change them: comparison metrics and a picture of the differences, per-channel statistics and histograms, unique colors, opacity and gray checks, perceptual hashes for near-duplicates, and a pixel signature. They take any pixel type and match ImageMagick's numbers (Python's imagehash for the hashes). Types live in Egami.Analysis. Compare two images // Every cheap metric in one pass, per channel and overall, on the 0 to 1 scale; SSIM on request. CompareResult result = Raster.Compare(expected, actual, new CompareOptions { Ssim = true, Fuzz = 0.02f }); Console.WriteLine($"PSNR {result.Overall.Psnr:F1} dB, SSIM {result.Overall.Ssim:F4}, {result.DifferentPixels} pixels off by more than 2%"); bool sameLook = result.Overall.Psnr >= 40; Raster.Compare reads both images once and returns a CompareResult: for red, green, blue, alpha and overall, a ChannelDifference with the mean absolute error, mean squared error, RMSE, PSNR (+∞ for equal images) and the peak error, all on the 0 to 1 scale, so 8-bit and 16-bit results line up; and DifferentPixels, the pixels with a channel off by more than Fuzz (ImageMagick's AE). Overall averages the color channels, plus alpha when either image has it, as ImageMagick's "all" line. The images must be the same size but may have different pixel types: an Rgb8 and an Rgba8 copy of one picture are identical. Color profiles are not reconciled, so convert both with ConvertColor first when they differ. Alpha. Colors are premultiplied by alpha first (AlphaCompare.Premultiplied, the default), so two fully transparent pixels are equal whatever color is stored under them, which is what a viewer sees and what ImageMagick 7's metrics do. AlphaCompare.Straight compares the stored channels. SSIM. With Ssim = true, each channel also gets the structural similarity of Wang et al. (2004) with an 11 × 11 Gaussian window (σ 1.5) and DSSIM = (1 − SSIM) / 2. It costs about as much as four blurs. ImageMagick 7.1 computes SSIM on straight channels, so use AlphaCompare.Straight to reproduce its numbers on images with transparency. Region compares one rectangle and Frame another frame. Results do not depend on the thread count. Visual regression tests // A visual regression check: pass when the render is close to the stored baseline, else save a picture of what moved. CompareResult result = Raster.Compare(baseline, rendered, new CompareOptions { Fuzz = 0.05f }); if (result.DifferentPixels > 0 || result.Overall.Psnr < 45) { using Raster where = Raster.Difference(baseline, rendered, DifferenceStyle.Highlight, new DifferenceOptions { Fuzz = 0.05f }); where.Save("regression.png"); } A picture of the differences // ImageMagick compare's red-over-faded picture, and the plain per-channel difference turned up 8 times. using Raster highlight = Raster.Difference(a, b); using Raster gaps = Raster.Difference(a, b, DifferenceStyle.Absolute, new DifferenceOptions { Amplify = 8 }); highlight.Save("highlight.png"); gaps.Save("gaps.png"); DifferenceStyle.Highlight is ImageMagick compare's picture: pixels that differ in HighlightColor (#F1001E) and the rest in LowlightColor (white), with 20% of the first image, flattened onto white, showing through (LowlightOpacity). Set LowlightOpacity = 0 for a plain mask. DifferenceStyle.Absolute shows |a − b| per color channel, times Amplify. Statistics // Per-channel statistics on the 0 to 1 scale, as identify -verbose prints them. RasterStatistics stats = photo.Statistics(); Console.WriteLine($"red mean {stats.Red.Mean:F3} ± {stats.Red.StdDev:F3}, luma {stats.Luma.Min:F2} to {stats.Luma.Max:F2}"); bool dark = stats.Luma.Mean < 0.25; Statistics returns a RasterStatistics with a ChannelStatistics for red, green, blue, alpha and the Rec. 709 luma: the minimum, maximum, mean, sample standard deviation, skewness, excess kurtosis and entropy, as ImageMagick's identify -verbose reports them. Entropy is the Shannon entropy of the values at 16-bit precision divided by its largest possible value for the number of distinct values present, so it is 1 when every distinct value is equally common. Histograms // How the brightness is spread: 256 bins, and the levels below which 1% and 99% of the pixels lie. Histogram histogram = photo.Histogram(ColorChannel.Luminance); double shadows = histogram.Percentile(0.01), highlights = histogram.Percentile(0.99); long midtones = histogram.Counts.Skip(64).Take(128).Sum(); Histogram counts pixels in equal bins over 0 to 1 (256 by default, one per 8-bit value) for one channel or the luma. Percentile(p) and Median return the level of the bin where the running count reaches that fraction. Colors, opacity and gray // Unique colors, the palette of a small image, and quick checks before choosing an output format. long count = photo.CountColors(); IReadOnlyList<Rgba16>? palette = photo.GetColors(256); // null: more than 256 colors bool needsAlpha = !photo.IsOpaque(); bool grayscale = photo.IsGray(tolerance: 1 / 255f); CountColors counts the distinct stored values exactly, as ImageMagick's %k. Pixel types of up to 3 bytes use a 2 MB table; wider types keep a set of the colors seen, and its worst case (every pixel distinct, about 24 bytes a pixel) counts against MaxTotalBytes. GetColors(limit) returns the colors as Rgba16 when there are at most limit, and stops scanning once there are more. IsOpaque and IsGray stop at the first pixel that fails and answer at once for types without alpha and gray types; both check every frame unless given one. // A scan that is gray in all but name can be stored as one channel: a third of the size, no visible change. if (gray.IsGray(tolerance: 2 / 255f)) { using Raster<Gray8> oneChannel = gray.As<Gray8>(); oneChannel.Save("scan-gray.png"); } Near-duplicates // Find near-duplicate photos: hash each once, store the 64-bit keys, and call a pair a duplicate within about 10 bits. ulong a = PerceptualHash.Dct(original), b = PerceptualHash.Dct(copy), c = PerceptualHash.Dct(other); bool duplicate = PerceptualHash.Distance(a, b) <= 10; bool unrelated = PerceptualHash.Distance(a, c) > 10; string key = a.ToString("x16", System.Globalization.CultureInfo.InvariantCulture); Keep the 64-bit hashes in a database column; a lookup within a few bits finds recompressed and resized copies. PerceptualHash.Dct (pHash style) and PerceptualHash.Difference (dHash) reduce the first frame's brightness, flattened onto white, to 32 × 32 or 9 × 8 with a Lanczos filter and keep one bit per low frequency or neighbour pair. The same picture after JPEG recompression, resizing or a small brightness change stays within about 6 bits; unrelated photos average about 32 bits apart. The bits are in reading order, so ToString("x16") matches Python imagehash's hex string to within a few bits. Signatures // The same pixels give the same signature, whatever the file or pixel type: dedupe exact copies. using Raster<Rgba16> wide = png.As<Rgba16>(); bool same = png.Signature() == wide.Signature(); Signature is the SHA-256 of the size, the frame count and each frame's delay and pixels as 16-bit RGBA, as 64 hex digits: equal exactly when the pixels are, whatever the file or pixel type. It is not ImageMagick's %#, whose bytes vary between versions.

articles/guides/animation.html.title: Animation | Egami
articles/guides/animation.html.summary: Animation A raster holds one or more frames, all the size of the raster and the same pixel type. GIF and APNG files load with every frame composited to full size, as a browser shows them, so each frame is a complete picture you can edit on its own. using Raster<Rgba8> anim = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("pan.gif"); Console.WriteLine($"{anim.FrameCount} frames, plays {anim.Metadata.LoopCount} times (0 = forever)"); anim.Frames.RemoveAt(0); // frames are removed, anim.Frames.Add(anim.Frames[0]).Metadata.Delay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500); // copied in, anim.Frames.Move(anim.FrameCount - 1, 0); // and moved anim.Apply(ops => ops.Fit(64, 64), Ct); // operations run on every frame anim.Save("pan-small.gif"); // or .png for an APNG using Raster<Rgba8> still = anim.CopyFrame(0); // one frame as its own raster Frames.Add and Frames.Insert copy the frame you pass, from this raster or another of the same size. FrameMetadata.Delay is how long a frame shows; RasterMetadata.LoopCount is how many times the animation plays, 0 for forever. Every operation in a chain runs on every frame. DrawImage draws its image's first frame onto each one. Reading part of an animation // Only the first frame, decoding nothing after it: a fast preview of an animation. using Raster first = Raster.Load("pan.gif", options: new ReaderOptions { Frames = ..1 }); ReaderOptions.Frames takes a range: ..1 for the first frame, ^1.. for the last (which has to read every frame to find it), 2..5 for three in the middle. Raster.Probe counts the frames without decoding them. Writing animations Saving a raster with more than one frame as GIF or PNG writes an animation. The writers work out each frame's stored rectangle, disposal and blend from the pixels, so an edited animation stays small: only what changed between frames is stored. GIF holds at most 256 colors per frame and has on-or-off transparency; APNG keeps full color and partial alpha. The GIF and PNG and APNG pages have each writer's options. Frame by frame Raster<TPixel>.Frames is a FrameList<TPixel>: index, add, insert, move and remove frames. Each frame's FrameMetadata holds its delay, how it is disposed (FrameDisposal) and blended (FrameBlend) when written as APNG, and the area that changed. using Raster<Rgba8> clip = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("pan.gif"); FrameList<Rgba8> frames = clip.Frames; // Play the clip forward and then backward: append the middle frames in reverse. for (int i = frames.Count - 2; i > 0; i--) { Frame<Rgba8> copy = frames.Add(frames[i]); copy.Metadata.Delay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(80); copy.Metadata.Disposal = FrameDisposal.None; copy.Metadata.Blend = FrameBlend.Source; } frames.RemoveAt(0); clip.Save("pan-bounce.gif"); using Raster<Rgba8> clip = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("pan.gif"); TimeSpan length = TimeSpan.Zero; foreach (Frame<Rgba8> frame in clip.Frames) { FrameMetadata timing = frame.Metadata; length += timing.Delay; Console.WriteLine($"{timing.Delay.TotalMilliseconds} ms, {timing.Disposal}, {timing.Blend}, changed area {timing.Bounds}"); } Animation tools Six steps work on the whole animation rather than on each frame. They run in Apply, Derive and Transcode (which then decodes the whole animation first) and mix with per-frame steps, but not inside Within, since a scope is an area of every frame. Frames in memory are already full pictures of what is on screen, so Egami needs no Coalesce, and the writers find each frame's changed area themselves, so it needs no Optimize. // Shrink a screen recording: merge frames that barely change, drop frames no viewer shows, then resample to 25 fps. recording.Apply(ops => ops.MergeDuplicates(tolerance: 0.01f).DropZeroDelay().Retime(25), Ct); recording.Save("recording.gif"); MergeDuplicates(tolerance) removes each frame equal to the one before it and adds its delay to the frame that stays, as ImageMagick's -layers RemoveDups; what is on screen at every moment is unchanged. DropZeroDelay() removes frames with no delay, which viewers never show, as -layers RemoveZero (nothing, when every delay is zero). Retime(fps) samples fixed ticks, each showing the frame visible when it starts, as ffmpeg's fps filter, then merges neighbours showing the same frame. It never adds frames and keeps the total duration; a rate at or above the animation's own changes nothing. Browsers show GIF delays under 20 ms as 100 ms, so 50 fps is the useful ceiling for GIF. // Twice as fast, then backwards: a boomerang clip is the clip followed by its reverse. using Raster fast = clip.Derive(ops => ops.ChangeSpeed(2), Ct); using Raster backwards = fast.Derive(ops => ops.Reverse(), Ct); ChangeSpeed(factor) divides every delay, rounded to whole milliseconds; Reverse() plays the frames backwards with their delays. One animation on another // A looping sticker on an animated background: the sticker keeps its own speed and loops for the background's whole length. background.Apply(ops => ops.DrawAnimation(sticker, new Point(10, 10), new AnimationOverlayOptions { Repeat = 0, Opacity = 0.9f }), Ct); background.Save("with-sticker.gif"); DrawAnimation cuts both timelines at every frame boundary of either (boundaries closer than 10 ms snap together, since GIF counts in hundredths), and each piece shows the base frame and the overlay frame of that moment, drawn as DrawImage draws with AnimationOverlayOptions.Blend and Opacity, so an overlay at another speed keeps its speed. Repeat plays the overlay that many times (0 loops it for the base's whole length) from Start. A still base lasts as long as the overlay plays and takes its loop count. AnimationTiming.ByIndex pairs base frame i with overlay frame i instead, as ImageMagick's -layers Composite does. The number of frames the result will have is checked against MaxFrames and MaxTotalBytes before anything is drawn. Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Make an animated GIF from frames // Start from one picture and add frames: each Add copies the frame you pass. using Raster<Rgba8> animation = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("duck.png"); animation.Apply(ops => ops.Fit(120, 120)); using Raster<Rgba8> next = animation.Derive(ops => ops.HueRotate(120)); using Raster<Rgba8> last = animation.Derive(ops => ops.HueRotate(240)); animation.Frames.Add(next.Frames[0]); animation.Frames.Add(last.Frames[0]); foreach (Frame<Rgba8> frame in animation.Frames) { frame.Metadata.Delay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(400); } animation.Metadata.LoopCount = 0; // forever animation.Save("hues.gif"); Run it samples/Animation is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Animation writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/audio-filters.html.title: Audio filters | Egami
articles/guides/audio-filters.html.summary: Audio filters Egami.Video's audio filters change level, time and placement of decoded audio as it streams: gain and gain envelopes, fades and crossfades, mixing and panning, delay, padding, trimming and new timestamps, and tempo and speed changes. They live in Egami.Video.Audio.Filters and work on the AudioFrames that AudioReader and the decoders hand out (see Audio). The filter loop Every filter is an IAudioFilter with the same calls as Resampler: Send a frame, TryReceive the frames that are ready, Flush at the end of the input and Reset after a seek. Latency says how much input a filter holds back, such as the lookahead of Tempo. Frames of any sample format go in and are converted once to planar float; frames come out as SampleFormat.F32Planar with exact timestamps. The filters that keep the length work on the frame in place, so a steady stream allocates no sample memory. Times you give a filter, such as where a fade starts or a trim cuts, are the frames' own timestamps, not counted from the first sample, as in FFmpeg: audio that starts at 1.4 s fades at 1.4 s only if you say so. Put a Retime first to count from zero. AudioFilterChain runs several filters on one input in one pass and is itself a filter. It owns the filters added to it. Egami.Video's filters derive from AudioFilter, which takes the rate and channels from the first frame and refuses frames that differ; to put a filter of your own in a chain, implement IAudioFilter. // Fade in over 2 s, then turn down 3 dB: frames of any format go in, F32 planar frames come out. using AudioFilterChain chain = new AudioFilterChain(48000, ChannelLayout.Stereo) .Add(new AudioFade(FadeDirection.In, MediaTime.Zero, MediaTime.FromSeconds(2))) .Add(new Gain(-3)); foreach (AudioFrame frame in frames) { chain.Send(frame); while (chain.TryReceive(out AudioFrame? output)) { samples += output.SampleCount; // write it to an AudioWriter or encoder here output.Dispose(); } } chain.Flush(); Gain Gain changes the level by a fixed number of Decibels or a linear Factor. Changing either between frames moves to the new gain over 5 ms, so it does not click; unity gain passes samples through unchanged. Its Envelope, a GainEnvelope, changes the gain over time: a list of Keyframes on the frames' time line, values in decibels, each with an Easing (linear, ease in, ease out, ease in and out, or hold) to the next. The same Keyframe type animates layers in video editing. // Duck to -12 dB from 1 s to 2 s, easing down and back up over a quarter second. using Gain duck = new() { Envelope = new GainEnvelope( new Keyframe(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.75), 0, Easing.EaseInOut), new Keyframe(MediaTime.FromSeconds(1), -12), new Keyframe(MediaTime.FromSeconds(2), -12, Easing.EaseInOut), new Keyframe(MediaTime.FromSeconds(2.25), 0)), }; Fades and crossfades AudioFade fades in (FadeDirection.In, silent before its start) or out (FadeDirection.Out, silent after its end) over a stretch of the time line, and reaches full level or silence on the exact sample. FadeCurve has five shapes with the same gains as FFmpeg's afade curves: Linear (tri, the default), EqualPower (qsin), Logarithmic (log), Exponential (exp) and SCurve (hsin). // A 3 s clip: fade out over its last second along an S curve. using AudioFade fadeOut = new(FadeDirection.Out, MediaTime.FromSeconds(2), MediaTime.FromSeconds(1), FadeCurve.SCurve); Crossfade joins two streams with an overlap, like FFmpeg's acrossfade: the first stream's end fades out as the second's start fades in, EqualPower by default so unrelated material keeps its loudness. It has two inputs, so it takes Send(input, frame) and Complete(input) instead of the single-input calls. // Join two clips with a 1 s equal-power overlap: 3 s + 2 s - 1 s = 4 s of output. using Crossfade crossfade = new(MediaTime.FromSeconds(1)); foreach (AudioFrame frame in first) { crossfade.Send(0, frame); } crossfade.Complete(0); foreach (AudioFrame frame in second) { crossfade.Send(1, frame); } crossfade.Complete(1); int samples = 0; while (crossfade.TryReceive(out AudioFrame? output)) { samples += output.SampleCount; output.Dispose(); } Mixing and panning AudioMixer adds several inputs, each times its weight (SetWeight), and places each by its timestamps, so a clip that starts later comes in at its time. Inputs at another rate or with other channels are resampled and remixed on the way in. It does not divide by the number of inputs unless Normalize is set, so a voice over music keeps its level. MixDuration says when the mix ends: with the longest input (the default), the shortest, or input 0. Pan places a mono input in stereo with the constant-power law (-3 dB in each channel at the centre), turns one side of a stereo input down with Position or Balance, swaps the channels and flips their polarity. For any other channel matrix use ChannelMixer. // A mono voice at 44.1 kHz over stereo music at 48 kHz, the music at half level: the voice is panned a little left, // then resampled and placed by its timestamps on the way into the mixer. using Pan pan = new(-0.3); using AudioMixer mixer = new(48000, ChannelLayout.Stereo, inputs: 2); mixer.SetWeight(0, 0.5); foreach (AudioFrame frame in music) { mixer.Send(0, frame); } foreach (AudioFrame frame in voice) { pan.Send(frame); while (pan.TryReceive(out AudioFrame? panned)) { mixer.Send(1, panned); panned.Dispose(); } } mixer.Flush(); Timing Delay puts silence in front of each channel, by one delay or one per channel, and hands out the delayed tail on Flush. Pad adds silence at the end, a fixed amount or up to a length (Pad.ToLength). Trim keeps the part between two times, cut on the exact sample, and keeps its timestamps; Retime gives the stream new timestamps that start at a time and run on without gaps. // Keep 0.5 s to 2.5 s, start it at zero, delay the right channel 20 ms and add half a second of silence. using AudioFilterChain chain = new AudioFilterChain(48000, ChannelLayout.Stereo) .Add(new Trim(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5), MediaTime.FromSeconds(2.5))) .Add(new Retime()) .Add(new Delay([MediaTime.Zero, MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.02)])) .Add(new Pad(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5))); Tempo and speed Tempo plays faster or slower and keeps the pitch, from a quarter of the speed to four times, with WSOLA (waveform similarity overlap-add). TempoPreset.Music uses longer windows for steady rhythm and low notes, TempoPreset.Speech shorter ones for speech. The output lasts the input's length divided by the factor, to the sample. Speed changes speed and pitch together by resampling, like a tape played faster, and costs less. // A quarter faster with the pitch kept (3 s becomes 2.4 s); Speed would raise the pitch too, like a tape. using Tempo tempo = new(1.25, TempoPreset.Speech); using Speed speed = new(1.25);

articles/guides/audio.html.title: Audio | Egami
articles/guides/audio.html.summary: Audio Egami.Video decodes and encodes audio with the same send and receive loop as video. It is fully managed and ships: Codecs: FLAC (RFC 9639) decode and encode, integer and float PCM, Opus (RFC 6716) decode and encode, Apple Lossless (ALAC) decode and encode, Vorbis I decode, MPEG audio (MP3, MP2 and MP1) decode, Dolby AC-3 (ATSC A/52) decode and G.711 μ-law and A-law decode. Containers: WAV with RF64 and BW64 for files over 4 GB, Sony Wave64, native FLAC, Ogg, MP3, AIFF and AIFF-C, Apple CAF and raw AC-3 and E-AC-3, read and written; these codecs in Matroska, WebM and MP4 too. A resampler between any two rates, sample format conversion with dither, and channel layouts with downmix and upmix. Streaming filters for gain, fades and crossfades, mixing and panning, delay and trimming, and tempo and speed: see Audio filters. Other audio tracks, such as AAC and E-AC-3, are copied through untouched. Frames An AudioFrame holds SampleCount samples for every channel of its Layout, its SampleRate, its Format (a SampleFormat) and the Timestamp of its first sample. Frame memory comes from the context's memory source; dispose each frame. AsSpan<T>(channel) reads a channel of a planar frame, or every channel of an interleaved one; GetSpan<T> writes. // A frame holds samples for every channel, a sample rate, a layout, a sample format and the time of its first sample. using AudioFrame frame = new(SampleFormat.F32Planar, ChannelLayout.Stereo, 48000, 480, MediaTime.Zero); Span<float> left = frame.GetSpan<float>(channel: 0); for (int i = 0; i < left.Length; i++) { left[i] = MathF.Sin(2 * MathF.PI * 1000 * i / 48000); } Console.WriteLine($"{frame.SampleCount} samples, {frame.Duration.ToTimeSpan().TotalMilliseconds} ms, {frame.Layout}"); SampleFormat has unsigned 8-bit, signed 16, 32 and 64-bit, and 32 and 64-bit float samples, each interleaved or planar. Integer frames say how many low bits they use in ValidBits: 24-bit audio is S32 with 24 valid bits, so WAV and FLAC round trip exactly. Convert and CopyTo change the format, with triangular dither when AudioConvertOptions.Dither is set; SampleFormatExtensions gives the size and kind of each format. // Integer samples carry their valid bits: 24-bit audio is S32 with ValidBits 24, from -2^23 to 2^23 - 1. using AudioFrame pcm24 = tone.Convert(SampleFormat.S32Planar); Console.WriteLine($"{pcm24.Format}, {pcm24.Format.BytesPerSample()} bytes, planar: {pcm24.Format.IsPlanar()}"); // Down to interleaved 16-bit with triangular dither. using AudioFrame cd = tone.Convert(SampleFormat.S16, options: new AudioConvertOptions { Dither = true }); ReadOnlySpan<short> interleaved = cd.AsSpan<short>(); Reading audio AudioReader opens a file and decodes its first audio track (or the one AudioReaderOptions.TrackNumber names). Frames come as planar float by default; AudioReaderOptions asks for another SampleFormat (or null for the codec's own), another SampleRate (resampled, with a ResamplerQuality) and another Layout (mixed). Codec delay and the packets an MP4 edit list leaves out are trimmed, so the audio has exactly the samples the encoder was given; KeepAllSamples keeps them. Seek is sample exact. // The first audio track of any file, as planar float by default; seeking is sample exact. using AudioReader reader = AudioReader.Open("tone.flac"); Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.CodecId} {reader.SampleRate} Hz {reader.Layout}"); reader.Seek(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5)); double peak = 0; while (reader.TryRead(out AudioFrame? frame)) { using (frame) { foreach (float sample in frame.AsSpan<float>(channel: 0)) { peak = Math.Max(peak, Math.Abs(sample)); } } } // Or ask for one format, rate and layout, and let the reader convert. AudioReaderOptions options = new() { SampleFormat = SampleFormat.S16, SampleRate = 22050, Layout = ChannelLayout.Mono }; using AudioReader mono = AudioReader.Open("tone.wav", options); Writing audio AudioWriter encodes frames into a file or stream; the container comes from the extension. AudioWriterOptions sets the Codec (FLAC for .flac, Opus for Ogg and WebM, PCM elsewhere by default), the SampleRate and Layout to write (converted when the frames differ), the BitsPerSample and the compression Level. Frames may have any length and format. // FLAC for .flac files, PCM for .wav, .w64, .mka and .mp4 unless the options name a codec; FLAC levels run 0 to 8. using (AudioWriter writer = AudioWriter.Create("tone.flac", new AudioWriterOptions { Level = 8, BitsPerSample = 24 })) { writer.Write(tone); } // 16-bit WAV at 44.1 kHz: the writer resamples and converts. using (AudioWriter writer = AudioWriter.Create("tone.wav", new AudioWriterOptions { SampleRate = 44100, BitsPerSample = 16 })) { writer.Write(tone); } VideoWriterOptions.AudioCodec, with AudioSampleRate and AudioLayout, adds an audio track to a VideoWriter, which WriteAudio fills. // A video writer can encode an audio track next to the video. VideoWriterOptions options = new() { AudioCodec = FlacCodec.Instance, AudioSampleRate = 48000, AudioLayout = ChannelLayout.Stereo }; using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("clip.mkv", options)) { for (int i = 0; i < 30; i++) { writer.WriteFrame(picture); } writer.WriteAudio(tone); } MediaFile.Transcode copies a file like MediaFile.Remux but decodes its audio and encodes it again with another codec, keeping video and the other tracks as they are. // Keep every other track as it is and turn the audio into FLAC. MediaFile.Transcode("talk.mka", "talk-flac.mkv", audio: FlacCodec.Instance, audioLevel: 8); Channel layouts and mixing A ChannelLayout lists the Speakers its channels feed, in WAVE_FORMAT_EXTENSIBLE order, which every decoder hands out whatever order its codec stores. Presets run from Mono to Surround714; Unpositioned is for ambisonic or unknown channels, and ForChannelCount gives the layout WAV and FLAC assume when a file names none. // Channels come in WAVE_FORMAT_EXTENSIBLE order whatever the codec stored: 5.1 is FL, FR, FC, LFE, BL, BR. ChannelLayout layout = ChannelLayout.Surround51; int lfe = layout.IndexOf(Speakers.LowFrequency); Speakers fourth = layout.GetSpeaker(3); ChannelLayout custom = new(Speakers.FrontLeft | Speakers.FrontRight | Speakers.TopFrontLeft | Speakers.TopFrontRight); ChannelLayout ambisonic = ChannelLayout.Unpositioned(4); ChannelMixer mixes one layout into another with a matrix. The default one follows ITU-R BS.775: center and surrounds at -3 dB, LFE dropped unless given a level, and upmixing only routes the speakers both layouts share. A matrix of your own works too. // ITU-R BS.775 downmix: center and surrounds at -3 dB, LFE dropped unless given a level. ChannelMixer downmix = new(ChannelLayout.Surround51, ChannelLayout.Stereo); using AudioFrame stereo = downmix.Mix(surround); float centerInLeft = downmix[0, 2]; // Or a matrix of one's own, indexed [output, input]. ChannelMixer swap = new(ChannelLayout.Stereo, ChannelLayout.Stereo, new float[,] { { 0, 1 }, { 1, 0 } }); Resampling Resampler converts between any two rates with a polyphase windowed-sinc filter. ResamplerQuality.Good, the default, is flat within 0.1 dB to 0.9 of the lower Nyquist frequency and 100 dB down above it; Fast and Best (140 dB) trade speed for steepness. Time stays exact: the first output sample has the first input sample's time, and the output has the input's length at the new rate. // 48 kHz to 44.1 kHz with the default quality (100 dB stopband); frames go in and come out like a codec's. using Resampler resampler = new(48000, 44100, ChannelLayout.Stereo, ResamplerQuality.Good); resampler.Send(tone); resampler.Flush(); long samples = 0; while (resampler.TryReceive(out AudioFrame? frame)) { using (frame) { samples += frame.SampleCount; } } Codecs by hand An AudioCodec creates an IAudioDecoder for a track and an IAudioEncoder from AudioEncoderOptions; AudioCodecs finds them in a MediaContext. PcmCodec has little-endian, big-endian and float instances; FlacCodec encodes at levels 0 to 8 with the reference encoder's meaning, default 5, and sizes within 1 % of libFLAC's. Decoders take AudioDecoderOptions: Errors as a DecodeErrorMode, and VerifyChecksums for FLAC's frame CRCs and STREAMINFO MD5 (reported as Flac.BadCrc and Flac.Md5Mismatch). IAudioDecoder.SendLoss reports a lost packet. // An encoder takes frames of any length and format and cuts packets of its frame size. using IAudioEncoder encoder = FlacCodec.Instance.CreateEncoder( new AudioEncoderOptions { SampleRate = 48000, Layout = ChannelLayout.Stereo, BitsPerSample = 16, Level = 5 }, MediaContext.Default); encoder.Send(tone); encoder.Flush(); List<EncodedPacket> packets = []; while (encoder.TryReceive(out EncodedPacket? packet)) { packets.Add(packet); } // The same send and receive loop as video, for the track the encoder describes (or one a demuxer read). using IAudioDecoder decoder = AudioCodecs.CreateDecoder(encoder.Track); long decoded = 0; foreach (EncodedPacket packet in packets) { using (packet) { decoder.Send(packet); } while (decoder.TryReceive(out AudioFrame? frame)) { using (frame) { decoded += frame.SampleCount; } } } // FLAC decodes to its own integers: S16Planar up to 16 bits, S32Planar above. Opus OpusCodec decodes every Opus stream: SILK (speech), CELT (music) and hybrid frames at every bandwidth, mono, stereo and the multichannel mappings of RFC 7845 (families 0, 1 and 255). Frames come out as planar float at 48 kHz, Opus's own rate, with the channels in the canonical order; ask AudioReaderOptions.SampleRate for another rate. The pre-skip (the track's CodecDelay) and the end padding are trimmed. A lost packet, reported with IAudioDecoder.SendLoss or seen as a gap in the timestamps, is concealed, or recovered from the next packet's in-band FEC when it carries some. The decoder passes the RFC 8251 test vectors. // Opus decodes to planar float at 48 kHz; pre-skip and end padding are trimmed, so the length is the original's. using AudioReader reader = AudioReader.Open("talk.opus"); Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.CodecId}, {reader.Track.Channels} channels, pre-skip {reader.Track.CodecDelay?.ToTimeSpan()}"); long samples = 0; while (reader.TryRead(out AudioFrame? frame)) { using (frame) { samples += frame.SampleCount; } } OpusCodec encodes too, with the packets libopus 1.5.2 makes: see Encoding Opus. Vorbis VorbisCodec decodes Vorbis I streams from Ogg, WebM, Matroska and MP4: mono to 255 channels, every rate, both floor types and all three residue types (floor 0, which no current encoder writes, is untested). Frames come out as planar float at the stream's rate, with 3 to 8 channels remapped from Vorbis order to the canonical order. The end is trimmed to Ogg's last granule position, or to Matroska's DiscardPadding, and output matches libvorbis to within 2^-16 of full scale. A packet that cannot be decoded is reported as Vorbis.CorruptPacket and, with DecodeErrorMode.Conceal, left as silence; the decoder starts its overlap again at the next packet. // Vorbis decodes to planar float at the stream's rate, trimmed to the last granule position; here it becomes FLAC. using (AudioReader reader = AudioReader.Open("song.ogg")) { Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.CodecId}, {reader.SampleRate} Hz, {reader.Layout.ChannelCount} channels"); } MediaFile.Transcode("song.ogg", "song.flac", audio: FlacCodec.Instance); MP3 Mp3Codec decodes MPEG audio (ISO/IEC 11172-3 and 13818-3): Layers I, II and III of MPEG-1, MPEG-2 and MPEG-2.5, every rate from 8 to 48 kHz, mono, stereo, joint and dual channel, and free-format bit rates. Frames come out as planar float, one per MPEG frame, and pass the ISO/IEC 11172-4 compliance streams at full accuracy. The decoder is translated from minimp3 (CC0). Damaged frames are found by resynchronizing on three matching headers, and a frame whose CRC-16 does not match is reported as Mp3.BadCrc; with DecodeErrorMode.Conceal a bad frame becomes silence of its own length, so the timing stays right. Mp3Format reads .mp3, .mp2, .mp1 and .mpa files: ID3v2.2 to 2.4 tags (text frames as tags, pictures as attachments with the front cover named cover.*, CHAP frames as chapters), ID3v1 and APEv2 tags, and the Xing, Info or VBRI frame. The LAME tag's encoder delay and padding become the track's CodecDelay and the last packet's duration, so the audio is gapless: a LAME file decodes to exactly the samples the encoder was given. Seeks are exact: the first seek reads every frame header into an index, and the reader starts early enough to fill the bit reservoir. Set Mp3Format.FastSeek (registered with MediaContext.WithContainer) to seek by the Xing table instead, which reads nothing first but lands within about a percent. The writer stores an ID3v2.4 tag and the frames, with a Xing header and LAME tag on a seekable stream, so MP3 leaves Matroska or MP4 without a re-encode. // MP3 decodes to planar float; the LAME tag's delay and padding are trimmed, so the length is the source's exact length. MediaInfo info = MediaFile.Probe("podcast.mp3"); Console.WriteLine($"{info.Tags["TITLE"]}: {info.Duration?.ToTimeSpan()}, {info.Chapters.Count} chapters, cover {info.Attachments[0].Name}"); using (AudioReader reader = AudioReader.Open("podcast.mp3")) { reader.Seek(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.15)); // exact: the next sample is the one at 150 ms Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.CodecId}, {reader.SampleRate} Hz, {reader.Layout.ChannelCount} channels"); } // An MP3 track leaves Matroska without a re-encode; the .mp3 gets an ID3v2.4 tag and a Xing header. MediaFile.Remux("episode.mka", "episode.mp3"); Containers WavFormat.Instance reads WAV, RF64 and BW64 (PCM, float, WAVE_FORMAT_EXTENSIBLE with its channel mask, and streamed files whose sizes were never filled in), and writes WAV that turns into RF64 by itself past 4 GB. WavFormat.Wave64 is Sony Wave64. LIST/INFO and id3 tags become MediaInfo.Tags, and cue points become chapters. FlacFormat reads and writes native FLAC: Vorbis comments as tags, pictures as attachments (cover.* for the front cover), and a seek table every 10 seconds. // WAV, Wave64 and FLAC are containers like the others: remux PCM from WAV into Wave64 without decoding. MediaFile.Remux("tone.wav", "tone.w64"); MediaInfo info = MediaFile.Probe("tone.w64"); AudioTrackInfo track = (AudioTrackInfo)info.Tracks[0]; Console.WriteLine($"{info.FormatName}: {track.CodecId}, {track.SampleRate} Hz, {track.BitsPerSample} bits, {track.Layout}"); AiffFormat reads AIFF and AIFF-C (.aiff, .aif, .aifc): big-endian PCM of 8 to 32 bits, AIFF-C's little-endian sowt, in24, in32, fl32 and fl64 samples, and G.711 ulaw and alaw, which G711Codec decodes to 16-bit samples (it decodes G.711 in WAV, AVI and MOV too). Other AIFF-C compressions, such as ima4, MACE and QDesign, pass through undecoded with an X_AIFC/ codec id. NAME, AUTH, (c) and ANNO chunks and an ID3 chunk become tags, MARK markers become chapters, and a CHAN chunk gives the channel layout. The writer stores integer PCM as AIFF and float as AIFF-C, the title, artist, copyright and comment in text chunks, other tags and cover art in an ID3 chunk, and chapters as markers. AIFF's sizes come before the samples, so a non-seekable output is written through a temporary file; AIFF holds at most 4 GB. // AIFF holds big-endian PCM; remuxing turns WAV's samples around without decoding. Metadata goes into its text chunks. MediaFile.Remux("tone.wav", "tone.aiff"); using (AudioWriter writer = AudioWriter.Create("titled.aiff", new AudioWriterOptions { Metadata = new MediaMetadata { Tags = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["TITLE"] = "Tone" } }, })) { writer.Write(tone); } // AIFF-C's G.711 (ulaw, alaw), sowt and float samples decode like any other track. using AudioReader reader = AudioReader.Open("titled.aiff"); Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.CodecId}: {reader.Track.SampleRate} Hz, {MediaFile.Probe("titled.aiff").Tags["TITLE"]}"); CafFormat reads and writes Apple's Core Audio Format (.caf): PCM of 8 to 32 bits in either byte order, 32 and 64-bit float, G.711, ALAC, Opus, AAC, MP3, AC-3 and FLAC, with 64-bit chunk sizes and so no 4 GB limit. The packet table (pakt) cuts variable-size packets and gives the priming frames, which become the track's CodecDelay, and the padding at the end; the magic cookie (kuki) becomes the track's CodecPrivate. The info chunk becomes tags, markers and regions named by the strg chunk become chapters, and a chan chunk gives the layout. Other formats pass through with an X_CAF/ codec id. The writer streams PCM and G.711: on a non-seekable output the data chunk's size is -1, meaning "to the end of the file". For other codecs it puts the packet table after the samples, or before them through a temporary file when the output cannot seek, so the file can be read as a stream. Reading a file whose packet table follows the samples needs a seekable stream. // CAF has no 4 GB limit and streams PCM: on a pipe the data chunk simply runs to the end of the file. using (AudioWriter writer = AudioWriter.Create("tone.caf")) { writer.Write(tone); } // Opus, AAC, MP3, AC-3, FLAC and ALAC packets are cut by the packet table, which also gives the priming frames. using (AudioWriter writer = AudioWriter.Create("tone-opus.caf", new AudioWriterOptions { Codec = AudioCodecs.Opus })) { writer.Write(tone); } AudioTrackInfo opus = (AudioTrackInfo)MediaFile.Probe("tone-opus.caf").Tracks[0]; Console.WriteLine($"{opus.CodecId}: {opus.Duration}, {opus.CodecDelay} priming"); Ac3Format reads and writes raw Dolby AC-3 and E-AC-3 streams (.ac3, .eac3, .ec3). Each packet is one AC-3 sync frame, or one E-AC-3 independent frame with the dependent substreams that follow it, as MP4 and Matroska store them; the track's rate, channels and layout come from the first frame's header (CodecIds.Ac3, CodecIds.EAc3). Bytes between frames are skipped, and a seek builds a frame index in one pass. Both pass through MP4 (ac-3 and ec-3 sample entries; the writer builds the dac3 or dec3 box from the first frame), Matroska and CAF unchanged. // A raw .ac3 or .eac3 stream: each packet is one sync frame (E-AC-3: an independent frame and its substreams). MediaInfo info = MediaFile.Probe("surround.ac3"); AudioTrackInfo track = (AudioTrackInfo)info.Tracks[0]; Console.WriteLine($"{track.CodecId}: {track.SampleRate} Hz, {track.Channels} channels, {info.Duration}"); // Into MP4 (an ac-3 sample entry with its dac3 box), Matroska or CAF without decoding. MediaFile.Remux("surround.ac3", "surround.mp4"); Ac3Codec decodes AC-3 (ATSC A/52) in every channel mode, 1/0 to 3/2 and dual mono, with or without the LFE, at 32, 44.1 and 48 kHz and 32 to 640 kbit/s, from raw .ac3 files and from AC-3 tracks in MP4, Matroska, AVI and CAF. Frames are 1536 samples of planar float in Egami.Video's channel order. Both frame CRCs are checked unless VerifyChecksums is off; a damaged frame is reported as Ac3.BadCrc or Ac3.CorruptFrame and handled as Errors says, and Conceal puts silence of its length in its place. The stream's dynamic range control is applied in full, as the standard asks; Ac3DecoderOptions.DynamicRange scales it (0 turns it off) and Ac3DecoderOptions.Downmix mixes to a smaller layout with the stream's own center and surround mix levels, scaled so the mix cannot clip. An AudioReader whose Layout is mono or stereo uses that downmix on wider AC-3 tracks too. Dialogue normalization is left to the player. E-AC-3 passes through undecoded. // AC-3 decodes to planar float in Egami.Video's order: 5.1 is front left, front right, center, LFE, side left, side right. using (AudioReader reader = AudioReader.Open("surround.ac3")) { Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Layout}, {reader.SampleRate} Hz"); } // The full dynamic range (no DRC gain words), mixed down to stereo with the stream's center and surround levels. AudioReaderOptions stereo = new() { Decoder = new AudioDecoderOptions { Ac3 = new Ac3DecoderOptions { DynamicRange = 0, Downmix = ChannelLayout.Stereo } }, }; using (AudioReader reader = AudioReader.Open("surround.ac3", stereo)) { Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Layout.ChannelCount} channels"); } // Decoded and encoded again as FLAC, all six channels. MediaFile.Transcode("surround.ac3", "surround.flac", FlacCodec.Instance); AlacCodec decodes and encodes Apple Lossless (ALAC) at 16, 20, 24 and 32 bits with 1 to 8 channels. It is translated from Apple's reference codec, so its packets are the bytes Apple's encoder makes: level 1, the default, searches the stereo matrix and predictor order, and level 0 is Apple's fast mode. Each packet holds 4096 samples unless FrameSize says otherwise, and the track's CodecPrivate is the 24-byte ALACSpecificConfig. ALAC goes in MP4 and M4A (an alac box), QuickTime MOV (read from its wave atom), Matroska (A_ALAC) and CAF. ALAC fixes the speakers by the channel count (for example center, left, right and back center for four channels), so a frame with the same number of channels is stored as it is and read back with ALAC's layout. Extracting an ALAC track with the CLI makes an .m4a file. // Apple Lossless in an .m4a file (also .mov, .mka and .caf): level 1 (the default) or 0, Apple's fast mode. using (AudioWriter writer = AudioWriter.Create("tone.m4a", new AudioWriterOptions { Codec = AlacCodec.Instance, BitsPerSample = 24 })) { writer.Write(tone); } // Decoding gives the 24-bit samples back exactly. using AudioReader reader = AudioReader.Open("tone.m4a", new AudioReaderOptions { SampleFormat = null }); Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.CodecId}, {reader.Track.BitsPerSample} bits"); OggFormat reads and writes Ogg (.ogg, .opus, .oga) with Opus, Vorbis and FLAC. Timestamps come from the granule positions, seeking from an index built in one pass over the page headers, and pages with a bad CRC are skipped with an ogg-crc warning. A chained file (one stream after another) reads as one track when the settings stay the same, each link's TITLE a chapter; a link that changes them ends the track with an ogg-chained-stream warning. // An Opus track moves from WebM to an .opus file and back without decoding; the tags travel in OpusTags. MediaFile.Remux("music.webm", "music.opus"); MediaInfo info = MediaFile.Probe("music.opus"); Console.WriteLine($"{info.FormatName}: {info.Tracks[0].CodecId}, {info.Duration?.ToTimeSpan()}, {info.Chapters.Count} chapters");

articles/guides/barcode-reading.html.title: Reading barcodes | Egami
articles/guides/barcode-reading.html.summary: Reading barcodes Egami.Barcodes reads every symbology it writes: QR Code, Data Matrix (DMRE too), PDF417 (compact too), Aztec Code (runes too), Code 128 and GS1-128, Code 39, ITF and ITF-14, EAN-13, EAN-8, UPC-A and UPC-E with their add-ons. It reads rendered barcodes, scans and photos: turned, in perspective, blurred, noisy, light on dark or mirrored, several in one image. Reading an image ReadBarcodes, an extension method in BarcodeReader, finds every barcode in a raster of any pixel type and returns a BarcodeResult for each: its Format, its Text, the Bytes it holds, the Corners it was found at, its Eci, its GS1 element strings in Gs1, and how many codewords error correction restored. ReadBarcode returns the first one, or null. // Every barcode in the image, of any format. foreach (BarcodeResult result in scan.ReadBarcodes()) { Console.WriteLine($"{result.Format}: {result.Text} at {result.Corners[0]}"); } Text is decoded with the symbol's ECI; without one, as ISO 8859-1, or as UTF-8 or Shift JIS when the bytes clearly are. GS1 data comes back in its human-readable form, such as (01)09501101530003(10)AB12. For EAN and UPC, Text holds the main digits and AddOn the digits of an EAN-2 or EAN-5 add-on, or null. BarcodeReaderOptions narrows or widens the search. Formats names the symbologies to look for, as BarcodeFormat flags (BarcodeFormat.Qr | BarcodeFormat.DataMatrix, or Linear, Matrix and All); fewer read faster. Effort, 0 to 10, decides how many binarizations, scan lines and rotations are tried, never what counts as a valid read; from effort 5 light symbols on a dark background are tried too (TryInverted). Region limits the search to part of the image. PureBarcode reads an image that holds one upright symbol and its quiet zone, such as a rendered barcode, without searching. // Only the formats you expect, searched harder; a rendered barcode can skip the search. BarcodeResult? result = label.ReadBarcode(new BarcodeReaderOptions { Formats = BarcodeFormat.DataMatrix | BarcodeFormat.Qr, Effort = 7, }); if (result?.Gs1 is { } elements) { foreach (Gs1ElementString element in elements) { Console.WriteLine($"{element.Title}: {element.Value}"); } } BarcodeResult? rendered = label.ReadBarcode(new BarcodeReaderOptions { PureBarcode = true }); Camera frames A camera frame's 8-bit luminance (the Y plane of a YUV frame) reads in place, without a copy: BarcodeReader.ReadBarcodes and ReadBarcode take the bytes with the width, height and stride. The buffer is only read, and only during the call. // A camera frame's Y plane (8-bit luminance, rows padded to the stride), read in place. BarcodeResult? code = BarcodeReader.ReadBarcode(yPlane, width, height, stride); The Y plane is read where it is, so a frame from a camera API needs no conversion or copy. How each symbology is found Linear barcodes are found along scan lines: rows, columns from effort 3 and diagonals from effort 7, each read in both directions with its edges placed between pixels, so low-resolution and blurred photos read. From effort 5 rows are also read through the local threshold, which keeps bars under glare apart. A linear barcode counts once two scan lines agree on it. ITF, whose check is weakest, is read from 4 digits on. QR Codes are found by their three finder patterns, at any rotation and in perspective; from version 2 the alignment pattern corrects the perspective (each one near the expected place is tried, nearest first), and a mirrored symbol reads too. Data Matrix symbols are found by their L-shaped finder, square and rectangular (DMRE too), at any rotation and in perspective, on a label lighter than its background or not; the clock tracks count the modules. PDF417 symbols are found by their start and stop patterns at any rotation and in perspective; a compact symbol, which has no stop pattern, is read from its start pattern on, and one cut off before its start pattern from its stop pattern back. Rows and columns that cannot be read are filled in by error correction. Aztec Codes are found by their bullseye at any rotation and in perspective, compact, full-range and runes; on larger full-range symbols the reference grid places the modules out to the edge. Many symbols, inverted and mirrored Every symbol in the image comes back once, in reading order: top to bottom, then left to right. A linear read inside a 2D symbol is dropped as part of it. Inverted tells which symbols were light on dark, Mirrored which were read from behind or flipped. Large images are searched on several threads, up to the MaxParallelism of the options' Context; the results are the same at any thread count. // All symbols on a page, top to bottom and left to right, each once; at most four threads. IReadOnlyList<BarcodeResult> parcels = page.ReadBarcodes(new BarcodeReaderOptions { Context = EgamiContext.Default with { MaxParallelism = 4 }, }); foreach (BarcodeResult parcel in parcels) { Console.WriteLine($"{parcel.Text} (inverted: {parcel.Inverted}, mirrored: {parcel.Mirrored})"); } GS1 data, ECI and add-ons GS1 symbols (GS1-128, GS1 QR Code, GS1 Data Matrix) come back with their element strings in Gs1, each with its AI, title and value, and Text in the human-readable form with the AIs in parentheses. A symbol that names an Extended Channel Interpretation has it in Eci, and its text is decoded with that character set. Bytes holds what the symbol carries before any character set is applied. // A GS1-128 label: the element strings by AI, and the text with the AIs in parentheses. BarcodeResult? code = label.ReadBarcode(new BarcodeReaderOptions { Formats = BarcodeFormat.Code128 }); string? expiry = code?.Gs1?.FirstOrDefault(e => e.Ai == "17")?.Value; // "261231" string? batch = code?.Gs1?.FirstOrDefault(e => e.Ai == "10")?.Value; // "AB12" What reads well Two pixels or more per module. Linear barcodes read down to about one pixel per narrow bar, as their edges are placed between pixels. The quiet zone the symbology asks for, or most of it: 10 modules beside Code 128 and Code 39, 4 around a QR code. Contrast between bars and background; uneven light is fine, as each part of the image gets its own threshold. A sharp image. Blur that merges neighbouring modules cannot be undone, although error correction fills in damaged parts of 2D symbols. Speed The reader allocates per call only and can run on many threads at once. On one thread it reads the ZXing test images in about the time zxing-cpp takes (0.9 times over 817 images, each read for its own symbology). These settle how long a call takes: Formats: only the symbologies you expect. Each detector skipped saves its time. Effort: 5 is the default. Lower efforts try fewer scan lines and rotations and no inverted image; higher ones try more. Region: only the part of the image where the symbol is. PureBarcode for a rendered symbol with nothing else in the image: it reads without searching. Images of a quarter of a megapixel or more are searched on several threads, up to the Context's MaxParallelism.

articles/guides/barcodes.html.title: Barcodes | Egami
articles/guides/barcodes.html.summary: Barcodes Egami.Barcodes writes and reads barcodes. It draws them through Egami.Drawing's canvas, so a barcode stays vector on a PDF page or in SVG output, and reads them from rasters. It is fully managed. It writes and reads QR Code, Data Matrix, PDF417 and Aztec Code, and the linear Code 128 (with GS1-128), Code 39, ITF and ITF-14, EAN-13, EAN-8, UPC-A and UPC-E. Each has its own factory on Barcode with typed options; Barcode.Create takes a format chosen at run time with the default options. // Labels from a table that stores each barcode's format with its data. (BarcodeFormat Format, string Data)[] rows = [ (BarcodeFormat.Ean13, "590123412345"), (BarcodeFormat.Code128, "SHIP-0042"), (BarcodeFormat.Qr, "https://inexin.github.io/Egami/"), ]; foreach ((BarcodeFormat format, string data) in rows) { Barcode barcode = Barcode.Create(format, data); using Raster<Gray8> image = barcode.ToRaster(pixelsPerModule: 3); } QR Code Barcode.Qr writes a QR Code from text, bytes or GS1 element strings. Text is split into numeric, alphanumeric, byte and Kanji segments that give the fewest bits. Text in ISO 8859-1 is written as it is, text that Shift JIS holds is written in Shift JIS (its kanji in Kanji mode), and anything else as UTF-8 with an ECI that tells readers so. By default the symbol is the smallest that holds the data at level M, and the level is then raised to Q or H while the symbol stays the same size, so spare room goes to error correction. QrOptions fixes the level, the version (1 to 40) or the mask instead. // Level M, raised to Q or H when that fits in the same size; segments chosen for the fewest bits. Barcode link = Barcode.Qr("https://inexin.github.io/Egami/"); // A fixed size and level, for a layout that must not change. Barcode fixedSize = Barcode.Qr("ORDER-1180042", new QrOptions { Version = 3, ErrorCorrection = QrErrorCorrection.H }); // Bytes as they are, and GS1 element strings with FNC1. Barcode bytes = Barcode.Qr([0x45, 0x67, 0x61, 0x6D, 0x69]); Barcode gs1 = Barcode.Qr(Gs1.Parse("(01)09501101530003(10)AB12")); using Raster<Gray8> image = link.ToRaster(pixelsPerModule: 4); Data Matrix Barcode.DataMatrix writes Data Matrix ECC 200 from text, bytes or GS1 element strings. The six encodation modes (ASCII, C40, Text, X12, EDIFACT and Base 256) are switched for the fewest codewords, and the symbol is the smallest that holds them. Text in ISO 8859-1 is written as it is, anything else as UTF-8 with an ECI. Symbols are square by default. DataMatrixOptions.Shape allows rectangular symbols, or the smallest of either, and AllowDmre adds the rectangular sizes of ISO/IEC 21471 (DMRE), which older readers may not read. // Square by default; the encodation modes are switched for the fewest codewords. Barcode part = Barcode.DataMatrix("PN 4711-0815 / LOT 2026-10"); // A narrow label: rectangular sizes, the DMRE ones too. Barcode narrow = Barcode.DataMatrix("PN 4711-0815 / LOT 2026-10", new DataMatrixOptions { Shape = DataMatrixShape.Rectangle, AllowDmre = true, }); // GS1 Data Matrix, as on medicine packs. Barcode pack = Barcode.DataMatrix(Gs1.Parse("(01)09501101530003(17)261231(10)AB12(21)XYZ")); PDF417 Barcode.Pdf417 writes PDF417 from text or bytes, as on boarding passes and driving licences. Text, numeric and byte compaction are chosen run by run. The error correction level follows the standard's recommended minimum for the amount of data, and the columns are picked so the symbol is about three times as wide as tall; Pdf417Options sets either, or asks for compact PDF417, which leaves out the right row indicators for a narrower symbol. Rows are 3 modules tall. // About three times as wide as tall, error level from the standard's table for the amount of data. Barcode ticket = Barcode.Pdf417("PASSENGER DOE/JANE FLIGHT EG1234 SEAT 12A GATE B17"); // Six data columns and error level 5, or the compact form for a narrow space. Barcode wide = Barcode.Pdf417("PASSENGER DOE/JANE", new Pdf417Options { Columns = 6, ErrorLevel = 5 }); Barcode compact = Barcode.Pdf417("PASSENGER DOE/JANE", new Pdf417Options { Compact = true }); Aztec Code Barcode.Aztec writes Aztec Code from text or bytes, as on rail and airline tickets. The text is written in the Upper, Lower, Mixed, Punctuation and Digit modes and Binary Shift, switched for the fewest bits. The symbol is the smallest compact (up to 4 layers) or full-range (up to 32 layers) one that leaves at least 23 % of its codewords, plus 3, for error correction; AztecOptions raises that share or fixes the form and layers. Aztec Code finds itself by its bullseye, so it needs no quiet zone. Barcode.AztecRune makes an Aztec Rune, an 11 x 11 core that holds one value from 0 to 255. // The smallest compact or full-range symbol with at least 23 % error correction; no quiet zone needed. Barcode ticket = Barcode.Aztec("EG1234 BER-MUC 2026-10-19 SEAT 12A DOE/JANE"); // More error correction for a ticket that gets folded, or a fixed compact size. Barcode robust = Barcode.Aztec("EG1234 BER-MUC", new AztecOptions { ErrorCorrectionPercent = 50 }); Barcode compact = Barcode.Aztec("EG1234", new AztecOptions { Compact = true, Layers = 2 }); // A rune: one value from 0 to 255 in an 11 x 11 core. Barcode rune = Barcode.AztecRune(42); Linear barcodes Code 128 Barcode.Code128 writes any text of characters 0 to 255. It picks the code sets A, B and C, and the changes and shifts between them, that give the shortest symbol, so runs of digits go in pairs. Code128Options.Height sets the bar height in modules when the barcode is drawn at a module size; drawn into a rectangle, the bars fill it. // The shortest mix of code sets A, B and C; the digits go in pairs. Barcode code = Barcode.Code128("ORDER-1180042", new Code128Options { Height = 40 }); using Raster<Gray8> image = code.ToRaster(pixelsPerModule: 2); GS1-128 and GS1 element strings Gs1.Parse reads GS1 element strings written with each Application Identifier in parentheses, such as (01)09501101530003(17)261231, and checks each one against the GS1 General Specifications: the AI is defined, the characters and lengths fit it, and check digits, dates and times are right. A bad field throws a FormatException that says which AI is wrong and how; Gs1.TryParse returns false instead. Each Gs1ElementString has its Ai, Value and GS1's Title for the AI. A parenthesis inside a value is written \(. Barcode.Gs1Code128 encodes element strings as Code 128 with FNC1 first, and an FNC1 after each field whose AI has no predefined length, unless it is the last. // Each element string is checked: the AI, the length, the GTIN's check digit, the date. IReadOnlyList<Gs1ElementString> elements = Gs1.Parse("(01)09501101530003(17)261231(10)AB12"); Barcode label = Barcode.Gs1Code128(elements); // Mistakes say what is wrong. if (!Gs1.TryParse("(01)09501101530004", out _)) { Console.WriteLine("(01) has a wrong check digit"); } The checks come from the GS1 Barcode Syntax Dictionary. Checks that need outside lists (country and currency codes, company prefixes) and the rules about which AIs go together are not applied. Code 39 Barcode.Code39 writes digits, capital letters, space and - . $ / + %. Text with other ASCII characters, such as lowercase letters, is written as Full ASCII, which spells them as pairs; Code39Options.FullAscii forces it on or off. A reader has to be set to Full ASCII to read such text back. Code39Options.CheckDigit adds the mod 43 check character, and WideRatio makes wide elements 2 (the default) or 3 times as wide as narrow ones. // Capitals, digits and a few symbols; lowercase switches to Full ASCII on its own. Barcode part = Barcode.Code39("PART-0042", new Code39Options { CheckDigit = true }); Console.WriteLine(part.HumanReadableText); // PART-0042 and its mod 43 check character ITF and ITF-14 Barcode.Itf writes Interleaved 2 of 5 from digits; an odd number of digits gets a leading zero. Barcode.Itf14 writes a GTIN-14 for cartons: 13 digits get their check digit added, 14 are checked, and bearer bars 5 modules thick frame the symbol and its quiet zone. ItfOptions sets the wide ratio (3 by default), the bearer bars and the height. // A GTIN-14 on a carton: the check digit is added, and bearer bars frame the symbol. Barcode carton = Barcode.Itf14("1540014128876"); using Raster<Gray8> image = carton.ToRaster(pixelsPerModule: 3); // Plain Interleaved 2 of 5 with a 2:1 wide ratio and no bearers. Barcode itf = Barcode.Itf("0123456789", new ItfOptions { WideRatio = 2 }); EAN and UPC Barcode.Ean13, Barcode.Ean8, Barcode.UpcA and Barcode.UpcE write retail barcodes. The check digit is added when it is left out and checked when it is given; a wrong one throws. Barcode.UpcE also takes a UPC-A number and writes its zero-suppressed form, or throws when the number has too few zeros. EanUpcOptions.AddOn adds a 2-digit or 5-digit add-on to the right, such as a magazine's issue or a book's price. With a font, the digits are drawn as on a product: EAN-13's first digit left of the symbol and the others between the guard bars, which reach down into the text line, and an add-on's digits above its bars. Bar heights default to the standards' nominal heights. // A book: the ISBN as EAN-13, its check digit added, and the price as an EAN-5 add-on. Barcode book = Barcode.Ean13("978020137962", new EanUpcOptions { AddOn = "52495" }); // Fitted into a rectangle, with the digits between the guard bars. using Raster<Rgba8> label = Raster.Create(400, 200, Rgba8.White); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = label.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawBarcode(book, new RectF(10, 10, 380, 180), Rgba8.Black, new BarcodeDrawOptions { Font = font }); } // A UPC-A number written in its short UPC-E form. Barcode small = Barcode.UpcE("042100005264"); Reading barcodes raster.ReadBarcodes() finds every barcode in an image and raster.ReadBarcode() the first. Reading barcodes covers the options, photos, camera frames, GS1 data and speed. // Every barcode in the image, of any format. foreach (BarcodeResult result in scan.ReadBarcodes()) { Console.WriteLine($"{result.Format}: {result.Text} at {result.Corners[0]}"); } Drawing on a canvas DrawBarcode, an extension method in CanvasBarcodeExtensions, draws on any canvas: a raster, a PDF or SVG page, a recording. The whole symbol is one filled path, a rectangle for each run of dark modules in a row, so a QR code is a few hundred rectangles rather than one per module, and neighbouring rectangles leave no seams. Given a rectangle, the barcode is fitted into it and centered, with its quiet zone kept clear inside it. 2D symbols keep square modules; linear bars fill the rectangle's height. On a raster canvas with no rotation or skew, the module size snaps to whole pixels, the largest that still fits, so every edge is sharp. using Raster<Rgba8> label = Raster.Create(300, 200, Rgba8.White); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = label.CreateCanvas()) { // Fitted into the rectangle and centered, quiet zone inside it; on a raster, modules snap to whole pixels. canvas.DrawBarcode(qr, new RectF(20, 20, 160, 160), Rgba8.Black); } Given a point and a module size instead, the barcode is drawn at that size, the X dimension of the standards, with the top-left corner of its quiet zone at the point. Linear bars are then BarcodeModules.Height modules tall. BarcodeDrawOptions changes how it is drawn: QuietZone keeps the quiet zone clear; it is on by default. Turn it off only when the space around the symbol is blank anyway. BarWidthReduction draws each dark bar or module narrower by that much, half from each side, to make up for ink spreading on a printer. It changes drawing only, never the modules. Font draws the human-readable text under the bars, centered, in that font and size. Without a font no text is drawn; Egami.Barcodes ships no font of its own. // A 0.33 mm module (the X dimension) in points, with the text under the bars and 0.05 mm taken off each bar // for ink spread. The quiet zone's top-left corner goes at (36, 36). float module = 0.33f / 25.4f * 72; page.DrawBarcode(code, new Vector2(36, 36), module, Rgba8.Black, new BarcodeDrawOptions { Font = font, BarWidthReduction = 0.05f / 25.4f * 72, }); Paths and rasters ToPath returns the symbol as one path, with the quiet zone's top-left corner at the origin, ready for Path.ToSvg or your own drawing. It holds no text. // One path, a rectangle per run of dark modules; the quiet zone's corner is at the origin. Path path = qr.ToPath(moduleSize: 4); string svg = path.ToSvg(); ToRaster renders black on white into a Raster<Gray8>, each module a square of whole pixels, with the quiet zone and, with a font, the text. // Black on white, 4 pixels a module, quiet zone included. using Raster<Gray8> image = qr.ToRaster(pixelsPerModule: 4); Barcodes from modules A Barcode is one symbol: its BarcodeFormat, its Modules, the QuietZone its standard asks for in modules (4 for QR, 1 for Data Matrix, 2 for PDF417, none for Aztec; at each end of a linear symbol, 10 for Code 128, Code 39 and ITF, 11 for EAN-13, 7 for EAN-8 and 9 for UPC) and the HumanReadableText printed under a linear symbol. Barcode.FromModules makes one from modules you already have, such as from another encoder. // Modules from another encoder become a barcode with the quiet zone of their standard: 4 modules for QR. Barcode qr = Barcode.FromModules(BarcodeFormat.Qr, modules); Console.WriteLine($"{qr.Format}: {qr.Modules.Width} modules plus {qr.QuietZone} on each side"); Modules Every symbol is a BarcodeModules: a grid of dark and light modules for a 2D code, or a row of bars and spaces for a linear one. Width and Height are in modules, the indexer says whether a module is dark, and a linear symbol also lists its bar and space widths in Runs. A grid holds the symbol only, without its quiet zone. BarcodeModules.Create and BarcodeModules.CreateLinear make one from modules you already have, for example from another encoder. // A 2D grid, row by row from the top; true is a dark module. BarcodeModules grid = BarcodeModules.Create(3, 3, [ true, false, true, false, true, false, true, false, true, ]); // A linear symbol: bar and space widths in modules, starting and ending with a bar. BarcodeModules bars = BarcodeModules.CreateLinear([2, 1, 1, 1, 3], height: 20); for (int y = 0; y < grid.Height; y++) { for (int x = 0; x < grid.Width; x++) { Console.Write(grid[x, y] ? '#' : '.'); } Console.WriteLine(); } Console.WriteLine($"{bars.Width} modules wide, bars {string.Join(' ', bars.Runs.ToArray())}"); Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Put a QR code on a label // A 600 x 300 label: a QR code on the left, the address beside it. using Raster<Rgba8> label = Raster.Create(600, 300, Rgba8.White); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = label.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawBarcode(Barcode.Qr("https://example.com/track/4711"), new RectF(20, 20, 260, 260), Rgba8.Black); canvas.DrawText("Parcel 4711", new Vector2(300, 80), font, Rgba8.Black); canvas.DrawText("Track at example.com", new Vector2(300, 120), font, Rgba8.Black); } On a raster, the QR code's modules snap to whole pixels, so its edges stay sharp at any size. Save a barcode as SVG // The symbol as one path, 4 units a module, drawn on Egami.Svg's canvas over a white quiet zone. Barcode barcode = Barcode.DataMatrix("PN 4711-0815"); Path path = barcode.ToPath(moduleSize: 4); float width = (barcode.Modules.Width + (2 * barcode.QuietZone)) * 4, height = (barcode.Modules.Height + (2 * barcode.QuietZone)) * 4; using (FileStream stream = File.Create(file)) using (var canvas = new Egami.Svg.SvgCanvas(stream, width, height)) { canvas.FillRect(new RectF(0, 0, width, height), Rgba8.White); canvas.FillPath(path, Rgba8.Black); } Barcode.ToPath gives the whole symbol as one path, so any canvas can take it; Egami.Svg's SvgCanvas writes it as one SVG <path>. Egami.Barcodes itself does not depend on Egami.Svg. Print a GS1 shipping label // A 4 x 6 inch label in points: an SSCC as GS1-128 at 0.5 mm a module with its text, and a GS1 Data Matrix. float module = 0.5f / 25.4f * 72; Barcode sscc = Barcode.Gs1Code128("(00)106141411234567897"); page.DrawBarcode(sscc, new Vector2(18, 300), module, Rgba8.Black, new BarcodeDrawOptions { Font = font }); page.DrawBarcode(Barcode.DataMatrix(Gs1.Parse("(01)09501101530003(10)AB12")), new RectF(18, 18, 100, 100), Rgba8.Black); At a module size in points, the barcode has the X dimension a scanner expects, on a PDF page or any other canvas.

articles/guides/color-management.html.title: Color management | Egami
articles/guides/color-management.html.summary: Color management Egami reads color information from every file and keeps it, but changes no pixel unless you ask: a file's numbers load as stored. The types below say what those numbers mean, and convert between them. Profiles A ColorProfile says what a raster's numbers mean: the color model (ColorModel.Rgb, Gray or Cmyk), the primaries and white point, and the transfer function. The built-ins cover sRGB, linear sRGB, Display P3, Adobe RGB, ProPhoto RGB, Rec. 2020, the two Rec. 2100 HDR encodings, gray, and one CMYK print profile, Fogra39 (offset on coated paper); ColorProfile.Create makes any other RGB encoding. // A ColorProfile says what a raster's numbers mean. The built-ins cover the common encodings... ColorProfile web = ColorProfile.Srgb; ColorProfile wide = ColorProfile.DisplayP3; ColorProfile hdr = ColorProfile.Rec2100Pq; // ...and Create makes any other RGB encoding from primaries and a transfer function. ColorProfile camera = ColorProfile.Create(ColorPrimaries.AdobeRgb, TransferFunction.Gamma(2.2), "Camera RGB"); Console.WriteLine($"{camera.Name}: {camera.Model}, HDR {camera.IsHdr}, same as Adobe RGB: {camera.IsEquivalentTo(ColorProfile.AdobeRgb)}"); Primaries and white points ColorPrimaries holds the CIE 1931 Chromaticity of red, green, blue and white. The named sets are BT.709 (sRGB's), Display P3, BT.2020, Adobe RGB and ProPhoto, with the D65 and D50 white points. // Primaries are the chromaticities of red, green, blue and white. ColorPrimaries p3 = ColorPrimaries.DisplayP3; Chromaticity red = p3.Red; Console.WriteLine($"P3 red is x {red.X}, y {red.Y}; white is D65: {p3.White == Chromaticity.D65}"); ColorPrimaries custom = new(new(0.68, 0.32), new(0.265, 0.69), new(0.15, 0.06), Chromaticity.D65); Transfer functions A TransferFunction decodes stored values to linear light and back: sRGB, linear, a pure gamma, BT.709, the ICC parametric curve, a sampled table, and the HDR curves PQ and HLG. Single values use exact double arithmetic; rows use a vectorized form within 1e-5 of it, the same on every CPU. Linear 1.0 is reference white, which for PQ and HLG is 203 cd/m² (ITU-R BT.2408), so HDR highlights are values above 1. // A transfer function decodes stored values to linear light and back; HDR curves put reference white at 1.0. double linear = TransferFunction.Srgb.ToLinear(0.5); // 0.214 double nits = TransferFunction.Pq.ToLinear(0.75) * 203; // a 75% PQ signal is about 983 cd/m² float[] row = [0f, 0.25f, 0.5f, 1f]; TransferFunction.Srgb.ToLinear(row, row); // a whole row at once, in place ICC profiles IccData parses an ICC profile (versions 2 and 4): the header fields (version, IccProfileClass, data and connection spaces, the suggested RenderingIntent, creation date), the description and copyright text, and every tag with its bytes. Like ExifData, it never throws: offsets or sizes outside the profile, a missing acsp signature or more bytes than SafetyLimits.MaxMetadataBytes mark it damaged, with Warnings saying why, and what could be read stays available. ColorProfile.FromIcc turns a profile into an encoding. Egami converts with RGB, gray and CMYK profiles of the input, display, output and color space classes, whether they convert through a matrix and curves or through lut8, lut16, lutAtoB and lutBtoA tables; a damaged tag that conversion needs throws CorruptDataException, and other classes or data spaces throw UnsupportedFormatException. A matrix profile gets its primaries and curve, so IsEquivalentTo recognizes an ICC profile written for one of the built-ins, and a version 4.4 cicp tag naming PQ or HLG wins over the rest. // IccData reads a profile's header and tags; it never throws, and says what was wrong with a damaged one. IccData icc = IccData.Parse(bytes); Console.WriteLine($"{icc.Description}: version {icc.Version}, {icc.ProfileClass}, {icc.DataSpace} to {icc.ConnectionSpace}, damaged: {icc.IsDamaged}"); foreach (IccTag tag in icc.Tags) { Console.WriteLine($" {tag.Signature} ({tag.Type}), {tag.Data.Length} bytes"); } // ColorProfile.FromIcc makes an encoding from it: a matrix profile gets its primaries and curve, so an ICC profile written // for Display P3 is equivalent to the built-in. ColorProfile profile = ColorProfile.FromIcc(icc); bool isP3 = profile.IsEquivalentTo(ColorProfile.DisplayP3); Converting Nothing converts unless asked. RasterMetadata.GetColorProfile says what a raster's pixels mean, from its ICC profile, its sRGB or linear tag or its gamma, and sRGB when the file said nothing. RasterOps.ConvertColor converts in place to another encoding of the same model and records the result: no profile for sRGB, the target's ICC profile otherwise. // What the pixels mean, from the file's ICC profile, tags and gamma; sRGB when it said nothing. ColorProfile stored = raster.Metadata.GetColorProfile(); // Convert in place to sRGB for the web: the metadata then says sRGB, so no profile is written. raster.Apply(ops => ops.ConvertColor(ColorProfile.Srgb)); What a file says is kept in the metadata: the 1.0 IccProfile, ColorSpace hint and Gamma as before, and now CodePoints (PNG cICP), Primaries (PNG cHRM, BMP calibrated endpoints) and Hdr (PNG mDCV and cLLI, as HdrMetadata). GetColorProfile resolves them in one order for every format: code points, then the ICC profile, then an sRGB tag, then a gamma or linear tag with the primaries, then a camera's EXIF Adobe RGB marker, and sRGB when the file said nothing. PNG's gAMA 45455 (1/2.2) without other chromaticities than sRGB's counts as sRGB, which is what such files mean. // What an HDR file says about its mastering display and light levels, alongside its code points.
