SVG path data Path.ParseSvg reads the d attribute grammar of SVG 1.1 and 2; TryParseSvg returns false instead of throwing SvgPathException, and lenient: true keeps every complete command before the first error. ToSvg writes path data, absolute or relative, compact or spaced, to a precision (SvgPathFormat). // An icon from SVG path data, drawn four times larger, and written back as compact relative data. Path heart = Path.ParseSvg("M12 21.35l-1.45-1.32C5.4 15.36 2 12.28 2 8.5 2 5.42 4.42 3 7.5 3c1.74 0 3.41.81 4.5 2.09" + "C13.09 3.81 14.76 3 16.5 3 19.58 3 22 5.42 22 8.5c0 3.78-3.4 6.86-8.55 11.54L12 21.35z"); string d = heart.Transform(Matrix3x2.CreateScale(4)).ToSvg(new SvgPathFormat { Relative = true, Compact = true }); // Untrusted data: TryParseSvg says whether it is valid; lenient keeps what comes before an error, as browsers draw it. bool valid = Path.TryParseSvg("M0 0 L10 10 L20", out Path? strict); Path drawn = Path.ParseSvg("M0 0 L10 10 L20", lenient: true); try { Path.ParseSvg("M0 0 X"); } catch (SvgPathException e) { Console.WriteLine($"{e.Problem} at character {e.Position}"); } In an operation chain Draw adds a step that draws on each frame with a canvas over the step's pixels (DrawingExtensions). // Draw as a step in an operation chain: inside Within the canvas covers the area, with its origin at the area's corner. raster.Apply(ops => ops .Draw(canvas => canvas.FillRect(new RectF(0, 0, 300, 200), new Rgba8(240, 240, 255, 255))) .Within(new Rect(100, 50, 100, 100), area => area.Draw(canvas => canvas.FillCircle(new Vector2(50, 50), 40, Rgba8.Red))), Ct); // On an animation the step runs once per frame, and can be told which. raster.Apply(ops => ops.Draw((canvas, frame) => canvas.FillCircle(new Vector2(20 + (frame * 4), 20), 10, Rgba8.Black)), Ct); Printing inks InkCanvas draws into an InkRaster's plates instead of RGB pixels. It shares the raster canvas's rasterizer, clips and layers, so shapes, strokes and text cover the same pixels; where the RGB canvas blends colours, it sets each plate. Ink paints print their inks by name, and RGB colours, gradients and images convert into the process inks as InkCanvasOptions says (the RGB encoding, intent and black point compensation). InkCanvas.Clear(InkColor.None) leaves blank paper. // Plates for CMYK and a spot; an RGB photo converts through FOGRA39, the logo prints on its own plate. Egami.Colors.InkSet inks = Egami.Colors.InkSet.FromProfile(Egami.Colors.ColorProfile.Fogra39) .WithSpot("PANTONE 186 C", Egami.Colors.InkAppearance.Cmyk(0, 1, 0.81f, 0.04f)); using InkRaster page = new(inks, 300, 200); using (InkCanvas canvas = new(page)) { canvas.Clear(Egami.Colors.InkColor.None); // paper canvas.FillRect(new RectF(0, 0, 300, 120), new Rgba8(80, 140, 200, 255)); // RGB: converted to CMYK canvas.FillCircle(new Vector2(150, 100), 40, new SolidPaint(Egami.Colors.InkColor.Spot(inks[4], 1))); } Other backends Canvas is abstract. Each public call is checked, tracked (transform, clip bounds, save stack) and then ends in one protected hook, so a backend sees shapes and pens as data: a PDF page can write a rectangle as re and a pen as w, J, j and M. Hooks a backend leaves alone have defaults: rectangles, round rectangles and ovals become paths. A backend that cannot express a call (a blend mode its format lacks, a CustomPaint, a filtered layer) can draw it into pixels with RasterizeFallback, which returns a FallbackImage. Layers reach a backend through OnSaveLayer and OnRestoreLayer; a PDF page would write a transparency group with its opacity, blend mode and soft mask. OnDrawMesh and OnDrawPatch let a PDF page write shading types 4 to 7, OnDrawPicture a form XObject drawn once and referenced each time, and OnDrawImageLattice and OnDrawAtlas images per cell or sprite; by default meshes go through the raster fallback, patches become meshes, and the others become images and meshes. // A backend overrides hooks; the base class has already checked the arguments and tracks the transform and clip bounds. // This one writes SVG elements, keeping rectangles as rectangles and strokes as stroke settings. public sealed class SvgCanvas(float width, float height) : Canvas(width, height) { private readonly System.Text.StringBuilder _body = new(); public string Document => $"<svg xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/2000/svg\" width=\"{Width}\" height=\"{Height}\">{_body}</svg>"; protected override void OnDrawRect(RectF rect, Stroke? stroke, Paint paint) => _body.Append(FormattableString.Invariant($"<rect x=\"{rect.X}\" y=\"{rect.Y}\" width=\"{rect.Width}\" height=\"{rect.Height}\" {Style(stroke, paint)}/>")); protected override void OnDrawPath(Path path, Stroke? stroke, Paint paint) { System.Text.StringBuilder d = new(); int p = 0; foreach (PathVerb verb in path.Verbs) { int count = verb switch { PathVerb.Quad => 2, PathVerb.Cubic => 3, PathVerb.Close => 0, _ => 1 }; d.Append(verb switch { PathVerb.Move => "M", PathVerb.Line => "L", PathVerb.Quad => "Q", PathVerb.Cubic => "C", _ => "Z" }); foreach (Vector2 point in path.Points.Slice(p, count)) { d.Append(FormattableString.Invariant($"{point.X},{point.Y} ")); } p += count; } _body.Append(System.Globalization.CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, $"<path d=\"{d}\" {Style(stroke, paint)}/>"); } protected override void OnClipPath(Path path, ClipOp op, bool antialias) { // Clips would become <clipPath> elements; this sketch leaves them out. } protected override void OnDrawImage(Raster image, RectF source, RectF destination, SamplingOptions sampling, Paint? paint) { // An image would be embedded as a PNG data URI. } private string Style(Stroke? stroke, Paint paint) { Rgba8 c = paint is SolidPaint solid ? solid.Color.ToRgba8() : Rgba8.Black; string color = $"#{c.R:x2}{c.G:x2}{c.B:x2}"; string transform = Matrix.IsIdentity ? "" : FormattableString.Invariant($" transform=\"matrix({Matrix.M11} {Matrix.M12} {Matrix.M21} {Matrix.M22} {Matrix.M31} {Matrix.M32})\""); return stroke is null ? $"fill=\"{color}\"{transform}" : FormattableString.Invariant($"fill=\"none\" stroke=\"{color}\" stroke-width=\"{stroke.Width}\" stroke-linecap=\"{stroke.Cap.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()}\"{transform}"); } } Accuracy and speed Fills are within a mean level of SkiaSharp's and closer than SkiaSharp's to the exact covered area. Boolean operations, outlines, dashes, effects and SVG parsing give paths within a mean level of SkiaSharp's, and measured lengths agree within 1e-3. The figures are in the 2.6.1 and 2.6.2 release notes. Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Draw a rounded badge // A rounded badge with an outline and a dot, drawn at twice the size for a sharp result on high-density screens. using Raster<Rgba8> badge = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(240, 80); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = badge.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.Scale(2); RoundRect pill = new(new RectF(2, 2, 116, 36), 18); canvas.FillRoundRect(pill, new Rgba8(46, 160, 67, 255)); canvas.StrokeRoundRect(pill, new Stroke(2), new Rgba8(20, 100, 40, 255)); canvas.FillCircle(new Vector2(22, 20), 7, Rgba8.White); } Drawing at twice the size through Scale(2) keeps every shape's coordinates as designed. Draw chart axes // Axes, ticks and a data line for a chart: hairlines stay one pixel wide whatever the scale. double[] values = [3, 7, 4, 9, 6, 11, 8]; using Raster<Rgba8> chart = Raster.Create(420, 260, Rgba8.White); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = chart.CreateCanvas()) { Rgba8 axis = new(60, 60, 60, 255); canvas.DrawLine(new Vector2(40.5f, 20), new Vector2(40.5f, 230.5f), Stroke.Hairline, axis); canvas.DrawLine(new Vector2(40, 230.5f), new Vector2(400, 230.5f), Stroke.Hairline, axis); for (int i = 0; i < values.Length; i++) { float x = 40.5f + (i * 55); canvas.DrawLine(new Vector2(x, 230), new Vector2(x, 236), Stroke.Hairline, axis); } Vector2[] points = [.. values.Select((v, i) => new Vector2(40 + (i * 55), 230 - (float)(v * 18)))]; canvas.DrawPoints(PointMode.Polygon, points, new Stroke(3) { Join = LineJoin.Round, Cap = LineCap.Round }, new Rgba8(30, 90, 200, 255)); canvas.DrawPoints(PointMode.Points, points, new Stroke(8) { Cap = LineCap.Round }, new Rgba8(30, 90, 200, 255)); } Hairlines on half-pixel coordinates fill exactly one column or row of pixels. Clip a photo to a circle // A round avatar: clip to a circle, draw the photo scaled to fill it, then ring it. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.png"); using Raster<Rgba8> avatar = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(256, 256); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = avatar.CreateCanvas()) { Path circle = Path.Circle(new Vector2(128, 128), 120); canvas.Save(); canvas.ClipPath(circle); int side = Math.Min(photo.Width, photo.Height); RectF square = new((photo.Width - side) / 2, (photo.Height - side) / 2, side, side); canvas.DrawImage(photo, square, new RectF(8, 8, 240, 240)); canvas.Restore(); canvas.StrokePath(circle, new Stroke(6), Rgba8.White); } avatar.Save("avatar.png"); Animate a line drawing itself // Frames of a signature drawing itself: each frame strokes a longer part of the path. Path signature = Path.ParseSvg("M10 60 C30 10 50 110 70 60 S110 10 130 60 S170 110 190 40"); List<Raster<Rgba8>> frames = []; for (int i = 1; i <= 24; i++) { Raster<Rgba8> frame = Raster.Create(200, 100, Rgba8.White); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = frame.CreateCanvas()) { Stroke pen = new(3) { Cap = LineCap.Round, Effect = PathEffect.Trim(0, i / 24f) }; canvas.StrokePath(signature, pen, new Rgba8(20, 40, 120, 255)); } frames.Add(frame); } PathEffect.Trim keeps a fraction of the path's length; stepping it from 0 to 1 gives the frames. Paint a dusk sky // A dusk sky: stops in Oklch so the hues turn smoothly, dithered so the wide soft ramp shows no bands, and a sun. using Raster<Rgba8> sky = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(800, 450); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = sky.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawPaint(new LinearGradient( new Vector2(0, 0), new Vector2(0, 450), new GradientStop(0, new Rgba8(20, 30, 90, 255)), new GradientStop(0.6f, new Rgba8(220, 110, 120, 255)), new GradientStop(1, new Rgba8(255, 200, 120, 255))) { Interpolation = GradientInterpolation.Oklch(), Dither = true, }); canvas.FillCircle(new Vector2(560, 380), 160, new RadialGradient(new Vector2(560, 380), 160, new RgbaF32(1, 0.95f, 0.8f, 0.9f), new RgbaF32(1, 0.8f, 0.5f, 0))); } sky.Save("sky.png"); Mixing in Oklch keeps the hues from turning gray between stops, and Dither hides the bands of a wide soft ramp. See Gradients. Draw a card with a shadow // A UI card: a Material-style shadow from its elevation, the card, and a soft inner highlight along its top edge. using Raster<Rgba8> screen = Raster.Create(400, 260, new Rgba8(236, 239, 244, 255)); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = screen.CreateCanvas()) { RoundRect card = new(new RectF(50, 40, 300, 170), 14); canvas.DrawShadow(Path.RoundRect(card), new ShadowOptions { Elevation = 16 }); canvas.FillRoundRect(card, Rgba8.White); canvas.Save(); canvas.ClipRoundRect(card); canvas.FillRect(new RectF(50, 40, 300, 30), new LinearGradient(new Vector2(0, 40), new Vector2(0, 70), new RgbaF32(0.85f, 0.9f, 1, 1), new RgbaF32(1, 1, 1, 1))); canvas.Restore(); } screen.Save("card.png"); Fade a photo's edges // A photo whose edges fade to transparent: an alpha soft mask of a radial gradient, opaque in the middle. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.png"); using Raster<Rgba8> faded = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(photo.Width, photo.Height); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = faded.CreateCanvas()) { Vector2 center = new(photo.Width / 2f, photo.Height / 2f); float radius = MathF.Min(photo.Width, photo.Height) / 2f; SoftMask vignette = new( mask => mask.DrawPaint(new RadialGradient(center, radius, new GradientStop(0.6f, Rgba8.Black), new GradientStop(1, new Rgba8(0, 0, 0, 0)))), SoftMaskKind.Alpha); canvas.SaveLayer(new LayerOptions { Mask = vignette }); canvas.DrawImage(photo, Vector2.Zero); canvas.Restore(); } faded.Save("faded.png"); Fade a group as one // A translucent logo made of overlapping parts: drawn in a layer at 60%, the overlaps do not show through. using Raster<Rgba8> banner = Raster.Create(300, 120, new Rgba8(30, 40, 60, 255)); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = banner.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.SaveLayer(0.6f); canvas.FillCircle(new Vector2(60, 60), 40, new Rgba8(255, 200, 0, 255)); canvas.FillRoundRect(new RoundRect(new RectF(60, 40, 200, 40), 20), new Rgba8(255, 200, 0, 255)); canvas.Restore(); } banner.Save("banner.png"); See Layers. Stretch a button image to any size // One small button image serves every size: corners stay round, the label sits on the stretched center. using Raster<Rgba8> button = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(200, 48); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = button.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawImageNinePatch(skin, new Rect(12, 12, 6, 6), new RectF(0, 0, 200, 48), new SamplingOptions { Filter = ResampleFilter.Bilinear }); } The corners keep their size and the edges and center stretch. An Android .9.png carries its own lattice: see Nine-patches and lattices. Shade a gradient mesh // A gradient mesh, as an illustration app draws one: a 3×3 grid of colored points, smoothly shaded. Vector2[] grid = new Vector2[16]; RgbaF32[] colors = new RgbaF32[16]; for (int j = 0; j < 4; j++) { for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { grid[(j * 4) + i] = new Vector2(i * 60, j * 40) + new Vector2(MathF.Sin(j) * 8, MathF.Cos(i) * 6); colors[(j * 4) + i] = new RgbaF32(i / 3f, 0.3f + (j * 0.2f), 1 - (i / 3f), 1); } } int[] indices = [.. Enumerable.Range(0, 9).SelectMany(k => new[] { k + (k / 3), k + (k / 3) + 1, k + (k / 3) + 5, k + (k / 3), k + (k / 3) + 5, k + (k / 3) + 4 })]; using Raster<Rgba8> mesh = Raster.Create(200, 140, Rgba8.White); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = mesh.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.Translate(10, 10); canvas.DrawMesh(new Mesh(MeshMode.Triangles, grid, colors, indices: indices), Rgba8.White); } See Meshes and patches. Separations of a CMYK page with spot colours // A CMYK page with two spot colours: a photo converted into the process inks, a Pantone band and a gold rule. InkSet inks = InkSet.FromProfile(ColorProfile.Fogra39) .WithSpot("PANTONE 186 C", InkAppearance.Cmyk(0, 1, 0.81f, 0.04f)) .WithSpot("Gold", InkAppearance.Lab(new LabColor(70, 5, 60))); using InkRaster page = new(inks, 600, 400); using (InkCanvas canvas = new(page)) { canvas.Clear(InkColor.None); canvas.DrawImage(photo, new RectF(40, 40, 360, 240)); canvas.FillRect(new RectF(0, 320, 600, 50), new SolidPaint(InkColor.Spot(inks[4], 1))); canvas.FillRect(new RectF(40, 300, 520, 4), new SolidPaint(InkColor.Spot(inks[5], 1))); } // Every plate as its own gray image (ink shows light), and all of them as one separated TIFF for the RIP. foreach (InkPlate plate in page.Plates) { using Raster<Gray8> gray = plate.AsRaster<Gray8>(); gray.Save($"page-{plate.Name}.png"); } page.Save("page.tif"); InkCanvas draws on plates with any Canvas call; RGB images and colours convert through the ink set's profile. See Printing inks. A spot-colour label with overprint // A label in one spot colour over a CMYK background, overprinted so the press needs no trapping: the background's // plates stay under the spot. Black text overprints too, leaving every other plate alone where it prints. using (InkCanvas canvas = new(page)) { canvas.FillRect(new RectF(0, 0, 300, 120), new SolidPaint(InkColor.Cmyk(0.1f, 0.05f, 0.4f, 0))); canvas.FillPath(Path.RoundRect(new RoundRect(new RectF(20, 20, 260, 80), 12)), new SolidPaint(InkColor.Spot(inks[4], 1)) { Overprint = Overprint.On }); canvas.FillPath(Path.Circle(new Vector2(150, 60), 20), new SolidPaint(InkColor.Cmyk(0, 0, 0, 1)) { Overprint = Overprint.NonZero }); } Overprint.On paints only the inks a colour names; NonZero also leaves the plates of a CMYK colour's zero components alone, as PDF's overprint mode 1. Check total ink coverage before printing // Before sending a page to a press with a 300% total ink limit: where is there too much ink, and how much of the page? InkCoverage coverage = page.MeasureCoverage(limit: 3.0f); if (coverage.MaxTotal > coverage.Limit) { Console.WriteLine($"{coverage.MaxTotal:P0} at {coverage.MaxAt}; {coverage.ShareOver:P1} of the page is over {coverage.Limit:P0}."); } // A soft proof shows how it will look on paper, the paper's own tone included. using Raster<Rgba8> proof = page.Proof<Rgba8>(new ProofOptions { SimulatePaper = true });

articles/guides/edges-and-morphology.htm.title: Edges and morphology | Egami
articles/guides/edges-and-morphology.htm.summary: Edges and morphology Edge operators measure how fast the image changes at each pixel; Canny's detector turns that into thin edge lines; and morphology grows, shrinks and cleans up shapes by taking the maximum or minimum over a neighbourhood. All of them keep the image's size, so they work inside Within scopes. Operation Does Edges(op, grayscale) The gradient magnitude of a fixed kernel, 0 to 1; gray by default, or per channel CannyEdges(sigma, low, high) Thin white edges on black, as ImageMagick's -canny Morphology(op, shape, iterations) Dilate, erode, open, close, gradient, top hat or bottom hat over a StructuringElement Dilate(radius), Erode(radius) The maximum or minimum over a square; Dilate(rx, ry) and Erode(rx, ry) over a rectangle Find edges using Raster edges = photo.Derive(o => o.Edges(), Ct); // Sobel, gray, 0 to 1 using Raster crisp = photo.Derive(o => o.Edges(EdgeOperator.Scharr), Ct); // rotation-steady using Raster colored = photo.Derive(o => o.Edges(EdgeOperator.Sobel, grayscale: false), Ct); // per channel using Raster lines = photo.Derive(o => o.Blur(1).Edges(EdgeOperator.Laplacian3x3), Ct); // second derivative EdgeOperator picks the kernels. Every operator is scaled so a full black-to-white step gives 1, so their results can be compared and thresholded alike. Operator Kernels Notes Sobel (default) 3 × 3 pair, weights 1, 2, 1 The usual choice Scharr 3 × 3 pair, weights 3, 10, 3 Its strength depends least on the edge's direction Prewitt 3 × 3 pair, weights 1, 1, 1 RobertsCross 2 × 2 diagonal differences Sharpest and noisiest; the pixel and the one below right Kirsch, Robinson Eight 3 × 3 compass kernels The strongest of the eight directions Laplacian3x3, Laplacian5x5 One kernel, absolute value Second derivative: edges come out as double lines LaplacianOfGaussian 5 × 5, absolute value A Laplacian smoothed against noise Gradient pairs write sqrt(gx² + gy²); the compass operators keep the largest of their eight responses. The edges are measured on premultiplied values, so transparent areas count as black, and alpha is kept. With grayscale: true (the default) the pixels are first reduced to Rec. 709 luma and the magnitude is written as gray; with false red, green and blue each get their own. Past the border the edge pixel repeats. A selection from Canny // Thin white edges on black. A gray raster works as a Mask as it is; an RGBA one needs MaskChannel.Luminance, // because a Mask of a raster with alpha reads its alpha. using Raster<Gray8> edges = Raster.Load<Gray8>("duck.png"); edges.Apply(o => o.CannyEdges(sigma: 1.4f).Dilate(1), Ct); // thin edges, thickened photo.Apply(o => o.Within(new Mask(edges), s => s.FillColor(Rgba8.Red)), Ct); // paint over them Canny's white-on-black map works directly as a Mask; thicken it with Dilate first to catch the pixels beside each edge. CannyEdges runs the four steps of Canny's detector: a Gaussian blur of the luma with standard deviation sigma, the gradient from Canny's own 2 × 2 first differences, non-maximum suppression (a pixel is kept only if neither neighbour across its edge is stronger), and hysteresis: pixels at least high times the image's strongest gradient start edges, and edges follow 8-connected pixels down to low times it. The output is white edges, one pixel wide, on black, with alpha kept. The parameters mean what ImageMagick's -canny 0x{sigma}+{low × 100}%+{high × 100}% means, and the edge maps match it pixel for pixel except where ImageMagick stops a trace early: it keeps its trace stack in one image row, so a trace deeper than the image is wide ends part way. Egami follows every connected pixel, so it finds the same edges plus the rest of those traces. A gray edge map is a Mask as it is. A color raster used as a Mask is read by its alpha, so for an RGBA edge map pass MaskChannel.Luminance: new Mask(edges, Channel: MaskChannel.Luminance). Clean a scanned form with Close // Close removes dark specks smaller than the shape (dust and toner dots on the paper) and keeps strokes wider than it; // Open does the opposite, for light pinholes in dark areas. using Raster<Gray8> scan = Raster.Load<Gray8>("scan.tif"); scan.Apply(o => o.Morphology(MorphologyOp.Close, StructuringElement.Disk(1)), Ct); // The outlines of shapes, and the light details smaller than a disk. using Raster outlines = scan.Derive(o => o.Morphology(MorphologyOp.Gradient, StructuringElement.Square(1)), Ct); using Raster details = scan.Derive(o => o.Morphology(MorphologyOp.TopHat, StructuringElement.Disk(5)), Ct); Morphology is flat: dilation takes each channel's maximum over the shape, erosion the minimum, on the stored values, so 8 and 16-bit results are exact. The rest combine them: MorphologyOp Is Use Dilate Maximum Grow light areas, close dark gaps Erode Minimum Shrink light areas, remove light specks Open Erode, then dilate Remove light details smaller than the shape; never brightens Close Dilate, then erode Remove dark details smaller than the shape; never darkens Gradient Dilate minus erode Outlines as wide as the shape TopHat Image minus its open The light details the open removed BottomHat Its close minus the image The dark details the close removed iterations repeats each dilation and erosion: Open with 2 erodes twice, then dilates twice, as ImageMagick's Open:2. Alpha is dilated and eroded with the color, so a logo's shape grows and shrinks with it; Gradient, TopHat and BottomHat keep alpha, since a difference of alpha would make an opaque image transparent. Past the border the edge pixel repeats, as ImageMagick does. Shapes StructuringElement disk = StructuringElement.Disk(4); // x² + y² ≤ 16, ImageMagick's Disk:4 StructuringElement diamond = StructuringElement.Diamond(3); // |x| + |y| ≤ 3 StructuringElement plus = StructuringElement.Cross(2); // ImageMagick's Plus:2 StructuringElement corner = StructuringElement.FromMask( new[,] { { true, true, true }, { true, false, false }, { true, false, false }, }, new Point(0, 0)); // [y, x] cells; the origin sits on the pixel using Raster rounded = photo.Derive(o => o.Morphology(MorphologyOp.Open, disk, iterations: 2), Ct); The factories make ImageMagick's kernels of the same name, so -morphology Dilate Disk:4 and Morphology(MorphologyOp.Dilate, StructuringElement.Disk(4)) give identical pixels. Cross(r) is ImageMagick's Plus:r. Shape Cells Square(r) The (2r + 1) square Rectangle(rx, ry) The (2rx + 1) × (2ry + 1) rectangle, Skia's dilate and erode radii Disk(r) x² + y² ≤ r² Diamond(r) |x| + |y| ≤ r Cross(r) The row and column through the origin, 2r + 1 long FromMask(cells, origin) Any set of cells, [y, x], with the origin on the pixel being computed Erosion reads the cells as offsets from the pixel and dilation reads them mirrored, as ImageMagick does, so Open and Close work as expected for lopsided shapes too. Squares and rectangles cost the same per pixel whatever their size (van Herk and Gil-Werman's running maximum down the columns); other shapes cost in proportion to their height. using Raster grown = photo.Derive(o => o.Dilate(3), Ct); // light areas grow 3 px: a 7 × 7 square using Raster shrunk = photo.Derive(o => o.Erode(3), Ct); // light areas shrink 3 px using Raster wide = photo.Derive(o => o.Dilate(6, 1), Ct); // 13 × 3, as Skia's dilate radii

articles/guides/effects.html.title: Effects | Egami
articles/guides/effects.html.summary: Effects The editor's effects menu: a vignette, glows and bloom, pixelate, oil paint, Kuwahara, spread, drop and inner shadows. Every effect keeps the image's size, except DropShadow, which by default grows the canvas to hold the shadow. Operation Does Vignette(radius, softness, color, center) Darkens or tints outside an ellipse fitted to the image, with a soft edge: ImageMagick's -vignette shape Glow(sigma, color, spread, inner) An outer glow behind the alpha shape, or an inner glow inside it, as an editor's layer style Bloom(threshold, sigma, intensity) Bright areas blurred and screened back in linear light: the photographic glow Pixelate(cellSize, origin) Each cell becomes its premultiplied average OilPaint(radius, levels) Each pixel becomes a pixel of the most common intensity in its square: ImageMagick's -paint Kuwahara(radius, sigma) Each pixel takes its value from the least varied of four squares: ImageMagick's -kuwahara Spread(radius, seed) Each pixel takes a random neighbour's value within the radius: ImageMagick's -spread DropShadow(dx, dy, sigma, color, options) Skia's DropShadow: the alpha moved, blurred and colored, with the image on top InnerShadow(dx, dy, sigma, color) A shadow inside the alpha shape, cast by everything outside it, as an editor's layer style Vignette, glow and bloom // Darken the corners: the edge of the ellipse passes through the corners and fades over half the radius. using Raster dark = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Vignette(), Ct); // A tighter, softer, warm-white vignette, off-center toward the subject. using Raster light = photo.Derive( ops => ops.Vignette(0.6f, softness: 0.8f, color: new Rgba8(255, 245, 230, 255), center: new System.Numerics.Vector2(photo.Width * 0.4f, photo.Height * 0.5f)), Ct); radius is a fraction of the half-diagonal: 1 puts the edge of the ellipse through the corners. The ellipse has the image's proportions and its center is the image's middle unless center moves it. softness is the share of the radius the edge fades over. The fade is the profile of a blurred edge, computed per pixel from the distance to the ellipse, so it costs the same at any softness. While the ellipse stays inside the image the result is within 5 levels of ImageMagick's -vignette (which blurs a drawn ellipse, so it bends where the ellipse leaves the image). The color is mixed source-over on premultiplied values; its alpha is the vignette's strength. // A soft yellow glow around the badge, behind it; spread hardens it before it fades. using Raster outer = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Glow(8, new Rgba8(255, 210, 0, 230), spread: 0.3f), Ct); // A white glow coming in from the badge's edges, inside it only. using Raster inner = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Glow(5, Rgba8.White, inner: true), Ct); Glow is built from Egami's own steps and gives exactly what the same chain gives by hand: a layer that is the color with the image's alpha (or 1 − alpha for an inner glow), blurred with BlurMethod.Fast, its alpha multiplied by 1 / (1 − spread) and by the color's alpha; then the image is drawn over the layer, or the layer drawn over the image with BlendMode.SourceAtop so it stays inside the shape. An opaque image has no edge to glow from: glow a logo or a cut-out. // Highlights above 80% bleed light into their surroundings, added in linear light as a lens does. photo.Apply(ops => ops.Bloom(threshold: 0.8f, sigma: 12, intensity: 1.5f), Ct); Bloom is a chain too: each channel's part above threshold (stored values), stretched to 0..1 and scaled by intensity, blurred in linear light with BlurMethod.Fast, and screened onto the image in linear light, so light adds as it does in a lens. Pixelate, oil paint, Kuwahara and spread // 12-pixel cells, each the average of what it covers. using Raster blocks = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Pixelate(12), Ct); Cells start at origin and repeat both ways; cells cut by the image's edges average what they hold. The average is taken on premultiplied values, so transparent pixels do not darken a cell; for Rgba8 and Bgra8 it is computed in whole numbers and rounded once, so it is exact. using Raster painted = photo.Derive(ops => ops.OilPaint(radius: 4, levels: 20), Ct); using Raster magick = photo.Derive(ops => ops.OilPaint(3, levels: 256), Ct); // ImageMagick's -paint 3, pixel for pixel OilPaint follows ImageMagick's -paint: a (2r + 1) square window, intensity in 256 bins (fewer with levels), and the output is a whole pixel of the most common bin, picked by ImageMagick's scan order. With 256 levels the result equals ImageMagick's pixel for pixel at 8 bits; the default 20 levels make broader strokes. The histogram slides along each row. // Flattens texture into patches while keeping edges; a small blur first, as ImageMagick's -kuwahara 4x1. using Raster smooth = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Kuwahara(4, sigma: 1), Ct); Kuwahara follows ImageMagick's -kuwahara radius x sigma: an optional Gaussian blur with ImageMagick's kernel (σ, out to the radius), then of the four (r + 1) squares with the pixel at a corner, the one whose luma varies least gives the pixel its value, sampled at its middle. Summed-area tables make the cost independent of the radius. Results are within a few levels of ImageMagick's, where near-equal variances may pick another square. // Frosted glass: every pixel takes a neighbour's value up to 3 pixels away; the same seed gives the same result. using Raster frosted = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Spread(3, seed: 42), Ct); Spread moves no pixel further than the radius. The offsets come from a hash of the seed and the position (SplitMix64), so a seed gives the same pixels on any machine, at any thread count and inside a scope. Drop shadows // Skia's DropShadow: 6 px right and down, blurred with sigma 8, black at 55%; the canvas grows to hold the shadow. using Raster shadowed = logo.Derive(ops => ops.DropShadow(6, 6, 8, new Rgba8(0, 0, 0, 140)), Ct); // Keep the size, or keep only the shadow (as Skia's DropShadowOnly and ImageMagick's -shadow). using Raster same = logo.Derive(ops => ops.DropShadow(4, 4, 3, Rgba8.Black, new DropShadowOptions { Expand = false }), Ct); using Raster shadow = logo.Derive(ops => ops.DropShadow(0, 10, 12, Rgba8.Black, new DropShadowOptions { ShadowOnly = true, SigmaY = 6 }), Ct); The parameters mean what Skia's do: the offset moves the shadow, sigma is the Gaussian's standard deviation (σx, with SigmaY for a different σy), and the color's alpha is the shadow's opacity. Fractional offsets move the shadow by fractions. Expand (the default) grows the canvas by 3σ plus the offset on the sides the shadow reaches past the image, so the shadow is never cut off; the image moves right and down by what was added on the left and top. ImageMagick's -shadow adds round(2σ) on every side instead, which cuts about 2% of a shadow's edge. A growing step cannot run inside Within; with Expand = false the size stays and it can. Method is BlurMethod.Fast by default, whose cost does not grow with sigma; BlurMethod.Exact uses the Gaussian kernel and is within a level of the same chain built from Pad, Offset, ColorMatrix, Convolve and DrawImage. Inner shadows // A shadow inside the badge, cast from up and left, as a pressed button looks. using Raster pressed = logo.Derive(ops => ops.InnerShadow(2, 3, 3, new Rgba8(0, 0, 0, 140)), Ct); InnerShadow is the chain written by hand: the color with 1 − alpha, moved by the offset rounded to whole pixels with the uncovered strips counted as outside, blurred fast, faded by the color's alpha and drawn source-atop. With glows and drop shadows it covers an editor's layer styles, and on a canvas layer it is a LayerOptions.Filter. Cookbook A drop shadow for a logo // A logo on a page: a soft shadow under it, then the result flattened onto white for a JPEG. logo.Apply(ops => ops .DropShadow(5, 7, 6, new Rgba8(0, 0, 0, 110)) .Flatten(Rgba8.White), Ct); logo.Save("logo-shadow.jpg"); The canvas grows to hold the shadow; pass Expand = false to keep the size, as inside Within. Blur a face // Hide a face: pixelate only the rectangle around it, with the grid starting at its corner so cells line up with it. Rect face = new(100, 40, 72, 64); photo.Apply(ops => ops.Within(face, o => o.Pixelate(12, new Point(face.X, face.Y))), Ct); Inside Within, cells stay on the grid that origin sets, and each cell averages all of its pixels, including those outside the rectangle, so the result inside equals pixelating the whole image there. Start the grid at the rectangle's corner so whole cells fill it. An oil-paint look // A painted look: a light blur to calm noise, the oil paint, then a touch more saturation and a vignette. using Raster painting = photo.Derive(ops => ops .Blur(0.8f) .OilPaint(radius: 4, levels: 24) .Saturation(1.15f) .Vignette(0.9f, softness: 0.6f), Ct); painting.Save("painting.png");

articles/guides/egdr-format.html.title: The .egdr format | Egami
articles/guides/egdr-format.html.summary: The .egdr format An Egami drawing file holds a recorded Picture: the calls a PictureRecorder kept, and the images, paths and nested drawings they use. Picture.Save writes it and Picture.Load reads it; this page is the format's specification, version 1.1, for anyone writing a reader or writer of their own. See Drawing for the API. Layout All numbers are little-endian. u8, u16 and u32 are unsigned integers of 1, 2 and 4 bytes, i32 a signed 4-byte integer, f32 an IEEE 754 single, and bool a u8 that is 0 or 1. A file is a 12-byte header followed by chunks: Bytes Field Value 0 to 7 Signature 89 45 47 44 52 0D 0A 1A (\x89EGDR\r\n\x1A, after PNG's: it catches text-mode transfers and stops type) 8 to 9 Major version u16, 1. A reader rejects a major version it does not know. 10 to 11 Minor version u16, 1. A reader accepts any minor version of its major version. Each chunk is a 4-byte ASCII type, a u32 payload length, and the payload. A reader skips the payload of a chunk type it does not know, which is how later minor versions add to the format. The chunk types of version 1.1: Type Payload Defines IMAG A PNG file The next image, numbered from 0 PATH A path, below The next path, numbered from 0 DRAW A drawing, below The next drawing, numbered from 0 ENCI An encoded image file (a JPEG, a PNG, any format Egami reads), its bytes as they were given The next encoded image, numbered from 0 INKS Ink entries, below (since 1.1) Nothing: it annotates the DRAW chunk right after it DEND Empty The end. The file's drawing is the last DRAW chunk before it. A chunk refers to images, paths and drawings by number, and only to ones defined by earlier chunks, so a file is read in one pass and cannot hold a cycle. A writer writes each image, path and drawing once, however often it is used. Bytes after DEND are ignored. Paths Field Type Fill rule u8: 0 nonzero, 1 even-odd Verb count u32 Verbs u8 each: 0 move, 1 line, 2 quadratic, 3 cubic, 4 close Point count u32, the sum of the verbs' points: 1 for a move or a line, 2 for a quadratic, 3 for a cubic, 0 for a close Points f32 x and y each, finite A line, quadratic or cubic must follow a move, or another segment, in its contour: after a close, a new contour starts with a move. Drawings Field Type Bounds Rectangle Call count u32 Calls One after another, each an opcode u8 and its operands The payload must end exactly after the last call. A rectangle is four f32: x, y, width and height. A matrix is six f32: M11, M12, M21, M22, M31, M32, as .NET's Matrix3x2, which maps a row vector (x, y, 1). A color is four f32: red, green, blue and straight alpha, encoded (sRGB) values from 0 to 1. A point is two f32. A string is a u32 byte count and that many bytes of UTF-8. A round rectangle is a rectangle and the x and y radii of its corners: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left. An enum is a u8 with the value Egami's enum of that name has. Every number must be finite. Opcode Call Operands 1 Save None 2 Restore (also ends a layer) None 3 SaveLayer Opacity f32, BlendMode, a flags u8 (1 isolated, 2 knockout), has-bounds bool, bounds rectangle if it has them 4 SetMatrix Matrix 5 ClipRect Rectangle, ClipOp, antialias bool 6 ClipRoundRect Round rectangle, ClipOp, antialias bool 7 ClipPath Path number u32, ClipOp, antialias bool 8 DrawPaint Paint 9 DrawRect Rectangle, has-stroke bool, stroke if it has one, paint 10 DrawRoundRect Round rectangle, has-stroke bool, stroke, paint 11 DrawOval Rectangle, has-stroke bool, stroke, paint 12 DrawPath Path number u32, has-stroke bool, stroke, paint 13 DrawPoints PointMode, count u32, points, stroke, paint 14 DrawImage Image number u32, source rectangle (inside the image), destination rectangle, sampling, has-paint bool, paint 15 DrawLattice Image number, lattice, destination rectangle, sampling, has-paint bool, paint 16 DrawAtlas Image number, count u32, that many sprite transforms (four f32: ScaleCos, ScaleSin, Tx, Ty), that many source rectangles, has-colors bool, that many colors if it has them, BlendMode, sampling, has-paint bool, paint 17 DrawMesh Mesh, paint, BlendMode, stops 18 DrawPatch Patch, paint, BlendMode, stops 19 DrawPicture Picture number u32, matrix, has-paint bool, paint, cache-as-image bool 20 DrawEncodedImage Encoded image number u32, source rectangle (inside the image), destination rectangle, sampling, has-paint bool, paint 21 DrawAnnotation Area rectangle, AnnotationKind, the URL or name as a string 22 BeginMarkedContent Tag as a string, a flags u8 (1 node id, 2 actual text, 4 alternate text), then the node id i32 and the two strings for the flags set 23 EndMarkedContent None; every BeginMarkedContent in a drawing has its EndMarkedContent in the same drawing 24 DrawImageMask Image number u32, destination rectangle, sampling, paint Coordinates are those the recorder's hooks received: local coordinates under the matrix last set. Replaying a drawing sets each recorded matrix after the matrix the drawing is replayed under. Text is written as DrawPath of its outlines, filled, since a file holds no fonts. A stroke is width f32 (0 for a hairline), LineCap, LineJoin, miter limit f32, has-dash bool, and for a dash an interval count u32, the intervals as f32 and the phase f32. Path effects never reach a file: the canvas applies them before the hook. Sampling is ResampleFilter, ColorSpace, EdgeMode and the background color as four u8 (red, green, blue, alpha). Stops are a count u32, then each stop's offset f32 (0 to 1) and color. A lattice is the x division count u32 and the divisions as i32, the same for y, has-bounds bool and the bounds as four i32 (x, y, width, height), has-kinds bool and one LatticeCellKind per cell, has-colors bool and one color per cell. There are (x divisions + 1) · (y divisions + 1) cells, row by row. A mesh is MeshMode, the vertex count u32, the positions, a flags u8 (1 colors, 2 texture coordinates, 4 values, 8 indices), then for each flag set in that order: a color per vertex, a point per vertex, an f32 per vertex, and an index count u32 with that many i32 indices, each below the vertex count. Colors and values are not both present, and a mesh with values has at least one stop. A patch is PatchKind (0 Coons, 1 tensor), its 12 or 16 points, a flags u8 (1 colors, 2 texture coordinates, 4 values), then four corner colors, four corner points and four corner f32 values for the flags set, in that order. Paints A paint is its kind u8, the fields every paint has, then its own: Field Type BlendMode u8 Opacity f32, 0 to 1 Flags u8: 1 antialias, 2 dither, 4 has a mask blur Local matrix Matrix Mask blur Sigma f32 and BlurStyle, when flag 4 is set Kind Paint Own fields 1 SolidPaint Color 2 LinearGradient Start point, end point, gradient fields 3 RadialGradient Center point, radius f32, gradient fields 4 ConicalGradient Start point, start radius f32, end point, end radius f32, gradient fields 5 SweepGradient Center point, start angle f32, end angle f32, gradient fields 6 ImagePaint Image number u32, TileMode x, TileMode y, sampling 7 NoisePaint NoisePaintKind, base frequency x and y f32, octaves i32, seed i32, has-tile bool, tile width and height i32 8 BlendPaint Destination paint, source paint, BlendMode 9 ColorMatrixPaint Source paint, the 20 matrix values f32, row by row 10 PicturePaint Picture number u32, TileMode x, TileMode y, tile rectangle The gradient fields are the stops (at least one), TileMode, a flags u8 (1 extend start, 2 extend end, 4 premultiplied), InterpolationSpace and HueMethod. A simplex noise uses its x frequency. A CustomPaint runs C# and has no kind: saving a drawing that uses one throws, and so does saving a layer with a filter, a backdrop or a soft mask, naming the call. Inks A drawing made with ink colours (InkColor), overprint or layers with a ColorSpace keeps them in an INKS chunk written just before its DRAW chunk, which holds every colour as its sRGB appearance. A 1.0 reader skips INKS and draws the appearances; an ink canvas reading 1.1 prints the inks. The payload is an entry count u32, then each entry: the byte offset u32 in the next DRAW chunk's payload that it is about, its kind u8, a data length u32 and the data. Each offset appears once and must be the start of what its kind names: Kind At Data 1 A color: a SolidPaint's, a stop's, a mesh vertex's or a patch corner's An ink colour 2 A paint's kind u8 Overprint u8: 1 on, 2 nonzero (absent means off) 3 A SaveLayer opcode The layer's colour space as an ICC profile An ink colour is a flags u8 (1 for a process CMYK colour, whose four inks are Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Black in that order), an ink count u32, and per ink: its name as a string, ColorantKind u8 (0 process, 1 spot, 2 technical), an appearance u8 (0 none, 1 CMYK, 2 sRGB, 3 Lab D50) with four f32 when there is one (RGB and Lab leave the fourth 0), and its tint f32. A mesh's or patch's vertices have inks all or none. Reading untrusted files Egami's reader checks every count against the bytes left before it allocates, puts every value through the constructors that check it, reads images with the PNG reader under the context's SafetyLimits, counts what it decodes toward MaxTotalBytes, and limits drawings to 64 levels of nesting and 50 million calls with nested drawings expanded, so a small file cannot ask for an exponential replay. Any failure is an EgamiException. The reader has a fuzz target, egdr.

articles/guides/extending.html.title: Custom operations and formats | Egami
articles/guides/extending.html.summary: Custom operations and formats Everything here uses only Egami's public API; Egami's own test suite has an outside project that does each of these things. Operations An operation implements IRasterOperation: it says what size it makes and fills the destination rows. /// <summary>Swaps red and blue, in parallel bands of rows.</summary> public sealed class SwapRedBlue : IRasterOperation { public Size OutputSize(Size input) => input; public void Run<TPixel>(OperationInput<TPixel> input) where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> { input.ForEachBand((start, end) => { for (int y = start; y < end; y++) { Span<TPixel> source = input.Source.Row(y); Span<TPixel> destination = input.Destination.Row(y); for (int x = 0; x < source.Length; x++) { Vector4 v = source[x].ToScaled(); destination[x] = TPixel.FromScaled(new Vector4(v.Z, v.Y, v.X, v.W)); } } }); } } image.Apply(ops => ops.Fit(100, 100).Add(new SwapRedBlue()), TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); OutputSize is asked while the chain is planned, before any pixel changes. Throw there for arguments that cannot work. When the size stays the same, Source and Destination may be the same plane (IsInPlace); read a row before you write it. ForEachBand runs bands of rows on up to EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads and checks the cancellation token between bands. A step that changes the size updates the EXIF dimensions and drops the thumbnail, as the built-in resizes do. TPixel.Layout tells you the pixel type, so you can take a fast path for the types you know and fall back to ToScaled and FromScaled for the rest. Check Layout.Alpha before you assume straight alpha. To run a chain on part of a larger picture, such as a tile or a canvas layer, pad the part by how far the chain reads: RasterOps.Reach returns that as an OperationReach, or null when a step reads the whole image (a resize, a turn, a custom operation). // How far a chain reads around each pixel: run it on a part of a picture padded by this much, and the part comes out as it // would in the whole picture. OperationReach? reach = RasterOps.Reach(ops => ops.Blur(3).Glow(4, Rgba8.White)); if (reach is OperationReach r) { Console.WriteLine($"pad by {r.X} × {r.Y}"); } // A resize reads the whole image: its reach is unknown. Assert.Null(RasterOps.Reach(ops => ops.Resize(100, 100))); Formats A new file format plugs in through a FormatInfo with your own reader and writer; Your own format shows how. Pixel types A pixel type is an unmanaged struct implementing IPixelType<TSelf>. Its Layout says how it is stored: a layout Egami knows (Rgba with Unorm8, say) lets Egami take its fast paths; anything else uses PixelChannelOrder.Other, and Egami converts it only through its own ToScaled and FromScaled. Wrapping memory Raster.Wrap puts a raster over memory you own, without copying: a Memory<TPixel> with a stride in pixels, or a Memory<byte> with a stride in bytes, such as a video frame whose rows are padded. Pass an IDisposable owner to have the raster release the memory when it is disposed. Rows and planes For a one-off pass over pixels, ForEachRow runs a lambda on each row in parallel; no operation class needed. using Raster<Rgba8> image = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(256, 64); // A horizontal gradient; rows run in parallel, each row is a Span over the pixels. image.ForEachRow((row, y) => { for (int x = 0; x < row.Length; x++) { row[x] = new Rgba8((byte)x, (byte)(y * 4), 128, 255); } }); Each frame's pixels are a PixelPlane<TPixel>: rows of Span<TPixel>, and the whole frame as one span when it is stored in one block. PixelPlane<Rgba8> plane = image.Frames[0].Plane; if (plane.TryGetContiguous(out Span<Rgba8> all)) { all.Fill(Rgba8.White); // one Span over every pixel when the rows are stored back to back } else { for (int y = 0; y < plane.Height; y++) { plane.Row(y).Fill(Rgba8.White); } } RasterOps records each step of a chain; built-in steps and your own mix freely. // RasterOps records steps; Apply runs them in one pass where it can, in place when the size stays. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("egret.png"); photo.Apply(ops => ops .AutoOrient() .Cover(400, 300, Anchor.Center) .Saturation(1.1f) .Sharpen(1, 0.6f)); /// <summary>Black or white per pixel: ForEachBand gives each worker a band of rows from start to end.</summary> private sealed class Threshold(float level) : IRasterOperation { public Size OutputSize(Size input) => input; public void Run<TPixel>(OperationInput<TPixel> input) where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> { RowBandAction band = (start, end) => { for (int y = start; y < end; y++) { Span<TPixel> source = input.Source.Row(y), destination = input.Destination.Row(y); for (int x = 0; x < source.Length; x++) { Vector4 v = source[x].ToScaled(); float on = ((0.2126f * v.X) + (0.7152f * v.Y) + (0.0722f * v.Z)) >= level ? 1 : 0; destination[x] = TPixel.FromScaled(new Vector4(on, on, on, v.W)); } } }; input.ForEachBand(band); } } Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Interop with raw buffers // Pixels from somewhere else, such as a camera SDK: 640 × 480 BGRA, rows 2,560 bytes apart. byte[] buffer = new byte[2560 * 480]; // Wrap them without copying, work on them, and save. using (Raster<Bgra8> frame = Raster.Wrap<Bgra8>(buffer, 640, 480, byteStride: 2560)) { frame.Apply(ops => ops.FillColor(Rgba8.Black).Opacity(1)); frame.Save("frame.png"); } // Or copy the pixels out of a raster into your own buffer, row by row. using Raster<Rgba8> image = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("duck.png"); Rgba8[] pixels = new Rgba8[image.Width * image.Height]; for (int y = 0; y < image.Height; y++) { image.Row(y).CopyTo(pixels.AsSpan(y * image.Width, image.Width)); } Run it samples/Extending is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Extending writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/filters.html.title: Filters | Egami
articles/guides/filters.html.summary: Filters using Raster soft = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Blur(3), Ct); // Gaussian, sigma in pixels using Raster boxed = photo.Derive(ops => ops.BoxBlur(4), Ct); // fast, radius in pixels using Raster crisp = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Sharpen(0.8f, 1.5f), Ct); // unsharp mask: amount, sigma // Any kernel: here a 3 × 3 emboss, with edges clamped and alpha left alone. ConvolutionKernel emboss = new(3, 3, [-2, -1, 0, -1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 2]); using Raster embossed = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Convolve(emboss, EdgeMode.Clamp, preserveAlpha: true), Ct); Operation Does Blur(sigma, colorSpace) Gaussian blur, separable; exact up to sigma 100, three box passes above Blur(sigma, colorSpace, BlurMethod.Fast) Gaussian blur in constant time per pixel at any sigma, for shadows, glows and large blurs BoxBlur(radius) Mean of a square, in constant time per pixel whatever the radius Sharpen(amount, sigma) Unsharp mask: adds amount times the difference from a Gaussian blur Convolve(kernel, edge, preserveAlpha) Any ConvolutionKernel, separable ones in two passes Median(radius, includeAlpha) The median of each channel over a square: removes salt-and-pepper noise, keeps edges LensBlur(radius, options) An out-of-focus lens: points become discs or polygons BilateralBlur(spatialSigma, rangeSigma) Smooths flat areas, keeps edges MotionBlur(radius, sigma, angle) A streak in one direction, as ImageMagick's -motion-blur RotationalBlur(degrees, center) A spin around a point, as ImageMagick's -rotational-blur ZoomBlur(amount, center) Streaks along rays from a point AddNoise(kind, amount, monochrome, seed) ImageMagick's six noise kinds, the same for a seed at any thread count Despeckle() Crimmins' speckle removal, as ImageMagick's -despeckle Large blurs Blur(sigma) computes the exact Gaussian, so its cost grows with sigma. BlurMethod.Fast runs three box passes per axis whose widths and fractional end weights give exactly the Gaussian's variance (Gwosdek et al., 2011): it costs the same at sigma 5 or 500, about six times less than the exact blur at sigma 20, and stays within 50 dB PSNR of it from sigma 3 up. // A large, soft background blur: Fast costs the same at any sigma and is within 50 dB of the exact Gaussian from sigma 3. using Raster soft = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Blur(40, ColorSpace.Linear, BlurMethod.Fast), Ct); Median and despeckle Median works on the stored values, so 8 and 16-bit results are exactly ImageMagick's -statistic Median. Its cost per pixel does not grow with the radius. Despeckle is gentler: it nudges values a level at a time toward their neighbours and leaves edges alone, exactly as ImageMagick's -despeckle. // Salt-and-pepper noise disappears and edges stay sharp; radius 2 is a 5 × 5 window. photo.Apply(ops => ops.Median(2), Ct); // Clean a scan: specks shrink, edges and text stay. Median(1) is the stronger alternative. scan.Apply(ops => ops.Despeckle(), Ct); For heavy salt-and-pepper noise use Median(1) or Median(2) instead; both keep edges, and both give ImageMagick's pixels. Lens and bilateral blur LensBlur convolves with an aperture: a disc, or a polygon of 5 to 12 blades turned by Rotation. It works in linear light, since a lens adds light, and HighlightGain brightens light above HighlightThreshold before the blur, so small lights bloom into bright discs. It runs by FFT on tiles, so its cost does not grow with the radius. // Blur the background like a wide-open lens with a six-blade aperture: bright points become hexagons. LensBlurOptions lens = new() { Blades = 6, Rotation = 15, HighlightGain = 4, HighlightThreshold = 0.8f }; photo.Apply(ops => ops.Within(new Rect(0, 0, photo.Width, photo.Height / 3), o => o.LensBlur(12, lens)), Ct); LensBlur works in linear light, so bright points stay bright discs instead of gray smudges; Within with a mask feathers the edge between the sharp subject and the blurred background. BilateralBlur weighs each neighbour by its distance and by how different its color is, so noise flattens and edges stay. The color difference is the root-mean-square difference of red, green and blue on 0..1; on gray images the sigmas mean what ImageMagick's -bilateral-blur means, with its intensity sigma 255 times rangeSigma. // Smooth skin or sky while keeping edges: neighbours count less the more their color differs (0.1 on the 0..1 scale). using Raster smooth = photo.Derive(ops => ops.BilateralBlur(spatialSigma: 4, rangeSigma: 0.1f), Ct); Directional blurs MotionBlur takes ImageMagick's parameters: 2⌈radius⌉ + 1 samples along angle (clockwise, y down), weighted by a Gaussian of sigma. Egami reads between pixels bilinearly where ImageMagick rounds to the nearest pixel, so diagonal streaks are smoother. RotationalBlur and ZoomBlur take about one sample per pixel of path; their center is in pixels, with pixel centers at +0.5. using Raster moving = photo.Derive(ops => ops.MotionBlur(radius: 12, sigma: 4, angle: 15), Ct); // a streak toward 15° using Raster spinning = photo.Derive(ops => ops.RotationalBlur(8), Ct); // 8° around the center using Raster zooming = photo.Derive(ops => ops.ZoomBlur(0.2f, new System.Numerics.Vector2(320, 200)), Ct); Noise AddNoise adds ImageMagick's +noise kinds to red, green and blue, never alpha, with amount as ImageMagick's -attenuate. Each value's noise is a hash of the seed, frame and position, so the same seed gives the same pixels at any thread count, and inside Within an area gets the noise the whole image would get there. // Film grain: gray Gaussian noise at a third of ImageMagick's default strength; the same seed gives the same grain. photo.Apply(ops => ops.AddNoise(NoiseKind.Gaussian, 0.3f, monochrome: true, seed: 42), Ct); The grain depends only on the seed and the pixel's position, so a batch of frames with the same seed grains alike. Edges EdgeMode says what a kernel sees past the border: Clamp repeats the edge pixel (the default), Mirror reflects the image, Wrap tiles it, and Transparent treats it as transparent black. The filters above repeat the edge pixel, as ImageMagick's default virtual pixel does. Alpha Blurs work on premultiplied values internally, so transparent pixels do not bleed their color into opaque ones. preserveAlpha: true keeps the alpha channel as it was, for effects that should only change color. Median and Despeckle keep alpha unless asked; AddNoise never touches it. Run it samples/Filters is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Filters writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/h264.html.title: H.264 | Egami
articles/guides/h264.html.summary: H.264 Egami.Video.H264 decodes H.264 (AVC), the codec of most MP4 and MOV files from phones, cameras and the web. It is a separate, opt-in package because H.264 is covered by patents (see Patents); Egami.Video itself contains no H.264 decoder and copies H.264 tracks through untouched when this package is not registered. Profiles: Constrained Baseline, Main, High, High 10 and High 4:2:2, at 8 and 10 bits, 4:0:0, 4:2:0 and 4:2:2, and their Intra profiles. CAVLC and CABAC, B-frames with spatial and temporal direct prediction, weighted prediction, the 8x8 transform and scaling matrices, long-term references and several slices per frame. Interlaced streams: field pictures (PAFF) and MBAFF frames, whose macroblock pairs are each two frame or two field macroblocks. A frame's two fields come out woven into one frame, as FFmpeg gives them; see Interlaced video. Containers: MP4, MOV, Matroska and AVI through Egami.Video's readers, and raw Annex B .h264 files through H264Format. Frames equal FFmpeg's decode sample for sample on every clip in the test corpus and on the interlaced and FRExt conformance bitstreams of ITU-T H.264.1. Not decoded: 4:4:4 and lossless (High 4:4:4), and the Extended profile's data partitions, FMO, ASO and SP and SI slices. They give UnsupportedFormatException. Registering WithH264() (from H264MediaContextExtensions) adds the decoder, H264Codec, and the raw stream reader, H264Format, to a MediaContext. Nothing registers them on its own; set the context as the default with MediaContext.SetDefault to use it everywhere. // Opt in to H.264 once: WithH264() adds the decoder and the raw .h264 reader to a context. MediaContext.SetDefault makes it // the default for every call. MediaContext context = MediaContext.Default.WithH264(); using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("h264.mp4", context: context); Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.CodecId} {reader.Track.Width}x{reader.Track.Height}"); Decoding Frames come out in display order through VideoReader, like any other codec, as YuvVideoFrames with the stream's own planes (8-bit samples in bytes, 10-bit in ushorts) or converted to a pixel type. The colour comes from the stream's VUI, then the container, and otherwise BT.601 for 576 lines and fewer and BT.709 above; HDR10 mastering display and content light level SEI become the frame's Hdr, and HDR10+ user data SEI its Hdr10Plus. // Frames come out in display order, B-frames included; a broken slice is concealed from the frame before. using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("h264.mp4", new VideoReaderOptions { Errors = DecodeErrorMode.Conceal }, context); int count = 0; foreach (VideoFrame<Rgb8> frame in reader.ReadFrames<Rgb8>()) { using (frame) { if (count++ == 0) { frame.Raster.Save("first.png"); } } } Broken data follows VideoReaderOptions.Errors. A slice that cannot be read reports H264.CorruptFrame, and the macroblocks it leaves out are filled from the previous frame (Conceal, and Skip, the default) or the frame is finished and the error thrown (Throw). Decoding that starts in the middle of a stream waits for the next IDR or recovery point; a reference frame that is missing is replaced by the nearest one. Slices decode in parallel when a frame has several, and deblocking runs on EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads as a wave down the frame. Interlaced video An interlaced frame holds two fields, every other row each, filmed one after the other. The decoder gives the frame with both fields woven together and says how on the frame: FieldOrder is TopFieldFirst or BottomFieldFirst for an interlaced frame and Progressive otherwise, and RepeatFields counts the fields a frame is shown for beyond its two (3:2 pulldown and frame doubling). Both come from the picture timing SEI's pic_struct when the stream has it, else from how the frame was coded (two field pictures or an MBAFF frame) and the order of its fields, as ffprobe reports them. Deinterlacing is up to you; InterlaceDetector finds interlaced stretches in decoded video. // An interlaced frame comes out with its two fields woven; FieldOrder says which was filmed first. using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("interlaced.h264", context: context); foreach (VideoFrame frame in reader.ReadFrames()) { using (frame) { Console.WriteLine($"{frame.Timestamp}: {frame.FieldOrder}, {frame.RepeatFields} repeated fields"); orders.Add(frame.FieldOrder); } } A field without its second field, as a cut stream can end, comes out with its rows doubled into the missing field and reports H264.UnpairedField. Raw .h264 files H264Format reads raw Annex B streams (.h264, .264 and .avc), as encoders and ffmpeg -f h264 write them. Such a stream has no timestamps, so frames are timed by the stream's VUI frame rate, or 25 frames a second, unless FrameRate is set. Seeking goes back to the IDR frame before the target. // A raw .h264 stream has no timestamps: frames are timed by the stream's own frame rate, or 25 a second, unless you // register the format with a rate of your own. MediaContext context = MediaContext.Default.WithH264().WithContainer(new H264Format { FrameRate = new Rational(30, 1) }); using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("camera.h264", context: context); Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.Width}x{reader.Track.Height} at {reader.Track.FrameRate} fps"); // Remuxing keeps the stream as it is, here into MP4. MediaFile.Remux("camera.h264", "camera.mp4", context: context); Patents H.264 is covered by patents. Egami's authors grant no patent rights and are not lawyers. Whether you need a patent licence depends on your country and on how you use and distribute this package; commercial products may need one from the AVC patent pools or holders. Egami.Video does not depend on this package.

articles/guides/hdr.html.title: HDR images | Egami
articles/guides/hdr.html.summary: HDR images HDR images hold light brighter than SDR white. Egami loads HDR pixels as linear light in floating point, unclamped, with 1.0 as reference white (203 cd/m²), the same scale the color management guide's tone mapping and HDR metadata use. Radiance (.hdr) and OpenEXR (.exr) files hold such pixels directly; see the Radiance and OpenEXR pages. Phone photos carry HDR as a gain map beside an SDR picture, which this guide covers. PQ and HLG images are covered with their formats: AVIF, HEIC and JPEG XL. Gain maps An Ultra HDR JPEG, as Android phones, Chrome and Photoshop write it, is an SDR picture any viewer shows, followed (through MPF) by a gain map: how much brighter each part of the picture is in the HDR rendition. ISO 21496-1, Adobe's hdrgm XMP (Ultra HDR 1.0) and Apple's HDRGainMap are three ways of writing the same idea down; GainMapFormat says which a file used, and GainMapInfo holds its values, in log2 units as the standards give them. A load gives the SDR picture as stored, with the map in RasterMetadata.GainMap as a GainMap (GainMapValues per channel); a damaged map is dropped with Jpeg.GainMapDropped. ReaderOptions.Hdr asks for the HDR rendition instead: HdrDecode.Headroom is how much brighter than SDR white the display can go (or the map's full capacity), and the load gives linear RgbaF16, within about 1% of libultrahdr's decode. GainMap.Apply does the same for a raster in hand. // As stored: the SDR base image, with the gain map in the metadata. using Raster sdr = Raster.Load("ultrahdr.jpg"); GainMap? map = sdr.Metadata.GainMap; // null for a plain JPEG // The HDR rendition for a display 4x as bright as SDR white: linear half floats, 1.0 = SDR white. using Raster<RgbaF16> hdr = Raster.Load<RgbaF16>("ultrahdr.jpg", options: new ReaderOptions { Hdr = new HdrDecode { Headroom = 4 } }); // The same from a raster in hand, at the map's full capacity. using Raster<RgbaF16> full = map!.Apply(sdr); Saving as JPEG writes the map back, in both metadata forms, as Skia and libultrahdr write them. Crops, turns, flips and resizes move the map with the picture; operations that change pixel values drop it (Operation.GainMapDropped), as do other formats (Save.GainMapDropped) and JpegWriterOptions.KeepGainMap = false. // Crops, turns, flips and resizes move the gain map with the picture; saving as JPEG writes it back. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("ultrahdr.jpg"); using Raster cropped = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Crop(16, 16, 200, 150).Rotate(90)); cropped.Save("cropped.jpg"); // still Ultra HDR // Operations that change pixel values drop it (Operation.GainMapDropped), and so do formats other than JPEG // (Save.GainMapDropped); KeepGainMap = false leaves it out on purpose. cropped.Save("sdr-only.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { KeepGainMap = false }); To write an HDR raster as Ultra HDR, set JpegWriterOptions.GainMap: the raster is tone mapped to the SDR picture and GainMap.Create makes the map that brings it back. GainMapOptions has libultrahdr's defaults (a full-size, color map, gamma 1, quality 95) and each can be changed; Create also takes an SDR rendition you graded yourself. // An HDR raster as Ultra HDR: the SDR base, tone mapped with BT.2390, and a gain map that brings the HDR raster back. using Raster<RgbaF32> hdr = Raster.Load<RgbaF32>("render.exr"); hdr.Save("render.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90, GainMap = new GainMapOptions() }); // Or choose the SDR rendition: the map goes in its metadata, and saving as JPEG writes both. using Raster<Rgb8> sdr = hdr.Derive(ops => ops.ToneMap(ToneMapping.Reinhard)).As<Rgb8>(); sdr.Metadata.GainMap = GainMap.Create(hdr, sdr, new GainMapOptions { Scale = 4 }); sdr.Save("graded.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90 }); Saving HDR to an SDR format PNG, JPEG and the other 8 and 16-bit formats hold 0 to 1. Saving a floating-point raster to them clamps, as other libraries do; when the raster holds light above reference white, the save also reports Save.HdrClipped, naming ToneMap, which rolls the highlights off instead of cutting them. Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Show an Ultra HDR photo as HDR // An Ultra HDR photo for an HDR display whose peak is displayHeadroom times SDR white: linear light, 1.0 = SDR white, // here written as a half-float OpenEXR file; an SDR display shows the JPEG as it is. using Raster<RgbaF16> photo = Raster.Load<RgbaF16>("ultrahdr.jpg", options: new ReaderOptions { Hdr = new HdrDecode { Headroom = displayHeadroom } }); photo.Save("photo-hdr.exr"); The gain map is applied for the display's headroom: 1 gives the SDR picture, and the map's own capacity (leave Headroom null) the full HDR rendition. Make an Ultra HDR JPEG from an OpenEXR render // An HDR render as a JPEG every viewer opens, which HDR displays (Android, Chrome, Apple Photos) show brighter. using Raster<RgbaF32> render = Raster.Load<RgbaF32>("render.exr"); render.Save("render-ultrahdr.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90, GainMap = new GainMapOptions { Scale = 2 } }); The SDR picture is the render tone mapped with BT.2390; the gain map, half the size here, brings the HDR render back.

articles/guides/index.html.title: Guides | Egami
articles/guides/index.html.summary: Guides Each guide covers one area of Egami: what it does, the options and their defaults, and the limits. Many guides end with Recipes, short answers to common tasks such as making a favicon or blurring a face, with code you can copy. Every code sample compiles and runs in Egami's test run. The guides are grouped by package, and within Egami the groups go from the basics to the specialized. Within a group, pages are in alphabetical order. Each file format has its own page in Formats. If you are new, read Getting started first. Egami: basics What every user meets: pixel types, metadata, and how Egami uses memory and handles untrusted files. Diagnostics: warnings about damaged or unusual files, and how to log or reject them. Memory and threading: pooled memory, streaming decode and parallel work. Metadata: EXIF, IPTC and XMP, kept, edited or stripped. Performance: what keeps loading, editing and saving fast. Pixel types: how pixels are stored, and which type to pick. Security: the limits that make untrusted files safe to load. Formats The overview says what each format reads and writes and how a format is detected; then one page per format, with its options: AVIF BMP CCITT fax GIF HEIC (in the Egami.Heic package) ICO and CUR JBIG2 JPEG JPEG 2000 JPEG XL Netpbm OpenEXR PNG and APNG PSD and PSB QOI Radiance TGA TIFF VP8 video frames WebP Your own format: plug in a reader and writer for a format Egami does not have Egami: editing images Operations that run on a raster through Apply and Derive. Color: brightness, contrast, saturation and other CSS-style color filters. Compositing: blend modes and drawing one image over another. Edges and morphology: edge detection, Canny, and dilate, erode, open and close. Effects and shadows: vignette, glow, pixelate, oil paint and shadows. Filters: blurs, sharpening, convolution, noise and median. Keying and arithmetic: transparent colors, flood fill and arithmetic between images. Lighting and relief: bevels, embossing and lighting from a height map. Regions, masks and channels: edit part of an image, and move channels around. Resizing and geometry: resize, crop, rotate, warp and combine images. Tone and color: levels, curves, grading, auto fixes and thresholds. Egami: color and HDR Color management: ICC profiles, converting between color spaces, CMYK. HDR images: HDR pixels, gain maps and Ultra HDR photos. Planar YUV: video-style YUV planes in and out of JPEG, AVIF and video frames. Egami: analysis, palettes and animation Animation: frames, timing and animated GIF, APNG and WebP. Comparing and measuring: differences, statistics, hashes and visual regression tests. Palettes and dithering: reducing colors and indexed images. Text recognition (OCR): one shape for every OCR engine, any OCR program as an engine, and hOCR and ALTO files. Egami: extending Custom operations and formats: write your own operation or pixel type, or wrap your own memory. Egami.Drawing Drawing: paths, shapes, strokes, paints, layers and recorded drawings on a canvas. Drawing files (.egdr): the file format for recorded drawings. Egami.Fonts Fonts and text: loading fonts, drawing text and preparing fonts for PDF. Paragraph layout: line breaking, justification, columns and vertical text. Unicode text and shaping: complex scripts, bidirectional text and emoji. Matching System.Drawing text: drawing UI text as GDI+ and GDI do on Windows. Egami.Svg and Egami.Css CSS: parse style sheets, match selectors and run the cascade. SVG: read, edit, save and draw SVG. Egami.Metafiles Windows metafiles: play WMF, EMF and EMF+ pictures onto a canvas. Egami.SystemDrawing System.Drawing drop-in: System.Drawing's Bitmap, Image and codec API on every OS. Egami.Video Video: probe, read, write and remux video, with Egami rasters as frames. Streaming MP4: fragmented MP4 for forward-only streams, and HLS and DASH segments. Audio: decode, encode, resample and mix audio. Encoding Opus: Opus files, settings and WebM audio. Subtitles: read, edit, retime and convert SRT, WebVTT and ASS subtitle files. Egami.Barcodes Barcodes: write 1D and 2D barcodes. Reading barcodes: find and decode barcodes in images.

articles/guides/keying-and-arithmetic.ht.title: Keying and arithmetic | Egami
articles/guides/keying-and-arithmetic.ht.summary: Keying and arithmetic Operations that ImageMagick users expect: making a color transparent, replacing a color, flood fill, arithmetic with a constant, and stacking several images. Each matches its ImageMagick option exactly at 8 and 16 bits. For green and blue screens there is also a chroma key with spill removal. Color tolerance Keying compares colors with ImageMagick's -fuzz distance on the stored values: a tolerance from 0 (the exact color) to 1 (every color). Alpha counts three times as much as each color channel, and colors count in proportion to how visible both pixels are, so two fully transparent pixels always match. Make a color transparent // Remove a green screen: within 0.15 of pure green becomes transparent, and alpha ramps back over the next 0.1 for soft edges. photo.Apply(ops => ops.MakeTransparent(new Rgba8(0, 177, 64, 255), tolerance: 0.15f, softness: 0.1f), Ct); Raise the tolerance until the screen is gone, then add softness for clean hair and edges. MakeTransparent clears alpha where a pixel lies within the tolerance and keeps its color, as ImageMagick's -transparent does. softness ramps alpha back up over the next band of distance, for antialiased edges; with no softness the result is ImageMagick's. Key out a green or blue screen // Key out a green screen by chroma, so its lighter and darker patches go too, soften the edge, and take the green cast off // what is left; then put the result over a new background. photo.Apply(ops => ops .ChromaKey(new Rgba8(0, 177, 64, 255), similarity: 0.12f, blend: 0.06f) .Despill(DespillColor.Green, mix: 0.5f), Ct); backdrop.Apply(ops => ops.DrawImage(photo, new Point(0, 0)), Ct); ChromaKey compares chroma alone: the distance between the Rec. 709 Cb and Cr of each pixel and of the screen color, as a share of the largest such distance (green to magenta). Luma is left out, so lighter and darker patches of an unevenly lit screen stay closer to the key than they do by MakeTransparent's RGB distance. similarity sets the distance that becomes fully transparent and blend the band over which alpha returns to full. Pixels keep their color and their alpha is scaled, so an already transparent pixel stays transparent. Types without alpha are left as they are. Despill removes the screen's colored cast from what remains. It holds green (or blue, with DespillColor.Blue) down to a limit taken from the other two channels: their average with mix 0, the larger of them with mix 1, which leaves neutral colors alone. expand lowers the limit further for heavy spill. Despill works on any raster, keyed or not. Replace a color photo.Apply(ops => ops.ReplaceColor(Rgba8.White, new Rgba8(250, 245, 230, 255), tolerance: 0.05f), Ct); Flood fill // Fill the region around (10, 10) whose colors are close to its own, as a paint bucket does. photo.Apply(ops => ops.FloodFill(new Point(10, 10), Rgba8.White, tolerance: 0.1f), Ct); FloodFill fills the region connected to the seed whose colors lie within the tolerance of the seed's own. It spreads to the four side neighbours by default, as ImageMagick does; Connectivity.Eight adds the diagonals. Its visited set, one bit a pixel, counts against MaxTotalBytes. Inside a scope, the region is found within the scope's area. Select by color // Select by color, then edit only the selection: a magic wand from a point, and every pixel close to a color. using Raster<Gray8> wand = photo.FloodMask(new Point(30, 30), tolerance: 0.12f); using Raster<Gray8> reds = photo.ColorMask(new Rgba8(200, 40, 30, 255), tolerance: 0.2f); photo.Apply(ops => ops .Within(new Mask(wand), o => o.Blur(4)) .Within(new Mask(reds), o => o.Saturation(1.4f)), Ct); ColorMask and FloodMask return a Gray8 mask, 255 inside the selection, for Within(Mask, …). Arithmetic with a constant // Lift the shadows with a log curve, then cap the highlights; values are on a 0 to 1 scale, as ImageMagick's -evaluate. photo.Apply(ops => ops .Arithmetic(PixelMath.Log, 3) .Arithmetic(PixelMath.Min, 0.95f), Ct); Arithmetic applies a PixelMath operator (add, subtract, multiply, divide, pow, log, min, max, set) to the chosen channels, on values scaled 0 to 1 and clamped. 8-bit and 16-bit pixels are evaluated as 16-bit samples and rounded as ImageMagick's Q16 build rounds them, so the result equals -evaluate exactly. Stack images // Average a burst of photos to smooth noise; the median removes things that appear in only a few frames. using Raster mean = Raster.Stack([first, second, third], StackMode.Mean); using Raster clean = Raster.Stack([first, second, third], StackMode.Median); Raster.Stack combines the same channel of the same pixel across two or more rasters (StackMode: mean, median, min, max), as ImageMagick's -evaluate-sequence does for mean, min and max. The median is taken per channel, as Photoshop's median stack does; ImageMagick's picks the whole pixel whose intensity is the median. Stack works a few rows at a time, holding one row of each input.

articles/guides/lighting-and-relief.html.title: Lighting and relief | Egami
articles/guides/lighting-and-relief.html.summary: Lighting and relief Three steps treat an image as a height field and light it. Lighting is the SVG 1.1 lighting filters, with Skia's parameters; Emboss and Shade are the two quick relief effects ImageMagick users know. Operation Does Lighting(light, model, options) SVG's feDiffuseLighting or feSpecularLighting with a distant, point or spot light: returns the light map, or blends it onto the image Emboss(angle, depth, sigma, grayscale) Blurs, takes the slope toward the light, and adds mid gray: flat areas become 0.5 Shade(azimuth, elevation, colored) ImageMagick's -shade (gray relief) or +shade (the shading multiplied onto the colors), identical at 8 bits Lights and surfaces // Three light sources, as SVG and Skia have them. Positions are pixels: x right, y down, z up out of the image. Light sun = new DistantLight(azimuth: 225, elevation: 40); // from the top left, 40° up Light bulb = new PointLight(new Vector3(60, 20, 80)) { Color = new Rgba8(255, 240, 210, 255) }; Light spot = new SpotLight(new Vector3(0, 0, 150), target: new Vector3(120, 60, 0), exponent: 4, coneAngle: 30); // Two ways a surface reflects: matte (N·L) or shiny (a highlight, (N·H)^shininess). LightingModel matte = LightingModel.Diffuse(kd: 1.2f); LightingModel shiny = LightingModel.Specular(ks: 1, shininess: 20); using Raster<Rgba8> map = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(sun, matte), Ct); // the light map, opaque using Raster<Rgba8> glints = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(bulb, shiny), Ct); // alpha = brightest channel using Raster<Rgba8> pool = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(spot, matte), Ct); The height is alpha by default, as in SVG and Skia: a logo on a transparent canvas stands up from it. SurfaceScale is the height of a fully opaque (or white) pixel, in pixels, so larger values give steeper slopes. Normals come from SVG's 3 × 3 Sobel stencils, with SVG's own stencils on the edges and corners of the image. DistantLight(azimuth, elevation) shines from one direction everywhere. The azimuth is SVG's: degrees clockwise from the x axis, with y down, so 225 is the top left. PointLight(position) and SpotLight(position, target, exponent, coneAngle) sit at a point in pixel coordinates, with z above the image; pixel centers are at x + 0.5, as Skia evaluates them. A spot light fades as cos(angle)^exponent away from its axis and stops at the cone angle, with Skia's soft cone edge. LightingModel.Diffuse(kd) gives the light's color times kd times N·L, and an opaque map. LightingModel.Specular(ks, shininess) gives a highlight, ks times (N·H)^shininess, and a map whose alpha is its brightest channel. Light colors and the light map are not color-managed: they work on stored values, as Skia does in its working space. SVG's default of computing filters in linear light is not applied; convert the image first if you need it. // A photo's luminance as the height: light areas stand up. SurfaceScale is the height of white, in pixels. LightingOptions relief = new() { Height = HeightSource.Luminance, SurfaceScale = 6 }; using Raster lit = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(new DistantLight(300, 50), LightingModel.Diffuse(), relief), Ct); // The same light blended onto the photo instead of replacing it. using Raster shaded = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(new DistantLight(300, 50), LightingModel.Diffuse(1.3f), relief with { Blend = BlendMode.Overlay }), Ct); A bevelled logo With Blend, the light map is blended onto the image with a 2.5.1 BlendMode, the light map as the source, and the image keeps its alpha, so the light changes the color and never the shape. Multiply shades the slopes away from the light; Screen adds a specular highlight on the slopes that face it. // A logo on a transparent canvas: alpha is the height, so soften its edges first to give them a slope. logo.Apply(ops => ops .Blur(2.5f) .Lighting(new DistantLight(225, 35), LightingModel.Diffuse(1.4f), new LightingOptions { SurfaceScale = 5, Blend = BlendMode.Multiply }) // shade the slopes .Lighting(new DistantLight(225, 35), LightingModel.Specular(0.8f, 24), new LightingOptions { SurfaceScale = 5, Blend = BlendMode.Screen }), Ct); // and add a highlight logo.Save("bevel.png"); Embossed text Emboss turns a page or a photo into gray relief: it blurs with sigma, takes the slope toward the light with a 3 × 3 Sobel stencil, scales it by depth and adds mid gray, so paper becomes flat gray and strokes rise.
