The angle is counterclockwise from the right with y up, as ImageMagick's -shade azimuth (135 is the top left). grayscale: false embosses each color channel on its own; alpha is kept. // Gray relief: flat paper becomes mid gray, strokes rise toward the light at the top left. using Raster embossed = page.Derive(ops => ops.Emboss(angle: 135, depth: 3, sigma: 1), Ct); // Each color channel on its own, softer and deeper. using Raster colored = page.Derive(ops => ops.Emboss(angle: 45, depth: 6, sigma: 2, grayscale: false), Ct); ImageMagick's -emboss shares only the name: it sharpens along a diagonal and then equalizes the histogram, so its results differ from this classic emboss. Shade Shade is ImageMagick's -shade: the luminance is the height, and each pixel becomes the Lambertian shading by a light at the azimuth (counterclockwise from the right, y up) and elevation; flat areas get sin(elevation). colored: true multiplies the shading onto the colors, as +shade does. Results are identical to ImageMagick 7 (Q16 HDRI) at 8 bits; alpha is kept. // ImageMagick's -shade 30x30 (identical at 8 bits) and +shade 120x45. using Raster gray = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Shade(azimuth: 30, elevation: 30), Ct); using Raster colored = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Shade(azimuth: 120, elevation: 45, colored: true), Ct); Edges and regions All three keep the size and read one pixel past each output (Emboss also the blur's reach), repeating the edge pixel past the border. They work inside Within and OnChannels: inside a region they read the real pixels around it, and a point or spot light keeps its position in the raster's coordinates.

articles/guides/lossless-archiving.html.title: Lossless archiving with FFV1 | Egami
articles/guides/lossless-archiving.html.summary: Lossless archiving with FFV1 FFV1 (RFC 9043) is the lossless video codec memory institutions archive with: a decode gives back every sample, each slice of every frame carries a CRC, and every frame can stand on its own. Egami.Video reads and writes it in Matroska and AVI with no native code, frame for frame equal to FFmpeg's decoder, and FFmpeg decodes Egami.Video's files to the same samples. Writing a master Pick VideoCodecs.Ffv1 and write frames as you would with any codec. Planes keep their layout and depth (4:2:0, 4:2:2, 4:4:4, 4:1:1, 4:1:0 or gray, with or without alpha, 8 to 16 bits), so a 10-bit 4:2:2 capture stays 10-bit 4:2:2. Write Matroska (.mkv), the usual archival pairing; AVI works too. // An uncompressed 10-bit 4:4:4 capture into an FFV1 master: the planes keep their layout and depth, and the defaults are // the archival profile (version 3, every frame a keyframe, a CRC on every slice). using (VideoReader capture = VideoReader.Open("capture.y4m")) using (VideoWriter master = VideoWriter.Create("master.mkv", new VideoWriterOptions { Codec = VideoCodecs.Ffv1, FrameRate = capture.Track.FrameRate ?? new Rational(25, 1), })) { foreach (YuvVideoFrame frame in capture.ReadFrames()) { using (frame) { master.WriteFrame(frame); } } } The defaults are the profile archives use, which FFmpeg users get by adding -level 3 -g 1 -slicecrc 1 -slices 16: Setting Default FFmpeg flag Version 3, with a configuration record in the container -level 3 Keyframes every frame (KeyframeInterval 1) -g 1 Slice CRCs on (Ffv1EncoderOptions.SliceCrc) -slicecrc 1 Slices 1 up to 352×288, 4 up to 720p, 16 up to 1440p, 24 above -slices Coder range coder with a custom state table -coder range_tab Context model small (Effort up to 6) -context 0 Files come within 1 % of FFmpeg's size at the same settings, and slices are coded in parallel on EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads with the same file at any thread count. Checking fixity Ffv1Codec.Verify checks the configuration record's CRC and every slice's without decoding a picture, about 50 times faster than a decode, so it suits routine checks of a whole collection. Ffv1VerifyResult.Errors names each damaged frame and slice. A decode with Errors = DecodeErrorMode.Conceal reports the same damage as Ffv1.SliceCrc and shows the last good frame in the damaged slice's place. After a migration, a full check decodes the master and compares it with the source: // A routine fixity check: every slice's CRC, without decoding a picture. Ffv1VerifyResult check = Ffv1Codec.Verify("master.mkv"); Console.WriteLine($"{check.Frames} frames, {check.Slices} slices: {(check.IsIntact ? "intact" : $"{check.Errors.Count} damaged")}"); // A full check after migration: decode the master and compare every sample with the source. using VideoReader source = VideoReader.Open("capture.y4m"); using VideoReader master = VideoReader.Open("master.mkv"); int frames = 0, different = 0; foreach (YuvVideoFrame original in source.ReadFrames()) { using (original) using (YuvVideoFrame copy = master.ReadFrame()!) { frames++; different += SamePlanes(original.Raster, copy.Raster) ? 0 : 1; } } Console.WriteLine($"{frames} frames compared, {different} differ"); Version 0 and 1 files, and version 3 files written without slice CRCs, have nothing to check per slice: HasSliceCrcs is false. RGB sources Scanned film, graphics and screen captures in RGB stay RGB: frames given as RGB rasters (8 or 16 bits a channel) are coded through FFV1's reversible color transform, and decode as G, B and R planes tagged YuvMatrix.Identity, which convert back to RGB exactly. // Scanned film or graphics in RGB stays RGB: frames given as RGB rasters are coded through FFV1's reversible color // transform and come back exactly, here as 16-bit RGB for a restoration tool. using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("scan.mkv", new VideoWriterOptions { Codec = VideoCodecs.Ffv1, FrameRate = new Rational(24, 1) })) { writer.WriteFrame(duck); } using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("scan.mkv"); using VideoFrame<Rgb16> restored = reader.ReadFrames<Rgb16>().First(); Planes decoded from a 9, 11, 13, 14 or 15-bit source sit in 10, 12 or 16-bit planes with their samples shifted up; set Ffv1EncoderOptions.BitDepth to write them back at the source depth. The track's BitDepth gives the depth a file holds. Working copies For copies made to work on rather than to keep, Golomb-Rice coding is faster than the range coder, spacing keyframes makes files smaller, and more slices use more cores. Quality does not apply to FFV1, and setting it reports Ffv1.QualityIgnored. // Smaller and faster masters for a working copy: Golomb-Rice coding, a keyframe every second, more slices for more cores. // Slice CRCs stay on, so Ffv1Codec.Verify still checks every frame. VideoWriterOptions mezzanine = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.Ffv1, FrameRate = new Rational(25, 1), KeyframeInterval = 25, Ffv1 = new Ffv1EncoderOptions { Coder = Ffv1Coder.GolombRice, Slices = 24 }, };

articles/guides/memory-and-threading.htm.title: Memory and threading | Egami
articles/guides/memory-and-threading.htm.summary: Memory and threading The context // Everything that is not specific to one call lives in an immutable EgamiContext. Change it with `with`. EgamiContext context = EgamiContext.Default with { MaxParallelism = 4, // threads one operation may use; 1 is sequential Limits = SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxPixels = 50_000_000 }, }; using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.png", context); image.Apply(ops => ops.Blur(2)); // uses the raster's context: 4 threads at most A raster remembers the context it was loaded or created with, and its operations use it. EgamiContext.Default serves every call that passes none; EgamiContext.SetDefault replaces it once, at startup, before anything reads it. Threads Operations split the image into bands of rows and run them on up to MaxParallelism threads (the processor count by default). Small images run on one thread, where splitting would cost more than it saves. Decoding is mostly sequential by nature; JPEG splits files at their restart markers, pipelines progressive scans and converts in parallel bands, and animated formats map frames in parallel. PNG compresses large images on several threads when PngWriterOptions.ParallelCompression is set, with the same bytes at any thread count. Rasters are not thread-safe: do not run two chains on the same raster at once. Separate rasters, contexts and loads are independent, and readers, writers and contexts can be shared freely. Streaming RasterDecoder decodes a band of rows or a frame at a time, so an image never has to exist whole: // A band of rows at a time: memory is the band plus the format's working set, whatever the image size. using RasterDecoder decoder = RasterDecoder.Open("egret.png"); Console.WriteLine($"{decoder.Info.Width}×{decoder.Info.Height}, {decoder.Info.Access}, holding {decoder.Info.WorkingBytes:N0} bytes"); using Raster<Gray8> band = Raster.Create<Gray8>(decoder.Info.Width, 64); int rows; while ((rows = decoder.ReadRows(band)) > 0) { for (int y = 0; y < rows; y++) { foreach (Gray8 pixel in band.Row(y)) { sum += pixel.L; } } } ReaderOptions.Region decodes only a rectangle and MinimumSize a reduced size, in Load, Probe and the decoder alike. RasterInfo.Access says whether a format streams its rows (RasterAccess.Streamed) or is decoded into a buffer first (RasterAccess.Buffered), and WorkingBytes how much the decode holds besides your band: // Only a rectangle, at a quarter of its size or a little more. ReaderOptions options = new() { Region = new Rect(100, 200, 256, 256), MinimumSize = new Size(64, 64) }; RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("egret.png", options: options); // Access and WorkingBytes before decoding using Raster tile = Raster.Load("egret.png", options: options); Raster.LoadInto decodes into a raster you already have, and ReadFrame gives an animation one composed frame at a time: // Decode into a raster you already have: video frames and pooled images reuse their memory. using Raster<Rgb8> reused = Raster.Create<Rgb8>(480, 640); Raster.LoadInto("egret.png", reused); // An animation one composed frame at a time, into one reused canvas. using RasterDecoder gif = RasterDecoder.Open("pan.gif"); using Raster<Rgba8> canvas = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(gif.Info.Width, gif.Info.Height); while (gif.ReadFrame(canvas) is Metadata.FrameMetadata frame) { Console.WriteLine($"frame {count++}, shown for {frame.Delay.TotalMilliseconds} ms"); } RasterDecoder.OpenIncremental decodes while the bytes are still arriving: Append each chunk as it comes, read the rows finished so far, and call EndOfInput after the last. Status (a DecodeStatus) says whether rows are ready, more bytes are needed, or the frame or image is done, and RenderPreview draws an interlaced PNG, a progressive JPEG or a GIF frame as far as it has arrived. Files that are decoded into a buffer first (such as bottom-up BMP and TGA) wait for the end. // Decode while the bytes arrive, a chunk at a time, as from a download. using RasterDecoder decoder = RasterDecoder.OpenIncremental(); Raster<Rgb8>? band = null; foreach (ReadOnlyMemory<byte> chunk in file.Chunk(4096).Select(c => new ReadOnlyMemory<byte>(c))) { decoder.Append(chunk.Span); if (decoder.HeaderRead) { band ??= Raster.Create<Rgb8>(decoder.Info.Width, 16); int rows; while ((rows = decoder.ReadRows(band)) > 0) { rowsSoFar += rows; // the rows finished so far; an interlaced file shows RenderPreview instead } } } decoder.EndOfInput(); while (decoder.ReadRows(band!) is int rest and > 0) { rowsSoFar += rest; } band?.Dispose(); On a server, RasterDecoder.OpenAsync reads an asynchronous stream the same way, and LoadAsync from a stream that cannot seek, such as a request body, no longer holds the whole file while it decodes: // On a server: read rows as the upload arrives, without holding the whole file. await using Stream upload = File.OpenRead("egret.png"); using RasterDecoder decoder = await RasterDecoder.OpenAsync(upload, cancellationToken: TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); using Raster<Gray8> band = Raster.Create<Gray8>(decoder.Info.Width, 32); int rows; while ((rows = await decoder.ReadRowsAsync(band, TestContext.Current.CancellationToken)) > 0) { for (int y = 0; y < rows; y++) { sum += band.Row(y)[0].L; } } RasterEncoder writes the other way: a band of rows or a frame at a time, into a file or stream, with the bytes Save writes. Options that need every pixel before the first byte, such as an automatic palette, PNG's Reduce or choosing alpha by looking at the pixels, throw NotSupportedException at Create and say what to set instead. BMP and TGA store rows bottom-up: on a stream that cannot seek they are written top-down, as is run-length TGA, and an APNG there needs PngWriterOptions.FrameCount. An interlaced PNG (PngWriterOptions.Interlace) holds the rows until the last one, since its first pass needs the whole height. // A huge image written a band at a time: only the band is ever in memory. const int Width = 8_000, Height = 6_000; using Raster<Rgb8> band = Raster.Create<Rgb8>(Width, 64); using RasterEncoder<Rgb8> encoder = RasterEncoder.Create<Rgb8>("big.png", Width, Height); for (int top = 0; top < Height; top += band.Height) { int rows = Math.Min(band.Height, Height - top); for (int y = 0; y < rows; y++) { band.Row(y).Fill(new Rgb8((byte)(top + y), 128, 200)); } encoder.WriteRows(band, rows); } encoder.Complete(); // writes IEND; without it the file is deleted on dispose // An animation written a frame at a time, each frame from one reused canvas. using Raster<Rgba8> canvas = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(120, 80); using FileStream file = File.Create("spinner.gif"); using RasterEncoder<Rgba8> gif = RasterEncoder.Create<Rgba8>(file, GifFormat.Info, 120, 80); for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) { for (int y = 0; y < canvas.Height; y++) { canvas.Row(y).Fill(new Rgba8(255, 255, 255, 255)); } canvas.Row(40)[(i * 10)..((i * 10) + 10)].Fill(new Rgba8(200, 0, 0, 255)); gif.WriteFrame(canvas, new Metadata.FrameMetadata { Delay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(80) }); } gif.Complete(); WriteRowsAsync and CompleteAsync write each band out asynchronously, and SaveAsync now does the same instead of encoding the whole file into memory first: // On a server: send each band as it is encoded, without holding the file. using RasterDecoder source = RasterDecoder.Open("egret.png"); using Raster<Rgb8> band = Raster.Create<Rgb8>(source.Info.Width, 32); using RasterEncoder<Rgb8> encoder = RasterEncoder.Create<Rgb8>(response, JpegFormat.Info, source.Info.Width, source.Info.Height); int rows; while ((rows = source.ReadRows(band)) > 0) { await encoder.WriteRowsAsync(band, rows, TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); } await encoder.CompleteAsync(TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); Raster.Transcode joins the two: rows go from the decoder through a short chain of operations into the encoder, so a thumbnail of a 20,000 × 20,000 PNG holds well under a megabyte of pixels instead of 1.6 GB. When the chain starts with Fit, Cover or Resize, the decoder already shrinks by a whole factor (MinimumSize), and a leading Crop becomes Region. The chain may crop, resize, mirror left to right and adjust colors pixel by pixel; anything that needs rows out of order or the whole image, such as Blur or Rotate, throws NotSupportedException before anything is written. // A thumbnail of a big file without ever holding the full image: the decoder already shrinks by a whole factor. Raster.Transcode("egret.png", "thumb.jpg", x => x.Fit(256, 256).Saturation(1.1f)); // On a server: an upload to a 512-pixel PNG preview, streamed both ways. await using Stream upload = File.OpenRead("egret.png"); await Raster.TranscodeAsync(upload, response, PngFormat.Info, x => x.Fit(512, 512), cancellationToken: TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); Pixel memory Pixel memory never lives on the garbage-collected heap as large arrays. PooledPixelMemorySource.Shared hands out pooled arrays for small blocks and 64-byte-aligned unmanaged memory for large ones, keeps up to 128 MB of freed blocks for reuse, and splits very large images into blocks of whole rows. Trim() frees what it keeps. You can plug in your own source through EgamiContext.Memory by implementing IPixelMemorySource. Finding leaks PixelMemoryUsage usage = PooledPixelMemorySource.Shared.Usage; Console.WriteLine($"{usage.LiveBlocks} blocks, {usage.LiveBytes:N0} bytes in use"); // Looking for a raster someone forgot to dispose: track leaks for a while, with stack traces. usage.CaptureStackTraces = true; usage.LeakDetected += (_, leak) => Console.WriteLine($"{leak.Bytes:N0} bytes never disposed, allocated at\n{leak.StackTrace}"); usage.TrackLeaks = true; LiveBlocks and LiveBytes are always counted, at the cost of one atomic addition per allocation. TrackLeaks gives each new block a small finalizable tracker, so turn it on only while you look; CaptureStackTraces makes allocations much slower still. LeakDetected runs on the finalizer thread. Leaks come only through LeakDetected, never through the diagnostics handler, which reports what one call found. Your own memory source // Every pixel buffer comes from the context's IPixelMemorySource; wrap the pooled one to count what it hands out. CountingSource counting = new(PooledPixelMemorySource.Shared); EgamiContext context = EgamiContext.Default with { Memory = counting }; using (Raster<Rgba8> image = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(512, 512, context)) { image.Apply(ops => ops.Blur(2)); } Console.WriteLine($"{counting.Blocks} blocks, {counting.Bytes:N0} bytes"); private sealed class CountingSource(IPixelMemorySource inner) : IPixelMemorySource { public int Blocks; public long Bytes; public int MaxBlockBytes => inner.MaxBlockBytes; public IMemoryOwner<byte> Allocate(int byteLength, ClearMode clear) { Interlocked.Increment(ref Blocks); Interlocked.Add(ref Bytes, byteLength); return inner.Allocate(byteLength, clear); // ClearMode.Zero when the caller needs zeroed memory } } // In tests or debug builds: report a raster that was never disposed, and where it was allocated. PooledPixelMemorySource memory = new(); memory.Usage.TrackLeaks = true; memory.Usage.CaptureStackTraces = true; memory.Usage.LeakDetected += (sender, e) => Console.Error.WriteLine($"Leaked {e.Bytes:N0} bytes, allocated at:\n{e.StackTrace}"); Run it samples/MemoryAndThreading is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/MemoryAndThreading writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/metadata.html.title: Metadata | Egami
articles/guides/metadata.html.summary: Metadata raster.Metadata holds what a file says beside its pixels. It is kept apart from the pixels, survives operations unless an operation makes it wrong, and is written back by every format that can carry it. Item Read from Written to Exif (ExifData) JPEG, PNG (eXIf, and the legacy "Raw profile type" chunks) JPEG, PNG Iptc (IptcData) JPEG (APP13), PNG ("Raw profile type iptc") JPEG, PNG Xmp, XmpData JPEG (with extended XMP), PNG, GIF JPEG, PNG, GIF IccProfile JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP (V5) JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP Text PNG text chunks, GIF comments, PNM comments, TGA author and comments The same Resolution PNG, JPEG, BMP PNG, JPEG, BMP ColorSpace, Gamma PNG, QOI, TGA PNG, QOI LoopCount, frame Delay GIF, APNG GIF, APNG FormatDetails Every format: what only it has The same format, for round trips Warnings Every reader: what a lenient read recovered from Never RasterMetadata metadata = image.Metadata; metadata.Text.Add(new TextEntry("Comment", "Made with Egami")); metadata.Resolution = new Resolution(300, 300, ResolutionUnit.PerInch); Console.WriteLine($"{metadata.ColorSpace}, ICC {metadata.IccProfile.Length} bytes, XMP {metadata.Xmp.Length} bytes"); foreach (EgamiDiagnostic warning in metadata.Warnings) { Console.WriteLine($"Recovered from: {warning.Message} ({warning.Id})"); } image.Save("duck-300dpi.png"); EXIF if (image.Metadata.Exif is ExifData exif) { Console.WriteLine($"{exif.CameraMake} {exif.CameraModel}, {exif.DateTaken}, {exif.Location}"); if (exif.TryGet(ExifKey.ExposureTime, out ExifEntry? exposure)) { Console.WriteLine($"1/{1 / exposure.AsDouble():0} s"); } exif.Set(ExifKey.Copyright, "© 2026 Example"); exif.Remove(ExifKey.GpsLatitude); } Common values have typed properties (Orientation, DateTaken, CameraMake, CameraModel, Location); any tag can be read with TryGet and written with Set. A block you do not edit is saved back byte for byte; an edited one is laid out again, in tag order. A damaged block keeps its raw bytes and sets IsDamaged, and the pixels still load. ExifData.Parse reads a block on its own, capped by SafetyLimits.MaxMetadataBytes. What operations do to metadata Rotating, flipping and AutoOrient set the EXIF orientation to Normal and drop the embedded thumbnail, which would otherwise show sideways. Resizing and cropping, including your own operations that change the size, update the EXIF pixel dimensions and drop the embedded thumbnail, which no longer matches. Every geometry operation moves the EXIF SubjectArea and SubjectLocation with the picture: shifted by crops and pads, scaled by resizes, mirrored and turned with flips and rotations, clipped to a crop and dropped when the subject leaves it. Their XMP copies, and the XMP tiff:Orientation, exif:PixelXDimension and exif:PixelYDimension, follow the same rules. A tag the file does not have is never added. Color operations change nothing in the metadata. Removing metadata // Every writer's options have StripMetadata: the pixels are written, EXIF, XMP, ICC and text are not. image.Save("clean.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { StripMetadata = true }); Typed EXIF values using Raster photo = Raster.Load("sideways.jpg"); ExifData exif = photo.Metadata.Exif ?? new ExifData(); // Typed values go in with their EXIF type; fractions are exact numerator / denominator pairs. exif.Set(ExifKey.ExposureTime, new ExifFraction(1, 250)); exif.Set(ExifKey.Artist, "A. Photographer"); if (exif.TryGet(ExifKey.ExposureTime, out ExifEntry? entry) && entry.Type == ExifType.Rational) { Console.WriteLine($"Exposure {entry.AsFraction()} s = {entry.AsFraction().ToDouble()} s, in the {entry.Key.Ifd} IFD"); } if (exif.Location is GeoPosition where) { Console.WriteLine($"Taken at {where.Latitude:F5}, {where.Longitude:F5}"); } The IFD1 thumbnail decodes as a raster, and a new one is made from any raster. Crops, resizes, flips and turns drop the thumbnail, since it no longer shows the image: using Raster photo = Raster.Load("sideways.jpg"); // The thumbnail as stored, if the file has one; ReadThumbnail returns null otherwise. using (Raster<Rgb8>? stored = photo.Metadata.Exif?.ReadThumbnail()) { Console.WriteLine(stored is null ? "No thumbnail" : $"Thumbnail {stored.Width} x {stored.Height}"); } // Turning the image drops the thumbnail, which would show sideways; make a new one from the result. photo.Apply(ops => ops.AutoOrient()); photo.Metadata.Exif?.SetThumbnail(photo); photo.Save("upright.jpg"); The Windows XP tags (ExifKey.XPTitle, XPComment, XPAuthor, XPKeywords, XPSubject) and the encoded strings (ExifKey.UserComment, GpsProcessingMethod, GpsAreaInformation) read and write as text through ExifEntry.AsString and ExifData.Set, in the encodings Windows Explorer and cameras use. EXIF stored somewhere else, such as a database, parses on its own: // EXIF from somewhere other than an image file (a database column, a sidecar), with a cap on the bytes of values read. ExifData exif = ExifData.Parse(tiff.Span, SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxMetadataBytes = 64 * 1024 }); foreach (string warning in exif.Warnings) { Console.WriteLine($"EXIF: {warning}"); } IPTC IptcData holds IPTC-IIM datasets, as news agencies, stock libraries and Lightroom write them. Each IptcEntry has an IptcKey (record and dataset, such as 2:25 for keywords), and typed getters cover the common ones. Values longer than the IIM specification allows are refused on Set and Add; long text belongs in XMP. Text that is not ASCII switches the block to UTF-8. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("sideways.jpg"); IptcData iptc = photo.Metadata.Iptc ?? new IptcData(); iptc.Headline = "Harbour at dawn"; iptc.Keywords = [.. iptc.Keywords, "harbour", "Bergen"]; // Any dataset by its key; Add appends to the repeatable ones. iptc.Set(IptcKey.City, "Bergen"); // Text that is not ASCII sets the coded character set (1:90) to UTF-8, so other programs read it right. iptc.Caption = "Fishing boats at Bryggen, Bergen — first light"; foreach (IptcEntry entry in iptc.Entries) { Console.WriteLine($"{entry.Key} {entry.AsString()}"); } // JPEG saves it in its Photoshop resource block (APP13), with the digest Photoshop and Lightroom check. photo.Metadata.Iptc = iptc; photo.Save("captioned.jpg"); IPTC stored somewhere else parses on its own: // IPTC datasets from somewhere other than an image file, with a cap on the bytes of values read. IptcData iptc = IptcData.Parse(iim.Span, SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxMetadataBytes = 64 * 1024 }); Console.WriteLine($"{iptc.Get(IptcKey.ObjectName)}: {iptc.Entries.Count} datasets, damaged: {iptc.IsDamaged}"); XMP XmpData is a parsed XMP packet. Properties are addressed by XmpName (a namespace URI from XmpNamespaces and a local name), never by prefix. A property is a simple value, an XmpArray (bag, sequence or language alternatives, an XmpArrayKind) or an XmpStruct; typed properties cover the Dublin Core, XMP Basic, Photoshop and TIFF values apps use most. An edited packet is written as canonical RDF/XML with padding; properties Egami does not know are kept. XmpData xmp = new() { Title = "Harbour at dawn", Creators = ["A. Photographer"], Keywords = ["harbour", "Bergen"], Rating = 4, }; // Any property, by namespace URI and local name; structures and arrays nest. XmpStruct contact = new(); contact.Set(new XmpName(XmpNamespaces.IptcCore, "CiEmailWork"), "photo@example.com"); xmp.Set(new XmpName(XmpNamespaces.IptcCore, "CreatorContactInfo"), contact); if (xmp.TryGet(new XmpName(XmpNamespaces.DublinCore, "title"), out object? title) && title is XmpArray languages) { languages.SetLanguage("nb-NO", "Havn ved daggry"); } ReadOnlyMemory<byte> packet = xmp.ToBytes(); // canonical RDF/XML with padding RasterMetadata.XmpData is a live view of RasterMetadata.Xmp: it parses the packet on first use, and once edited, the edit is the packet every format saves. JPEG, PNG (an iTXt chunk) and GIF carry XMP. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("sideways.jpg"); // The parsed view of the packet; it is null when the file has none, so start one. XmpData xmp = photo.Metadata.XmpData ??= new XmpData(); xmp.Keywords = [.. xmp.Keywords, "harbour"]; xmp.Rating = 5; // The edit is the packet now: Metadata.Xmp returns it and every format saves it. photo.Save("rated.png"); Lightroom, Bridge and Windows read the keywords and rating from XMP. For news and stock workflows, set the same keywords in IPTC too. // An XMP packet from a sidecar file or a database; DTDs are refused and nothing outside it is read. XmpData xmp = XmpData.Parse(packet.Span, SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxMetadataBytes = 1024 * 1024 }); Console.WriteLine(xmp.IsDamaged ? string.Join(" ", xmp.Warnings) : $"Label: {xmp.Label}"); Color space RasterMetadata.ColorSpace says what the file declared about its colors. Egami keeps the declaration and the profile bytes; it does not convert between color spaces. using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.png"); string note = image.Metadata.ColorSpace switch { ColorSpaceHint.Srgb or ColorSpaceHint.Unknown => "sRGB: shown as is", ColorSpaceHint.Linear => "linear light: encode before showing", ColorSpaceHint.Gamma => "a file gamma other than sRGB", ColorSpaceHint.EmbeddedIcc => "an ICC profile describes the colors", _ => "unknown", }; Run it samples/Metadata is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Metadata writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/metafiles.html.title: Windows metafiles | Egami
articles/guides/metafiles.html.summary: Windows metafiles Egami.Metafiles plays Windows metafiles, the vector pictures Office and Windows programs exchange: WMF (Windows Metafile), EMF (Enhanced Metafile) and EMF+ (GDI+ records inside an EMF), and their gzip forms WMZ and EMZ. It draws them through Egami.Drawing's canvas, so a chart pasted from Excel stays vector on a PDF page or in SVG output and rasterizes the same on any OS. It only reads and plays: it does not write metafiles. It is fully managed. Loading Metafile.Load reads a file, a stream or bytes in memory; gzip is detected by its first bytes. Metafile.Kind says what it holds (a MetafileKind: Wmf, Emf, EmfPlusDual or EmfPlusOnly), and the header gives the picture's size: Size and Frame are in points: an EMF's frame rectangle (0.01 mm), a placeable WMF's box and units per inch, or, for a WMF without a placeable header, its window extent at 96 DPI (with a Metafile.NoPlaceableHeader warning). Dpi is the resolution the records were made at, and Description an EMF's application and picture names. Loading is lenient: a record that runs past the end of the file ends the walk with a warning, and what came before it plays. Warnings lists what the load found; MetafileLoadOptions.Context sets the limits (the file size and what EMZ and WMZ inflate to) and the diagnostics handler. // Untrusted files: the context's limits bound the file size and what EMZ and WMZ inflate to; a record that runs past // the end is skipped with a warning, and what came before it plays. MetafileLoadOptions options = new() { Context = EgamiContext.Default with { Limits = SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxTotalBytes = 16 << 20 } }, }; Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(new MemoryStream(bytes), options); if (picture.Kind is MetafileKind.EmfPlusDual or MetafileKind.EmfPlusOnly) { Console.WriteLine("Drawn by its EMF+ records, as GDI+ draws it."); } A picture taken out of a document is often already in memory; Load takes the bytes as they are. // A picture taken out of a document, already in memory: no stream needed. Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(bytes); using Raster<Rgba8> page = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(200, 150); using RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = page.CreateCanvas(); picture.Draw(canvas, new RectF(0, 0, 200, 150)); Drawing Metafile.Draw plays the picture on any canvas: in points from the canvas's origin, or with its frame stretched to a box, as Word stretches a picture to its frame. Metafile.Rasterize draws into a new raster at a DPI (96 by default) or a width and height, over a background: // WMF, EMF and EMF+ alike, and the gzip forms WMZ and EMZ. Metafile chart = Metafile.Load(path); Console.WriteLine($"{chart.Kind}, {chart.Size.X} by {chart.Size.Y} points"); // At twice the screen's resolution, over white; text uses the installed fonts. using Raster<Rgba8> image = chart.Rasterize<Rgba8>(new MetafileRenderOptions { Dpi = 192, Background = new RgbaF32(1, 1, 1, 1), }); image.Save(output); Egami.Metafiles plays the records as Windows does (GDI for WMF and EMF, GDI+ for EMF+), in managed code on any OS. Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(path); // The frame is stretched to the box, as Word stretches a picture to its frame. The same calls draw on a PDF page. using Raster<Rgba8> page = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(400, 300); using RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = page.CreateCanvas(); canvas.Clear(new RgbaF32(1, 1, 1, 1)); picture.Draw(canvas, new RectF(50, 50, 300, 200)); MetafileRenderOptions carries the rest: Antialias is on by default; off, GDI records draw aliased as GDI itself draws them, which is what to compare with Windows. EMF+ records follow the file's own smoothing either way. Playback (a MetafilePlayback) picks which records of a dual file play: Auto, the EMF+ records as GDI+ plays them, or Gdi, the GDI records only, as programs without GDI+ draw the file. Fonts and FontSubstitutions choose the faces for text; TextAsPaths draws text as outlines. // A dual EMF+ file plays its EMF+ records by default, as Office and GDI+ do; Gdi plays only the GDI records, as // programs without GDI+ draw it. Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(path); using Raster<Rgba8> gdi = picture.Rasterize<Rgba8>(new MetafileRenderOptions { Playback = MetafilePlayback.Gdi }); Text and fonts Text records name a face, and each glyph's place comes from the record itself, so a line keeps its length in another face. A face the fonts lack is replaced by a metric-compatible open font where one exists (Arial by Liberation Sans or Arimo, Times New Roman by Liberation Serif or Tinos, Courier New by Liberation Mono or Cousine, Calibri by Carlito, Cambria by Caladea), then by your FontSubstitutions, then by the generic family; each substitution is a Metafile.FontSubstituted warning. Symbol and Wingdings text maps to Unicode in a substitute. Text given as glyph indices (Word writes these for complex scripts) is drawn only in the face it was made for, since another face would show the wrong letters. // Faces the machine lacks: the built-in table maps Calibri to Carlito, Arial to Liberation Sans and so on; add your own. Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(path); using Raster<Rgba8> image = picture.Rasterize<Rgba8>(new MetafileRenderOptions { FontSubstitutions = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["Segoe UI"] = "Noto Sans" }, Antialias = false, // GDI's own aliased look, for comparing with Windows }); Each glyph still goes where the file put it, so lines keep their length in a substitute face. The open fonts are found only when they are installed, and many servers have none. The Egami.Fonts.Substitutes package bundles Liberation, Carlito and Caladea, so put its faces in the Fonts you pass: // The same pictures on a machine without Arial or Calibri: the bundled substitutes first, then the installed fonts. var fonts = new FontCollection(); foreach (FontFamily family in SubstituteFonts.Collection) { foreach (Typeface face in family.Faces) { fonts.Add(face); } } fonts.AddSystemFonts(); using Raster<Rgba8> image = Metafile.Load(path).Rasterize<Rgba8>(new MetafileRenderOptions { Fonts = fonts }); Raster.Load Registered with EgamiContext.WithFormat, MetafileFormat lets Raster.Load draw a metafile at its size at 96 DPI onto a transparent Rgba8 raster, and Raster.Probe give that size from the header without drawing. MetafileDecodeOptions.Dpi sets another resolution. // Register the format once; Raster.Load then draws metafiles at their own size at 96 DPI. EgamiContext context = EgamiContext.Default.WithFormat(MetafileFormat.Info); using Raster raster = Raster.Load(path, context); RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe(path, context); // the size from the header, nothing drawn // MetafileDecodeOptions sets the resolution; Raster.Load then draws at that DPI. using Raster sharp = Raster.Load(path, context, new MetafileDecodeOptions { Dpi = 300 }); What plays, and how close it is The GDI records of WMF and EMF play as GDI plays them: map modes, the world transform, pens and brushes (hatches and pattern brushes sized from the reference device, so they scale with the picture), paths, clipping regions, bitmaps through Egami's BMP reader, and text. Drawn aliased, the synthetic test files match Windows GDI within a mean of one level and 99% of pixels within 16 levels, family by family; text is measured with a looser bound, since GDI hints glyphs to whole pixels. Raster operations Egami draws with the nearest blend: AND as multiply, OR as lighten, XOR as difference, and the common transparent-bitmap idioms as one masked image; others draw as a copy with a Metafile.RasterOperation warning. EMF+ records play as GDI+ plays them: the world and page transforms, containers, clips with all six combine modes, smoothing, pixel offset and compositing; solid, hatch, texture, linear and path gradient brushes (path gradients as a Gouraud mesh); pens with dashes, compound lines, inset alignment and anchor and arrow caps; cardinal curves; images, with JPEG and PNG handed to the canvas unchanged so a PDF page embeds them as they are, and metafile images played as vectors up to eight levels deep; GDI+ 1.1 image effects; DrawString laid out in its rectangle and DrawDriverString. In a dual file the GDI records play only where GDI+ hands drawing to GDI (EmfPlusGetDC). Flood fills, OpenGL records, escapes and PostScript carried in comments are skipped with a Metafile.SkippedRecord warning. The diagnostics page lists every Metafile.* id.

articles/guides/ocr.html.title: Text recognition (OCR) | Egami
articles/guides/ocr.html.summary: Text recognition (OCR) Egami does not recognize text itself. It gives every OCR engine one shape, so code that needs text from an image works with whichever engine you plug in: a program such as Tesseract, the OS's own OCR or a cloud service. Egami ships no engine and links no native code. It also reads and writes hOCR and ALTO, the two files engines write. Types live in Egami.Ocr. The engine shape // An engine is one method: an image in, lines of words out. This one finds a single word; a real one wraps an OCR program, // an OS service or a cloud API (see samples/Ocr). public sealed class OneWordEngine : IOcrEngine { public OcrEngineInfo Info { get; } = new("one-word") { Languages = ["eng"], IsThreadSafe = true }; public Task<OcrResult> RecognizeAsync(OcrRequest request, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) { OcrQuad box = OcrQuad.FromBounds(10, 10, request.Image.Width / 2, 20); OcrLine line = new([new OcrWord("Duck", box, Confidence: 0.9, Language: "eng")]); return Task.FromResult(new OcrResult([line]) { ImageSize = new Size(request.Image.Width, request.Image.Height) }); } } An IOcrEngine has one method, RecognizeAsync, and an OcrEngineInfo that says what it can do: its Name, the Languages it reads, the MaxImageDimension it takes (callers scale larger images down and the boxes back up), whether it FindsOrientation and whether calls may overlap (IsThreadSafe, the default; a caller runs one page at a time when it is false). // Any IOcrEngine reads a Raster<Rgba8>; say the resolution and languages when you know them. OneWordEngine engine = new(); using Raster<Rgba8> page = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("duck.png"); OcrResult result = await engine.RecognizeAsync(new OcrRequest(page) { Dpi = 300, Languages = ["eng"] }, Ct); Console.WriteLine(result.Text); foreach (OcrWord word in result.Words) { Console.WriteLine($"{word.Text} at {word.Box.Bounds}, {word.Confidence:P0} sure"); } An OcrRequest carries a Raster<Rgba8> that the engine must not change or dispose, its Dpi (300 by default; engines use it to judge text size), the Languages to read as the engine names them, most likely first, and the PageIndex when the image is a page of a document. The OcrResult has Lines of OcrWords in reading order, each with its Text, its Box, a Confidence from 0 to 1 when the engine gives one, and a Language. Text joins words with spaces and lines with line feeds; Words lists them all. Rotation is the clockwise quarter turn that would put the image upright, for engines that look, and ImageSize the size of the image the boxes refer to. All engines are async. A network engine that blocks a thread while it waits can deadlock a caller with a synchronization context, so there is no synchronous form; a console app can simply await. Boxes are quads // Boxes are quads, corners named as the word reads, so turned and skewed words keep their shape. OcrQuad upright = OcrQuad.FromBounds(100, 50, 200, 40); OcrQuad upThePage = OcrQuad.FromBounds(20, 300, 40, 200, angle: 90); // TopLeft is the bottom left of the box Console.WriteLine($"{upThePage.Angle}° from {upThePage.TopLeft} to {upThePage.TopRight}"); // Map boxes back from an image the engine saw at half size, or into another space. OcrQuad full = upright.Transform(Matrix3x2.CreateScale(2)); An OcrQuad holds a word's four corners in image pixels with the origin at the top left, named as the word reads: a word that runs up the page has its TopLeft at the bottom left of its box. Rotated and skewed scans keep each word's shape, which a PDF text layer needs for selection that matches the picture. FromBounds makes the quad of an upright word, or of a word turned by a quarter turn; Bounds gives the whole-pixel rectangle around it, Angle the reading direction in degrees counterclockwise, and Transform maps the corners through a matrix, such as back from an image the engine saw at a smaller size. Any OCR program: CommandOcrEngine // Any OCR program that writes hOCR or ALTO is an engine. No shell runs the command, and each run has its own temp folder. CommandOcrEngine tesseract = new("tesseract {image} {output} -l {langs} --dpi {dpi} hocr", new CommandOcrOptions { Languages = ["eng"], Timeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2), }); try { OcrResult result = await tesseract.RecognizeAsync(new OcrRequest(page), Ct); Console.WriteLine(result.Text); } catch (OcrEngineException e) { Console.WriteLine($"{e.Message} {e.ErrorOutput}"); } CommandOcrEngine runs a program for each image and reads the hOCR or ALTO it writes, so any engine with a command line plugs in without code. The command is split into words at spaces, with quotes around a word that holds spaces, and run without a shell: an image path or a language can never become a command. Words may hold placeholders: Placeholder Becomes {image} The image, written as a PNG file in the run's own temporary folder {output} A path without extension for the output file; the engine reads it, or the one file the program wrote with an extension added {langs} The request's languages joined by + (Tesseract's form), or CommandOcrOptions.Languages when the request names none {dpi} The request's resolution as a whole number {page} The request's page index Without {output}, the engine reads the program's standard output, so tesseract {image} - -l {langs} hocr works as well. CommandOcrOptions sets the Output format (OcrOutputFormat.Auto, the default, tells hOCR from ALTO by the content), a Timeout (5 minutes; the program and its children are stopped), the WorkingDirectory, the engine Name and the Read limits for what the program writes. A program that cannot start, exits with an error, times out or writes no hOCR or ALTO throws OcrEngineException, with its ExitCode and the end of its ErrorOutput. Each run has its own temporary folder, deleted afterwards, so runs may overlap. hOCR and ALTO files // Read hOCR from Tesseract or any other engine, under limits for files you did not make. using FileStream file = File.OpenRead("page.hocr"); IReadOnlyList<OcrResult> pages = Hocr.Read(file, new OcrReadOptions { MaxWords = 100_000 }); Console.WriteLine($"{pages.Count} page, {pages[0].Words.Count()} words: {pages[0].Lines[0].Text}"); // Write results back as hOCR (or Alto.Write for ALTO). using FileStream copy = File.Create("copy.hocr"); Hocr.Write(copy, pages); Hocr reads and writes hOCR, the HTML that Tesseract, OCRopus and kraken write: ocr_page pages, ocr_line lines (and ocrx_line, ocr_header, ocr_caption and ocr_textfloat) and ocrx_word words with bbox, x_wconf (confidence as a percentage), textangle and lang. It reads HTML the way browsers do, not only XHTML, so missing end tags and unquoted attributes are fine. A line with textangle 90, 180 or 270 gives turned quads. A document with neither a page nor a word throws CorruptDataException. // ALTO from ABBYY, Tesseract or a library's digitization: positions in 1/10 mm or 1/1200 inch become pixels at Dpi. IReadOnlyList<OcrResult> pages = Alto.Parse(File.ReadAllText("page.xml"), new OcrReadOptions { Dpi = 300 }); Console.WriteLine($"{pages[0].ImageSize}: {pages[0].Text}"); // Turn it into hOCR, or write ALTO 4 in pixels. using FileStream hocr = File.Create("page.hocr"); Hocr.Write(hocr, pages); using FileStream alto = File.Create("page-v4.xml"); Alto.Write(alto, pages); Alto reads ALTO 1 to 4, the XML of library digitization that ABBYY, Tesseract and Transkribus write: Page, TextLine and String with HPOS, VPOS, WIDTH, HEIGHT, WC and LANG, a HYP hyphen joined to the word before it. Positions in 1/10 mm (mm10) or 1/1200 inch (inch1200) become pixels at OcrReadOptions.Dpi. It writes ALTO 4 in pixels. Both readers take untrusted files: OcrReadOptions limits the size (MaxBytes, 256 MB) and the words (MaxWords, 4 million), breaking either throws LimitExceededException, and no DTD, schema or other file is ever fetched. Both writers replace characters XML cannot hold with U+FFFD. Sample engines Egami's samples hold three adapters you can copy, built with the rest of the repository but never packed: samples/Ocr has Tesseract, through its program and CommandOcrEngine, and Azure AI Document Intelligence's Read model, through its REST API with HttpClient and no SDK. It draws a page of text, reads it back and writes text, hOCR and ALTO: dotnet run --project samples/Ocr -- tesseract (or azure, with AZURE_DOCUMENT_INTELLIGENCE_ENDPOINT and AZURE_DOCUMENT_INTELLIGENCE_KEY set). samples/OcrWindows has Windows' own OCR (Windows.Media.Ocr) for Windows 10 and 11: dotnet run --project samples/OcrWindows -- scan.png en-US. Engines differ in what they report. Tesseract gives confidences and no page orientation in hOCR; Windows OCR gives upright word rectangles and no confidence; Document Intelligence gives polygons, confidences and the page's angle.

articles/guides/opus-encoding.html.title: Encoding Opus | Egami
articles/guides/opus-encoding.html.summary: Encoding Opus Opus (RFC 6716) is the audio codec of WebM and of .opus files, and the best general-purpose lossy codec for both speech and music. Egami.Video encodes it fully managed: the encoder is translated from libopus 1.5.2 and gives the same packets, byte for byte, in every mode, so the quality and the bitrate are libopus's. SILK (speech), CELT (music) and hybrid frames, chosen per frame from the content and the bitrate, as libopus chooses. 1 to 8 channels: mono and stereo in one stream (mapping family 0), and 3 to 8 channels as surround streams in Vorbis channel order (mapping family 1, up to 7.1), with libopus's surround masking and its bitrate split between streams. 8, 12, 16, 24 and 48 kHz coded directly; other rates are resampled to 48 kHz first. Variable, constrained variable and constant bitrate, frames of 2.5 to 120 ms, in-band FEC and DTX. Writing .opus files AudioWriter writes Opus by default for Ogg (.opus, .ogg, .oga) and WebM files; set AudioWriterOptions.Codec to AudioCodecs.Opus for Matroska (.mka, .mkv) and MP4. AudioWriterOptions.Opus takes an OpusEncoderOptions; leave it out for the defaults, which suit music and most speech. // Speech at 32 kbit/s. Opus codes 8, 12, 16, 24 and 48 kHz, so this 44.1 kHz audio is resampled to 48 kHz; the // header keeps 44.1 kHz as the rate the audio came at. using (AudioWriter writer = AudioWriter.Create("voice.opus", new AudioWriterOptions { Opus = new OpusEncoderOptions { Bitrate = 32_000, Application = OpusApplication.Voice }, })) { writer.Write(tone); } The packets are timed at 48 kHz, as Opus always decodes. The encoder looks 6.5 ms ahead (2.5 ms with OpusApplication.LowDelay), so the stream starts with that much extra audio: the pre-skip, which the header (OpusHead) and the track's CodecDelay record and every decoder drops. At the end the encoder codes silence until the look-ahead is out, and the last packet's duration says where the input ended: Ogg writes it as the last granule position, Matroska and WebM as DiscardPadding and MP4 as the edit list. AudioReader, opusdec and FFmpeg give back exactly the samples written (FFmpeg ignores the end of an MP4 edit list, so it keeps the padding of an MP4 file). Settings OpusEncoderOptions Default What it does Bitrate 64 kbit/s per channel Bits per second for all channels together. Opus codes 6 to 510 kbit/s for stereo; 24 kbit/s is good speech, 64 to 96 kbit/s stereo is transparent for most music. RateMode Vbr Vbr spends bits where the audio needs them, so the average follows the content; ConstrainedVbr keeps a short window near the bitrate, for streaming; Cbr gives every packet the same size. Application Audio Audio codes for fidelity; Voice favours SILK and intelligibility; LowDelay turns SILK off and cuts the look-ahead to 2.5 ms. FrameDuration 20 ms 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 or 120 ms. Short frames lower the delay and cost bits; long ones save a little on speech. Effort 10 0 to 10, libopus's complexity. Below 10 the tonality analysis is off and the searches are simpler. Bandwidth automatic The widest band coded, from OpusBandwidth.Narrowband (4 kHz) to Fullband (20 kHz). InbandFec off Speech packets carry a coarse copy of the packet before, which a decoder uses when that one is lost. ExpectedLoss 0 % The share of packets expected to be lost, which the encoder protects against. Dtx off Speech silence is sent as one tiny packet every 400 ms. With Vbr the bitrate is an average over typical content, not a cap: a clip of pure tones may come out 20 % over it and noise 15 % under, exactly as with libopus. Use ConstrainedVbr when the rate must hold over each second. The encoder by hand AudioCodecs.Opus.CreateEncoder gives the IAudioEncoder the writer uses. AudioEncoderOptions.Opus carries the settings; FrameSize and Level are not used by Opus. // Constant bitrate with 10 ms frames for a link that wants packets of one size: 96 kbit/s gives 120 bytes each. OpusEncoderOptions options = new() { Bitrate = 96_000, RateMode = OpusRateMode.Cbr, FrameDuration = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(10), Bandwidth = OpusBandwidth.Superwideband, }; using IAudioEncoder encoder = AudioCodecs.Opus.CreateEncoder( new AudioEncoderOptions { SampleRate = 48000, Layout = ChannelLayout.Stereo, Opus = options }, MediaContext.Default); encoder.Send(tone); encoder.Flush(); int packets = 0; while (encoder.TryReceive(out EncodedPacket? packet)) { using (packet) { Console.WriteLine($"{packet.Timestamp}: {packet.Data.Length} bytes"); packets++; } } Transcoding to WebM WebM holds only Opus and Vorbis audio. MediaFile.Transcode with no codec and a WebM output copies Opus and Vorbis tracks and encodes the others in Opus, so a Matroska or MP4 file with FLAC or PCM audio becomes a valid WebM. Audio that no registered codec decodes is copied, and the WebM writer refuses it. // WebM holds only Opus and Vorbis audio, so without a codec Transcode encodes the FLAC track in Opus. MediaFile.Transcode("talk.mka", "talk.webm"); Compared with libopus and FFmpeg The packets are libopus 1.5.2's, so files match what opusenc or ffmpeg -c:a libopus make with the same settings, apart from the container. FFmpeg's own opus encoder is a different, CELT-only encoder.

articles/guides/palettes.html.title: Palettes and dithering | Egami
articles/guides/palettes.html.summary: Palettes and dithering The palette machinery behind the GIF, palette PNG, BMP and TGA writers, opened up: build a palette or bring your own, reduce an image to it in its own pixel type, get the indices, and pick from the published dithers. Types live in Egami.Quantization. Reduce colors // A 16-color poster with Atkinson's dither; the pixel type stays as it was. photo.Apply(ops => ops.Quantize(new PaletteOptions { MaxColors = 16, Dither = DitherMode.Atkinson }), Ct); photo.Save("poster.png"); RasterOps.Quantize gives each frame a palette (its own colors when they fit, Wu's quantizer otherwise) and replaces each pixel by its palette color, keeping the pixel type: an Rgba16 image stays Rgba16 with at most MaxColors distinct values. The PaletteOptions that the writers take drive it: MaxColors, Dither and AlphaThreshold, as in 1.0. FixedPalette: a fixed palette instead of building one. Every writer that takes PaletteOptions honours it, and throws, naming both numbers, when it has more colors than the format allows. DitherStrength, 0 to 1: how much of the error is diffused, or how tall the ordered pattern is. Serpentine: error diffusion alternates direction from row to row. RefineIterations: k-means passes (Lloyd's algorithm on every fourth pixel) that polish Wu's palette; they never make it fit worse. ExactMatching: each color goes to its exact nearest palette color rather than through the 64-level lookup table. Kernel: a custom ErrorDiffusionKernel instead of Dither. The defaults are 1.0's: Wu's palette, Floyd–Steinberg at full strength, left to right, table matching. Every GIF, PNG, BMP and TGA file Egami wrote before stays the same byte for byte. Dithers DitherMode has 1.0's FloydSteinberg, Ordered (8 × 8 Bayer) and None, plus Atkinson, Burkes, Jarvis–Judice–Ninke, Sierra (three rows, two rows and Lite), Stevenson–Arce and Stucki error diffusion with their published kernels; Riemersma, error diffusion along a Hilbert curve; and Bayer2x2, Bayer4x4, Bayer16x16 and Ordered3x3 patterns. Error diffusion runs row after row; ordered patterns treat every pixel alike, so animation frames dither the same way. Posterize takes the same modes. // A custom error-diffusion kernel: half the error to the right, a quarter down and a quarter down-left, at 80% strength, // scanning every other row backwards. ErrorDiffusionKernel kernel = new(new[,] { { 0, 0, 2 }, { 1, 1, 0 } }, divisor: 4, origin: 1); photo.Apply(ops => ops.Quantize(new PaletteOptions { MaxColors = 8, Kernel = kernel, DitherStrength = 0.8f, Serpentine = true }), Ct); Fixed palettes // Map onto a fixed palette: here an e-ink display's six inks. Palette inks = Palette.FromColors([Rgba8.Black, Rgba8.White, new(255, 0, 0, 255), new(255, 255, 0, 255), new(0, 0, 255, 255), new(0, 255, 0, 255)]); photo.Apply(ops => ops.Remap(inks, DitherMode.FloydSteinberg), Ct); Palette.FromColors takes up to 256 colors and an optional transparent entry. RasterOps.Remap maps onto a palette as ImageMagick's -remap does, keeping each pixel's alpha when the palette is opaque. Palette.Build and Palette.FromRaster build one from every frame of an image; Nearest and NearestIndex look colors up. // Build one palette from an image, polished by k-means, and use it for other images and for every GIF frame. Palette shared = Palette.Build(first, new PaletteOptions { MaxColors = 64, RefineIterations = 6 }); second.Apply(ops => ops.Remap(shared), Ct); second.Save("egret.gif", new GifWriterOptions { Palette = new PaletteOptions { FixedPalette = shared, Dither = DitherMode.Bayer4x4 } }); Palettes has ready-made ones: // Ready-made palettes: web-safe colors, black and white, gray levels, and color cubes such as 3-3-2. using Raster web = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Remap(Quantization.Palettes.WebSafe, DitherMode.Ordered), Ct); using Raster bilevel = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Remap(Quantization.Palettes.BlackAndWhite, DitherMode.Riemersma), Ct); using Raster fourGrays = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Remap(Quantization.Palettes.Grayscale(4)), Ct); using Raster rgb332 = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Remap(Quantization.Palettes.Uniform(8, 8, 4), DitherMode.Bayer16x16), Ct); Indices // Indices plus palette, for a PDF indexed-color image or a format of your own. using IndexedImage indexed = photo.ToIndexed(new PaletteOptions { MaxColors = 64 }); byte[] lookup = [.. indexed.Palette.Colors.SelectMany(c => new[] { c.R, c.G, c.B })]; byte[] samples = indexed.Indices.ToArray(); Raster.ToIndexed returns an IndexedImage: a byte per pixel and the palette, as a palette PNG would store them. The indices are pooled, so dispose it. Dominant colors // The main colors and how much of the picture each covers, e.g. to pick brand colors from a logo or a placeholder color. IReadOnlyList<WeightedColor> colors = logo.DominantColors(5); foreach ((Rgba8 color, double weight) in colors) { Console.WriteLine($"#{color.R:X2}{color.G:X2}{color.B:X2} covers {weight:P0}"); } Raster.DominantColors returns WeightedColors, largest share first. The image is averaged down to at most DominantColorOptions.MaxSamples pixels, transparent ones left out, and clustered by k-means in Oklab, seeded by Wu's palette so the result is the same on every run; clusters closer than MergeDistance merge. The weights of the colors returned sum to 1.

articles/guides/paragraph-layout.html.title: Paragraph layout | Egami
articles/guides/paragraph-layout.html.summary: Paragraph layout Egami.Fonts lays out paragraphs in the Egami.Fonts.Layout namespace: it finds where lines may break (UAX #14), turns styled text into shaped runs with the shaper from Unicode text and shaping, and builds lines at a width, with alignment and justification, line height, spacing, tabs, max lines and ellipsis, inline placeholders, vertical lines, decorations and shadows, and carets and selection for editors. The result is plain geometry (lines of GlyphRuns and decoration shapes), so Egami.Drawing's canvas, a PDF canvas and SVG draw it the same way. Line breaking LineBreaks.Enumerate walks a text's break opportunities through a LineBreakEnumerator that allocates nothing. Each LineBreak gives the index the next line would start at, whether the line must end there (after a newline, CR LF, NEL, VT, FF, U+2028 or U+2029) and whether the break follows a soft hyphen (U+00AD), which shows a hyphen when a line ends there. The last break is always at the end of the text. // Where lines may end: after spaces and hyphens, and always at the end; a line must end after a newline. List<int> breaks = []; foreach (LineBreak b in LineBreaks.Enumerate("A well-known fact.\nNext")) { breaks.Add(b.Index); // 2, 7, 13, 19 (mandatory), 23 } // CSS switches: break-all lets letters break like ideographs. LineBreakOptions breakAll = new(WordBreak: WordBreak.BreakAll); int count = 0; foreach (LineBreak b in LineBreaks.Enumerate("word", breakAll)) { count++; // 4: after every letter } The rules are Unicode's line breaking algorithm (UAX #14) from Egami's own Unicode 17.0 tables, with each character's LineBreakClass from UnicodeData.GetLineBreakClass. LineBreakOptions adds CSS Text 3's switches: WordBreak.BreakAll lets letters and digits of any script break like ideographs; WordBreak.KeepAll keeps ideographs, kana and Hangul together like the letters of a word, for Korean text with spaces. LineBreakStrictness sets how Chinese and Japanese text breaks. Auto is CSS's default and the same as Normal: a line may start with a small kana, and in Chinese and Japanese (Language "zh" or "ja") with the hyphens U+2010, U+2013, U+301C and U+30A0. Loose also lets iteration marks, centred punctuation, wide prefixes and suffixes and inseparable characters break in Chinese and Japanese. Strict is UAX #14's own rules, which pass Unicode's LineBreakTest.txt in full. Anywhere breaks between any two grapheme clusters. OverflowWrap says whether a piece too wide for its line may break between grapheme clusters; line filling uses it. Thai, Lao, Khmer and Myanmar text breaks only at spaces and zero width spaces: Egami has no dictionaries. An object replacement character (U+FFFC, as placeholders use) breaks before and after. Rich text and paragraphs A RichText is a string with StyleSpans over it (start and length in UTF-16 units, never overlapping) and a Placeholder for each object replacement character (U+FFFC). RichTextBuilder builds one: Push a TextStyle, Append text, AddPlaceholder for an inline box, Pop back. Pushed styles nest, and the result has one flat span per stretch of equal style. // Font families come from a collection; later families cover what the first lacks. FontCollection fonts = new(); fonts.AddFile(System.IO.Path.Combine(folder, "NotoSans-Regular.ttf")); fonts.AddFile(System.IO.Path.Combine(folder, "NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf")); fonts.TryGetFamily("Noto Sans", out FontFamily latin); fonts.TryGetFamily("Noto Sans Arabic", out FontFamily arabic); // Styles nest: the inner span keeps the outer one's size and adds a color and an underline. RichText text = new RichTextBuilder() .Append("Peace is ") .Push(new TextStyle { Size = 20 }) .Append("\u0633\u0644\u0627\u0645 ") .Push(new TextStyle { Color = new Rgba8(200, 30, 30, 255), Decoration = new TextDecoration() }) .Append("in Arabic") .Pop() .Pop() .AddPlaceholder(new Placeholder(16, 16, PlaceholderAlignment.Middle)) .ToRichText(); ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [latin, arabic], Size = 16, LineHeight = LineHeight.Multiple(1.4f) }, Align = TextAlign.Justify, LineBreaking = new LineBreakOptions(WordBreak: WordBreak.Normal), }; // Shaped once: lay it out at any width later. Paragraph paragraph = Paragraph.Create(text, style); Every TextStyle field is optional. An unset field takes the enclosing builder style's, then the ParagraphStyle's DefaultStyle, then Egami's default (16 units, black, normal line height): Fonts: FontFamilies in order of preference (later families and the paragraph's Fallback cover what the first lacks, per grapheme cluster), Size, FontStyle, Variations, Language and OpenType Features. Paint: Color (an Rgba8), or a Paint, which is any ITextPaint; Egami.Drawing's Paint is one, so gradients and image paints reach text. Background or BackgroundPaint fill behind the text, Decoration adds a TextDecoration (its TextDecorationLines, TextDecorationStyle and TextDecorationSkipInk), and Shadows a list of TextShadows. Spacing: LetterSpacing after each grapheme cluster (which turns optional ligatures off), WordSpacing, a LineHeight (Normal, a Multiple of the font size or an Absolute height, by its LineHeightKind) and a BaselineShift. A Placeholder has a width, a height and a PlaceholderAlignment: on the baseline at a given offset, above or below it, or at the line box's top, bottom or middle. Bidi, line breaking and indexes treat it as one character. ParagraphStyle holds the rest: the DefaultStyle, the paragraph Direction, TextAlign, TextAlignLast and TextJustify, the LineBreakOptions in LineBreaking, LineFill (greedy or balanced), the Hyphen and Ellipsis strings, MaxLines and MaxHeight, a Strut, TrimEdges, TabSize or TabStops with their TabAlignment, the WritingMode and TextOrientation, and the font Fallback. Paragraph.Create prepares the text once: it resolves the styles, finds the bidi levels and break opportunities, splits the text into runs where the bidi level, script, font or a shaping field changes, and shapes each run. Paint fields never split a run, so a color change inside a ligature keeps the ligature. A paragraph is immutable and safe to share between threads. Laying out lines Paragraph.Layout lays a paragraph out at a width and returns a TextLayout: its Width and Height, the LongestLine, and its Lines. Each TextLine has its text range (Start, Length), its line box (Top, Ascent, Descent, Baseline), its content's Left and Width (trailing spaces hang outside it), whether it ends at a HardBreak, and its LayoutRuns in visual order. A run is glyphs (Glyphs, a GlyphRun already at its layout position), a placeholder's box, a tab or a break, by its LayoutRunKind, with its BidiLevel and StyleIndex. ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [family], Size = 16 } }; Paragraph paragraph = Paragraph.Create("A paragraph is shaped once and laid out at any width.", style); // Each width gives an immutable layout: lines of glyph runs, positioned from the box's top-left corner. TextLayout narrow = paragraph.Layout(120); TextLayout wide = paragraph.Layout(400); foreach (TextLine line in narrow.Lines) { string text = paragraph.Text[line.Start..line.End]; // the line's text, its trailing space included float baseline = line.Baseline; // y of the baseline foreach (LayoutRun run in line.Runs) { GlyphRun? glyphs = run.Glyphs; // glyphs at their layout positions } } // No wrapping: the box is as wide as the longest line. TextLayout unbounded = paragraph.Layout(float.PositiveInfinity); Lines fill greedily, as browsers do: each takes the text up to the last break opportunity that fits. A taken soft hyphen shows the Hyphen string, counted in the line's width. A piece too wide for any line overflows, or with OverflowWrap breaks between grapheme clusters. Where a line breaks inside a shaped run at a point the shaper marks unsafe (an Arabic join, a contextual substitution), the pieces on each side are shaped again, so a line has the glyphs it would have on its own. Each line reorders its own bidi runs (UAX #9 rules L1 and L2): trailing spaces take the paragraph's direction. LineFill.Balanced evens the lines of a short paragraph (up to 6 lines): of the breaks that fit, the ones that leave the least squared space on every line, the last included, as Chromium's text-wrap: balance does. float.PositiveInfinity lays the paragraph out without wrapping; the box is then as wide as the longest line. Line boxes and spacing Line boxes follow CSS Inline Layout 3, with the numbers browsers use: Each run's inline box is its font's ascent and descent, rounded to whole units as browsers round them, plus the leading its LineHeight adds: Normal adds the font's line gap, Multiple and Absolute set the height (a computed height is floored to 1/64 unit, browsers' layout unit, so stacked lines do not drift). The leading is split half above and half below, the top half rounded down. A BaselineShift moves the box down (or up, when negative). Every line also holds the root inline box, from the paragraph's DefaultStyle, as CSS's strut does; a Strut adds a minimum box of its own, and with Force it alone sets every line box, for line grids. Placeholders sit by their alignment: on the baseline at an offset, above or below it, or at the middle (half the default font's x-height above the baseline, as CSS's middle); boxes aligned to the line's top or bottom stretch it last. TrimEdges drops the space above the first line's text and below the last one's (CSS text-box-trim). Letter spacing follows each grapheme cluster and word spacing each word separator; tabs advance to the next of the TabStops, which align the text after them at their start, end, centre or first decimal separator, or else to the next multiple of TabSize spaces, at least half a space on. Characters take the first family that has them, as CSS matches fonts, so spaces and punctuation between words of another script stay in the first family. Line boxes equal Chromium's within 0.01 unit on every line-height, strut, spacing, tab, placeholder and mixed-font case, and glyph positions equal its within 0.01 once its 1/64 layout unit is allowed for. Alignment and justification TextAlign places each line: Start and End follow the paragraph's direction, Left, Right and Center do not, and Justify stretches lines to the full width. The last line, and lines before a hard break, use TextAlignLast, whose Auto is the start for justified paragraphs. Trailing spaces hang past the line's end and never count for alignment. TextJustify says where justified lines stretch: InterWord at word separators, InterCharacter between any two grapheme clusters except inside cursive scripts such as Arabic, and Auto (the default) at word separators and around Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters, as browsers justify. None leaves justified lines at the start. Kashida justifies Arabic the way Word and Arabic typesetting do: words grow with tatweels (U+0640, kashida) before the spaces widen. Each word gets one point, the best one the shaping marks safe for a tatweel (after Seen or Sad, before a final Heh, Alef or Lam, and so on), and whole tatweel glyphs of the run's font go there; ParagraphStyle.Kashida caps them at one (Low), two (Medium, the default) or four (High) per word, and word spaces take the rest. Lines break as they would without kashida, text in other scripts and fonts without a tatweel justify at spaces, and vertical lines never get kashida. The tatweels join the character before them, so carets, selections and hit tests stay on character boundaries, and DrawTextLayout marks them with an empty ActualText so extracted text keeps the paragraph's words. // Justified Arabic lengthens words with tatweels (kashida) before it widens spaces, as Word does. ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [arabic], Size = 16 }, Align = TextAlign.Justify, Justify = TextJustify.Kashida, Kashida = KashidaLevel.Medium, // up to two tatweels a word; Low one, High four }; TextLayout layout = Paragraph.Create(text, style).Layout(260); canvas.DrawTextLayout(layout, new System.Numerics.Vector2(20, 10)); Line limits and the ellipsis MaxLines and MaxHeight stop the lines: at the limit, or before the line whose bottom would pass the height. When text is cut, TextLayout.DidExceed is true and HiddenRange says what was hidden; the last kept line drops whole grapheme clusters from its end until its text and the Ellipsis (U+2026 by default, shaped in the style of the last kept character) fit, and the ellipsis ends the line in the paragraph's direction, flagged Ellipsized; a line with room keeps its trailing space before it, as Chromium's line clamp does. A null Ellipsis cuts at the line's end. Ellipses sit where Chromium's -webkit-line-clamp puts them in Latin, Arabic and Chinese. Metrics A TextLayout also answers how big its text is: MinIntrinsicWidth (CSS min-content, the widest piece that cannot break; OverflowWrap.Anywhere lowers it to the widest grapheme cluster) and MaxIntrinsicWidth (max-content, the widest line without wrapping), equal to Chromium's; FirstBaseline and LastBaseline for aligning boxes on text; InkBounds, the union of the glyphs' ink and placeholder boxes, which can reach past the layout box; PlaceholderRects, one TextBounds per placeholder in order, where the caller draws them; and GetLineAt and GetLineAtY to find the line holding a character or a height. Hit testing, carets and selection Editors and selectable text build on four queries, all read-only and safe from any thread: HitTest turns a point into the nearest TextPosition: a UTF-16 index at a grapheme cluster boundary and a TextAffinity that says which side it belongs to where an index has two places (the end of one line and the start of the next, or a direction change). Points outside the lines go to the nearest one; at a direction change, the position is the one the surrounding text gives the edge, as browsers resolve it. GetCaret says where to draw a Caret: its primary CaretLine, and at a bidi boundary a secondary one at the other direction's edge. Inside a ligature, carets use the font's GDEF caret values, or split the ligature evenly by grapheme. MoveCaret steps by CaretMove: grapheme, word, line start and end, paragraph start and end, and line up and down keeping a preferred x across short lines. GetSelectionRects covers a range with rectangles, one per visually contiguous piece on each line, as tall as the line box or, with SelectionHeight.Tight, the fonts' ascent and descent. GetWordBoundary and GetLineBoundary give the word and line around an index. // A click: the nearest caret position, then where to draw the caret. TextPosition position = layout.HitTest(new System.Numerics.Vector2(40, 30)); Caret caret = layout.GetCaret(position); CaretLine bar = caret.Primary; // x, top and bottom; Secondary at a bidi boundary // Arrow keys: logical moves, and line moves that keep the column. TextPosition right = layout.MoveCaret(position, CaretMove.NextGrapheme); TextPosition down = layout.MoveCaret(position, CaretMove.LineDown, preferredX: bar.X); // A selection: rectangles to fill, one per visually contiguous piece on each line. IReadOnlyList<TextBounds> highlight = layout.GetSelectionRects(position.Index, down.Index); Egami.Fonts.Unicode.TextSegment word = layout.GetWordBoundary(position.Index); // double-click Hit tests, carets and selection rectangles equal Chromium's (caretPositionFromPoint, collapsed ranges and Range.getClientRects) on Latin with ligatures, mixed bidi, Arabic, a right-to-left paragraph, emoji, hard breaks and a clamped paragraph. Decorations A TextDecoration on a TextStyle draws underlines, overlines and line-throughs, solid, double, dotted, dashed or wavy. TextLayout.Decorations gives each as a DecorationShape per decorated stretch of a line: one position and thickness for the stretch, and its Segments (each a DecorationSegment from left to right), with gaps cut where glyph ink crosses an underline or overline (SkipInk.Auto, the default; Chinese, Japanese and Korean glyphs never cut). AddTo writes a shape's outline, and TextLayout.ToPath writes the whole layout, glyphs then decorations, to any IGlyphOutlineSink. TextStyle underlined = new() { FontFamilies = [family], Decoration = new TextDecoration { Lines = TextDecorationLines.Underline, Style = TextDecorationStyle.Wavy }, }; TextLayout layout = Paragraph.Create("Typography, quickly", new ParagraphStyle { DefaultStyle = underlined }).Layout(400); foreach (DecorationShape line in layout.Decorations) { // Top and Thickness place the line; Segments skip the descenders of y, p, g and q. System.Console.WriteLine($"{line.Line} at {line.Top}: {line.Segments.Count} pieces"); } // Or everything as outlines, to fill with any path renderer. PathRecorder path = new(); layout.ToPath(path); Positions follow Chromium's text-decoration rules rather than the font's underline values: the thickness is a tenth of the font size, floored to whole pixels; the underline sits half a thickness below the baseline (or UnderlineOffset below it); the overline on the ascent; the line-through a third of the ascent up. Thicknesses, positions and skip-ink gaps equal Chromium's ink within half a pixel on sans and serif text. Vertical layouts have no decorations yet. Drawing paragraphs Canvas.DrawTextLayout (Egami.Drawing) draws a layout with its top-left corner at a point, line by line in CSS's order: text shadows, run backgrounds, underlines and overlines, glyphs and placeholders, then line-throughs. A run's paint is its style's Paint (an Egami.Drawing Paint) or Color; shadows blur with a standard deviation of half their blur radius, as CSS. Lines outside the clip or the optional visible rectangle are skipped, and a PlaceholderPainter draws each placeholder in its box. Canvas.DrawText into a RectF lays out and draws in one call, placing the lines by VerticalAlign, and TextLayout.ToPath(origin) gives glyphs and decorations as one Path. On a PDF canvas the glyph runs keep their text, and an ellipsis or a soft hyphen's hyphen is marked content whose ActualText is the text it stands for. ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [family], Size = 18, Color = new Rgba8(30, 30, 60, 255), Shadows = [new TextShadow(new System.Numerics.Vector2(1, 1), 2, new Rgba8(0, 0, 0, 80))], }, Align = TextAlign.Justify, }; // One call: wrap into a box, centred across the lines. TextLayout boxed = canvas.DrawText("Paragraphs wrap, justify and drop shadows.", new RectF(10, 10, 300, 80), style, VerticalAlign.Center); // Or lay out once and draw where needed, skipping lines outside the visible part. TextLayout layout = Paragraph.Create("Laid out once, drawn many times.", style).Layout(300); canvas.DrawTextLayout(layout, new System.Numerics.Vector2(10, 110), visibleRect: new RectF(0, 0, 320, 200)); // Inline placeholders (an icon, a badge) are drawn by a painter called with each one's box. canvas.DrawTextLayout(layout, new System.Numerics.Vector2(10, 130), placeholderPainter: (c, index, box) => c.FillRoundRect(new RoundRect(box, 3), new Rgba8(200, 60, 40, 255))); // The same text as one path: glyphs and decorations. Egami.Drawing.Path outline = layout.ToPath(new System.Numerics.Vector2(10, 150)); Vertical lines WritingMode.VerticalRl stacks top-to-bottom lines from right to left, as Chinese and Japanese books, and VerticalLr from left to right. TextOrientation.Mixed (the default) stands each character as UAX #50's Vertical_Orientation says: Chinese, Japanese and Korean upright, shaped top to bottom with the font's vertical metrics and alternates, and Latin turned a quarter clockwise on the central baseline; Upright stands everything upright and Sideways turns whole lines. The width given to Layout is the lines' length; the layout's Height is that length and its Width the columns added up. Along a line, positions are y (a line's Left and Width, a run's X, a caret's X), across the lines x (a line's Top, Baseline and Bottom); glyph runs and rectangles stay in x and y. Line breaks, line boxes, positions, hit tests, carets and selections equal Chromium's writing-mode output on Japanese, Chinese and mixed Latin. LineFlow lays a paragraph out one line at a time, each at its own width, to flow text across columns and pages or around images: Paragraph.CreateFlow, then NextLine until it returns null. Each line's top is 0; place it where it goes, and Rewind to a line's start to take back a line that does not fit. // One line at a time, each at its own width: two columns of four lines, the second wrapping around an image. LineFlow flow = paragraph.CreateFlow(); List<TextLine> first = [], second = []; while (first.Count < 4 && flow.NextLine(150) is TextLine line) { first.Add(line); } while (flow.NextLine(second.Count < 2 ? 90 : 150) is TextLine line) { second.Add(line); // narrower beside the image } Line breaks equal headless Chromium's on a corpus of eleven scripts at five widths each, and on the feature cases; the few differences are Chromium's own (its older quotation mark rule, no break at U+2028, no break after a slash in URLs, letter spacing in Arabic). Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. A caption in a box // A caption wrapped into the bottom of a photo, centred, on a translucent band as tall as the lines. RectF box = new(20, 200, 360, 80); ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [family], Size = 15, Color = Rgba8.White }, Align = TextAlign.Center, MaxLines = 3, }; TextLayout layout = Paragraph.Create("Harbour at dawn, seen from the old lighthouse; the fishing boats leave before the ferries.", style).Layout(box.Width); float top = box.Y + box.Height - layout.Height; canvas.FillRect(new RectF(box.X - 8, top - 6, box.Width + 16, layout.Height + 12), new SolidPaint(new Rgba8(0, 0, 0, 140))); canvas.DrawTextLayout(layout, new System.Numerics.Vector2(box.X, top)); The layout's height is known before drawing, so the band behind the text fits the lines exactly; MaxLines stops a long caption from climbing up the photo. A justified article column // A justified column: each paragraph balanced, indented by its first line, with space between paragraphs. ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [family], Size = 13, LineHeight = LineHeight.Multiple(1.4f) }, Align = TextAlign.Justify, LineFill = LineFill.Balanced, }; float y = 10; foreach (string text in paragraphs) { TextLayout layout = Paragraph.Create(text, style).Layout(260); canvas.DrawTextLayout(layout, new System.Numerics.Vector2(20, y)); y += layout.Height + 8; } Balanced filling evens out line lengths, so justified lines stretch less; soft hyphens break long words only where a line needs them. A chat bubble with an emoji // A chat bubble: at most two lines, cut with an ellipsis; the bubble shrinks to the longest line, so short messages get // short bubbles. Emoji come from the second family, character by character. ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [text, emoji], Size = 15, Color = Rgba8.White }, MaxLines = 2, }; TextLayout message = Paragraph.Create("See you at the caf\u00E9 at eight? I will bring the maps, the snacks and the long list of places we still have not seen \U0001F389", style).Layout(240); RoundRect bubble = new(new RectF(12, 12, message.LongestLine + 24, message.Height + 16), 14); canvas.FillRoundRect(bubble, new SolidPaint(new Rgba8(0, 120, 255, 255))); canvas.DrawTextLayout(message, new System.Numerics.Vector2(24, 20)); bool cut = message.DidExceed; // true: offer "show more" LongestLine is the width the lines actually use, which is what a bubble should wrap; DidExceed and HiddenRange say what the ellipsis cut. Japanese vertical text // Japanese set vertically, columns right to left: the width given to Layout is the column height, and DrawText into a // rectangle puts the first column at its right edge.
