SvgTextMode.Text writes text elements with the font's family, size, weight and style and each cluster's position, so the text stays searchable and lines up with Egami's layout; with EmbedSubset each font's glyphs used are embedded as an OpenType subset in an @font-face rule (unless the font's license forbids it, reported as Svg.FontNotEmbedded). Synthetic bold and italic are drawn as Egami draws them, as a stroke and a slant. // By default text is glyph outlines, each written once and reused, so the file needs no fonts. // SvgTextMode.Text writes text elements instead, searchable and selectable; EmbedSubset adds the glyphs used as a font. SvgWriteOptions options = new() { Text = SvgTextMode.Text, EmbedSubset = true }; using (SvgCanvas canvas = new(file, 300, 60, options)) { canvas.DrawText("Hello, SVG", new Vector2(10, 40), new Font(face, 28), new Rgba8(20, 20, 20, 255)); } Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Render an SVG to PNG // An SVG drawn 256 pixels wide and saved as PNG; the height keeps the aspect ratio. SvgDocument document = SvgDocument.Load(input); using Raster<Rgba8> raster = document.Rasterize<Rgba8>(new SvgRenderOptions { Width = 256 }); raster.Save(output); Egami.Svg draws as resvg does where SVG leaves a choice. Recolor an SVG icon // Every fill and stroke of a one-color icon set to a brand color, then drawn: edits redraw at once. SvgDocument icon = SvgDocument.Parse(Icon); foreach (SvgElement element in icon.Root.Descendants()) { foreach (string paint in (string[])["fill", "stroke"]) { if (element.Attributes[paint] is string value && value != "none") { element.Attributes[paint] = "#7b2ff7"; } } } using Raster<Rgba8> branded = icon.Rasterize<Rgba8>(new SvgRenderOptions { Width = 64 }); Draw icons from an SVG sprite sheet // Each symbol of a sprite sheet drawn into its own 32-pixel cell of a toolbar strip. SvgDocument sheet = SvgDocument.Parse(Sheet); string[] icons = ["plus", "dot", "plus"]; using Raster<Rgba8> strip = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(32 * icons.Length, 32); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = strip.CreateCanvas()) { for (int i = 0; i < icons.Length; i++) { sheet.Draw(canvas, icons[i], new RectF(32 * i, 0, 32, 32)); } } A symbol's viewBox fits it into each cell; the same calls draw on a PDF page. Flow SVG text into a shape // SVG 2 text that wraps: inside a circle (as Inkscape writes flowed text), or in lines 160 units long. SvgDocument card = SvgDocument.Parse(""" <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="400" height="200" font-family="Noto Sans" font-size="14"> <circle id="area" cx="100" cy="100" r="90" fill="#eef"/> <text style="shape-inside: url(#area); shape-padding: 6px; text-align: center"> Text flows into the circle line by line, each line as wide as the circle is at that height. </text> <text x="220" y="40" style="inline-size: 160px">Wrapped at 160 units, as a paragraph fills a column.</text> </svg> """, options); using Raster<Rgba8> raster = card.Rasterize<Rgba8>();

articles/guides/system-drawing-text.html.title: Matching System.Drawing text | Egami
articles/guides/system-drawing-text.html.summary: Matching System.Drawing text Egami can draw small UI text the way System.Drawing does on Windows, for images that replace ones made with Graphics.DrawString (GDI+) or TextRenderer (GDI), such as buttons in emails. The settings come from measurements of GDI and GDI+ on Windows; Fonts and text explains each of them. GDI+ ClearTypeGridFit Font.WithGdiPlusLook() and CanvasOptions.GdiPlusClearType together give GDI+'s ClearTypeGridFit look. The font's TrueType instructions run for GDI+, with Microsoft's ClearType compatibility rules (FontHinting.Full, TrueTypeTarget.GdiPlus). Advances are grid-fitted (FontMetrics.GridFitted), as DrawString lays out text with the default StringFormat, and glyph origins sit on whole pixels. GDI+ rounds an advance up from about 0.458 of a pixel rather than 0.5, and the GDI+ target does the same. With StringFormat.GenericTypographic GDI+ pulls lines back toward their design width. Use FontMetrics.GridFittedToDesign for that: a run that hinted advances would make more than 2.1 pixels wider than designed keeps its design advances, rounded up to sixteenths of a pixel. LCD edging uses GDI+'s filter (LcdFilter.Gdi) and sampling (LcdSampling.Gdi): six on-or-off samples per pixel across the stripes, on each pixel's centre line, so every channel's coverage is a whole number of sixths. The blend uses GDI+'s gamma: TextGamma 1.4, which is 1 + Graphics.TextContrast / 10 at the default contrast of 4. With LcdSampling.Gdi it goes through GDI+'s 8-bit gamma tables, as measured: the drawn values equal GDI+'s for every coverage on every gray background tested. // Text that looks like System.Drawing's Graphics.DrawString with TextRenderingHint.ClearTypeGridFit: the font's own hints // and grid-fitted advances, GDI+'s ClearType filter, sampling and gamma. Font label = new Font(face, 16).WithGdiPlusLook(); using (RasterCanvas<Rgb8> canvas = button.CreateCanvas(CanvasOptions.GdiPlusClearType)) { float width = label.MeasureText("Start the course").Advance; canvas.DrawText("Start the course", new Vector2(MathF.Round((200 - width) / 2), 26), label, Rgba8.White); } // A different Graphics.TextContrast (0 to 12) is a different text gamma: 1 + contrast / 10. CanvasOptions contrast8 = CanvasOptions.GdiPlusClearType with { TextGamma = 1 + (8 / 10f) }; For a white Trebuchet MS label at 16 pixels on a black or a #0078d4 button, the result is within 0.5% of GDI+'s brightness. The mean per-pixel difference is 0.67 levels out of 255 on black and 0.38 on blue, against 9.5 and 5.4 for Egami's default text. Fonts that GDI+ draws from embedded bitmaps at small sizes, such as Calibri, still differ: Egami draws their outlines. Shapes Two canvas settings match what Graphics does with shapes at its defaults, SmoothingMode.AntiAlias and PixelOffsetMode.None. CanvasOptions.GdiPlusClearType sets both. PixelOffset.None puts whole coordinates on pixel centres, as GDI+'s None, Default and HighSpeed offset modes do. Paths, their paints and clips move half a pixel right and down. Text moves only when it is unhinted, just as GDI+ moves its AntiAlias text but not its grid-fitted text, and images do not move. PixelOffset.Half, Egami's default, is GDI+'s Half. Antialiasing.GdiPlus samples like AntiAlias and HighQuality, which are the same mode. Each pixel has 8 samples across and 4 down, and a sample on a left or top edge is inside. Pens of 1.5 device pixels or less draw as GDI+'s thin lines: one pixel thick across the line's major axis, at full strength, with pointed ends and no caps. // Shapes as System.Drawing draws them at its defaults (SmoothingMode.AntiAlias, PixelOffsetMode.None): whole coordinates on // pixel centres, GDI+'s 8 by 4 samples a pixel, and pens up to 1.5 px drawn as its one-pixel thin lines. // CanvasOptions.GdiPlusClearType sets both too. var options = new CanvasOptions { PixelOffset = PixelOffset.None, Antialiasing = Antialiasing.GdiPlus }; using (RasterCanvas<Rgb8> canvas = raster.CreateCanvas(options)) { canvas.FillOval(new RectF(4, 4, 20, 20), new SolidPaint(new Rgba8(0, 90, 200, 255))); canvas.DrawLine(new Vector2(30, 6), new Vector2(60, 26), new Stroke(0.5f), new SolidPaint(Rgba8.Black)); } On rectangles, polygons, ovals and lines at fractional positions, the mean difference from GDI+ is 0.12 levels, down from 1.94 with Egami's closest settings before. Rectangles and polygons match to the level. Ovals and round caps still differ a little, because GDI+ flattens curves its own way. GDI ClearType For TextRenderer or GDI's ExtTextOut: Set Font.HintingTarget = TrueTypeTarget.Gdi and Font.Metrics = FontMetrics.Compatible. GDI's compatible widths equal GetCharABCWidths for 9,688 of 9,690 glyph sizes measured. Set TextGamma to the system's ClearType contrast divided by 1000. That is 1.2 when it is 1200, and Windows' default is 1.4. DrawString's layout Graphics.DrawString at a point, with the default StringFormat, starts the text 1/6 em right of the point, rounded to a whole pixel. The first baseline sits the font's ascent below the point. MeasureString adds about 0.275 em on each side and 1/8 em to the height. StringFormat.GenericTypographic drops all of this padding. These rules belong to System.Drawing's layout, not to the text, so Egami keeps them in a sample rather than in the library: // Graphics.DrawString(text, font, brush, x, y) with the default StringFormat starts the text 1/6 em right of the point (to a // whole pixel) with the first baseline the font's ascent below it; StringFormat.GenericTypographic drops that padding. // MeasureString with the default format adds about 0.275 em on each side and 1/8 em to the height (measured on Windows). public static Vector2 DrawStringOrigin(Font font, Vector2 point, bool typographic = false) => new(point.X + (typographic ? 0 : MathF.Round(font.Size / 6)), point.Y + font.Extents.Ascent); public static (float Width, float Height) MeasureStringSize(Font font, string text, bool typographic = false) { TextMeasure m = font.MeasureText(text); return typographic ? (m.Advance, m.Height) : (m.Advance + (0.55f * font.Size), m.Height + (font.Size / 8)); }

articles/guides/system-drawing.html.title: System.Drawing drop-in | Egami
articles/guides/system-drawing.html.summary: System.Drawing drop-in Egami.SystemDrawing gives code written for System.Drawing.Common its API on every OS, in managed code: Bitmap, Image, Icon, pixel formats, LockBits, the codecs and their encoder parameters, frames and property items. System.Drawing.Common runs only on Windows since .NET 6; with this package the same code runs on Linux, macOS and in containers, drawn by Egami. The package is a preview (1.0.0-preview.1). This release has bitmaps, pixel access, codecs, icons, and Graphics with pens, brushes, paths, transforms, clipping, regions and images. Fonts and text follow in the next previews. Moving code over Replace the System.Drawing.Common package reference with Egami.SystemDrawing. With implicit usings on, the package adds System.Drawing and Egami.SystemDrawing as implicit usings, so most files compile unchanged; files that name System.Drawing.Imaging types change that line to using Egami.SystemDrawing.Imaging;. Set EgamiSystemDrawingImplicitUsings to false in the project file to leave the implicit usings out. Color, Point, Size, Rectangle, their float forms, KnownColor, SystemColors and ColorTranslator are .NET's own System.Drawing.Primitives types, which every OS has, so values pass between your code, other libraries and Egami unchanged. Everything else (Bitmap, Image, PixelFormat, ImageFormat and the rest) is defined by the package with System.Drawing's names, members, overloads, defaults and exceptions: ArgumentException for "Parameter is not valid", ExternalException for GDI+'s generic error, OutOfMemoryException from Image.FromFile for a file it cannot read. The package is source-compatible, not binary-compatible: your code recompiles against it, while a DLL built against System.Drawing.Common keeps using System.Drawing.Common. // The same code as with System.Drawing.Common: only the using lines name Egami.SystemDrawing. using Bitmap bitmap = new(64, 32); for (int x = 0; x < 64; x++) { bitmap.SetPixel(x, 16, Color.FromArgb(255, x * 4, 0, 255 - (x * 4))); } Color middle = bitmap.GetPixel(32, 16); // ARGB(255, 128, 0, 127) bitmap.SetResolution(300, 300); bitmap.RotateFlip(RotateFlipType.Rotate90FlipNone); bitmap.Save(output, ImageFormat.Png); GraphicsUnit unit = GraphicsUnit.Inch; RectangleF bounds = bitmap.GetBounds(ref unit); // 32 by 64, in pixels GraphicsUnit and RotateFlipType (with System.Drawing's shared values, such as RotateNoneFlipY equal to Rotate180FlipX) live in Egami.SystemDrawing, as they do in System.Drawing. Bitmaps and pixel formats A Bitmap holds its pixels in GDI+'s own memory layout for each PixelFormat: rows of the format's bits, each padded to a multiple of four bytes. The 14 bitmap formats are all there, and pixels convert exactly as GDI+ converts them, measured on Windows for every 8-bit value and every color and alpha pair: 5 and 6-bit channels (Format16bppRgb555, Format16bppRgb565, Format16bppArgb1555) truncate when written and repeat their high bits when read; 1555's alpha bit is set from alpha 128. Format32bppPArgb premultiplies with rounding and divides out through GDI+'s 16-bit reciprocal of alpha. Format32bppRgb keeps the fourth byte it is given and reads as opaque. Format48bppRgb, Format64bppArgb and Format64bppPArgb hold linear light from 0 to 8192 through the sRGB curve, as GDI+ does, so 8-bit colors round-trip. Indexed formats look up their palette; SetPixel on them throws InvalidOperationException, and Format16bppGrayScale bitmaps exist but GetPixel and SetPixel throw, as in GDI+. Image.GetPixelFormatSize, IsAlphaPixelFormat, IsExtendedPixelFormat and IsCanonicalPixelFormat read the format's bits, and Image.Flags holds ImageFlags values: alpha, color space, and for a file, read-only and a stated resolution. // Every GDI+ pixel format, with GDI+'s conversions: 5-bit channels truncate when written and repeat their high bits when read. using Bitmap rgb555 = new(1, 1, PixelFormat.Format16bppRgb555); rgb555.SetPixel(0, 0, Color.FromArgb(10, 20, 30)); Color read = rgb555.GetPixel(0, 0); // ARGB(255, 8, 16, 24) // 48 and 64-bit formats hold linear light from 0 to 8192, as in GDI+. using Bitmap deep = new(1, 1, PixelFormat.Format48bppRgb); deep.SetPixel(0, 0, Color.FromArgb(255, 200, 100, 50)); int bits = Image.GetPixelFormatSize(deep.PixelFormat); // 48 bool alpha = Image.IsAlphaPixelFormat(PixelFormat.Format64bppArgb); // true ImageFlags flags = (ImageFlags)new Bitmap(1, 1, PixelFormat.Format32bppArgb).Flags; // HasAlpha Clone(rect, format) copies an area into another format, ConvertFormat converts in place, MakeTransparent keys out a color (the bottom-left pixel's by default) into 32-bit ARGB, RotateFlip turns and mirrors, and GetThumbnailImage makes a 32-bit premultiplied copy. new Bitmap(image, size) draws another image at a size, bilinearly, as GDI+'s DrawImage does. A bitmap made with new Bitmap(width, height, stride, format, scan0) reads and writes the caller's memory in place. Locking pixels LockBits with an ImageLockMode returns a BitmapData: where the first locked row is, the bytes from one row to the next, and the size and format. Locked in the bitmap's own format, the pointer is into the bitmap's memory. Locked in another format, it is a converted copy, written back on UnlockBits when the lock writes. ImageLockMode.UserInputBuffer locks into a buffer the caller's BitmapData points to. While a bitmap is locked, GetPixel, SetPixel and a second lock throw ExternalException, as in GDI+. // Locked in its own format, the bitmap's pixels are its own memory; in another format they are a converted copy that // goes back into the bitmap on UnlockBits. BitmapData data = bitmap.LockBits(new Rectangle(0, 0, 16, 8), ImageLockMode.ReadWrite, PixelFormat.Format32bppArgb); byte[] row = new byte[data.Stride]; for (int y = 0; y < data.Height; y++) { Marshal.Copy(data.Scan0 + (y * data.Stride), row, 0, row.Length); for (int x = 0; x < data.Width; x++) { row[(x * 4) + 2] = 255; // red } Marshal.Copy(row, 0, data.Scan0 + (y * data.Stride), row.Length); } bitmap.UnlockBits(data); Palettes Indexed bitmaps start with GDI+'s default palettes: black and white, the 16 VGA colors, or for 8 bits the VGA colors, 24 transparent entries and a 6 by 6 by 6 cube. Image.Palette hands out a copy as a ColorPalette; set it back to change it. Its Flags hold PaletteFlags. new ColorPalette(PaletteType) builds GDI+'s fixed halftone palettes, and ColorPalette.CreateOptimalPalette builds one from a bitmap's colors with Egami's palette builder. Converting to an indexed format maps each color as GDI+ does, through a table of 16 levels a channel: Clone uses GDI+'s halftone palettes (2, 16 or 224 colors), a lock uses the format's default palette, and ConvertFormat the palette or PaletteType it is given. Every DitherType maps to the nearest color; Egami does not dither yet. // Indexed bitmaps keep GDI+'s default palettes; Palette hands out a copy to change and set back. using Bitmap indexed = new(4, 4, PixelFormat.Format8bppIndexed); ColorPalette palette = indexed.Palette; palette.Entries[0] = Color.Navy; indexed.Palette = palette; bool halftone = (palette.Flags & (int)PaletteFlags.Halftone) != 0; // true // ConvertFormat maps to a fixed palette, and Clone to an indexed format uses GDI+'s halftone palettes. using Bitmap photo = new(System.IO.Path.Combine(Images, "duck.png")); photo.ConvertFormat(PixelFormat.Format8bppIndexed, DitherType.None, PaletteType.FixedHalftone252); using Bitmap bilevel = photo.Clone(new Rectangle(0, 0, photo.Width, photo.Height), PixelFormat.Format1bppIndexed); Loading and saving Image.FromFile, Image.FromStream and the Bitmap constructors read through Egami's codecs, which read every format Egami does, more than GDI+. Images come in the pixel format GDI+ gives each file type: 24-bit PNG and JPEG as Format24bppRgb, palette PNG, GIF and BMP files as their indexed formats with their palettes, gray PNG and 16-bit gray TIFF as Format32bppArgb, gray JPEG and 8-bit gray TIFF as Format8bppIndexed with a gray palette, plain 32-bit BMP as Format32bppRgb, 16-bit RGB TIFF as Format48bppRgb, icons and animated GIFs as Format32bppArgb. The resolution is the file's, computed as GDI+ computes it (3780 pixels a meter is 96.01199), or 96. RawFormat is the file's ImageFormat. Save writes BMP, PNG, GIF, TIFF and JPEG, the encoders ImageCodecInfo.GetImageEncoders lists with GDI+'s class ids, MIME types and ImageCodecFlags. An EncoderParameters holds EncoderParameter settings, by Encoder: Encoder.Quality sets JPEG quality (75 by default), Encoder.Compression with an EncoderValue sets TIFF compression (LZW by default), Encoder.ColorDepth writes 1, 4 or 8-bit TIFF, and Encoder.SaveFlag with SaveAdd writes a multipage TIFF. EncoderParameterValueType says what type a setting's values have. GetEncoderParameterList lists what each encoder takes, as GDI+ lists it. // The encoders GDI+ lists, by MIME type, with encoder parameters for JPEG quality and TIFF compression. ImageCodecInfo jpeg = ImageCodecInfo.GetImageEncoders().First(c => c.MimeType == "image/jpeg"); using EncoderParameters settings = new(1); settings.Param[0] = new EncoderParameter(Encoder.Quality, 85L); using MemoryStream file = new(); photo.Save(file, jpeg, settings); file.Position = 0; using Image loaded = Image.FromStream(file); bool fromJpeg = loaded.RawFormat.Equals(ImageFormat.Jpeg); // true PixelFormat format = loaded.PixelFormat; // Format24bppRgb bool readOnly = ((ImageFlags)loaded.Flags).HasFlag(ImageFlags.ReadOnly); // true ImageCodecFlags can = jpeg.Flags; // Encoder, Decoder, SupportBitmap, Builtin EncoderParameterValueType type = settings.Param[0].ValueType; // ValueTypeLong EncoderValue lzw = EncoderValue.CompressionLZW; // for Encoder.Compression and TIFF BMP is written as GDI+ writes it, with the bitmap's own rows, so a 32-bit bitmap reads back as Format32bppRgb. GIF is written with the default 8-bit palette. Frames and properties A multipage TIFF counts its pages in FrameDimension.Page and an animated GIF its frames in FrameDimension.Time; GetFrameCount and SelectActiveFrame choose one. PropertyItems, GetPropertyItem, SetPropertyItem and RemovePropertyItem hold what GDI+ reports as PropertyItem values: the EXIF tags, every tag of a TIFF's first directory, a JPEG's quantization tables (0x5090 and 0x5091), a PNG's gamma and pixel size, and a GIF's frame delays, loop count, global palette, background and transparent index and comment, each with its tag id, type and little-endian bytes. // An animated GIF counts its frames in time; property items hold its delays (0x5100) and loop count (0x5101). using Image animation = Image.FromFile(System.IO.Path.Combine(Images, "loop.gif")); FrameDimension time = new(animation.FrameDimensionsList[0]); // FrameDimension.Time int frames = animation.GetFrameCount(time); PropertyItem delays = animation.GetPropertyItem(0x5100)!; // 4 bytes a frame, in hundredths of a second animation.SelectActiveFrame(time, frames - 1); // Thumbnails are 32-bit premultiplied. using Image thumbnail = animation.GetThumbnailImage(16, 12, null, IntPtr.Zero); GetThumbnailImage takes an Image.GetThumbnailImageAbort callback, which, as in GDI+, is never called. Icons Icon loads an ICO file and shows the image nearest the size asked for, 32 by 32 by default, chosen as System.Drawing chooses: the smallest difference in width plus height, then the most bits a pixel. ToBitmap gives it as 32-bit ARGB, and Save writes the file it came from. Image.FromFile on an icon takes the last image of the file, as GDI+'s decoder does. // An icon shows the image nearest the size asked for, as System.Drawing chooses it, and saves the file it came from. using Icon icon = new(System.IO.Path.Combine(Images, "app.ico"), 24, 24); using Bitmap image = icon.ToBitmap(); // 24 by 24, 32-bit ARGB using MemoryStream copy = new(); icon.Save(copy); Drawing with Graphics Graphics.FromImage draws on a bitmap of any pixel format GDI+ draws on; indexed formats throw ArgumentException, and 16-bit gray and 16-bit ARGB 1555 throw ExternalException, as in GDI+. Each call draws at once, so Flush does nothing, and the bitmap keeps what was drawn after Dispose; FlushIntention is accepted and changes nothing. As in GDI+, drawing goes through premultiplied ARGB with GDI+'s rounding, so a translucent copy onto a format without alpha keeps the premultiplied color. GDI+'s defaults are kept: shapes are aliased (SmoothingMode.None), pixel centers lie on whole coordinates (PixelOffsetMode.Default; Half and HighQuality move them half a pixel, to Egami's own centers), images are sampled bilinearly, and drawing blends (CompositingMode.SourceOver; SourceCopy replaces). CompositingQuality and QualityMode values are kept but blend the same way. Settings read back as GDI+ stores them: SmoothingMode.HighQuality reads as AntiAlias, HighSpeed and Default as None, InterpolationMode.Low as Bilinear and High as HighQualityBicubic. PageUnit and PageScale scale page coordinates at the bitmap's resolution; with GraphicsUnit.Display, the default, GDI+ ignores the page scale and so does the package. // Draw on a bitmap as with System.Drawing: GDI+'s defaults are aliased shapes and whole-pixel centers. using Bitmap bitmap = new(80, 60); using (Graphics g = Graphics.FromImage(bitmap)) { g.Clear(Color.White); g.SmoothingMode = SmoothingMode.AntiAlias; g.PageUnit = GraphicsUnit.Millimeter; // 1 mm is 96 / 25.4 pixels at the bitmap's 96 dpi using Pen pen = new(Color.Navy, 0.5f); g.DrawEllipse(pen, 2, 2, 15, 10); } Color corner = bitmap.GetPixel(0, 0); // white Transforms and states Matrix is a 3 by 2 affine transform with System.Drawing's members; MatrixOrder.Prepend, the default, applies a new transform before the existing one. The world transform takes the same calls on Graphics, and TransformPoints maps points between CoordinateSpace.World, Page and Device. Save and Restore keep the transform, page settings, clip and quality settings; restoring a state drops every state saved after it. BeginContainer returns a GraphicsContainer and starts again from the defaults inside the current transform and clip; with a destination and a source rectangle, the source is in the given unit and the container's own coordinates are pixels, as in GDI+. // Transforms prepend by default, so the last call applies first; Save and Restore bring settings back. using Bitmap bitmap = new(64, 64); using Graphics g = Graphics.FromImage(bitmap); g.TranslateTransform(32, 32); g.RotateTransform(45); GraphicsState saved = g.Save(); g.ScaleTransform(2, 2); PointF[] points = [new(1, 0)]; g.TransformPoints(CoordinateSpace.Device, CoordinateSpace.World, points); // (33.41, 33.41) g.Restore(saved); using Matrix matrix = new(); matrix.Rotate(90); matrix.Translate(10, 0, MatrixOrder.Append); float[] elements = matrix.Elements; // 0, 1, -1, 0, 10, 0 Clipping and regions The clip is kept in device pixels, as GDI+ keeps it, so a later transform does not move it, and it holds the pixels whose whole coordinates lie inside: closed at the top and left, open at the bottom and right, half a pixel in when the pixel offset is set. SetClip takes a CombineMode. ClipBounds and VisibleClipBounds are its pixels' bounds in world coordinates. A Region keeps its shape as given; GetRegionScans, IsEmpty, Equals and the bounds of a combined region are its pixels, rasterized the same way. GetRegionData writes GDI+'s region format as a RegionData, with the checksum left as zero. // The clip is kept in device pixels, as GDI+ keeps it: changing the transform afterwards does not move it. using Bitmap bitmap = new(64, 48); using Graphics g = Graphics.FromImage(bitmap); g.SetClip(new Rectangle(10, 10, 20, 20)); g.ExcludeClip(new Rectangle(15, 15, 5, 5)); g.TranslateTransform(100, 0); RectangleF bounds = g.ClipBounds; // (-90, 10, 20, 20) in the new world coordinates g.ResetTransform(); using SolidBrush brush = new(Color.Red); g.FillRectangle(brush, 0, 0, 64, 48); // paints only inside the clip using Region region = new(new Rectangle(0, 0, 4, 4)); region.Union(new RectangleF(2.5f, 2.5f, 4, 4)); RectangleF[] scans = region.GetRegionScans(new Matrix()); // the pixels, as rectangles Shapes DrawLine, DrawRectangle, DrawEllipse, DrawArc, DrawPie, DrawPolygon, DrawBezier, DrawCurve, DrawClosedCurve, DrawRoundedRectangle and their Fill forms take every System.Drawing overload, including the span ones. Arcs are measured on the ellipse as GDI+ measures them, cardinal splines use GDI+'s tension (0.5 by default), and a pen is never thinner than a pixel. Polygons and closed curves fill even-odd unless given FillMode.Winding. DrawPath and FillPath draw a GraphicsPath. // Lines, rectangles, arcs, pies, polygons, Beziers and cardinal splines, stroked with a pen or filled with a brush. using Bitmap bitmap = new(64, 48); using Graphics g = Graphics.FromImage(bitmap); using Pen pen = new(Color.Black, 2); using SolidBrush brush = new(Color.FromArgb(128, 255, 0, 0)); g.DrawLine(pen, 2, 2, 60, 2); g.FillRectangle(brush, 4, 6, 20, 12); g.DrawArc(pen, 30, 6, 30, 20, 0, 180); g.FillPie(brush, 4, 20, 24, 24, 30, 120); g.DrawCurve(pen, [new PointF(30, 40), new PointF(40, 30), new PointF(50, 44), new PointF(60, 34)], 0.5f); g.FillPolygon(brush, [new PointF(40, 4), new PointF(48, 16), new PointF(32, 16)], FillMode.Winding); Pens A Pen has GDI+'s settings and checks: StartCap and EndCap take every LineCap, the anchors centered on the end; LineJoin with MiterLimit (at least 1); a DashStyle whose DashPattern is in multiples of the width, with a DashCap and DashOffset (a solid pen's DashPattern throws InvalidOperationException, and Custom keeps the pattern of the style before it); CompoundArray strips; PenAlignment.Inset, the only alignment GDI+ draws differently from centered; and a Transform that shapes the nib, so a pen scaled 3 by 1 draws three times as wide across vertical lines. CustomEndCap and CustomStartCap take an AdjustableArrowCap or a CustomLineCap with a stroke path; as in GDI+, a CustomLineCap with a fill path throws NotImplementedException. PenType says what kind of brush the pen paints with. Pens and SystemPens hold one-unit pens of the named and system colors, which cannot be changed or disposed. // Pens take GDI+'s caps, joins, dash styles (in multiples of the width), compound lines, inset alignment and arrow caps. using Bitmap bitmap = new(80, 60); using Graphics g = Graphics.FromImage(bitmap); g.SmoothingMode = SmoothingMode.AntiAlias; using Pen dashed = new(Color.Navy, 3) { DashStyle = DashStyle.DashDot, StartCap = LineCap.Round, EndCap = LineCap.ArrowAnchor }; g.DrawLine(dashed, 5, 10, 75, 10); using Pen arrow = new(Color.DarkRed, 2) { CustomEndCap = new AdjustableArrowCap(4, 5) }; g.DrawLine(arrow, 5, 30, 70, 30); using Pen inset = new(Color.Black, 4) { Alignment = PenAlignment.Inset, LineJoin = LineJoin.Round }; g.DrawRectangle(inset, 5, 40, 30, 15); float[] pattern = dashed.DashPattern; // 3, 1, 1, 1 Brushes HatchBrush draws the 53 HatchStyle patterns pixel for pixel as GDI+ draws them on a bitmap, from the device origin moved by RenderingOrigin, including GDI+'s smoothed forward, backward and crossed diagonals. TextureBrush tiles an image (or part of it) through its transform, by its WrapMode; given ImageAttributes, it takes their wrap mode, Clamp unless they set one. LinearGradientBrush runs across a rectangle at an angle, a LinearGradientMode or between two points, with GDI+'s brush transform: the far corners lie on the end colors, and the diagonal modes and a scaleable angle work in the rectangle stretched to a square. Its Blend falls off from SetSigmaBellShape (511 samples of the normal curve, as GDI+ takes them) or SetBlendTriangularShape, or a ColorBlend sets preset colors, after which Blend is null. PathGradientBrush runs from a center color at the mean of the boundary's points out to the surrounding colors. Brushes and SystemBrushes hold solid brushes of the named and system colors; as in System.Drawing, the color of one of the Brushes can be changed. Every brush derives from Brush. // Hatch, texture and gradient brushes, and the Brushes and Pens of the named colors. using Bitmap bitmap = new(80, 60); using Graphics g = Graphics.FromImage(bitmap); using HatchBrush hatch = new(HatchStyle.DiagonalCross, Color.Black, Color.White); g.FillRectangle(hatch, 0, 0, 40, 30); using LinearGradientBrush linear = new(new Rectangle(40, 0, 40, 30), Color.Red, Color.Blue, LinearGradientMode.Horizontal); linear.SetSigmaBellShape(0.5f); g.FillRectangle(linear, 40, 0, 40, 30); using PathGradientBrush radial = new([new PointF(0, 30), new PointF(40, 30), new PointF(20, 60)]) { CenterColor = Color.White, SurroundColors = [Color.Green] }; g.FillRectangle(radial, 0, 30, 40, 30); using Bitmap tile = new(4, 4); tile.SetPixel(0, 0, Color.Orange); using TextureBrush texture = new(tile, WrapMode.TileFlipXY); g.FillRectangle(texture, 40, 30, 40, 30); g.DrawRectangle(Egami.SystemDrawing.Pens.Gray, 0, 0, 79, 59); g.FillEllipse(Egami.SystemDrawing.Brushes.Gold, 36, 26, 8, 8); Blend? blend = linear.Blend; // 511 factors: the bell, as GDI+ samples it Paths A GraphicsPath keeps GDI+'s points and PathPointType types, built as GDI+ builds them: lines, arcs, Beziers and curves join the open figure (a repeated point is dropped), while rectangles, ellipses, pies, polygons and closed curves are figures of their own. Arcs are cubic Beziers of 90 degrees of the ellipse's own angle from the start, the remainder last. PathPoints, PathTypes and PathData hand out copies. Flatten, Widen and Warp (a WarpMode of perspective or bilinear, from four points or three) replace the figures; Reverse keeps each segment's kind, the closes and the markers. GetBounds with a matrix transforms the bounds' corners and grows them for a pen as GDI+ does, and IsVisible and IsOutlineVisible test the pixel a point rounds to. GraphicsPathIterator walks figures, runs of one type and markers. A path also makes a Region, a clip, and a path gradient's boundary. // Paths keep GDI+'s points and point types; lines, arcs and curves join the open figure, closed shapes are their own. using GraphicsPath path = new(); path.AddLine(0, 0, 10, 10); path.AddArc(0, 0, 40, 20, 0, 90); path.CloseFigure(); path.AddEllipse(50, 0, 20, 20); byte[] types = path.PathTypes; // 0 1 1 3 3 3|128, then the ellipse's 13 points RectangleF bounds = path.GetBounds(); bool inside = path.IsVisible(60, 10); using GraphicsPathIterator iterator = new(path); int figures = iterator.SubpathCount; // 2 path.Widen(new Pen(Color.Black, 2)); using Bitmap bitmap = new(80, 30); using Graphics g = Graphics.FromImage(bitmap); g.FillPath(Egami.SystemDrawing.Brushes.Teal, path); g.SetClip(path); Images DrawImage(image, x, y) and DrawImageUnscaled draw an image at its physical size: its pixels at its resolution, in page units at the bitmap's resolution. The other overloads stretch an image or part of it into a rectangle or a parallelogram, with the source in any GraphicsUnit. As in GDI+, the edges fade where sampling reaches past the image, unless ImageAttributes sets a wrap mode; ImageAttributes also applies color matrices (with a ColorMatrixFlag for grays), gamma, thresholds, color keys, ColorMap remap tables (by ColorMapType) and ColorChannelFlag output channels, each for every ColorAdjustType or one of them. A DrawImageAbort callback that returns true stops the draw with ExternalException. DrawIcon stretches an icon, and DrawIconUnstretched draws it at its size. // DrawImage at a point draws at the image's physical size; ImageAttributes adjust its colors and tile it. using Bitmap source = new(8, 8); source.SetResolution(48, 48); // half the 96 dpi of the bitmap drawn on, so it is drawn twice as large using (Graphics s = Graphics.FromImage(source)) { s.Clear(Color.Orange); } using Bitmap bitmap = new(64, 48); using Graphics g = Graphics.FromImage(bitmap); g.DrawImage(source, 0, 0); // 16 by 16 pixels g.InterpolationMode = InterpolationMode.NearestNeighbor; using ImageAttributes attributes = new(); attributes.SetColorMatrix(new ColorMatrix { Matrix33 = 0.5f }); // half the alpha attributes.SetWrapMode(WrapMode.Tile); g.DrawImage(source, new Rectangle(20, 0, 40, 40), 0, 0, 16, 16, GraphicsUnit.Pixel, attributes); What throws on every OS Members that need Windows handles exist so code compiles, throw PlatformNotSupportedException with a message naming what to use instead, and carry [Obsolete] with one diagnostic id per group, so the compiler warns at each use. Suppress an id in the project file (<NoWarn>$(NoWarn);EGSD0001</NoWarn>), around a call (#pragma warning disable EGSD0001), or raise it to an error in .editorconfig. EGSD0001, Windows handles: Bitmap.GetHbitmap, GetHicon, FromHicon and FromResource, Image.FromHbitmap, Icon.Handle and Icon.FromHandle, Graphics.FromHdc, FromHwnd, GetHdc, ReleaseHdc and GetHalftonePalette, and Region.FromHrgn and GetHrgn. Use LockBits for the pixels, new Icon(path) for icons and Graphics.FromImage to draw. EGSD0002, screen capture: Graphics.CopyFromScreen, with or without a CopyPixelOperation. EGSD0003, Windows' own icons: Icon.ExtractAssociatedIcon and Icon.ExtractIcon. Load an icon file instead. Known differences The package is measured against System.Drawing on Windows with the same probe programs compiled against both (egami-compare, sysdrawing/). Pixel formats, conversions, palettes, strides, locks and the codec list match GDI+ exactly. Where it differs: JPEG and GIF files Egami writes differ from GDI+'s in their pixels: the JPEG encoder and GIF color mapping are Egami's. CreateOptimalPalette chooses different colors. CMYK JPEG and TIFF files load as Format24bppRgb; GDI+ gives them a CMYK format System.Drawing has no name for. Egami reads BMP files GDI+ rejects (OS/2, 2-bit, RLE24, embedded PNG and JPEG). Antialiased edges are Egami's: about 96 percent of the pixels of an antialiased shape match GDI+ within 8 levels, and aliased shapes match on about 99.8 percent of their pixels. HighQualityBilinear and HighQualityBicubic sample as plain bilinear and bicubic, without GDI+'s wider filters, and an image drawn much smaller is not prefiltered. Drawing onto 16-bit bitmaps does not dither, and SourceCopy with antialiasing blends its edges with what is below instead of making them transparent. Compound pens draw their strips on both sides of the line, and PathGradientBrush.FocusScales is kept but not drawn. Flatten takes as many steps as GDI+ but evaluates the curve exactly, so its points differ from GDI+'s, which are rounded to sixteenths of a pixel. Rounded rectangles have no zero-length segments, which GDI+'s float arithmetic adds.

articles/guides/text.html.title: Fonts and text | Egami
articles/guides/text.html.summary: Fonts and text Egami.Fonts is a separate package that reads TrueType, OpenType, WOFF, WOFF2 and variable fonts in managed code: faces, glyph outlines, metrics, kerning, installed fonts and subsets. Egami.Drawing uses it to draw and measure a line of text on a canvas. Egami.Drawing and Egami.Fonts are at 1.0 and their APIs are frozen. Egami.Fonts ships no font: text needs a face from a file, a stream, memory or the installed fonts, or from the opt-in substitute fonts package. Faces A Typeface is one face, immutable and shared by every thread. Typeface.FromFile, FromStream and FromMemory read TrueType (.ttf), OpenType CFF and CFF2 (.otf), collections (.ttc, .otc, with a face index), WOFF and WOFF2 (.woff, .woff2, collections too) and bare CFF; FromCff reads a bare CFF stream as PDF embeds it, with CffOptions for the units per em and widths it lacks. FontLoader.Probe tells a FontProbe (its FontFileKind, face count and FontOutlines) from the header, and FontLoader.LoadAll loads every face of a collection. // One face from a file; a collection takes an index. The bytes are read once and every table is parsed when first needed. Typeface face = Typeface.FromFile(FontFile); Console.WriteLine($"{face.FamilyName} {face.SubfamilyName}, {face.GlyphCount} glyphs, {face.UnitsPerEm} units per em"); // What a file holds, from its header alone. FontProbe probe = FontLoader.Probe(File.ReadAllBytes(FontFile)); Console.WriteLine($"{probe.Kind}, {probe.FaceCount} face(s), {probe.Outlines} outlines"); // Damaged fonts load leniently with diagnostics; Strict throws instead. var seen = new List<EgamiDiagnostic>(); var options = new FontLoadOptions { Context = EgamiContext.Default with { Diagnostics = seen.Add } }; Typeface lenient = Typeface.FromMemory(File.ReadAllBytes(FontFile), 0, options); The file is read into memory once and every table is a slice of it; tables are parsed when first used. Loading is lenient: a missing or damaged name, OS/2, hhea, hmtx, post or cmap table gets a documented default and a Font.MissingTable or Font.BadTable diagnostic, and a broken glyph draws empty with Font.BadGlyph. Only a font with no readable glyph data throws CorruptDataException. FontLoadOptions.Strict throws on the first problem instead. A WOFF or WOFF2 file is unwrapped once into an ordinary font in new memory (zlib, and Brotli through .NET's own decoder, with WOFF2's glyf, loca and hmtx transforms); the compressed bytes are not kept. Container says where a face came from, and GetWoffMetadata and GetWoffPrivateData return the file's own blocks. Every decoded table equals the reference decoders'. GetNames returns every FontNameRecord; TryGetTable returns any table's bytes by FontTag. Embedding reports the FontEmbedding permissions, which Egami never enforces. // A CFF stream as a PDF embeds it (FontFile3): no character map, glyphs by id; widths from the PDF when it gives them. Typeface embedded = Typeface.FromCff(fontFile3, new CffOptions { UnitsPerEm = 1000 }); float width = embedded.GetAdvance(1); // WOFF and WOFF2 files load like any font: they are unwrapped into an ordinary font in memory once. Typeface face = Typeface.FromFile(WebFile); FontFileKind container = face.Container; string? metadata = face.GetWoffMetadata(); Variable fonts A variable font is one file that holds a range of designs along its axes, such as weight from 100 to 900. IsVariable, VariationAxes (each a VariationAxis with its range) and NamedInstances (each a NamedInstance, such as "Bold") describe it. WithVariations returns the face at a position, given as FontVariation values, and WithNamedInstance at a named one: an ordinary immutable Typeface sharing the file's memory, whose outlines, advances, extents, kerning, names and subsets all answer for that position. Variations gives a face's position. // A variable font's axes and named instances, and the face at any position on them. Typeface flex = Typeface.FromFile(VariableFile); foreach (VariationAxis axis in flex.VariationAxes) { Console.WriteLine($"{axis.Tag} {axis.Name}: {axis.Min} to {axis.Max}, default {axis.Default}"); } Typeface semiBold = flex.WithVariations(FontVariation.Weight(600), FontVariation.Width(90)); Typeface black = flex.WithNamedInstance(flex.NamedInstances.Count - 1); // The optical size follows the font size unless the face sets it (OpticalSizing.None turns that off). var caption = new Font(semiBold, 11); Typeface drawn = caption.EffectiveTypeface; // For a PDF, the subset is a static font at the face's position, which every viewer draws as it is. FontSubset subset = FontSubsetter.Subset(semiBold, caption.Shape("Static at 600").Glyphs.ToArray()); Positions clamp to each axis; axes the font lacks are ignored, and the default position is the face itself. Faces at a position are cached, so drawing at one position costs what a static font costs. Outlines vary through gvar (TrueType) or CFF2's blends, advances through HVAR (or phantom points), the extents through MVAR and kerning through GDEF's deltas, with avar versions 1 and 2. At 25 positions in each test font every outline and advance equals fontTools' within 1/64 unit. A named instance takes the instance's names; another position keeps the default's names and gets a PostScript name of its own (Adobe Technical Note 5902), such as NotoSans_650wght. FontCollection lists a variable face's named instances as faces, and FontFamily.Match places the face anywhere its weight, width and slant or italic axes reach, as CSS does: weight 450 is drawn at 450, not snapped to 400. With Font.OpticalSizing at OpticalSizing.Auto (the default), a face with an opsz axis it leaves at the default is drawn at opsz equal to the size in canvas units; Font.EffectiveTypeface is the face drawn. SubsetOptions.Variations (by default the face's own position) makes the subset a static font at that position, written as an instancer would: the varied outlines rounded to whole units, metrics, OS/2 and post at the position, CFF2 written as CFF and the variation tables left out. Its outlines, advances and bearings equal fontTools' instancer's, so a PDF shows the position. A variable font's GSUB feature variations (glyph swaps by position) arrive with shaping in 2.8. Glyphs and metrics Everything a face returns is in font units with y up. GetGlyph maps a code point (with a variation selector, through cmap format 14), GetGlyphOutline sends an outline to an IGlyphOutlineSink, and GetAdvance, GetGlyphExtents (a GlyphExtents box) and GetKerning give the numbers. Glyph ids are ushort throughout, as OpenType caps a face at 65,535 glyphs. // Character map, advance, ink box and kerning, all in font units with y up. ushort a = face.GetGlyph('A'), v = face.GetGlyph('V'); float advance = face.GetAdvance(a); GlyphExtents ink = face.GetGlyphExtents(a); float kern = face.GetKerning(a, v); FontExtents extents = face.Extents; // An outline arrives through a sink: lines and quadratics for TrueType, lines and cubics for CFF. var counter = new SegmentCounter(); face.GetGlyphOutline(a, counter); TrueType outlines arrive as lines and quadratic curves and CFF outlines as lines and cubic curves, exactly as stored: every outline of the test fonts equals fontTools' point for point. Extents is a FontExtents with ascent, descent, line gap, cap and x heights, decoration lines and the italic angle, by the browsers' rule: OS/2 typo metrics when the face sets USE_TYPO_METRICS, else hhea. HheaMetrics, TypoMetrics and WinMetrics give each stored VerticalMetrics set. Typeface.GetKerning is GPOS pair positioning under the kern feature (the DFLT and latn scripts), else the kern table. Text drawn on a canvas is shaped with all of the font's OpenType features (see Unicode text and shaping). Text on a canvas A Font is a typeface at a size, the em in canvas units: pixels on a raster, points on a PDF page. Font.FromPoints sizes from points at a resolution. Canvas.DrawText puts the left end of the first line's alphabetic baseline at the origin. Font is a value type; default(Font) has no typeface, and its metrics, shaping and measuring throw InvalidOperationException. // A caption on a photo: white text with a dark shadow, its baseline 24 pixels above the bottom. using Raster<Rgba8> photo = Raster.Create(640, 360, new Rgba8(90, 120, 160, 255)); var font = new Font(Typeface.FromFile(FontFile), 28); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = photo.CreateCanvas()) { var origin = new Vector2(24, photo.Height - 24); canvas.DrawText("Lofoten, March", origin + new Vector2(2, 2), font, new Rgba8(0, 0, 0, 160)); canvas.DrawText("Lofoten, March", origin, font, Rgba8.White); } Font.Shape turns text into a GlyphRun with the full shaper: ligatures, kerning, marks, the script rules, bidi order, and a new line at each hard break (\n, \r\n, \r, U+0085, U+2028, U+2029). ShapingOptions set the direction, language, features and spans. A run has one font, so text that falls back to other fonts is shaped by TextShaper.Shape and drawn with Canvas.DrawShapedText; Canvas.DrawText does that by itself when the options ask for fallback. Nothing wraps; without fallback a missing character draws .notdef. A ShapedText drawn with Canvas.DrawShapedText is shaped once, so it can be measured, kept and drawn again. // Shape once, measure the result, draw it centred: no second shaping pass. using Raster<Rgba8> banner = Raster.Create(640, 120, Rgba8.White); Egami.Fonts.Shaping.ShapedText title = Egami.Fonts.Shaping.TextShaper.Shape("Office hours: 9 to 17", font); var origin = new Vector2((banner.Width - title.Advance) / 2, 70); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = banner.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawShapedText(title, origin, Rgba8.Black); } A run carries the source text and a cluster per glyph, so a PDF backend keeps text searchable. Canvas.DrawGlyphRun draws a run built elsewhere with GlyphRun.Create. Small glyphs are drawn from the GlyphCache of coverage masks, at whole device pixels, by the same rasterizer as paths, so caching changes speed, not pixels. Glyphs over 256 pixels per em, or under a rotation or skew, fill as paths. // Small text draws from a process-wide cache of glyph masks; give it more room for many fonts and sizes. GlyphCache.ByteLimit = 16 * 1024 * 1024; GlyphCache.Clear(); Rendering quality Four switches on a Font change how a raster draws it, never how it measures: MeasureText gives the same numbers whatever they are. // Small text for a screen: light hinting (vertical only), quarter-pixel origins (the default) and, for an RGB display // the image will not leave, LCD edging. var screen = new Font(face, 13) { Hinting = FontHinting.Light, Edging = FontEdging.Lcd }; using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = image.CreateCanvas(new CanvasOptions { PixelGeometry = PixelGeometry.RgbHorizontal })) { canvas.DrawText("Crisp caption", new Vector2(8, 24), screen, Rgba8.Black); // A face matched for bold italic it lacks is emboldened and slanted, unless AllowSynthesis is off. var synthetic = new Font(face, 13) { Synthesis = FontSynthesis.Bold | FontSynthesis.Italic }; canvas.DrawText("Synthetic bold italic", new Vector2(8, 48), synthetic, Rgba8.Black); } Font.Subpixel (on by default) keeps glyph origins at quarter pixels horizontally, each quarter its own cached mask, so small text is evenly spaced; off, origins snap to whole pixels as in 2.7.1. Vertical positions always snap to whole pixels. Font.Hinting = FontHinting.Light snaps the baseline, x-height and cap-height zones (a CFF font's blue zones, else zones measured from the face's own glyphs) to whole pixels, up to 48 pixels per em; x values and advances never move. There is no TrueType bytecode hinting. Font.Edging picks FontEdging.Antialias (the default), Alias (one bit, pixel centres inside the outline) or Lcd: three samples per pixel along the canvas's CanvasOptions.PixelGeometry, filtered and blended per channel. LCD text draws only onto an 8-bit RGB canvas outside layers with a solid source-over paint; anything else falls back to grayscale with one Text.LcdFallback diagnostic per canvas. Images that leave the screen they were made for carry the colour fringes with them, so LCD is opt-in. Font.Synthesis (set by matching) is drawn: bold outsets the outline by em/24 at 9 pixels down to em/32 at 36 and above, advances unchanged, and italic slants 14 degrees, CSS's default oblique. Glyph paths and ink bounds include it; Font.AllowSynthesis = false turns it off. Text gamma and contrast Two canvas settings change how heavy small text looks without touching its shapes. CanvasOptions.TextGamma (0.5 to 3, default 1) blends glyph coverage per channel as (a·src^γ + (1 − a)·dst^γ)^(1/γ) on the stored values, as GDI ClearType does: above 1, light text on a dark ground gets heavier and dark text on a light ground lighter. CanvasOptions.TextContrast (0 to 1, default 0) first boosts coverage a to a + (1 − a)·c·a, the contrast boost of Skia and DirectWrite, which thickens thin edges whatever the colours. // A white label on a blue button, weighted like GDI+'s ClearTypeGridFit text: a text gamma of 1.15 matched the brightness // GDI+ adds to within 1% for Trebuchet MS at 16 pixels. Shapes and images on this canvas blend as before. var options = new CanvasOptions { PixelGeometry = PixelGeometry.RgbHorizontal, TextGamma = 1.15f }; var label = new Font(face, 16) { Hinting = FontHinting.Light, Edging = FontEdging.Lcd, Subpixel = false }; using (RasterCanvas<Rgb8> canvas = button.CreateCanvas(options)) { canvas.DrawText("Start the course", new Vector2(40, 26), label, Rgba8.White); } // Thin dark text on a light page can take a contrast boost instead, as Skia and DirectWrite do. var boosted = new CanvasOptions { TextContrast = 0.25f }; Only glyphs drawn from the glyph cache (up to 256 pixels per em, under a scale-and-translate transform) take them; shapes, images, blurred text and text drawn as paths never do. The defaults draw exactly what Egami 1.2.0 drew. The gamma needs to read the canvas, so it applies to solid source-over text on an 8-bit RGB canvas outside layers, the text LCD edging can draw too; other text takes the contrast only. With ColorSpace.Linear the gamma is ignored, since that blend is already gamma-correct; the contrast still applies. To look like GDI+ ClearTypeGridFit (its default TextContrast of 4) with LCD edging, light hinting and whole-pixel origins, use a gamma of 1.15 and no contrast: the brightness a white Trebuchet MS label adds to a black or a #0078d4 button is then within 1% of GDI+'s. With the GDI filter and sampling below, use 1.25. Letter shapes and spacing still differ, since TrueType instructions are not run. LCD filter, sampling and ClearType level Three more canvas settings shape LCD text. CanvasOptions.LcdFilter spreads each subpixel's coverage over five taps that add up to 256: LcdFilter.Default (16, 64, 96, 64, 16, Egami's filter since 2.7.2), Balanced (8, 77, 86, 77, 8), Light (0, 85, 86, 85, 0), Gdi (the even three-subpixel spread measured from GDI and GDI+, the weights of Light) or LcdFilter.Custom. CanvasOptions.LcdSampling = LcdSampling.Gdi samples as GDI+ ClearType does: six on-or-off samples per pixel across the stripes, on each pixel's centre line, so edges along the stripes stay sharp and each channel of the Gdi filter is a whole number of sixths; Smooth, the default, takes exact areas. CanvasOptions.ClearTypeLevel (0 to 1, default 1) mixes the filtered coverage with the pixel's grayscale coverage, as Windows' ClearType level does. // GDI+ ClearType's look: its filter (an even spread over three subpixels), no smoothing along the stripes, and the text // gamma that then matched GDI+'s weight for a white Trebuchet MS label at 16 pixels. var gdiPlus = new CanvasOptions { PixelGeometry = PixelGeometry.RgbHorizontal, LcdFilter = LcdFilter.Gdi, LcdSampling = LcdSampling.Gdi, TextGamma = 1.25f, }; var label = new Font(face, 16) { Hinting = FontHinting.Light, Edging = FontEdging.Lcd, Subpixel = false }; using (RasterCanvas<Rgb8> canvas = button.CreateCanvas(gdiPlus)) { canvas.DrawText("Start the course", new Vector2(40, 26), label, Rgba8.White); } // Softer fringes: a balanced filter and half the colour of full ClearType. var soft = new CanvasOptions { PixelGeometry = PixelGeometry.RgbHorizontal, LcdFilter = LcdFilter.Balanced, ClearTypeLevel = 0.5f }; // Or weights of your own, normalised to add up to 256. var custom = new CanvasOptions { PixelGeometry = PixelGeometry.RgbHorizontal, LcdFilter = LcdFilter.Custom(1, 3, 4, 3, 1) }; With all three at their defaults LCD text is drawn as in Egami 1.2.0. TrueType hinting FontHinting.Full runs the font's own TrueType instructions, with Egami's interpreter, at a whole number of pixels per em. Font.HintingTarget picks what the interpreter tells the font it is: TrueTypeTarget.GdiPlus (the default) or Gdi, both with the answers measured from Windows and Microsoft's ClearType compatibility rules (x hinted on a 1/16-pixel grid), or FreeType (FreeType's minimal rules: x left alone). CFF faces, faces without instructions, variable faces and sizes the gasp table leaves unhinted fall back to FontHinting.Light. So does text under a transform that scales x and y differently or turns it. Font.Metrics = FontMetrics.GridFitted takes each glyph's advance from its hinted phantom points at that size, FontMetrics.GridFittedToDesign does the same but keeps design advances for a run they would widen by more than 2.1 pixels (GDI+'s GenericTypographic layout), and FontMetrics.Compatible takes GDI's compatible widths: the hdmx table's widths, the rounded design advance where the LTSH table says the glyph scales linearly, or the advance of a black-and-white run of the glyph's instructions. On the six Windows UI fonts from 8 to 24 pixels per em, these equal GDI's GetCharABCWidths for 9,688 of 9,690 glyph sizes. Shaping, measuring and layout use these whole-pixel advances, and drawing puts every glyph origin on a whole pixel, so measured text always matches drawn text. // The font's own TrueType instructions, run for GDI+, with its hinted advances: glyphs on whole pixels, spacing as Windows // lays out ClearType text. Together with GDI+'s filter, sampling and gamma (1 + TextContrast/10 = 1.4), this is the closest // Egami gets to System.Drawing's ClearTypeGridFit. var label = new Font(face, 16) { Hinting = FontHinting.Full, HintingTarget = TrueTypeTarget.GdiPlus, Metrics = FontMetrics.GridFitted, Edging = FontEdging.Lcd, }; var gdiPlus = new CanvasOptions { PixelGeometry = PixelGeometry.RgbHorizontal, LcdFilter = LcdFilter.Gdi, LcdSampling = LcdSampling.Gdi, TextGamma = 1.4f, }; using (RasterCanvas<Rgb8> canvas = button.CreateCanvas(gdiPlus)) { // Measuring uses the same hinted advances, so centring is exact. float width = label.MeasureText("Start the course").Advance; canvas.DrawText("Start the course", new Vector2(MathF.Round((200 - width) / 2), 26), label, Rgba8.White); } With the GDI+ settings in that sample, a white Trebuchet MS label on a button has the brightness GDI+'s ClearTypeGridFit gives it to within 0.5%, and the mean per-pixel difference from GDI+ falls from 9.5 levels (light hinting) to 0.67 on a black button: for that label the two are nearly pixel for pixel the same. Embolden and stem darkening Font.Embolden grows outlines on every side by an amount in the font's units (pixels on a raster), with round joins, on top of synthetic bold; advances never change, and glyph paths and ink bounds include it. Font.StemDarkening grows thin stems by the default darkening curve FreeType documents for its CFF engine (its darkening-parameters property): 0.4 pixel for stems up to 0.5 pixel wide, 0.275 from 1 to 1.667 pixels, nothing from 2.333, half on each side. The stem width is the face's own (a CFF font's StdVW, else measured across 'l'), so darkening fades as text grows. It follows the device size, so only drawing on a raster applies it. // A little more weight without a bold face: outlines grow 0.2 pixels on each side, advances stay as they are. var heavier = new Font(face, 14) { Embolden = 0.2f }; // Darkening for thin stems only: it fades out as the face's stems grow past 1.667 pixels. var caption = new Font(face, 9) { StemDarkening = true }; using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = image.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawText("Slightly heavier", new Vector2(8, 24), heavier, Rgba8.Black); canvas.DrawText("A darkened caption", new Vector2(8, 48), caption, Rgba8.Black); } Color fonts Emoji and other color glyphs draw in color by themselves. Per glyph, the first format the font has wins: COLR version 1 (a graph of layers, gradients, transforms and compositing), COLR version 0 (layers of solid outlines), sbix, then CBDT and CBLC (images); anything else draws its outline in the paint. Typeface.ColorFormats says what a face holds. // Color glyphs draw in color by themselves: COLR (layers and gradients), sbix and CBDT (images), per glyph. using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = image.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawText("Ship it", new Vector2(8, 40), new Font(text, 24), Rgba8.Black); canvas.DrawText("\U0001F680\U0001F389", new Vector2(100, 42), new Font(emoji, 32), Rgba8.Black); } // The palette is a font setting; the paint's color fills a glyph's foreground parts and its alpha the whole glyph. var darkMode = new Font(emoji, 32) { Palette = FontPalette.Dark }; ColorGlyphFormats formats = emoji.ColorFormats; // The paint graph is there to walk, for writers that draw color glyphs their own way. emoji.TryGetColorGlyph(emoji.GetGlyph(0x1F680), darkMode.Palette, out ColorGlyph? rocket); Font.Palette picks a CPAL palette by index or by FontPaletteBackground (FontPalette.Light, FontPalette.Dark), with FontPaletteEntry overrides; Typeface.Palettes lists each FontPaletteInfo. Font.ColorGlyphs = false draws outlines. The paint's color fills the glyph's foreground parts and its alpha and blend mode apply to the whole glyph, drawn as one group. Typeface.TryGetColorGlyph returns a ColorGlyph: a PaintColorGlyph whose ColorPaint graph an IColorPaintVisitor walks, with variable values taken at the face's position: ColorLayersPaint, ColorSolidPaint (a GlyphColor), ColorLinearGradientPaint, ColorRadialGradientPaint and ColorSweepGradientPaint (over a ColorLine of ColorStops with a ColorExtend), ColorGlyphPaint (a glyph-outline clip), ColorGlyphReferencePaint, ColorTransformPaint and ColorCompositePaint; or a BitmapColorGlyph with its image (BitmapGlyphEncoding) and placement, from the strike nearest above the size. Every canvas draws color glyphs: the default glyph hook turns them into clips, fills, gradients, layers and images, so a PDF page gets vector color. A raster caches them, up to 256 pixels per em, as color images keyed by palette. OpenType SVG glyphs are not drawn: Typeface.TryGetSvgDocument returns the document for callers with an SVG renderer, and such glyphs fall back to their COLR, bitmap or outline data. Drawing them arrives with Egami.Svg. Text on a path Canvas.DrawTextOnPath lays a line of text along a Path by SVG's textPath rules, through Font.ShapeOnPath: each glyph's advance midpoint sits on the path, turned to its direction, and glyphs past either end are left out. TextOnPathOptions sets the start (StartOffset in canvas units plus StartFraction of the length), the TextAnchor, the BaselineShift along the normal, the TextPathSide and whether a closed contour wraps. // A label along a curve: each glyph's midpoint on the path, turned to its direction, as SVG's textPath. The result is // still a glyph run, so a PDF backend writes it as searchable text. Path curve = new PathBuilder().MoveTo(20, 150).CubicTo(80, 20, 240, 20, 300, 150).ToPath(); var font = new Font(face, 18); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = image.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawTextOnPath("Text that follows the curve", curve, font, Rgba8.Black, new TextOnPathOptions { StartFraction = 0.5f, Anchor = TextAnchor.Center, BaselineShift = 4 }); } // Or place glyphs yourself, each with its own turn and scale. GlyphRun dial = GlyphRun.CreateTransformed(font, [face.GetGlyph('N'), face.GetGlyph('E')], [GlyphTransform.FromRotationScale(1, 0, new Vector2(150, 30)), GlyphTransform.FromRotationScale(1, 90, new Vector2(290, 90))]); The result is a GlyphRun with a GlyphTransform per glyph (a rotation and uniform scale, then an origin, as Skia's RSXform), so a PDF backend writes it as real, searchable text; GlyphRun.CreateTransformed builds such runs by hand. Glyphs that are only moved draw from the glyph cache like any text; turned or scaled ones fill as paths. Text is not warped: each glyph keeps its shape, as SVG and browsers draw it. Measuring Font.MeasureText lays text out exactly as DrawText does and returns a TextMeasure: the widest line's advance, the exact ink box as TextBounds, the line count and the vertical metrics. // A label shrunk until it fits a 200-pixel button, then centred on it. const string label = "Download the full report"; var box = new RectF(20, 20, 200, 40); var font = new Font(face, 24); while (font.MeasureText(label).Advance > box.Width - 16 && font.Size > 8) { font = new Font(face, font.Size - 1); } TextMeasure size = font.MeasureText(label); var origin = new Vector2( box.X + ((box.Width - size.Advance) / 2), box.Y + ((box.Height - size.Height) / 2) + size.Ascent); using Raster<Rgba8> image = Raster.Create(240, 80, Rgba8.White); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = image.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.FillRoundRect(new RoundRect(box, 8), new Rgba8(30, 90, 200, 255)); canvas.DrawText(label, origin, font, Rgba8.White); } MeasureText also takes a ReadOnlySpan<char>, so a slice of a longer text or a reused buffer is measured without making a string of it. // Measure each word of a longer text in place: a span is measured without making a string of it. ReadOnlySpan<char> text = "Measure every word of this sentence"; float widest = 0; foreach (Range word in text.Split(' ')) { widest = Math.Max(widest, font.MeasureText(text[word]).Advance); } Text as paths FontExtensions holds GetGlyphPath, GetTextPath and GlyphRun.ToPath, which give Paths in canvas units, y down, to stroke, clip to or combine. // Text as a shape: outline it, or clip a picture to it. Path title = font.GetTextPath("EGAMI", new Vector2(10, 80)); using Raster<Rgba8> image = Raster.Create(300, 100, Rgba8.White); using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = image.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.StrokePath(title, new Stroke(2), Rgba8.Black); canvas.ClipPath(title); canvas.FillRect(new RectF(0, 50, 300, 50), Rgba8.Red); } Installed fonts and matching FontCollection.System finds the installed fonts without native calls, by scanning the platform's font folders (and fontconfig's dir entries on Linux), and indexes them on first use from the name and OS/2 tables only. It is read-only. A FontCollection of your own takes faces, files and folders, and AddSystemFonts copies the installed fonts into it, so your fonts and the machine's are matched together. Families are found by typographic, legacy, full or PostScript name in any language, and FontFamily.Match picks a face by the CSS Fonts 4 rules for a FontStyle (weight, width and FontSlant). The FontMatch records the FontSynthesis a lighter or upright face would need; GenericFamily names fixed per-platform lists. // Installed fonts, found without native calls and indexed on first use; a style is matched by the CSS rules. FontMatch? match = FontCollection.System.Match(GenericFamily.SansSerif, FontStyle.Bold); // Your own fonts work the same way; System is read-only, so add the installed fonts to your collection to have both. var fonts = new FontCollection(); fonts.AddFile(FontFile); fonts.AddSystemFonts(); FontMatch noto = fonts.Match("Noto Sans", FontStyle.BoldItalic)!.Value; Font font = noto.ToFont(16); Substitute fonts Documents often name Arial, Helvetica, Times, Courier, Calibri or Cambria without carrying the font, and many machines (Linux servers and containers above all) have none of them. Egami.Fonts.Substitutes is a separate, opt-in package that bundles open fonts with the same glyph widths, so text set in a substitute keeps the original's line breaks: Liberation Sans for Helvetica and Arial, Liberation Serif for Times and Times New Roman, Liberation Mono for Courier and Courier New, Carlito for Calibri and Caladea for Cambria, each in four styles. It adds about 7 MB, which is why Egami.Fonts does not carry the fonts itself. The fonts are under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, and their licences ship in the package. SubstituteFonts.Find takes a family name or a common alias (ArialMT, Times-Roman, Courier New; spaces, hyphens and case are ignored) and returns the face in the nearest style, or null for any other name. SubstituteFonts.Collection holds all twenty faces as a FontCollection, to match by family name or to pass to anything that takes fonts, such as MetafileRenderOptions.Fonts or SvgFontOptions.Collection. // Bundled faces for the fonts documents name most, on any machine: Arial is Liberation Sans, Calibri is Carlito. Typeface? arial = SubstituteFonts.Find("Arial", FontStyle.Bold); Font body = new(SubstituteFonts.Find("Calibri", FontStyle.Normal)!, 11); // All twenty faces as a collection, matched by family name and style. FontMatch? mono = SubstituteFonts.Collection.Match("Liberation Mono", FontStyle.Italic); Subsets FontSubsetter.Subset writes a font with only some glyphs, as PDF embedding and SVG export want: TrueType, OpenType CFF or a bare CID-keyed CFF stream (SubsetFormat), closed over composites and accents, with unused CFF subroutines dropped. SubsetOptions sets the format, dense or kept glyph ids, the character map, extra tables and the subset tag; the FontSubset holds the bytes and the glyph map. // Keep only the glyphs a page uses, as a PDF writer embeds them: renumbered from 0, with the map to write the text with. GlyphRun run = new Font(face, 12).Shape("Invoice 2026-10"); FontSubset subset = FontSubsetter.Subset(face, run.Glyphs.ToArray(), new SubsetOptions { FontNamePrefix = "ABCDEF+", KeepCmap = false, }); byte[] fontFile2 = subset.Data.ToArray(); ushort first = subset.GlyphMap[run.Glyphs[0]]; // The face's embedding permissions are reported, never enforced: the writer decides. bool restricted = face.Embedding.HasFlag(FontEmbedding.Restricted); A PDF needs only the glyphs it draws. A subset that is to be shaped again, such as a web font for a known set of pages, sets SubsetOptions.LayoutClosure: the kept glyphs gain every glyph GSUB can substitute for them (OpenTypeLayout.GetClosure with the default features), and GSUB, GPOS and GDEF are copied unchanged. The copied tables use the old glyph ids, so it needs RetainGlyphIds. // Keep what the text's characters can become (ligatures, contextual forms) and the layout tables, so the subset shapes // the text as the full face does; the copied tables use the old glyph ids, so the ids are kept. ushort[] glyphs = [.. "office".Select(c => face.GetGlyph(c))]; FontSubset subset = FontSubsetter.Subset(face, glyphs, new SubsetOptions { RetainGlyphIds = true, LayoutClosure = true }); GlyphRun shaped = new Font(subset.ToTypeface(), 12).Shape("office"); Font data for PDF A PDF font reaches its glyphs in ways a text layout never does: by glyph name, by CID, through one particular cmap subtable or through the font program's own encoding. Typeface gives each as FreeType does, so a PDF reader built on Egami finds the glyphs PDFium finds. GetGlyphName and TryGetGlyphByName read a name-keyed CFF font's charset, else the post table (versions 1, 2 and 2.5). A simple font's /Differences array names glyphs this way. When two glyphs share a name the lower id wins. // A PDF simple font's /Differences array names glyphs: find each by name, and get names back for a ToUnicode guess. ushort aacute = face.TryGetGlyphByName("aacute", out ushort g) ? g : (ushort)0; string? name = face.GetGlyphName(aacute); A simple font's /Differences names glyphs; TryGetGlyphByName finds them in a CFF charset or a TrueType post table. CidSystemInfo, GetCid and TryGetGlyphByCid read a CID-keyed CFF font's ROS and charset, for CIDFontType0 fonts. // A CIDFontType0 font with /CIDToGIDMap absent reaches glyphs by CID through the CFF charset. CidSystemInfo? collection = cjk.CidSystemInfo; // Adobe-Identity-0 for this font ushort glyph = cjk.TryGetGlyphByCid(1, out ushort byCid) ? byCid : (ushort)0; int cid = cjk.GetCid(glyph); CharacterMaps lists every cmap subtable as stored and FindCharacterMap picks one by platform and encoding; a CharacterMap maps the subtable's own codes (bytes for (1,0) and (3,0)), never translated, and GetMappings lists them all as CharacterMappings. BuiltInEncoding is a name-keyed CFF font's own encoding as a platform 7 map (0 Standard, 1 Expert, 2 custom). GetGlyph(codePoint) keeps choosing its one Unicode subtable as before. // A symbolic TrueType font in PDF looks a code up in (3,0) first, then (1,0); a non-symbolic one uses (3,1). CharacterMap? map = trueType.FindCharacterMap(3, 0) ?? trueType.FindCharacterMap(1, 0) ?? trueType.FindCharacterMap(3, 1); ushort forA = map?.GetGlyph('A') ?? 0; // A Type1C font without /Encoding uses the CFF program's own encoding. CharacterMap? own = face.BuiltInEncoding; // platform 7, encoding 0: the Standard Encoding ushort forB = own?.GetGlyph('B') ?? 0; // Every code the map gives a glyph, in code order, for a PDF writer's /Widths or a ToUnicode table. int mapped = map?.GetMappings().Count() ?? 0; A symbolic TrueType font looks codes up in (3,0), then (1,0); a non-symbolic one in (3,1). A Type1C font without /Encoding uses the CFF program's own encoding, BuiltInEncoding. CffStandardStrings has the 391 standard strings and the Standard and Expert encodings, for writing CFF (a Type 1 font converted for embedding, say). // Converting a Type 1 font to CFF: standard glyph names take their standard SIDs, others go in the String INDEX. int sid = CffStandardStrings.TryGetSid("Aacute", out int standard) ? standard : -1; string atCode65 = CffStandardStrings.StandardEncoding[65]; // "A" Everything is read on first use, once per face, and is safe from several threads. Damaged data never throws: a name the post table cannot give is null, a subtable that cannot be read maps nothing, and each reports a warning (Font.BadTable) through the context's diagnostics, unless FontLoadOptions.Strict asks for an exception. On the 1,723 font programs embedded in Egap's corpus, names, CIDs, subtables and built-in encodings equal FreeType's and fontTools' (FreeType's where the two differ). Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. A label along a curve // A round badge: one label along the top of a circle and one along the bottom, both reading left to right and centred. // Each glyph sits on the curve at its midpoint, turned to the curve's direction, as SVG's textPath. var badge = new Font(face, 16); Path ring = new PathBuilder().AddOval(new RectF(20, 20, 160, 160)).ToPath(); Path top = new PathBuilder().MoveTo(40, 100).ArcTo(new Vector2(60, 60), 0, false, true, new Vector2(160, 100)).ToPath(); Path bottom = new PathBuilder().MoveTo(40, 100).ArcTo(new Vector2(60, 60), 0, false, false, new Vector2(160, 100)).ToPath(); var centred = new TextOnPathOptions { StartFraction = 0.5f, Anchor = TextAnchor.Center }; using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = image.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.StrokePath(ring, new Stroke(2), new SolidPaint(Rgba8.Black)); canvas.DrawTextOnPath("EGAMI QUALITY", top, badge, Rgba8.Black, centred); // Below, the glyphs hang under the curve: shift the baseline down by the cap height. canvas.DrawTextOnPath("since 2026", bottom, badge, Rgba8.Black, centred with { BaselineShift = -12 }); } A variable weight slider // A weight slider: each move draws the sample at the new weight. Faces at a position share the font's memory and are // cached, and glyph masks are cached per position, so dragging back and forth is cheap. Raster<Rgba8> Preview(float weight) { VariationAxis axis = flex.VariationAxes.First(a => a.Tag == new FontTag("wght")); Typeface face = flex.WithVariations(FontVariation.Weight(Math.Clamp(weight, axis.Min, axis.Max))); var font = new Font(face, 28); TextMeasure size = font.MeasureText("Weight"); Raster<Rgba8> preview = Raster.Create((int)MathF.Ceiling(size.Advance) + 16, (int)MathF.Ceiling(size.Height) + 8, Rgba8.White); using RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = preview.CreateCanvas(); canvas.DrawText("Weight", new Vector2(8, 4 + size.Ascent), font, Rgba8.Black); return preview; } Searchable text in a PDF // What a PDF writer needs to keep shaped text searchable: each glyph's cluster points back into the text. A glyph that // stands for several characters (the "ffi" ligature) maps to all of them in ToUnicode; a cluster whose glyphs were // reordered or merged (Indic, Arabic marks) goes in an ActualText span instead. GlyphRun run = new Font(face, 11).Shape("office hours"); var toUnicode = new Dictionary<ushort, string>(); for (int i = 0; i < run.Count; i++) { int start = run.Clusters[i]; int end = i + 1 < run.Count ? run.Clusters[i + 1] : run.Text!.Length; if (end > start) { toUnicode.TryAdd(run.Glyphs[i], run.Text![start..end]); } } A GlyphRun from the shaper carries the text and a cluster per glyph, in visual order; that is all a PDF writer needs for ToUnicode and ActualText. A variable font in a PDF // PDF has no variable fonts: embed a static instance at the position the page uses. The subset is an ordinary TrueType // font (glyf and hmtx at that position, no variation tables); its whole-unit advances are the ones to write in /W. Typeface heading = flex.WithVariations(FontVariation.Weight(720), FontVariation.Width(85)); GlyphRun run = new Font(heading, 24).Shape("Annual report"); FontSubset subset = FontSubsetter.Subset(heading, run.Glyphs.ToArray(), new SubsetOptions { FontNamePrefix = "EGAMIA+" }); Typeface embedded = subset.ToTypeface(); var widths = new SortedDictionary<ushort, int>(); foreach (ushort glyph in run.Glyphs) { ushort id = subset.GlyphMap[glyph]; widths[id] = (int)MathF.Round(embedded.GetAdvance(id) * 1000 / embedded.UnitsPerEm); } byte[] fontFile2 = subset.Data.ToArray(); The subset of a variable face is always a static instance; SubsetOptions.Variations gives the position without making a face.

articles/guides/tone-and-color.html.title: Tone and color | Egami
articles/guides/tone-and-color.html.summary: Tone and color Egami has the tone and color tools photo editors have: levels, gamma, curves and sigmoidal contrast; posterize, solarize, colorize, tint, duotone, thresholds and an accessibility filter; 3D lookup tables from .cube files and Hald images; and the adjustments that read the image first, from auto levels to white balance, equalization, CLAHE and local contrast. The tone steps follow ImageMagick's formulas, with values from 0 to 1 where ImageMagick takes percentages: Level(0.1f, 0.9f) is -level 10%,90%. They work on the stored, gamma-encoded values, as photo editors and LUT files do, change red, green and blue, keep alpha, and clamp to 0..1 after each step. Tone steps // A basic tone panel: levels with a midtone lift, a gentle S-curve, and a warm tint in the midtones. The three steps run as // one pass over the pixels. raster.Apply(o => o .Level(black: 0.04f, white: 0.96f, gamma: 1.1f) .SigmoidalContrast(4, midpoint: 0.5f) .Tint(new Rgba8(255, 200, 150, 255), 0.15f), Ct); raster.Save("duck-toned.jpg"); Levels, an S-curve and a tint run as one pass over the pixels. Step Does ImageMagick Level(black, white, gamma, outputBlack, outputWhite) Stretches black..white to outputBlack..outputWhite with a midtone gamma -level, +level Gamma(gamma) v^(1/gamma): 2.2 brightens -gamma SigmoidalContrast(contrast, midpoint, increase) An S-curve that adds contrast without clipping, or its inverse ±sigmoidal-contrast Posterize(levels, dither) Rounds each channel to evenly spaced levels, optionally with ordered or Floyd–Steinberg dithering -posterize Solarize(threshold) Inverts values above the threshold -solarize Threshold(level, mode, below, above) Two colors, by luminance, saturation, chroma or each channel (ThresholdMode) -threshold Colorize(color, amount) Blends toward a color -colorize Tint(color, amount) Pushes the midtones toward a color, keeping black and white -tint Duotone(shadows, highlights) Maps luminance onto a line between two colors -grayscale then +level-colors HighContrast(grayscale, invert, contrast) Skia's high-contrast accessibility filter (ContrastInvert) — SimulateColorBlindness(kind, severity) Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (2009), from mild anomaly to full -opia (ColorVisionDeficiency) — Every one of these matches ImageMagick 7 to within one level at 8 bits, and thresholds are identical, including where a pixel lies exactly on the level. Adjacent tone steps, color matrices and filters fuse into one pass over the pixels; on 8- and 16-bit images a fused chain is a lookup table per channel, rounded between steps, so it gives exactly the pixels the steps give one by one. // A two-color poster, then a check of how it reads to someone with deuteranopia. raster.Apply(o => o.Duotone(Rgba8.FromHex("#1b2a49"), Rgba8.FromHex("#f2c14e")).Posterize(4, DitherMode.Ordered), Ct); using Raster<Rgba8> preview = raster.Derive(o => o.SimulateColorBlindness(ColorVisionDeficiency.Deuteranopia), Ct); // High contrast for low vision: gray, lightness inverted so dark becomes light, and more contrast. using Raster<Rgba8> readable = raster.Derive(o => o.HighContrast(grayscale: true, ContrastInvert.Lightness, contrast: 0.3f), Ct); Color filters A ColorFilter is a color adjustment as a value, as Skia's color filters are: a function of one pixel's color, with no neighbours, position or statistics. Every tone step and color matrix has a factory; Curves takes ToneCurves, FromLut a 3D table; Then chains filters and Lerp mixes two, so a look can be applied at any strength. Run one with ApplyFilter, on your own pixels with Apply, or save it as a .cube file with ToLut3D. // A look as a value: build it once, mix it in at 70%, apply it to any image or to your own pixels. ColorFilter look = ColorFilter.Level(0.03f, 0.97f).Then(ColorFilter.Saturation(1.2f)).Then(ColorFilter.Tint(new Rgba8(255, 190, 140, 255), 0.2f)); ColorFilter subtle = ColorFilter.Lerp(ColorFilter.Identity, look, 0.7f); raster.Apply(o => o.ApplyFilter(subtle), Ct); Span<Rgba8> swatch = [new Rgba8(200, 120, 80, 255), new Rgba8(40, 60, 90, 255)]; subtle.Apply(swatch); ToneCurve.FromPoints draws a curve as photo editors do, a monotone cubic through the points (Fritsch and Carlson) that never overshoots; FromTable and FromFunction take a table or a function. // Curves as a photo editor draws them: a smooth curve through the points that never overshoots, here a mild S on all // three channels and a lift in the blue shadows. ToneCurve s = ToneCurve.FromPoints([(0, 0), (0.25f, 0.2f), (0.75f, 0.82f), (1, 1)]); ToneCurve blue = ToneCurve.FromPoints([(0, 0.06f), (0.5f, 0.5f), (1, 1)]); raster.Apply(o => o.ApplyFilter(ColorFilter.Curves(s, s, s.Then(blue))), Ct); 3D lookup tables A Lut3D is an N × N × N grid of output colors, with an optional 1D shaper before it. CubeFile reads and writes .cube files (Adobe's 1.0 specification and DaVinci Resolve's 1D-plus-3D form); the reader is strict and checks the limits before it allocates. Lut3D.FromHald and ToHald read and write Hald CLUT images, and Raster.HaldIdentity makes the identity to grade in an editor. LutInterpolation.Tetrahedral (the default, as Resolve and OpenColorIO read tables) keeps grays neutral; Trilinear matches ImageMagick's -hald-clut to within a level. // Export a grade for DaVinci Resolve or Premiere, then load a .cube file and apply it at 70%.
