ColorFilter grade = ColorFilter.Curves(ToneCurve.FromPoints([(0, 0), (0.25f, 0.2f), (0.75f, 0.82f), (1, 1)])) .Then(ColorFilter.Saturation(1.1f)); CubeFile.Write("my-grade.cube", grade.ToLut3D(size: 33), title: "My grade"); Lut3D lut = CubeFile.Read("my-grade.cube"); raster.Apply(o => o.ApplyFilter(ColorFilter.Lerp(ColorFilter.Identity, ColorFilter.FromLut(lut), 0.7f)), Ct); // Tables can also be built from a function, and read at any color. Lut3D warm = Lut3D.FromFunction(c => new Vector3(c.X, c.Y * 0.97f, c.Z * 0.9f), size: 17); Vector3 gray = warm.Evaluate(new Vector3(0.5f), LutInterpolation.Tetrahedral); // Export the identity Hald image, grade it in any editor, and load the graded image back as a table. using Raster<Rgba8> identity = Raster.HaldIdentity(level: 8); // 512 × 512, a 64³ table identity.Save("hald.png"); using Raster graded = Raster.Load("hald.png"); Lut3D fromHald = Lut3D.FromHald(graded); using Raster<Rgba16> back = fromHald.ToHald(level: 8); Adjustments that read the image AutoLevel, ContrastStretch, Normalize, AutoGamma, AutoWhiteBalance, Equalize and AutoThreshold measure the image before they change it: the chain runs up to the step, the step measures the result, and it becomes a plain filter for the rest of the chain. Inside Within or OnChannels they measure only the scope; transparent pixels do not count. An animation is measured as a whole, so its frames get one correction and do not flicker; perFrame: true measures each frame alone, as ImageMagick does. Black and white points, gammas and threshold levels equal ImageMagick's. // Fix a dull scan: stretch it to the full range, clipping the darkest 2% and lightest 1%, then set the midtones. raster.Apply(o => o.Normalize().AutoGamma(), Ct); // Or stretch each channel on its own, which also removes a cast. raster.Apply(o => o.AutoLevel(linked: false), Ct); // Measured steps measure only their scope: here the sky alone is stretched. raster.Apply(o => o.Within(new Rect(0, 0, raster.Width, raster.Height / 3), sky => sky.AutoLevel()), Ct); linked: true (the default) gives red, green and blue one pair of points, which keeps colors; false gives each channel its own, which also removes a cast. Each step has a Raster.Measure… helper that returns the filter without changing anything, to apply one correction to many images. // Measure once on a reference shot, then apply the same correction to the whole shoot. ColorFilter fix = reference.MeasureAutoLevel().Then(reference.MeasureWhiteBalance()); foreach (Raster<Rgba8> shot in shoot) { shot.Apply(o => o.ApplyFilter(fix), Ct); } // The other measured steps have their Measure helpers too. ColorFilter stretch = reference.MeasureContrastStretch(0.02f, 0.01f); ColorFilter midtones = reference.MeasureAutoGamma(); ColorFilter spread = reference.MeasureEqualize(); White balance WhiteBalance(temperature, tint) corrects for a light of a known color temperature with the Bradford transform, as a raw editor's sliders do; WhiteBalance(neutral) makes a picked color gray; AutoWhiteBalance finds the cast itself (WhiteBalanceMethod.GrayWorld, ImageMagick's -white-balance, or WhitePatch). Both fixed corrections are also filters, ColorFilter.WhiteBalance(neutral) and ColorFilter.WhiteBalance(temperature, tint), so they can join a chain or a paint. // Correct a tungsten-lit photo, as a raw editor's temperature slider does. raster.Apply(o => o.WhiteBalance(temperature: 3200), Ct); // Or pick a gray card's color and make it neutral. raster.Apply(o => o.WhiteBalance(new Rgba8(182, 170, 151, 255)), Ct); // Or let the image tell: ImageMagick's gray world, or the brightest pixels as white. raster.Apply(o => o.AutoWhiteBalance(WhiteBalanceMethod.GrayWorld), Ct); raster.Apply(o => o.AutoWhiteBalance(WhiteBalanceMethod.WhitePatch), Ct); Equalization, CLAHE and local contrast Equalize spreads the values evenly: of L* by default, so colors hold (EqualizeMode.Luminance), or of each channel as ImageMagick's -equalize (EqualizeMode.Channels). Clahe equalizes each tile of the image with a clipped histogram and blends the tiles smoothly (Zuiderveld's CLAHE, on L* as ImageMagick runs it); LocalContrast is ImageMagick's -local-contrast. Both look at neighbours, and each frame is its own. // Spread the lightness evenly without shifting colors, or each channel on its own as ImageMagick's -equalize. using Raster<Rgba8> even = raster.Derive(o => o.Equalize(EqualizeMode.Luminance), Ct); using Raster<Rgba8> strong = raster.Derive(o => o.Equalize(EqualizeMode.Channels), Ct); // Bring out detail in a flat, foggy landscape: CLAHE on 8 × 8 tiles, then ImageMagick's local contrast. raster.Apply(o => o.Clahe(tilesX: 8, tilesY: 8, clipLimit: 2).LocalContrast(radius: 0.1f, strength: 0.15f), Ct); Thresholds AutoThreshold finds the level with Otsu's, the triangle or Kapur's method (ThresholdMethod), as ImageMagick's -auto-threshold; Raster.FindThreshold returns the level alone. AdaptiveThreshold compares each pixel with the mean of the window around it (Bradley and Roth), for pages under uneven light. // Two colors: navy below half luminance, cream above; alpha is kept. using Raster<Rgba8> stamp = raster.Derive(o => o.Threshold(0.5f, ThresholdMode.Luminance, Rgba8.Navy, new Rgba8(250, 240, 220, 255)), Ct); // Threshold a scanned page for OCR: Otsu's level for an evenly lit page, or Bradley's local threshold for uneven light. float level = page.FindThreshold(ThresholdMethod.Otsu); using Raster<Gray8> even = page.Derive(o => o.AutoThreshold(ThresholdMethod.Otsu), Ct); using Raster<Gray8> uneven = page.Derive(o => o.AdaptiveThreshold(limit: 0.15f), Ct); Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Tint a photo // Tint toward sepia-orange, keeping the shading: Color takes the tint's hue and saturation and the photo's luminosity. photo.Apply(ops => ops.BlendColor(new Rgba8(220, 150, 80, 255), BlendMode.Color, opacity: 0.5f), Ct);

articles/guides/unicode-text.html.title: Unicode text and shaping | Egami
articles/guides/unicode-text.html.summary: Unicode text and shaping Egami.Fonts carries its own Unicode 17.0 data and the Unicode algorithms text shaping builds on: character properties, the bidirectional algorithm and text boundaries, in the Egami.Fonts.Unicode namespace. On top of them, Egami.Fonts.Shaping shapes text with a font's OpenType tables, as HarfBuzz does, with HarfBuzz's script shapers (Arabic, Syriac, N'Ko and Mongolian joining, Hebrew, the nine Indic scripts, Khmer, Myanmar, Thai, Lao, Hangul, and the Universal Shaping Engine for Tibetan, Sinhala, Javanese and the other complex scripts), itemization, font fallback and drawing on the canvas. The tables are generated from the Unicode Character Database by tools/make-unicode-tables.py and never come from the .NET runtime, so the same text gives the same answer on every runtime and machine. UnicodeData.UnicodeVersion says which version they follow. Character properties UnicodeData answers per code point: the general category (as the runtime's UnicodeCategory), the Script and its script extensions, the BidiClass, the mirroring character and BidiPairedBracketType, the JoiningType and JoiningGroup of Arabic and Syriac letters, the canonical combining class, the VerticalOrientation, the EastAsianWidth, the LineBreakClass (UAX #14), the emoji properties and whether a character is default ignorable. // Egami's own Unicode 17.0 tables: the same answer on every runtime and machine. Script script = UnicodeData.GetScript('\u0915'); // Devanagari ReadOnlySpan<FontTag> tags = script.OpenTypeTags; // dev2, then deva BidiClass bidi = UnicodeData.GetBidiClass('\u0627'); // ArabicLetter JoiningType joining = UnicodeData.GetJoiningType('\u0628'); // DualJoining JoiningGroup group = UnicodeData.GetJoiningGroup('\u0628'); // Beh VerticalOrientation upright = UnicodeData.GetVerticalOrientation('\u6F22'); // Upright EastAsianWidth width = UnicodeData.GetEastAsianWidth('\u6F22'); // Wide bool emoji = UnicodeData.IsEmojiPresentation(0x1F600); // true UnicodeData.TryGetBidiMirroringGlyph('(', out int mirror); // ')' BidiPairedBracketType bracket = UnicodeData.GetBidiPairedBracketType('['); // Open A Script has its ISO 15924 Code, its Unicode Name and the OpenType tags fonts use for it, newest first (dev2 then deva). Common, Inherited and Unknown are the shared scripts, and fonts know them as DFLT. Every lookup is a few array reads and allocates nothing. Code points run from 0 to 0x10FFFF; lone surrogates are code points too. Bidirectional text Bidi.Resolve runs the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX #9) in full: embeddings, overrides and isolates up to depth 125, paired brackets and the weak and neutral rules. It returns a BidiResult with a level per UTF-16 unit and the BidiRuns of equal level; Reorder gives one line's runs from left to right. TextDirection.Auto, the default, takes each paragraph's direction from its first strong character; LeftToRight and RightToLeft force it. // A Hebrew word inside English text: three runs, the middle one drawn right to left. string text = "abc \u05D0\u05D1\u05D2 def"; using BidiResult result = Bidi.Resolve(text, TextDirection.Auto); int paragraph = result.ParagraphLevel; // 0: the first strong character is Latin foreach (BidiRun run in result.Reorder(0, result.Length)) { Console.WriteLine($"{run.Start}+{run.Length} {(run.IsRightToLeft ? "right to left" : "left to right")}"); } Each paragraph separator ends a paragraph, and each paragraph is resolved on its own. Levels lays each paragraph out as one line. When text is wrapped, call Reorder per line: trailing spaces then take the paragraph's level, as rule L1 asks. The result rents its arrays; dispose it when done. Unicode's BidiTest.txt and BidiCharacterTest.txt pass in full. Graphemes and words TextSegmenter.Graphemes walks extended grapheme clusters (UAX #29): what a reader sees as one character, such as a letter with its accents, a Hangul syllable, a Devanagari conjunct or an emoji sequence. TextSegmenter.Words walks the segments between word boundaries with Unicode's default rules. Both return a TextSegment per segment through a GraphemeEnumerator or WordEnumerator that allocates nothing; IsGraphemeBoundary checks one index. // A family emoji is one grapheme cluster of eight UTF-16 units; "can't" is one word. string text = "\uD83D\uDC68\u200D\uD83D\uDC69\u200D\uD83D\uDC67 can't stop"; var graphemes = new List<TextSegment>(); foreach (TextSegment grapheme in TextSegmenter.Graphemes(text)) { graphemes.Add(grapheme); } var words = new List<string>(); foreach (TextSegment word in TextSegmenter.Words(text)) { words.Add(text.Substring(word.Start, word.Length)); } bool inside = TextSegmenter.IsGraphemeBoundary(text, 2); // false: inside the family Words use no dictionary, so Thai, Lao, Khmer and CJK text without spaces is not split into words. Line breaking (UAX #14) arrives with paragraph layout in 2.8.2. Unicode's GraphemeBreakTest.txt and WordBreakTest.txt pass in full. Shaping a run TextShaper.ShapeRun shapes one run of text in one font, as HarfBuzz's hb_shape: the font's GSUB substitutions (ligatures, contextual and alternate forms) and GPOS positioning (kerning, marks, cursive attachment) with the default features, normalization against the font's character map, and the fallbacks HarfBuzz uses for fonts that lack them. RunProperties gives the script (taken from the text when null), a BCP 47 language (none by default: the font's default forms, never the machine's culture), the direction, feature settings and the ClusterLevel. The result lands in a reusable GlyphBuffer: glyph ids, the UTF-16 index each glyph's cluster starts at, GlyphFlags and a GlyphPosition per glyph, in visual order and in the font's units. // One run, one font, as HarfBuzz's hb_shape: ligatures, kerning and marks from the font's GSUB and GPOS. var font = new Font(face, 24); var glyphs = new GlyphBuffer(); string text = "office"; TextShaper.ShapeRun(text, 0, text.Length, font, new RunProperties { Script = Script.Latin }, glyphs); for (int i = 0; i < glyphs.Count; i++) { ushort id = glyphs.GlyphIds[i]; int cluster = glyphs.Clusters[i]; // index in text the glyph came from GlyphPosition position = glyphs.Positions[i]; // in the font's units (pixels here) bool breakable = (glyphs.Flags[i] & GlyphFlags.UnsafeToBreak) == 0; } float width = glyphs.Advance; GlyphFlags.UnsafeToBreak marks where breaking the text needs shaping again; line layout uses it to re-shape only there. A run is one script in one direction; TextShaper.Shape splits real text into runs. The engine gives exactly hb-shape's glyphs, clusters, positions and flags on HarfBuzz's own tests and on Egami's corpus. Shaping text TextShaper.Shape shapes a whole string: it splits it into lines at hard breaks ( , , , U+0085, U+2028, U+2029), resolves each line's bidi levels, splits the line into runs of one level, one script, one span and one font, shapes each run as ShapeRun does and returns the runs in display order. Nothing wraps; that is line layout's job. // Whole text: lines at hard breaks, bidi levels, script runs, fallback fonts, runs in display order. var font = new Font(face, 24); var options = new ShapingOptions { Fallback = new FontFallback(fonts.Families) }; ShapedText shaped = TextShaper.Shape("Shalom: \u05E9\u05DC\u05D5\u05DD!", font, options); float x = 0; foreach (ShapedRun run in shaped.Lines[0].Runs) { GlyphRun glyphs = run.ToGlyphRun(new System.Numerics.Vector2(x, 0), shaped.Text); // what a canvas draws x += run.Advance; } ShapedText.Lines holds a ShapedLine per line, with its ParagraphLevel, its Runs from left to right, its Advance and the highest ascent and lowest descent of its fonts. Each ShapedRun has its Font, BidiLevel, Script, Language, text range and GlyphBuffer; ToGlyphRun turns it into the GlyphRun a canvas draws. ShapingOptions.Direction is Auto by default: each paragraph takes the direction of its first strong character. ShapingOptions.Spans give ranges their own font, language or features; spans must not overlap. // A styled range: its own font, language or features. var options = new ShapingOptions { Language = "en", Spans = [new TextSpan(6, 6) { Font = font with { Kerning = false }, Features = [FontFeature.SmallCaps] }], }; ShapedText shaped = TextShaper.Shape("Hello, World", font, options); Font fallback A font that does not map a character draws .notdef, unless ShapingOptions.Fallback names fonts to try. Fallback works on whole grapheme clusters, so a letter and its accents, or an emoji sequence, stay in one font: the first font that maps every character of the cluster takes it. The span's font comes first, then the FontFallback.Families (matched to the font's style), then the FontFallback.Resolver. Spaces and punctuation stay in the font before them when it has them, so fallback does not split words. Emoji presentation (a default-emoji character or VS16) prefers a color face (COLR, sbix or CBDT); VS15 prefers an outline face. // Characters the font lacks: the caller's families first, then installed fonts only when asked for. FontFallback mine = new(FontCollection.System.Families.Where(f => f.Name is "Segoe UI Emoji" or "Noto Color Emoji")); FontFallback system = FontFallback.System; // depends on the machine's fonts FontFallback none = FontFallback.None; // the default: missing characters draw as .notdef FontFallback.None, the default, keeps output independent of the machine: only the fonts passed are used. FontFallback.System resolves from the installed fonts through SystemFontFallback: fixed families per script on Windows, macOS and Linux (Segoe UI Emoji, Apple Color Emoji or Noto Color Emoji for emoji; the language picks Japanese, Chinese or Korean faces for Han), then any installed face that maps the cluster. Output then depends on the fonts installed. An IFontFallbackResolver of your own receives the cluster's text, script, language and the font's style. Features A FontFeature sets one OpenType feature for the whole run or a range of it: 0 turns a default feature off, 1 turns a feature on, higher values pick an alternate. FontFeature.Parse reads HarfBuzz's syntax (liga=0, +smcp, ss01, aalt=2, kern[3:5]=0); the presets cover common cases. // HarfBuzz's feature syntax, or the presets. FontFeature noLigatures = FontFeature.Parse("liga=0"); FontFeature figures = FontFeature.TabularFigures; FontFeature alternates = FontFeature.StylisticSet(1); FontFeature someKerning = FontFeature.Parse("kern[0:3]=0"); // off for the first three characters only var properties = new RunProperties { Features = [noLigatures, figures] }; TextShaper.ShapeRun(text, 0, text.Length, font, properties, glyphs); Layout tables Typeface.Layout returns an OpenTypeLayout, which lists the scripts, language systems and features the font's GSUB and GPOS offer. A table whose structure is damaged is ignored whole, with a Font.BadTable diagnostic, as HarfBuzz ignores it; a font that drives shaping past its limits stops with Font.ShapingLimit. // What the font's layout tables list. OpenTypeLayout layout = face.Layout; IReadOnlyList<FontTag> scripts = layout.Scripts; // DFLT, cyrl, grek, latn IReadOnlyList<FontTag> languages = layout.GetLanguageSystems(new FontTag("latn")); IReadOnlyList<FontTag> features = layout.GetFeatures(new FontTag("latn")); // liga, kern, ... Recipes Short answers to common tasks in this area. Each one compiles and runs in Egami's test run. Emoji in a caption // A caption mixing words and emoji: the emoji fall back to the color face, cluster by cluster, so a ZWJ sequence or a flag // stays whole; one call shapes and draws every run. string caption = "Launch day \U0001F680 thanks, team \U0001F389"; var fallback = new FontCollection(); fallback.Add(emoji); var options = new Egami.Fonts.Shaping.ShapingOptions { Fallback = new Egami.Fonts.Shaping.FontFallback(fallback.Families) }; using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = image.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawText(caption, new Vector2(8, 32), new Font(text, 20), Rgba8.Black, options); } Color glyphs draw in color on every canvas; on a raster they are cached as images, like other glyphs. A cluster with emoji presentation prefers a color face from the fallback list; text presentation (VS15) prefers an outline face. An Arabic caption // An Arabic caption, right-aligned: the shaper joins the letters and puts the words in right-to-left order, and the measured // advance places the line's right end at the margin. using Raster<Rgba8> photo = Raster.Create(640, 120, new Rgba8(40, 60, 80, 255)); var font = new Font(arabic, 32); string caption = "\u0645\u0631\u062D\u0628\u0627\u0020\u0628\u0627\u0644\u0639\u0627\u0644\u0645"; float width = font.MeasureText(caption).Advance; using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = photo.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawText(caption, new Vector2(photo.Width - 24 - width, 80), font, Rgba8.White); } The shaper picks each letter's joining form and the bidi algorithm orders the words; the origin is still the line's left end, so right alignment subtracts the measured advance. A Hindi label with fallback // A label in Hindi and English with a Latin font: Devanagari clusters (conjuncts, vowel signs, the reph) fall back whole to // the Devanagari face, and the Indic shaper reorders them. var families = new FontCollection(); families.Add(devanagari); var options = new Egami.Fonts.Shaping.ShapingOptions { Language = "hi", Fallback = new Egami.Fonts.Shaping.FontFallback(families.Families), }; using (RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = image.CreateCanvas()) { canvas.DrawText("Price: \u0915\u0940\u092E\u0924\u0020\u0915\u094D\u0937\u0947\u0924\u094D\u0930", new Vector2(10, 40), new Font(latin, 22), Rgba8.Black, options); } Fallback works on whole grapheme clusters, so a conjunct never splits across two faces. FontFallback.System would find an installed Devanagari face instead, at the cost of output that depends on the machine.

articles/guides/video-editing.html.title: Video editing | Egami
articles/guides/video-editing.html.summary: Video editing Egami.Video's editing library, in Egami.Video.Editing, joins clips with transitions, draws clips over clips, keys out green screens, lays clips side by side and runs Egami operations on the result, encoding it all again in one pass. An edit is a description: VideoEdit holds an EditCanvas, a main EditTrack of Clips with a Transition between each two, Layers drawn over it and EditEffects. Nothing is decoded until it renders, and then only the frames in use are held. The egami-video commands join, fade, overlay, pip, stack and edit build the same edits (see the command line). Joining clips Clips play one after another; each TrackItem on the track is a clip and the transition into it. They may differ in size, frame rate, pixel format and sound: the canvas sets the output's size, frame rate and audio format (from the first clip when there is no canvas), each clip is fitted with ClipFit (Contain with bars by default, Cover, Stretch or None) over the canvas Background, each output frame shows the source frame nearest its time, and the sound is resampled and remixed; a clip without sound adds silence. Clip.Trim cuts a clip on the exact frame and sample, and FadeIn and FadeOut fade the picture from and to a colour and the sound from and to silence. Render writes the result with a VideoWriter, whose settings EditRenderOptions.Writer carries; the sound goes into Opus unless another audio codec is set. // Three clips of different sizes and rates, fitted to one 320x180 canvas at 25 fps, with fades at both ends. VideoEdit edit = new(new EditCanvas(320, 180, new Rational(25, 1)) { Fit = ClipFit.Contain }); edit.Track .Add(Clip.Open("intro.avi").FadeIn(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5))) .Add(Clip.Open("talk.avi").Trim(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5), MediaTime.FromSeconds(1.5))) .Add(Clip.Open("outro.avi").FadeOut(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5))); EditPlan plan = edit.Render("joined.mkv", new EditRenderOptions { Writer = new VideoWriterOptions { Codec = MotionJpegCodec.Instance, Quality = 80 } }); Console.WriteLine($"{plan.FrameCount} frames, {plan.Duration.Seconds} s"); Plan lays the timeline out in whole frames before anything is decoded and returns an EditPlan: every PlannedClip and PlannedLayer with its frames, the length, and warnings about what it fixed up. An edit that cannot render, such as one with a trim past a clip's end or a transition longer than a clip, throws with every reason. ToJson and VideoEdit.FromJson save and load an edit as the JSON file the command line's edit runs. // Lay out the timeline before rendering, and save the edit as the JSON file 'egami-video edit' runs. VideoEdit edit = new(new EditCanvas(320, 180, new Rational(25, 1))); edit.Track.Add(Clip.Open("intro.avi")).Add(Clip.Open("talk.avi"), Transition.Fade(MediaTime.FromSeconds(1))); EditPlan plan = edit.Plan(); foreach (PlannedClip clip in plan.Clips) { Console.WriteLine($"clip {clip.Index}: frames {clip.StartFrame} to {clip.StartFrame + clip.FrameCount - 1}, {clip.SourceSize.Width}x{clip.SourceSize.Height}"); } foreach (string warning in plan.Warnings) { Console.WriteLine(warning); } File.WriteAllText("edit.json", edit.ToJson()); VideoEdit again = VideoEdit.FromJson(File.ReadAllText("edit.json")); Transitions A Transition overlaps the two clips it joins by its Duration, so the edit gets shorter by it, and crossfades their sound over the same time (AudioCurve, equal power by default). TransitionKind has ten built-in kinds: Fade (a cross-dissolve), FadeThroughColor, Dissolve, Wipe and Slide in a TransitionDirection, CircleOpen, CircleClose, Clock, Zoom, Pixelize and Blur. A wipe can have a soft edge (Softness), and any transition can ease its progress (Easing). The fades and wipes match FFmpeg's xfade to within its rounding and one pixel of the edge. // A dissolve, then a soft wipe with eased progress: each overlaps the two clips by its length, sound crossfading too. VideoEdit edit = new(new EditCanvas(320, 180, new Rational(25, 1))); edit.Track.Add(Clip.Open("intro.avi")) .Add(Clip.Open("talk.avi"), Transition.Dissolve(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5))) .Add(Clip.Open("outro.avi"), Transition.Wipe(TransitionDirection.Left, MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5)) with { Softness = 0.1, Easing = Easing.EaseInOut }); EditPlan plan = edit.Render("transitions.mkv"); An app's own transition implements ITransition, which draws one frame from the two clips' frames and the progress: // An app's own transition: the incoming clip appears from the top down. VideoEdit edit = new(new EditCanvas(320, 180, new Rational(25, 1))); edit.Track.Add(Clip.Open("intro.avi")).Add(Clip.Open("outro.avi"), Transition.Custom(new Blinds(), MediaTime.FromSeconds(1))); edit.Render("blinds.mkv"); private sealed class Blinds : ITransition { public void Render(Raster<Rgba8> outgoing, Raster<Rgba8> incoming, double progress, Raster<Rgba8> target) { int rows = (int)Math.Round(progress * target.Height); for (int y = 0; y < target.Height; y++) { (y < rows ? incoming : outgoing).Row(y).CopyTo(target.Row(y)); } } } Layers A Layer draws a clip over the main track: placed in a rectangle (Place(Rect)) or at an Anchor with a margin and a scale, with an opacity and an Egami BlendMode, inside a time window (Between), with fades. Animate moves its LayerProperty values (X, Y, Scale, Rotation and Opacity) through Keyframes, timed from the layer's start. A layer ends with its clip, or holds the last frame (HoldLastFrame). Its sound is mixed in unless its clip is muted. // Picture-in-picture: talk.avi in the bottom-right corner from 0.5 s to 1.5 s, sliding in from the right as it fades in. VideoEdit edit = new(new EditCanvas(320, 180, new Rational(25, 1))); edit.Track.Add(Clip.Open("intro.avi")); edit.Layers.Add(Layer.Of(Clip.Open("talk.avi").Muted()) .Place(Anchor.BottomRight, margin: 8, scale: 0.3) .Between(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5), MediaTime.FromSeconds(1.5)) .FadeIn(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.25)) .Animate(LayerProperty.X, new Keyframe(MediaTime.Zero, 60, Easing.EaseOut), new Keyframe(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.25), 0))); edit.Render("pip.mkv"); Layer.Key runs a ChromaKey on the layer's frames: Egami's chroma key takes out the pixels near the screen colour in the CbCr plane, so uneven lighting on the screen matters little, and despill takes the screen's colour out of hair and edges. // A green-screen clip over another: the key takes the studio green out and despill cleans its edges. VideoEdit edit = new(new EditCanvas(320, 180, new Rational(25, 1))); edit.Track.Add(Clip.Open("intro.avi")); edit.Layers.Add(Layer.Of(Clip.Open("presenter-green.avi")) .Key(new ChromaKey(Rgba8.FromHex("#00b140")) { Similarity = 0.12f, Blend = 0.06f, Despill = 0.6f }) .Place(new Rect(160, 90, 160, 90))); edit.Render("keyed.mkv"); Stacks Stack.Horizontal, Stack.Vertical and Stack.Grid (the three StackLayouts) make one clip of several shown at once, like FFmpeg's hstack, vstack and xstack. StackOptions sets a gap, the background, how grid cells fit, whether the stack ends with its shortest clip, and whether the sound is the first clip's or every clip's mixed. A stack is a clip, so it can be trimmed, faded and joined with a transition. // Two clips side by side with a 4-pixel gap, each scaled to the first one's height; a stack is a clip like any other. VideoEdit edit = new(); edit.Track.Add(Stack.Horizontal([Clip.Open("intro.avi"), Clip.Open("talk.avi")], new StackOptions { Gap = 4, MixAudio = true })); EditPlan plan = edit.Render("side-by-side.mkv"); Console.WriteLine($"{plan.Canvas.Width}x{plan.Canvas.Height}"); Speed, reverse, loops and freezes Clip.Speed plays a clip faster or slower, from a tenth of its speed to ten times: the picture takes the nearest frame, and the sound keeps its pitch through V9.1's Tempo (or follows it, like a tape, with keepPitch: false). Reverse plays a clip backwards, picture and sound, decoding one keyframe interval at a time, so memory stays bounded however long the clip is. Loop plays it several times, Freeze holds the frame at a time for a while (a ClipFreeze, with silence), and Hold keeps the last frame after the end. They apply in that order: speed, reverse, loops, freezes, then the hold. Frame counts and timestamps match FFmpeg's setpts with fps, reverse, loop and tpad. // Twice as fast with the pitch kept, then backwards, then twice in a row with a frame frozen for half a second. VideoEdit edit = new(new EditCanvas(320, 180, new Rational(25, 1))); edit.Track .Add(Clip.Open("talk.avi").Speed(2)) .Add(Clip.Open("intro.avi").Reverse()) .Add(Clip.Open("outro.avi").Trim(MediaTime.Zero, MediaTime.FromSeconds(1)).Loop(2).Freeze(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5), MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5)).Hold(MediaTime.FromSeconds(1))); EditPlan plan = edit.Render("timing.mkv"); Stills, colours and an app's own frames Clip.Still shows an image for a time, Clip.Animation plays an animated GIF, WebP or APNG at its own delays, and Clip.Color is one colour the canvas size. PanZoom moves the part of the picture shown from one rectangle to another (a PanZoomPath, in fractions of the picture), drawn with a sub-pixel transform from the full picture on every frame, so slow zooms do not jitter as whole-pixel crops do. Slideshow.Create builds an edit of images with transitions and, optionally, a pan and zoom for each from a seed (SlideshowOptions). Clip.FromSource takes an app's own IFrameSource, such as titles drawn with Egami.Drawing. // Photos as a slideshow with fades and a slow pan and zoom, then a title an app draws, on black. VideoEdit show = Slideshow.Create(["duck.png", "egret.png"], new SlideshowOptions { Each = MediaTime.FromSeconds(3), PanZoom = true, Canvas = new EditCanvas(320, 180, new Rational(25, 1)) { Fit = ClipFit.Cover }, }); show.Track.Add(Clip.Color(Rgba8.Black, MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5)), Transition.Fade(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5))); show.Track.Add(Clip.FromSource(new Title())); show.Track.Add(Clip.Still("duck.png", MediaTime.FromSeconds(2)) .PanZoom(new System.Drawing.RectangleF(0, 0, 1, 1), new System.Drawing.RectangleF(0.3f, 0.3f, 0.4f, 0.4f), Easing.EaseInOut)); show.Render("slideshow.mkv"); private sealed class Title : IFrameSource { public Size Size => new(320, 180); public MediaTime Duration => MediaTime.FromSeconds(1); public void Render(MediaTime time, Raster<Rgba8> target) { // A bar that grows across the frame: draw anything here, such as text with Egami.Drawing. int width = (int)(target.Width * time.Seconds / Duration.Seconds); for (int y = 0; y < target.Height; y++) { Span<Rgba8> row = target.Row(y); row.Fill(Rgba8.Black); if (y is > 80 and < 100) { row[..width].Fill(Rgba8.White); } } } } Effects EditEffect.Apply runs Egami operations or any IRasterOperation on each frame, and EditEffect.Of runs an app's own IFrameEffect, which gets the frame's time and its progress through the effect's window in a FrameEffectContext. Effects attach to the whole edit (VideoEdit.Effects), to a clip (Clip.WithEffect) or to a layer (Layer.WithEffect), and Between limits one to a time window. An effect keeps the frame size. // Blur the whole edit from 0.5 s to 1 s, and darken one clip with an app's own effect that knows the time. VideoEdit edit = new(new EditCanvas(320, 180, new Rational(25, 1))); edit.Track.Add(Clip.Open("intro.avi").WithEffect(EditEffect.Of(new Darken()))); edit.Effects.Add(EditEffect.Apply(ops => ops.Blur(4), "blur 4").Between(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5), MediaTime.FromSeconds(1))); edit.Render("effects.mkv"); private sealed class Darken : IFrameEffect { public void Apply(Raster<Rgba8> frame, FrameEffectContext context) { float keep = 1 - (0.5f * (float)context.Progress); for (int y = 0; y < frame.Height; y++) { foreach (ref Rgba8 p in frame.Row(y)) { p = new Rgba8((byte)(p.R * keep), (byte)(p.G * keep), (byte)(p.B * keep), p.A); } } } } Plug-in points An app adds its own pieces at five places, each an interface it implements: ITransition draws a transition between two clips' frames, IFrameEffect changes a frame knowing its time and progress, IRasterOperation (Egami's own operation interface) runs through EditEffect.Apply as an effect, IFrameSource makes a clip's frames, such as titles drawn by the app, and ChromaKey settings key a layer. All of them work on Egami rasters, so they need nothing from the video side. A model on every frame A machine-learning model, such as a style transfer or a denoiser, plugs in as an IRasterOperation. The adapter below turns each frame into a 1x3xHxW tensor of red, green and blue from 0 to 1, hands it to a model, and writes the model's tensor back. Here the model is a stand-in written in C# (a sepia tone), so the sample runs with the tests: /// <summary> /// Runs a model on each frame: the frame goes in as a 1x3xHxW tensor of red, green and blue from 0 to 1, and the model's /// tensor of the same shape comes back into the frame. Alpha is kept. /// </summary> public sealed class ModelOperation(Func<float[], int, int, float[]> model) : IRasterOperation { public Size OutputSize(Size input) => input; public void Run<TPixel>(OperationInput<TPixel> input) where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> { int width = input.Source.Width, height = input.Source.Height, plane = width * height; float[] tensor = new float[3 * plane]; float[] alpha = new float[plane]; for (int y = 0; y < height; y++) { Span<TPixel> row = input.Source.Row(y); for (int x = 0; x < width; x++) { Vector4 v = row[x].ToScaled(); int i = (y * width) + x; tensor[i] = v.X; tensor[plane + i] = v.Y; tensor[(2 * plane) + i] = v.Z; alpha[i] = v.W; } } float[] result = model(tensor, width, height); if (result.Length != tensor.Length) { throw new InvalidOperationException($"The model returned {result.Length} values, not {tensor.Length}."); } for (int y = 0; y < height; y++) { Span<TPixel> row = input.Destination.Row(y); for (int x = 0; x < width; x++) { int i = (y * width) + x; row[x] = TPixel.FromScaled(Vector4.Clamp(new Vector4(result[i], result[plane + i], result[(2 * plane) + i], alpha[i]), Vector4.Zero, Vector4.One)); } } } } /// <summary>A stand-in for a style model: a sepia tone, as a tensor in and a tensor out.</summary> public static float[] Sepia(float[] tensor, int width, int height) { int plane = width * height; float[] output = new float[tensor.Length]; for (int i = 0; i < plane; i++) { float r = tensor[i], g = tensor[plane + i], b = tensor[(2 * plane) + i]; output[i] = (0.393f * r) + (0.769f * g) + (0.189f * b); output[plane + i] = (0.349f * r) + (0.686f * g) + (0.168f * b); output[(2 * plane) + i] = (0.272f * r) + (0.534f * g) + (0.131f * b); } return output; } // A model as an effect: every frame of the edit from 0.2 s goes through it. VideoEdit edit = new(); edit.Track.Add(Clip.Open("clip.mkv")); edit.Effects.Add(EditEffect.Apply(new ModelOperation(Sepia), "sepia model").Between(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.2))); edit.Render("styled.mkv"); With ONNX Runtime, an app's own reference to the Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime package (Egami.Video has none), the stand-in becomes a call into an InferenceSession. These lines are app code shown as a sketch: they are not compiled or run with Egami's tests, and the input name and shape depend on the model. // Untested app code: needs the Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime package and a model file. using Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime; using Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime.Tensors; using InferenceSession session = new("style.onnx"); string inputName = session.InputMetadata.Keys.First(); float[] RunModel(float[] tensor, int width, int height) { DenseTensor<float> input = new(tensor, [1, 3, height, width]); using IDisposableReadOnlyCollection<DisposableNamedOnnxValue> results = session.Run([NamedOnnxValue.CreateFromTensor(inputName, input)]); return results.First().AsTensor<float>().ToArray(); } edit.Effects.Add(EditEffect.Apply(new ModelOperation(RunModel), "style model")); Smart render EditRenderOptions.SmartRender (the command line's --smart) copies the untouched parts of clips instead of encoding them again. Where one clip fills the picture with no transition, fade, layer, effect or change of time, its source has the canvas's size and frame rate, and its stream matches what the encoder writes (VP8, VP9, AV1 or Motion JPEG with the same profile, bit depth, chroma, color and, for AV1, sequence header), its packets are copied byte for byte from the first keyframe on, and the encoder starts again with a keyframe after each copied part. A source that does not match is encoded as usual, with a MediaWarning. The sound is always mixed and encoded. It is off by default. Stabilizing Stabilizing takes two passes, like FFmpeg's vidstabdetect and vidstabtransform. Stabilizer.Analyze measures the camera's motion from each frame to the next: it tracks corners with pyramidal Lucas-Kanade on a copy of the luma no wider than MotionAnalysisOptions.AnalysisWidth and fits a turn, a zoom and a move to them with RANSAC. The CameraMotion it returns saves as JSON, so the slow pass runs once; its Frames are FrameMotions, the move, turn and zoom from the frame before. Clip.Stabilize then smooths the camera's path with a Gaussian over StabilizeOptions.Smoothing frames either way and warps each frame onto the smooth path; the clip's Stabilization holds both as a ClipStabilization. StabilizeEdges says what fills the edges a correction uncovers: Zoom (the least zoom that hides them in every frame, up to StabilizeOptions.MaxZoom, 1.5 by default), Black or Blur. The command line's stabilize does both passes, and --save-motion and --motion split them. // Two passes: measure the camera's motion, then render the clip warped onto a smoothed path, zoomed to hide the edges. CameraMotion motion = Stabilizer.Analyze("talk.avi"); File.WriteAllText("talk.motion.json", motion.ToJson()); VideoEdit edit = new(); edit.Track.Add(Clip.Open("talk.avi").Stabilize(motion, new StabilizeOptions { Smoothing = 20, Edges = StabilizeEdges.Zoom })); edit.Render("steady.mkv");

articles/guides/video-encoding.html.title: Encoding video | Egami
articles/guides/video-encoding.html.summary: Encoding video Egami.Video encodes VP8 and VP9 into WebM, Matroska and IVF (VP9 into MP4 too), with alpha in WebM and Matroska, and AV1 into WebM, Matroska, MP4, IVF, raw OBU and Annex B files. VP8's frame coding is Egami's Vp8StreamEncoder, VP9's Egami.Video's own and AV1's Egami's Av1StreamEncoder; for all three, Egami.Video decides how each frame is coded: where keyframes go, which frames become references, and how many bits each frame gets. Motion JPEG and uncompressed video encode too, without these settings: every frame is a keyframe. Writing VP8 Set VideoWriterOptions.Codec to VideoCodecs.Vp8. Quality runs from 0 to 100 (default 60, the scale of Egami's AVIF writer) and Effort from 0 (fastest) to 10 (smallest files, default 4). Frames given as 8-bit 4:2:0 planes are coded as they are; anything else is converted to BT.601 limited range first. Frames with alpha get a second VP8 stream for the alpha plane, as WebM carries it. // VP8 in WebM at constant quality: Quality 0 to 100 (default 60) and Effort 0 to 10 (default 4). VideoWriterOptions options = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.Vp8, FrameRate = new Rational(30, 1), Quality = 70, Effort = 4 }; using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("duck.webm", options)) { for (int i = 0; i < 30; i++) { using Raster<Rgb8> frame = duck.Derive(ops => ops.Crop(new Rect(i * 4, i * 2, 320, 240))); writer.WriteFrame(frame); } } // Expert settings: no hidden alternate reference frames, and quantizer limits. VideoWriterOptions tuned = options with { Vp8 = new Vp8EncoderOptions { AlternateReference = false, MinQuantizer = 10, MaxQuantizer = 90 } }; Vp8EncoderOptions holds the expert settings: quantizer limits, alternate reference frames on or off, golden frame spacing, the temporal filter's frames and strength, token partitions, error resilience and alpha. Writing VP9 Set VideoWriterOptions.Codec to VideoCodecs.Vp9. Quality and Effort work as for VP8 (default 60 and 4); Quantizer runs from 0 to 255, and 0 is lossless. The encoder searches each 64x64 superblock's partition down to 4x4, its intra modes, motion vectors to 1/8 pixel with three interpolation filters, compound prediction from two references and its transform sizes by rate and distortion, quantizes with a trellis, and picks the loop filter level per frame. Hidden alternate references go out in a superframe with the next shown frame, so every packet shows one frame. // VP9 in WebM at constant quality, on the same Quality and Effort scales as VP8. VideoWriterOptions options = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.Vp9, FrameRate = new Rational(30, 1), Quality = 70, Effort = 2 }; using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("duck-vp9.webm", options)) { for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { using Raster<Rgb8> frame = duck.Derive(ops => ops.Crop(new Rect(i * 4, i * 2, 320, 240))); writer.WriteFrame(frame); } } // Expert settings: two tile columns, adaptive quantization, quantizer limits on VP9's 0 to 255 scale. VideoWriterOptions tuned = options with { Vp9 = new Vp9EncoderOptions { TileColumns = 2, AdaptiveQuantization = true, MinQuantizer = 20, MaxQuantizer = 200 }, }; Vp9EncoderOptions holds the expert settings: quantizer limits, alternate reference frames on or off, golden frame spacing, the temporal filter's frames and strength, tile columns, adaptive quantization by block detail (libvpx's aq-mode 1), error resilience, the bit depth and alpha. Frames are split into up to four tile columns by default (each at least 256 pixels wide), which the encoder searches on separate threads, superblock rows running as a wavefront within them. Bit depths, chroma and HDR 8-bit 4:2:0 planes are coded as they are (profile 0); 4:2:2 and 4:4:4 planes as profile 1; 10 and 12-bit planes as profile 2 (4:2:0) or 3. Vp9EncoderOptions.BitDepth codes another depth, and VideoEncoderOptions.ChromaFormat sets the chroma format for RGB frames. The track's color comes from the frames: their code points (primaries, transfer, matrix, range), and their static HDR metadata (mastering display, content light levels), which WebM and Matroska keep in the Colour element and MP4 in its colr, mdcv and clli boxes. Frames with alpha get a second, 8-bit 4:2:0 VP9 stream for the alpha plane. Alternate references of other formats than 8-bit 4:2:0 are their frame unfiltered. // 10-bit planes code profile 2 (4:2:0) or 3 (4:2:2, 4:4:4); the frames' code points and HDR metadata go into the // container's Colour (WebM, Matroska) or colr, mdcv and clli boxes (MP4). ColorCodePoints pq = new(9, 16, 9, false); HdrMetadata hdr = new() { MasteringMaxLuminance = 1000, MasteringMinLuminance = 0.005, MaxContentLightLevel = 1000, MaxFrameAverageLightLevel = 400 }; VideoWriterOptions options = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.Vp9, Quality = 80, Effort = 1 }; using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("hdr.mp4", options)) { for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { YuvRaster<ushort> planes = YuvRaster.Create(64, 48, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, 10, new YuvColor(YuvMatrix.Bt2020Ncl, YuvRange.Limited, ChromaSiting.Center)); using YuvVideoFrame frame = new(planes, new MediaTime(i, new Rational(1, 30)), color: pq) { Hdr = hdr }; writer.WriteFrame(frame); } } Writing AV1 Set VideoWriterOptions.Codec to VideoCodecs.Av1. Quality and Effort work as for VP8 and VP9 (default 60 and 4), and equal qualities give the same quantizer step as VP9's; Quantizer is AV1's base_q_idx, 0 to 255, and 0 is lossless. Each packet is a temporal unit of OBUs, as MP4 and Matroska store them, and the track's av1C comes from the sequence header. The frame coding is Av1StreamEncoder's: partitions, intra and inter modes from up to seven references with compound prediction, transform types and sizes chosen by rate and distortion, a trellis, delta quantizers per superblock, deblocking levels searched over every level at once, CDEF strengths and, on frames others predict from, Wiener loop restoration; from effort 5, 6 and 7 on it adds compound masks, overlapped and warped motion, dual filters and global motion. Egami.Video plans the references: each group of 16 frames is a pyramid. Its last frame, blended with its neighbours along their motion, is coded first as a hidden alternate reference, then a hidden frame halfway to it, halfway again and so on down to pairs, five layers in all; the frames left between them predict from both sides and nothing predicts from them. No hidden frame costs a frame of its own when its time comes: AV1 shows it again with show_existing_frame, a packet of a few bytes. Before a group is coded, it and the next run through Av1StreamEncoder.Analyze, which finds how much of each frame the frames after it reuse: the more, the finer the alternate reference's and the keyframe's quantizers, and the finer the superblocks that matter most. Deeper layers get coarser quantizers and spend fewer bits on what only they show. The temporal filter, on keyframes and alternate references, blends as much as each picture's noise and the frame's quantizer call for. // AV1 in MP4 at constant quality, on the same Quality and Effort scales as VP8 and VP9. Each group's hidden alternate // reference, and a hidden frame halfway to it, are shown later with show_existing_frame. VideoWriterOptions options = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.Av1, FrameRate = new Rational(30, 1), Quality = 70, Effort = 1 }; using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("duck-av1.mp4", options)) { for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { using Raster<Rgb8> frame = duck.Derive(ops => ops.Crop(new Rect(i * 4, i * 2, 320, 240))); writer.WriteFrame(frame); } } // Expert settings: no pyramid, no adaptive quantization, quantizer limits on AV1's 0 to 255 base_q_idx scale. VideoWriterOptions tuned = options with { Av1 = new Av1EncoderOptions { Pyramid = false, AdaptiveQuantization = false, MinQuantizer = 20, MaxQuantizer = 200 }, }; Av1EncoderOptions holds the expert settings: quantizer limits, alternate references and the pyramid on or off, golden frame spacing, the temporal filter's frames and strength (adaptive by default), adaptive quantization (from the temporal model on the base frames, by block detail on the others), screen content tools, error resilience and the bit depth. AV1 codes no alpha in video files (Matroska and MP4 have no standard place for it); animated AVIF, through Egami's AvifWriter, does. Profiles and HDR 8 and 10-bit 4:2:0 planes make Main profile streams, 4:4:4 High and 12-bit or 4:2:2 Professional, all coded as they are; Av1EncoderOptions.BitDepth codes another depth and VideoEncoderOptions.ChromaFormat sets the chroma format for RGB frames, which are converted to BT.601 limited range. The frames' code points (primaries, transfer, matrix, range) and the chroma siting of 4:2:0 planes go into the sequence header and the container. Their static HDR metadata goes into content light level and mastering display metadata OBUs on every keyframe, and into the container as for VP9; a frame's HDR10+ metadata goes into its own temporal unit as an ITU-T T.35 metadata OBU. The level is the smallest whose picture size and sample rate hold the stream. // 10-bit 4:2:0 planes code the Main profile (4:4:4 High; 12 bits or 4:2:2 Professional). The frames' code points go into // the sequence header and the container, their HDR metadata into metadata OBUs on every keyframe and into the container // (Matroska's Colour, MP4's mdcv and clli). ColorCodePoints pq = new(9, 16, 9, false); HdrMetadata hdr = new() { MasteringMaxLuminance = 1000, MasteringMinLuminance = 0.005, MaxContentLightLevel = 1000, MaxFrameAverageLightLevel = 400 }; VideoWriterOptions options = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.Av1, Quality = 80, Effort = 1 }; using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("hdr-av1.mkv", options)) { for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { YuvRaster<ushort> planes = YuvRaster.Create(64, 48, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, 10, new YuvColor(YuvMatrix.Bt2020Ncl, YuvRange.Limited, ChromaSiting.TopLeft)); using YuvVideoFrame frame = new(planes, new MediaTime(i, new Rational(1, 30)), color: pq) { Hdr = hdr }; writer.WriteFrame(frame); } } Writing FFV1 VideoCodecs.Ffv1 writes FFV1 version 3 (RFC 9043), the lossless codec archives use, in Matroska or AVI: a decode gives back every sample. Frames given as planes keep their layout (4:2:0, 4:2:2, 4:4:4, 4:1:1, 4:1:0 or gray, with or without alpha, 8 to 16 bits); RGB rasters, and 4:4:4 planes tagged YuvMatrix.Identity, are coded as RGB. The first frame sets the stream's layout. The defaults are the archival profile: every frame a keyframe, slice CRCs on (so Ffv1Codec.Verify can check the file), the range coder with a custom state table, and a slice grid picked from the frame size (16 slices at 1080p). KeyframeInterval spaces keyframes further apart, Effort 7 and up picks the large context model, and Ffv1EncoderOptions sets the slices, the coder (Ffv1Coder.GolombRice is faster and larger), the context model and BitDepth for planes that hold a 9, 11, 13, 14 or 15-bit source shifted up. Quality does not apply, and setting it reports Ffv1.QualityIgnored. Slices are coded in parallel, with the same file at any thread count. Files come within 1 % of FFmpeg's size at the same settings, and FFmpeg decodes them to the same samples. // FFV1 keeps every sample: RGB frames are coded as RGB and planes keep their layout and depth. The defaults are the // archival profile (version 3, every frame a keyframe, slice CRCs, the range coder with a custom table). VideoWriterOptions options = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.Ffv1, FrameRate = new Rational(25, 1) }; using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("master.mkv", options)) { for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { using Raster<Rgb8> frame = duck.Derive(ops => ops.Crop(new Rect(i * 4, i * 2, 320, 240))); writer.WriteFrame(frame); } } // Expert settings: more slices for more threads, Golomb-Rice for speed, a keyframe every 10 frames for smaller files. VideoWriterOptions fast = options with { KeyframeInterval = 10, Ffv1 = new Ffv1EncoderOptions { Slices = 16, Coder = Ffv1Coder.GolombRice, ContextModel = Ffv1ContextModel.Small }, }; // Check the archive without decoding it. bool intact = Ffv1Codec.Verify("master.mkv").IsIntact; How bits are spent RateControl picks one of four modes: Mode What it does For Quality (default) Every frame aims at Quality; files are as large as the content needs. Files Bitrate An average Bitrate, spread over frames by how hard they are; capped by MaxBitrate. Files of a known size, streaming ConstantBitrate Bitrate with a decoder buffer of BufferSize bits (one second by default) that never runs dry. Live streams, WebRTC Quantizer The same quantizer for every frame (Quantizer, or the one Quality maps to). Tests, comparisons // An average of 1 Mbit/s, the bits spread by how hard each frame is; ConstantBitrate keeps a decoder buffer from running dry. VideoWriterOptions options = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.Vp8, RateControl = RateControlMode.Bitrate, Bitrate = 1_000_000, }; using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("duck.mkv", options)) { for (int i = 0; i < 30; i++) { writer.WriteFrame(duck); } } Two passes A two-pass encode first reads the whole clip to learn how hard each frame is, then spreads the bitrate over all of it. VideoWriter.AnalyzeFirstPass runs the first pass over frames or a file and returns FirstPassStats, which can be saved and loaded; pass it as FirstPassStats with RateControlMode.Bitrate. // Pass one reads the clip and learns how hard each frame is; save it to run the passes apart. FirstPassStats stats = VideoWriter.AnalyzeFirstPass("clip.ivf"); stats.Save("clip.stats"); // Pass two spreads 500 kbit/s over the whole clip by what pass one learned. VideoWriterOptions options = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.Vp8, RateControl = RateControlMode.Bitrate, Bitrate = 500_000, FirstPassStats = FirstPassStats.Load("clip.stats"), }; using (VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("clip.ivf")) using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("clip.webm", options)) { foreach (YuvVideoFrame frame in reader.ReadFrames()) { using (frame) { writer.WriteFrame(frame); } } } Keyframes, groups and latency The encoder looks 25 frames ahead (LatencyMode.Quality, the default). It analyzes each frame on a half-size copy as it arrives and starts a keyframe at a scene cut, at least every 10 seconds (KeyframeInterval sets another spacing, in frames), and wherever EncodeFrameOptions.ForceKeyframe asks. Between keyframes it codes groups of 4 to 16 frames: the group's last frame is blended with its neighbours along their motion into a hidden alternate reference, coded first at a finer step, so the frames before it can predict from it. That happens only where the group's first frame still predicts its last well (still content); with motion, zooms or fades the group just ends in a golden frame. A VP8 hidden frame's packet carries the timestamp of the shown frame after it, and gives no frame when decoded; VP9 and AV1 put their hidden frames in the next shown frame's packet. Turn SceneCutKeyframes off for keyframes at a fixed spacing. LatencyMode.Realtime looks nowhere ahead: each packet comes out as soon as its frame goes in, there are no hidden frames, frames keep no probability updates for the next (so a lost packet spoils one frame), and 720p and larger VP8 frames get two or four token partitions so decoders can use more threads. // Live: no lookahead, so each packet comes out as soon as its frame goes in, at a constant bitrate. VideoEncoderOptions options = new() { Width = 320, Height = 240, LatencyMode = LatencyMode.Realtime, RateControl = RateControlMode.ConstantBitrate, Bitrate = 300_000, }; using IVideoEncoder encoder = VideoCodecs.Vp8.CreateEncoder(options, MediaContext.Default); using IMuxer muxer = MediaFile.CreateMuxer(stream, "webm", [encoder.Track], leaveOpen: true); for (int i = 0; i < 60; i++) { using VideoFrame<Rgb8> frame = new(Raster.Create(320, 240, new Rgb8((byte)i, 90, 160)), new MediaTime(i, new Rational(1, 30))); // A viewer joined: start a keyframe so they can decode from here. encoder.Send(frame, new EncodeFrameOptions { ForceKeyframe = i == 30 }); while (encoder.TryReceive(out EncodedPacket? packet)) { using (packet) { muxer.WritePacket(packet); } } } encoder.Flush(); muxer.Finish(); Threads and repeatability The output depends only on the frames and the options, never on the number of threads or the machine, so a test can compare hashes. EgamiContext.MaxParallelism on the MediaContext sets how many threads the encoder uses. VP9's tile columns depend on the frame width and Vp9EncoderOptions.TileColumns, never on the threads; AV1's are one per 4096 samples of width, so frames up to 4K are one tile, and its threads help little within a frame.

articles/guides/video.html.title: Video | Egami
articles/guides/video.html.summary: Video Egami.Video reads and writes video with Egami rasters as frames, so resizing, color and drawing from Egami work on video with no copying. It is fully managed and ships only royalty-free codecs: Containers: WebM and Matroska, AVI (with OpenDML for files over 1 GB), IVF and YUV4MPEG2, read and written, and headerless raw frames. Codecs: AV1 (8, 10 and 12 bit, 4:0:0 to 4:4:4, film grain, equal to libaom frame for frame), VP9 (all four profiles, 8, 10 and 12 bit, equal to libvpx frame for frame), VP8 (with WebM alpha) and Motion JPEG decode; VP8 (see Encoding video), Motion JPEG and uncompressed encode. Audio codecs such as FLAC, Opus, ALAC and AC-3 (see Audio); other tracks are copied through untouched. H.264 decodes with the opt-in Egami.Video.H264 package (see H.264). Probing a file MediaFile.Probe reads the headers and returns a MediaInfo: the container's FormatName, the Duration, and the Tracks. A TrackInfo gives a track's Number, Kind (a TrackKind) and CodecId (see CodecIds); a VideoTrackInfo adds its size, bit depth, chroma format, FieldOrder, frame rate, color and HDR metadata, and an AudioTrackInfo its sample rate and channels. MediaMetadata holds the tags, the chapters (ChapterInfo) and the attachments (AttachmentInfo). // What a file holds, without decoding: its container, duration, tracks, tags, chapters and attachments. MediaInfo info = MediaFile.Probe("metadata.mkv"); Console.WriteLine($"{info.FormatName}, {info.Duration?.ToTimeSpan()}"); foreach (TrackInfo track in info.Tracks) { string details = track switch { VideoTrackInfo v => $"{v.Width}x{v.Height} {v.BitDepth}-bit {v.ChromaFormat}, {v.FieldOrder}", AudioTrackInfo a => $"{a.SampleRate} Hz, {a.Channels} channels", _ => "", }; Console.WriteLine($"#{track.Number} {track.Kind} {track.CodecId} {details}"); } MediaMetadata metadata = info.Metadata; foreach (ChapterInfo chapter in metadata.Chapters) { Console.WriteLine($"{chapter.Start.ToTimeSpan()} {chapter.Title}"); } foreach (AttachmentInfo attachment in metadata.Attachments) { File.WriteAllBytes(attachment.Name, attachment.Data.ToArray()); } Reading frames VideoReader opens a file and decodes its first video track. ReadFrames<TPixel> gives VideoFrame<TPixel> frames of RGB pixels, each with its timestamp, duration and color; dispose each frame when done with it. // Every frame as RGB pixels: VP9, VP8, Motion JPEG or raw, from WebM, Matroska, AVI, IVF or YUV4MPEG2. using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("movie.webm"); Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.Width}x{reader.Track.Height} at {reader.Track.FrameRate?.ToDouble()} fps"); foreach (VideoFrame<Rgba8> frame in reader.ReadFrames<Rgba8>()) { using (frame) { frame.Raster.Save($"frame-{frame.Timestamp.ToTimeSpan().TotalMilliseconds:0000}.png"); } } ReadFrame and ReadFrames without a pixel type give a YuvVideoFrame: the codec's own planes as a YuvRaster, at the stream's subsampling and bit depth, with no conversion. Both kinds of frame are a VideoFrame, which is what encoders and writers take. // The codec's own planes, with no conversion: luma and chroma at the stream's subsampling and bit depth. using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("movie.webm"); using YuvVideoFrame first = reader.ReadFrame()!; YuvRaster planes = first.Raster; Console.WriteLine($"{planes.ChromaFormat} {planes.BitDepth}-bit, color {first.Color}"); VideoFrame frame = first; // the base type encoders and writers take using Raster<Rgb8> rgb = first.ToRaster<Rgb8>(); VideoReaderOptions picks the track, the codec's VideoDecoderOptions (such as DecodeAlpha for WebM alpha), and what a broken frame does, as a DecodeErrorMode: Skip (the default) reports it and drops frames up to the next keyframe, Conceal repeats the last good frame, and Throw throws. // How a reader decodes: which track, what a broken frame does (Skip, the default, drops it up to the next keyframe; // Conceal repeats the last good frame; Throw throws) and the codec's own options. VideoReaderOptions options = new() { TrackNumber = 1, Errors = DecodeErrorMode.Conceal, Decoder = new VideoDecoderOptions { DecodeAlpha = false }, }; using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("alpha.webm", options); using YuvVideoFrame frame = reader.ReadFrame()!; // Opening reads the headers; the async forms do that off the calling thread. using VideoReader reader = await VideoReader.OpenAsync("movie.webm", VideoReaderOptions.Default); using YuvVideoFrame? frame = reader.ReadFrame(); Seeking Seek takes a MediaTime and lands on the frame shown at that time, decoding from the keyframe before it; it is exact over VP9's hidden and show-existing frames too. SeekMode.Keyframe stops at the keyframe instead, which is faster. // An exact seek lands on the frame shown at the time; SeekMode.Keyframe stops at the keyframe before it, which is faster. using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("movie.webm"); reader.Seek(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5)); using YuvVideoFrame atHalf = reader.ReadFrame()!; reader.Seek(MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5), SeekMode.Keyframe); using YuvVideoFrame keyframe = reader.ReadFrame()!; Writing a clip VideoWriter encodes images or frames into a file or stream; VideoWriterOptions sets the codec, the frame rate (a Rational), the quality, the chroma format, the metadata and other tracks to copy in. // Images into a Motion JPEG clip; the container comes from the extension. VideoWriterOptions options = new() { Codec = VideoCodecs.MotionJpeg, FrameRate = new Rational(25, 1), Quality = 85 }; using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create("duck.mkv", options)) { for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { writer.WriteFrame(duck); } } // Or into a stream, in a format by name. using MemoryStream avi = new(); using (VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create(avi, "avi", options, leaveOpen: true)) { writer.WriteFrame(duck); } Remuxing MediaFile.Remux copies a file's packets into another container without decoding. For more control, an IDemuxer reads EncodedPackets (data, timestamps, the keyframe flag and PacketAdditions such as WebM alpha) and an IMuxer writes them. // Copy the packets into another container without decoding; the sound and the tags come along. long packets = MediaFile.Remux("camera.avi", "camera.mkv"); // Or packet by packet, choosing what goes through. using IDemuxer demuxer = MediaFile.OpenDemuxer("movie.webm"); using (IMuxer muxer = MediaFile.CreateMuxer("movie.ivf", [demuxer.Info.VideoTrack!])) { while (demuxer.ReadPacket() is { } packet) { using (packet) { // Data, the time and whether it starts a keyframe; WebM alpha travels in Additions. IReadOnlyList<PacketAddition> additions = packet.Additions; muxer.WritePacket(packet); } } muxer.Finish(); } Trimming MediaFile.Trim cuts the part of a file from a start up to an end into a new file whose timestamps start at 0. The cut's first frame is the first at or after the start, and it ends after the last frame that starts before the end; a time within half a tick of a frame, such as the millisecond Matroska keeps, counts as that frame's. TrimMode says what happens when the start falls between keyframes: TrimMode.Smart, the default, is frame-exact and encodes as little as it can. It decodes from the keyframe before the start and encodes the frames from the start up to the next keyframe again, as a new group that starts with a keyframe; every packet from that keyframe on is copied byte for byte. The new group matches the stream (codec, profile, size, bit depth, chroma format and color, and for AV1 the sequence header byte for byte, as MP4 and Matroska keep it in the track header) and is coded at the average quantizer of the packets it replaces, so the quality does not jump. A start on a keyframe, and Motion JPEG or uncompressed video, are a plain copy. TrimMode.Keyframe decodes nothing: the cut starts at the keyframe at or before the start, as ffmpeg -ss -c copy does. TrimMode.Reencode encodes every frame of the cut again, with the same codec at the source's quantizer. The end needs no encoding: VP8, VP9 and AV1 decode in packet order and code a hidden frame before the frames that show it, so the cut keeps every packet up to the one that shows its last frame and drops a hidden frame after it that nothing shows. Smart cut falls back where it must and says so in a MediaWarning, in TrimResult.Warnings and through MediaContext.Warnings: a codec Egami.Video cannot encode (H.264, HEVC) starts at the keyframe (trim-keyframe), as do frames that change size, and a stream the encoder cannot match (a VP8 version other than 0, 4:4:0 or monochrome AV1, an AV1 sequence header with frame ids or a decoder model) is encoded again whole (trim-reencode). TrimResult tells where the cut starts in the input, how many frames it holds and how many were encoded again. Audio and subtitles are copied. Audio is cut at the sample where the format can say so: PCM by slicing its packets, MP4 by its edit list, and Opus in Matroska and WebM by CodecDelay (with 80 ms of pre-roll) and DiscardPadding. Other audio is cut at the packet whose middle is nearest (trim-audio-packet). Subtitle cues shown across the cut are clipped to it, and so are chapters; tags and attachments are kept. A seekable input is read from a few seconds before the start. Trim takes a Stream in and out, progress and a token as the other jobs do. // Frame-exact: only the frames from 0.3 s up to the next keyframe are encoded again; every other packet is copied. TrimResult result = MediaFile.Trim("show.webm", "cut.webm", MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.3), MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.8)); Console.WriteLine($"{result.Frames} frames from {result.Start.Seconds:0.000} s, {result.ReencodedFrames} encoded again"); foreach (MediaWarning warning in result.Warnings) { Console.WriteLine(warning.Message); } // No decoding at all: the cut starts at the keyframe at or before 0.3 s. MediaFile.Trim("show.webm", "copy.webm", MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.3), MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.8), TrimMode.Keyframe); // Streams in and out, such as cloud blobs: a non-seekable input is read from its start. using Stream source = File.OpenRead("movie.webm"); using Stream upload = File.Create("cut.mkv"); IProgress<MediaProgress> progress = new Progress<MediaProgress>(p => Console.Write($"\r{p.Fraction ?? 0:P0}")); TrimResult result = MediaFile.Trim(source, upload, "mkv", MediaTime.FromSeconds(1), null, TrimMode.Smart, tracks: t => t.Kind == TrackKind.Video, leaveOpen: true, progress: progress, cancellationToken: cts.Token); On the command line, egami-video trim --smart cuts this way, and segment --scenes --exact starts every part on its scene. Progress, cancellation and streams MediaFile.Remux and MediaFile.Transcode take an IProgress<MediaProgress> and a CancellationToken as their last parameters. A MediaProgress report carries the position, the duration, a 0 to 1 Fraction, frames, packets, bytes read and written, the elapsed time and the speed (media seconds per second, like FFmpeg's speed=). Reports come once the output is open, then at most every 250 ms, then once more with IsFinal set and Fraction 1. The fraction comes from the time when the input has a duration, else from the bytes read over the input's length, else it is null; it never goes backwards. The handler runs on the job's thread; Progress<T> moves it to the UI thread. If the handler throws, the job stops with that exception. Without a handler, nothing is built or timed. // Reports arrive once the output is open, then at most every 250 ms, then once more with IsFinal set. // Progress<T> runs the handler on the caller's synchronization context: the UI thread in WinForms, WPF or MAUI. IProgress<MediaProgress> progress = new Progress<MediaProgress>(p => Console.Write($"\r{p.Position.ToTimeSpan():c} {p.Fraction ?? 0:P0} {p.Frames} frames {p.Speed:0.0}x")); long packets = MediaFile.Remux("camera.avi", "camera.mkv", progress: progress); The token is checked before each packet. A cancelled job throws OperationCanceledException and does not finish the output: a file the job created is deleted, and a stream you passed in keeps what was written so far. // Ctrl+C stops the job between two packets; the half-written camera.mkv is deleted. using CancellationTokenSource cts = new(); ConsoleCancelEventHandler onCtrlC = (_, e) => { e.Cancel = true; cts.Cancel(); }; Console.CancelKeyPress += onCtrlC; try { MediaFile.Remux("camera.avi", "camera.mkv", cancellationToken: cts.Token); } catch (OperationCanceledException) { Console.WriteLine("Cancelled."); } finally { Console.CancelKeyPress -= onCtrlC; } Both jobs also take a Stream in and a Stream out, with the output container named, so they can read from and write to cloud storage without a local copy. The input may be non-seekable; only MP4 files with moov after the media need a seekable one. Matroska, WebM, IVF and YUV4MPEG2 write to a non-seekable stream as they go, MP4 keeps its media in a temporary file and writes moov first, and AVI needs a seekable stream (NotSupportedException otherwise). leaveOpen keeps both streams open. The jobs are synchronous and block a thread while the network is slow; run them with Task.Run to keep a UI responsive. // Any Stream works, seekable or not: a cloud blob's read and upload streams, an HTTP response body, a pipe. // Files stand in for them here. using Stream source = File.OpenRead("movie.webm"); using Stream upload = File.Create("movie.mkv"); long packets = MediaFile.Remux(source, upload, "mkv", leaveOpen: true, cancellationToken: cts.Token); Codecs by hand VideoCodecs finds the codec for a track and creates an IVideoDecoder: send packets, receive frames. VideoCodecs.CreateDecoder<TPixel> gives an IVideoDecoder<TPixel> that hands out RGB frames. // A codec by hand: packets in, frames out. VideoCodecs finds the codec for a track's CodecId (CodecIds.Vp9 here). using IDemuxer demuxer = MediaFile.OpenDemuxer("movie.webm"); VideoTrackInfo track = demuxer.Info.VideoTrack!; bool isVp9 = track.CodecId == CodecIds.Vp9; using IVideoDecoder decoder = VideoCodecs.CreateDecoder(track, new VideoDecoderOptions { Errors = DecodeErrorMode.Throw }); int frames = 0; while (demuxer.ReadPacket() is { } packet) { using (packet) { decoder.Send(packet); } while (decoder.TryReceive(out YuvVideoFrame? frame)) { using (frame) { frames++; } } } decoder.Flush(); Each codec is a VideoCodec: Av1Codec, Vp9Codec, Vp8Codec, Ffv1Codec, MotionJpegCodec and RawVideoCodec. // The built-in codecs, for a MediaContext of your own or to create decoders directly. VideoCodec vp9 = Vp9Codec.Instance, vp8 = Vp8Codec.Instance, mjpeg = MotionJpegCodec.Instance, raw = RawVideoCodec.Instance; using IVideoDecoder decoder = vp9.CreateDecoder(track, VideoDecoderOptions.Default, MediaContext.Default); // Decoders that hand out RGB frames instead of planes. using IVideoDecoder<Rgba8> rgb = VideoCodecs.CreateDecoder<Rgba8>(track); An IVideoEncoder takes frames and gives packets, with VideoEncoderOptions for the size, frame rate and quality. // An encoder by hand: frames in, packets out, for a muxer of your own. VideoEncoderOptions options = new() { Width = duck.Width, Height = duck.Height, FrameRate = new Rational(30, 1), Quality = 90 }; using IVideoEncoder encoder = MotionJpegCodec.Instance.CreateEncoder(options, MediaContext.Default); using (VideoFrame<Rgb8> frame = new(Raster.Load<Rgb8>("duck.png"), MediaTime.Zero)) { encoder.Send(frame); } encoder.Flush(); List<EncodedPacket> packets = []; while (encoder.TryReceive(out EncodedPacket? packet)) { packets.Add(packet); } // Uncompressed frames go the same way, losslessly. using IVideoEncoder rawEncoder = RawVideoCodec.Instance.CreateEncoder(options with { ChromaFormat = ChromaFormat.Yuv444 }, MediaContext.Default); CodecHeaders.Describe lists a packet's header fields as CodecHeaderFields under the codec's own names, for VP8, VP9, AV1, FFV1 and Motion JPEG. // A packet's header fields under the codec's own names, as a hex dump with meaning. using IDemuxer demuxer = MediaFile.OpenDemuxer("movie.webm"); TrackInfo track = demuxer.Tracks[0]; using EncodedPacket packet = demuxer.ReadPacket()!; if (CodecHeaders.CanDescribe(track)) { foreach (CodecHeaderField field in CodecHeaders.Describe(track, packet)) { Console.WriteLine($"{field.Name} = {field.Value}"); } } AV1 Av1Codec decodes AV1 from WebM, Matroska, MP4 and IVF with Egami's AV1 decoder: every profile, 8, 10 and 12 bit, 4:0:0, 4:2:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4, film grain, scaled references and scalable streams. Every frame equals libaom's. A packet is a temporal unit; hidden frames give no frame, and a frame shown later with show_existing_frame comes out then. Frames come out at their own size, 8-bit planes for 8-bit streams and 16-bit planes above, 4:0:0 for monochrome. The color comes from the sequence header; the container's fills only what the header leaves unspecified. HDR metadata OBUs give the frames' Hdr and Hdr10Plus (see HDR). VideoDecoderOptions.ApplyFilmGrain = false gives the frames as coded, without the film grain the stream asks for. A keyframe is a temporal unit that starts with a shown key frame. A forward key frame, hidden and shown later, is not one, as FFmpeg flags them too. When a container's keyframe flag disagrees, the stream wins and Av1.KeyframeFlagMismatch is reported. A track's av1C (its CodecPrivate) gives the sequence header when the first unit has none. The IVF reader builds av1C from the first sequence header, and so does the Matroska writer for a track that has none, so IVF files remux to WebM, Matroska and MP4. Seeking decodes from the shown key frame at or before the time, so exact seeks give the frame decoding from the start gives. Broken data follows VideoReaderOptions.Errors: Skip (the default) reports Av1.CorruptFrame, or Av1.MissingReference for a unit that needs frames from before the first key frame, and resumes at the next shown key frame; Conceal repeats the last good frame in between. // AV1 from WebM, Matroska, MP4 or IVF reads like any other video: 10 and 12-bit streams give 16-bit planes. using (VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("av1.webm")) { foreach (YuvVideoFrame frame in reader.ReadFrames()) { using (frame) { Console.WriteLine($"{frame.Timestamp}: {frame.Width}x{frame.Height}, {frame.Raster.BitDepth} bit {frame.Raster.ChromaFormat}, {frame.Color}"); } } } // The frames as coded, without the film grain the stream asks for; broken units are skipped to the next key frame and // reported as Av1.CorruptFrame or Av1.MissingReference, or repeat the last good frame with Conceal. VideoReaderOptions options = new() { Decoder = new VideoDecoderOptions { ApplyFilmGrain = false }, Errors = DecodeErrorMode.Conceal, }; using VideoReader plain = VideoReader.Open("av1.webm", options); using YuvVideoFrame first = plain.ReadFrame()!; Raw AV1 streams are containers of their own: Av1ObuFormat reads and writes low-overhead OBU files (.obu, as aomenc --obu writes and aomdec and dav1d read), and Av1AnnexBFormat the length-delimited files of the specification's Annex B (as the conformance streams and aomenc --annexb=1 write). Both are detected from their first bytes; neither has timestamps, so frames are timed at the format's FrameRate, 30 a second unless you register one with another rate. Reading a file and writing it back gives the same bytes, and IVF, WebM, Matroska and MP4 tracks write to them. // Raw AV1 streams have no timestamps: frames are timed at the format's frame rate, 30 a second unless you register another. MediaContext context = MediaContext.Default.WithContainer(new Av1ObuFormat { FrameRate = new Rational(24, 1) }); // An IVF clip to a low-overhead .obu file (what aomdec and dav1d read) and to Annex B, then read back. MediaFile.Remux("clip-av1.ivf", "clip.obu"); using (IDemuxer demuxer = MediaFile.OpenDemuxer("clip-av1.ivf")) using (IMuxer annexB = Av1AnnexBFormat.Instance.CreateMuxer(File.Create("clip-annexb.obu"), demuxer.Tracks, MediaContext.Default, leaveOpen: false)) { while (demuxer.ReadPacket() is { } packet) { using (packet) { annexB.WritePacket(packet); } } } using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("clip.obu", context: context); Console.WriteLine($"{MediaFile.Probe("clip-annexb.obu").FormatName}; {reader.Track.FrameRate} fps"); Av1Packets splits a temporal unit into its frames and merges them back, and builds the av1C record from a sequence header. // An AV1 packet is a temporal unit: split it into its frames and join them back; build the av1C an MP4 or Matroska // track needs from its sequence header. using IDemuxer demuxer = MediaFile.OpenDemuxer("clip-av1.ivf"); using EncodedPacket packet = demuxer.ReadPacket()!; IReadOnlyList<ReadOnlyMemory<byte>> frames = Av1Packets.SplitFrames(packet.Data); byte[] unit = Av1Packets.MergeFrames(frames); byte[]? av1C = Av1Packets.ExtractConfig(packet.Data.Span); Console.WriteLine($"{frames.Count} frames, av1C of {av1C?.Length} bytes"); CodecHeaders.Describe lists an AV1 packet's OBUs, its sequence header and metadata fields, and the start of each frame header (up to error_resilient_mode). The rest of a frame header depends on the frames before it, so a CodecHeaderReader reads a track's packets in order, decoding them, and lists each frame header whole. // An AV1 frame header depends on the frames before it: a CodecHeaderReader reads the packets in order and lists each whole. using IDemuxer demuxer = MediaFile.OpenDemuxer("av1.webm"); using CodecHeaderReader headers = new(demuxer.Tracks[0]); while (demuxer.ReadPacket() is { } packet) { using (packet) { IReadOnlyList<CodecHeaderField> fields = headers.Describe(packet); Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", fields.Where(f => f.Name is "frame_type" or "order_hint" or "base_q_idx").Select(f => $"{f.Name} = {f.Value}"))); } } FFV1 Ffv1Codec decodes FFV1, the lossless codec archives use (RFC 9043), from Matroska (V_FFV1) and AVI (FourCC FFV1): versions 0, 1 and 3, Golomb-Rice and the range coder, YCbCr 4:2:0, 4:2:2, 4:4:4, 4:1:1, 4:1:0 and gray, RGB, each with or without alpha, at 8 to 16 bits. Every frame equals FFmpeg's sample for sample. Frames keep their planes: 8-bit planes, or 16-bit planes holding 10, 12 or 16 bits. Depths 9, 11, 13, 14 and 15 sit in the next of those with their samples shifted up, so nothing is lost; the track's BitDepth gives the source depth. RGB comes out as G, B and R planes tagged YuvMatrix.Identity, which ToRaster turns back into RGB exactly. A version 3 track's configuration record (its CodecPrivate) gives the depth and subsampling before any frame is decoded. Every slice CRC is checked. Broken data follows VideoReaderOptions.Errors: a damaged slice is reported as Ffv1.SliceCrc (or Ffv1.CorruptFrame when it cannot be read), a frame with no keyframe before it as Ffv1.MissingReference and a damaged configuration record as Ffv1.ConfigCrc. Skip drops the frame, Conceal shows the last good frame where the slice was. CodecHeaders.Describe lists the parameters, the keyframe flag and each slice's header and footer. // FFV1 archives from Matroska or AVI read like any other video. A 10-bit master gives 16-bit planes holding 10 bits; // the track says the depth and subsampling before any frame is decoded. using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("master.mkv", new VideoReaderOptions { Errors = DecodeErrorMode.Conceal }, context); Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.CodecId}: {reader.Track.BitDepth} bit {reader.Track.ChromaFormat}"); foreach (YuvVideoFrame frame in reader.ReadFrames()) { using (frame) { Console.WriteLine($"{frame.Timestamp}: {frame.Raster.BitDepth} bit {frame.Raster.ChromaFormat}"); } } // Every slice's CRC is checked: a damaged one is reported as Ffv1.SliceCrc and, with Conceal, shows the last good frame. Console.WriteLine($"{reported.Count(d => d.Id == "Ffv1.SliceCrc")} damaged slices"); Slices decode in parallel up to EgamiContext.MaxParallelism, with the same frame at any thread count. Ffv1Codec.Verify checks a file's fixity without decoding pictures: the configuration record's CRC and every slice's, far faster than a decode. The Ffv1VerifyResult says how many frames and slices it checked and lists each Ffv1VerifyError; a version 0 or 1 file, or one written without slice CRCs, has HasSliceCrcs false. // Check an archive's fixity without decoding pictures: the configuration record's CRC and every slice's. Ffv1VerifyResult result = Ffv1Codec.Verify("master.mkv"); Console.WriteLine($"{result.Frames} frames, {result.Slices} slices checked: {(result.IsIntact ? "intact" : "damaged")}"); foreach (Ffv1VerifyError error in result.Errors) { Console.WriteLine($"frame {error.Frame} at {error.Timestamp}, slice {error.Slice}: {error.Problem}"); } Writing FFV1 is in Encoding video; Lossless archiving with FFV1 puts writing, fixity checks and restores together. HDR A frame's Color and Hdr carry its color code points and static HDR metadata. YuvVideoFrame.ToRaster with a target ColorProfile converts through Egami's color pipeline and tone maps PQ and HLG to SDR. VP9 frames in WebM carry HDR10+ dynamic metadata as Hdr10PlusMetadata, with its Hdr10PlusPercentile distribution and Hdr10PlusToneCurve.
