AV1 frames take Hdr from the stream's content light level and mastering display metadata OBUs (or the track's av1C), and Hdr10Plus from an ITU-T T.35 metadata OBU. // An HDR10 frame tone mapped to SDR through Egami's color pipeline, from its mastering display and light levels. using (VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("hdr10.mkv")) using (YuvVideoFrame frame = reader.ReadFrame()!) using (Raster<Rgba8> sdr = frame.ToRaster<Rgba8>(ColorProfile.Srgb)) { sdr.Save("sdr.png"); } // HDR10+ dynamic metadata, frame by frame. using VideoReader plus = VideoReader.Open("hdr10plus.webm"); foreach (YuvVideoFrame frame in plus.ReadFrames()) { using (frame) { if (frame.Hdr10Plus is { } meta) { double maxScl = meta.MaxScl.Max(); // cd/m² Hdr10PlusPercentile median = meta.DistributionMaxRgb.First(p => p.Percentage == 50); Hdr10PlusToneCurve? curve = meta.ToneCurve; Console.WriteLine($"MaxSCL {maxScl}, median {median.Value} cd/m², knee {curve?.KneeX}"); } } } Measuring quality VideoQuality sums PSNR and SSIM over frames, plane by plane, as PlaneScores, and hashes frames the way libvpx's tests do. // PSNR and SSIM of a decode against a reference, plane by plane, and the MD5 of a frame as libvpx's tests take it. VideoQuality quality = new(); using (VideoReader reference = VideoReader.Open("movie.webm")) using (VideoReader distorted = VideoReader.Open("movie.webm")) { foreach ((YuvVideoFrame a, YuvVideoFrame b) in reference.ReadFrames().Zip(distorted.ReadFrames())) { using (a) using (b) { quality.Add(a.Raster, b.Raster); string md5 = VideoQuality.Md5(a.Raster); } } } PlaneScores psnr = quality.Psnr, ssim = quality.Ssim; Console.WriteLine($"{quality.Frames} frames: PSNR Y {psnr.Y:0.00} dB, SSIM {ssim.Average:0.0000}"); Scenes and analysis MediaAnalysis.Run reads a file once and hands every frame to its detectors: the SceneDetector by default, and any IVideoDetector or IAudioDetector you add. Each Scene has its first and last frame, its start and end time and how it starts (SceneStart): at the first frame, at a cut, or inside a fade through black. Cuts lists each SceneCut and Fades each fade out and fade in (FadeKind). // One pass over the file: the scene detector runs by default, and any detectors of your own run with it. MediaAnalysisResult result = MediaAnalysis.Run("shots.mkv"); foreach (Scene scene in result.Scenes) { Console.WriteLine($"Scene {scene.Number}: {scene.Start.ToTimeSpan()} to {scene.End.ToTimeSpan()}, starts with a {scene.StartKind}"); } SceneOptions picks the method and its threshold. SceneMethod.Adaptive weighs each frame's change against the frames around it, so a fast pan is not taken for a cut; Content compares with the frames just before, as ffmpeg's scene score does; Histogram compares luma histograms, which ignores motion inside a steady picture. A cut closer than MinSceneLength to the last is dropped, and with FlashMode.Merge a flash that comes back to the picture before it is no scene. A frame counts as black for fades when its mean luma is at or under FadeLevel (2 % of the range, so dark scenes keep their cuts). KeepSeries keeps every frame's score. // Content compares each frame with the one before, as ffmpeg's scene score does; Adaptive (the default) also weighs the // frames around it, so fast motion is not taken for a cut. Fades through black end a scene in the dark. SceneOptions options = new() { Method = SceneMethod.Content, Threshold = 0.3, MinSceneLength = MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5), DetectFades = true, KeepSeries = true, }; MediaAnalysisResult result = MediaAnalysis.Run("shots.mkv", new MediaAnalysisOptions { Scenes = options }); SceneScore sharpest = result.SceneScores.MaxBy(s => s.Score); Console.WriteLine($"{result.Cuts.Count} cuts; the sharpest at {sharpest.Time.ToTimeSpan()}"); A detector of your own takes frames in time order, and the SceneDetector runs on its own too: // A detector takes frames in time order; this one finds the darkest frame. The scene detector can run on its own too. DarkestFrame darkest = new(); SceneDetector scenes = new(new SceneOptions { Method = SceneMethod.Histogram }); using (VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("shots.mkv")) { foreach (YuvVideoFrame frame in reader.ReadFrames()) { using (frame) { darkest.Add(frame); if (scenes.Add(frame) is { } cut) { Console.WriteLine($"Cut at frame {cut.Frame}"); } } } scenes.Complete(reader.Info.Duration ?? MediaTime.Zero); } Console.WriteLine($"Darkest frame at {darkest.Time.ToTimeSpan()}, {scenes.Scenes.Count} scenes"); // Audio detectors get the audio in blocks, interleaved with the video by time, in the same pass. Peak peak = new(); MediaAnalysis.Run("shots.mkv", new MediaAnalysisOptions { AudioDetectors = [peak] }); Console.WriteLine($"Peak {20 * Math.Log10(peak.Value):0.0} dBFS"); SceneFrames.Read seeks to the first, middle or last frame of each scene, for thumbnails or a shot list: // A frame from each scene, read by seeking: the first, the middle or the last. MediaAnalysisResult result = MediaAnalysis.Run("shots.mkv"); using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("shots.mkv"); foreach (SceneFrame scene in SceneFrames.Read(reader, result.Scenes, ScenePosition.Middle)) { using (scene.Frame) using (Raster<Rgba8> picture = scene.Frame.ToRaster<Rgba8>()) { picture.Save($"scene-{scene.Scene.Number}.png"); } } TestSources makes pictures and sounds to test with: SMPTE color bars at their code values in any bit depth, a moving pattern with a frame counter, solid colors, gradients, tones, white or pink noise (NoiseColor) and sweeps. TestVideoFormat and TestAudioFormat set the size, rate and sample layout; ColorBarsStyle picks HD or SD bars. // Generated pictures and sounds for tests and demos: bars, a moving pattern, solid colors, gradients, tones and noise. TestVideoFormat format = new() { Width = 320, Height = 180, FrameRate = new Rational(25, 1) }; MediaTime second = MediaTime.FromSeconds(1); using VideoWriter writer = VideoWriter.Create(path, new VideoWriterOptions { FrameRate = format.FrameRate, AudioCodec = Egami.Video.Audio.Codecs.FlacCodec.Instance, AudioSampleRate = 48000, AudioLayout = ChannelLayout.Stereo, }); IEnumerable<YuvVideoFrame> shots = TestSources.ColorBars(format, second) .Concat(TestSources.Solid(format, second, new Rgba8(30, 40, 220, 255))) .Concat(TestSources.Pattern(format, second)); int index = 0; foreach (YuvVideoFrame frame in shots) { using (frame) { writer.WriteFrame(frame.Raster, new MediaTime(index++, format.FrameRate.Reciprocal())); } } foreach (AudioFrame block in TestSources.Sine(null, MediaTime.FromSeconds(3), frequency: 1000, level: -18)) { using (block) { writer.WriteAudio(block); } } More detectors run in the same pass, each keeping ffmpeg's documented measure and defaults with thresholds as fractions of the stream's range: BlackDetector (blackdetect) and FreezeDetector (freezedetect) return DetectedRanges, CropDetector (cropdetect) a CropReport with the rectangle that keeps every frame's picture, InterlaceDetector (idet) an InterlaceReport with field order counts, repeated fields and an InterlaceVerdict that spots 3:2 telecine, and DuplicateDetector (mpdecimate's test) runs of repeated frames. Each takes its own options record (BlackOptions, FreezeOptions, CropOptions with the runs of frames as CropRuns, InterlaceOptions, DuplicateOptions), and the black detector keeps every frame's ratio as a FrameValue series on request. // ffmpeg's detection filters as detectors, with their documented defaults: black and frozen stretches, black borders, // field order and repeated frames, all from one decode. BlackDetector black = new(new BlackOptions { MinDuration = MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5) }); using FreezeDetector freeze = new(new FreezeOptions { MinDuration = MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5) }); CropDetector crop = new(); InterlaceDetector fields = new(); DuplicateDetector duplicates = new(); MediaAnalysis.Run("shots.mkv", new MediaAnalysisOptions { VideoDetectors = [black, freeze, crop, fields, duplicates] }); foreach (DetectedRange range in freeze.Ranges) { Console.WriteLine($"Frozen from {range.Start.ToTimeSpan()} to {range.End.ToTimeSpan()}"); } Console.WriteLine($"{black.Ranges.Count} black stretches, crop to {crop.Report().Crop}, {fields.Report().Verdict}"); Console.WriteLine($"{duplicates.DuplicateCount} repeated frames"); SignalMeter reports what signalstats and colordetect do: the lowest, 10 %, mean, 90 % and highest code values of each plane as PlaneLevels, saturation, the share of pixels outside broadcast range, the SignalRange the samples really use and the AlphaUse of an alpha plane. With Blur and Blockiness on it also scores edge width and coding blocks, and KeepSeries keeps a SignalFrame per frame. // Levels, saturation and broadcast range as signalstats gives them, the range really used, and optional blur and // blockiness scores. SignalMeter meter = new(new SignalOptions { Blur = true, Blockiness = true }); MediaAnalysis.Run("shots.mkv", new MediaAnalysisOptions { Scenes = null, VideoDetectors = [meter] }); SignalReport report = meter.Report(); Console.WriteLine($"Y {report.Y.Min}..{report.Y.Max} (mean {report.Y.Mean:0.0}), {report.OutOfRange:P1} out of range, {report.Range} range"); Console.WriteLine($"Edges {report.Blur:0.00} px wide, blockiness {report.Blockiness:0.00}"); On the audio side, SilenceDetector finds silent stretches as silencedetect does, over all channels or each one, with its SilenceOptions; AudioLevelMeter returns an AudioLevelReport with ChannelLevels for each channel and overall: peak, RMS, DC offset, crest factor, clipped samples, noise floor, zero crossings and a 1 dB histogram, as volumedetect and astats report them. // Silent stretches as silencedetect finds them (under -60 dBFS for 2 s by default), and the sample levels volumedetect // and astats report, per channel and over all channels. SilenceDetector silence = new(new SilenceOptions { Noise = -50, MinDuration = MediaTime.FromSeconds(0.5) }); AudioLevelMeter levels = new(); MediaAnalysis.Run("shots.mkv", new MediaAnalysisOptions { Scenes = null, AudioDetectors = [silence, levels] }); Console.WriteLine($"{silence.Ranges.Count} silent stretches"); AudioLevelReport report = levels.Report(); Console.WriteLine($"Peak {report.Overall.Peak:0.0} dBFS, RMS {report.Overall.Rms:0.0} dBFS, {report.Overall.Clipped} clipped"); LoudnessMeter measures loudness as ITU-R BS.1770 and EBU R 128 define it, at any rate from 8 to 384 kHz: momentary and short-term loudness while audio comes in, and a LoudnessReport with the gated integrated loudness, the loudness range (EBU Tech 3342) and the true peak. LoudnessOptions turns the true peak off or keeps a LoudnessValue every 100 ms. // EBU R 128 loudness: integrated, range and true peak at the end, momentary and short-term while the audio plays. LoudnessMeter meter = new(new LoudnessOptions { KeepSeries = true }); MediaAnalysis.Run("shots.mkv", new MediaAnalysisOptions { Scenes = null, AudioDetectors = [meter] }); LoudnessReport loudness = meter.Report(); Console.WriteLine($"I {loudness.Integrated:0.0} LUFS, LRA {loudness.Range:0.0} LU, true peak {loudness.TruePeak:0.0} dBTP"); foreach (LoudnessValue value in meter.ShortTermSeries) { Console.WriteLine($"{value.Time.ToTimeSpan()}: {value.Loudness:0.0} LUFS"); } AudioPictures draws audio as a Raster<Rgba8>, reading it once with constant memory however long it runs. Waveform shows each column's min-to-max outline with the RMS level shaded inside, linear or in dB (WaveformScale), with the channels together or stacked (AudioPictureChannels); WaveformOptions sets the size and colors. Spectrogram shows frequency over time with a Hann-windowed FFT per column, on a linear or logarithmic FrequencyScale, colored by level from Floor to Ceiling with magma or grayscale (SpectrogramColors); SpectrogramOptions sets the window length too. The pictures carry no text: add axes and labels with Egami.Drawing. // A waveform with each channel in its own strip, and a spectrogram on a logarithmic frequency axis in magma colors. using Raster<Rgba8> waveform = AudioPictures.Waveform("shots.mkv", new WaveformOptions { Width = 1200, Height = 240, Channels = AudioPictureChannels.Stacked, }); waveform.Save("waveform.png"); using Raster<Rgba8> spectrogram = AudioPictures.Spectrogram("shots.mkv", new SpectrogramOptions { Width = 1200, Height = 400, Scale = FrequencyScale.Logarithmic, Floor = -100, }); spectrogram.Save("spectrogram.png"); Limits and warnings A MediaContext holds the containers and codecs, the Egami context (memory, threads, safety limits), the MediaLimits for files from outside (packet, header and index sizes, tracks, nesting) and a handler for MediaWarnings: what a reader recovered from. VP9 decodes tile columns and loop filter rows on up to MaxParallelism threads. // Limits for files from outside, and a handler for what a reader recovers from (a broken index, a cut-off cluster). List<MediaWarning> warnings = []; MediaContext context = MediaContext.Default with { Limits = MediaLimits.Default with { MaxPacketBytes = 8 << 20, MaxTracks = 8 }, Warnings = warnings.Add, Egami = EgamiContext.Default with { MaxParallelism = 2 }, }; using VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("movie.webm", null, context); foreach (MediaWarning warning in warnings) { Console.WriteLine($"{warning.Code}: {warning.Message}"); } MP4 and QuickTime Mp4Format reads .mp4, .m4v, .m4a and .mov files, flat or fragmented (CMAF and DASH segments, phone recordings), and writes ISO MP4. Every track is read: AV1, VP9, VP8, Motion JPEG, Opus, FLAC, PCM and mov_text with their settings, and H.264, HEVC, AAC or any other codec passed through, so a remux keeps them byte for byte. Opening a long file reads only its index. Edit lists are applied, as FFmpeg shows them: a delayed track starts later, and packets before the start are marked EncodedPacket.IsDiscardable (the reader decodes them and drops their frames). new Mp4Format { IgnoreEditLists = true } gives the media's own times. The display matrix is VideoTrackInfo.Orientation. Frames come out as coded; VideoReaderOptions.AutoOrient turns them. A timecode track gives MediaInfo.Timecode. Tags, cover art (as an attachment named cover.jpg or cover.png) and chapters (Nero chpl or a QuickTime chapter track) are read, and written back. MovTextSample reads and writes mov_text subtitles with their style runs (MovTextStyle: the characters each covers, MovTextFace bold, italic or underline, size and color). Writing puts moov before the media, so the file plays while it downloads. On a stream that can seek and read the media is moved forward at the end; on any other stream the file is written fragmented (see Streaming MP4, which also covers HLS and DASH segments). new Mp4Format { MoovAtEnd = true } writes moov last, straight to a seekable stream. A QuickTime file is written as MP4. // MP4 and QuickTime files read like any other: rotation from the display matrix, the start timecode, edit lists applied. MediaInfo phone = MediaFile.Probe("phone.mov"); Console.WriteLine($"{phone.FormatName}: turn {phone.VideoTrack!.Orientation} to show upright"); Console.WriteLine($"starts at timecode {MediaFile.Probe("camera.mov").Timecode}"); // Frames come out as coded; AutoOrient turns each one upright. using (VideoReader reader = VideoReader.Open("phone.mov", new VideoReaderOptions { AutoOrient = true })) { using VideoFrame<Rgb8> upright = reader.ReadFrames<Rgb8>().First(); Console.WriteLine($"{reader.Track.Width}x{reader.Track.Height} coded, {upright.Raster.Width}x{upright.Raster.Height} shown"); } // Writing MP4: moov before the media (the file plays while it downloads), tags, chapters and cover art kept. MediaFile.Remux("movie.webm", "movie.mp4"); MediaFile.Remux("metadata.mkv", "metadata.mp4"); // mov_text subtitles: each packet's text and style runs. using IDemuxer demuxer = MediaFile.OpenDemuxer("subtitled.mp4"); TrackInfo subtitles = demuxer.Tracks.First(t => t.CodecId == CodecIds.MovText); while (demuxer.ReadPacket() is { } packet) { using (packet) { if (packet.TrackNumber == subtitles.Number) { MovTextSample text = MovTextSample.Parse(packet.Data.Span); Console.WriteLine($"{packet.Timestamp.ToTimeSpan()}: {text.Text} ({text.Styles.Count} styles)"); } } } Broken files are read up to the damage, with a warning through MediaContext.Warnings: mp4-truncated (the file was cut off), mp4-bad-track, mp4-bad-box and mp4-bad-fragment (broken boxes, skipped), mp4-sample-table (tables that disagree), mp4-edit-list (an edit list with several media edits or another rate, not applied), mp4-sample-descriptions (a track that changes its sample description), mp4-fragment-track and mp4-track-id. Writers report mp4-timestamps (a packet decoding before the one before it), metadata-dropped, and for fragmented files mp4-fragmented and mp4-chapter-track. A file whose moov follows its media needs a stream that can seek. Containers Each container is a ContainerFormat: MatroskaFormat (WebM and Matroska), Mp4Format (MP4 and QuickTime), AviFormat, IvfFormat, Y4mFormat, Av1ObuFormat and Av1AnnexBFormat for raw AV1, and for audio WavFormat and FlacFormat. RawVideo reads and writes headerless frames in a layout you give. // The containers, by name or extension, and headerless raw frames in a layout you give. ContainerFormat? webm = MediaContext.Default.FindContainer("webm"); bool known = webm is MatroskaFormat && MediaContext.Default.FindContainer("avi") is AviFormat && MediaContext.Default.FindContainer("ivf") is IvfFormat && MediaContext.Default.FindContainer("y4m") is Y4mFormat; VideoTrackInfo track = new() { Number = 1, Kind = TrackKind.Video, CodecId = CodecIds.Uncompressed, FourCC = "I420", TimeBase = new Rational(1, 25), FrameRate = new Rational(25, 1), Width = 64, Height = 48, }; using MemoryStream frames = new(new byte[64 * 48 * 3 / 2 * 2]); using IDemuxer raw = RawVideo.OpenDemuxer(frames, track);

articles/packages.html.title: Packages | Egami
articles/packages.html.summary: Packages Egami is a family of packages. Each is fully managed C# with no dependencies outside the family, and you add only the ones you use. Packages at 1.0 or above keep their public API compatible within the major version; packages at 0.x may still change. Egami, Egami.Drawing, Egami.Fonts, Egami.Svg, Egami.Css, Egami.Heic, Egami.Formats.Extended, Egami.Cli and Egami.Cli.Host share one version and release together; the other packages have versions of their own. Each package name links to its source code. Images Package Version What it does Needs Docs Egami 1.x Rasters and pixel types, every format reader and writer, operations, color management, metadata, streaming decode Nothing Getting started, formats, all guides Egami.Heic 1.x Reads HEIC phone photos (HEVC-coded HEIF), opt-in because HEVC is covered by patents Egami, the same version HEIC Egami.Formats.Extended 1.x Extra image formats as plugins on core Egami's format API: PCX, SGI, Sun raster, XBM, XPM, WBMP and Farbfeld, read and written Egami, the same version Extended formats Drawing and text Package Version What it does Needs Docs Egami.Drawing 1.x Antialiased paths, shapes, strokes, clips, paints, layers, meshes and recorded drawings on a canvas Egami, Egami.Fonts Drawing, The .egdr format Egami.Fonts 1.x TrueType and OpenType fonts, glyph outlines and metrics, subsetting, text shaping and paragraph layout Egami Fonts and text, Unicode text and shaping, Paragraph layout Egami.Fonts.Substitutes 1.0 Bundled open fonts, metric-compatible with Arial, Helvetica, Times, Courier, Calibri and Cambria, for when those are not installed Egami.Fonts Fonts and text Egami.Barcodes 1.0 Writes and reads 1D and 2D barcodes Egami, Egami.Drawing, Egami.Fonts Barcodes, Reading barcodes Vector graphics Package Version What it does Needs Docs Egami.Svg 1.x Reads SVG 1.1 and SVG 2 into an editable element tree, saves it back, and draws it onto any canvas Egami, Egami.Drawing, Egami.Fonts, Egami.Css SVG Egami.Css 1.x CSS syntax, selectors, the cascade, media queries and value parsers Nothing CSS Egami.Metafiles 1.0 Plays WMF, EMF and EMF+ pictures onto a canvas Egami, Egami.Drawing, Egami.Fonts Windows metafiles Compatibility Package Version What it does Needs Docs Egami.SystemDrawing 1.0 preview System.Drawing.Common's API on every OS, in managed code: Bitmap, Image, Icon, pixel formats, LockBits and the codecs so far Egami, Egami.Drawing, Egami.Fonts, Egami.Metafiles System.Drawing drop-in Video and audio Package Version What it does Needs Docs Egami.Video 1.0 Reads and writes video and audio with Egami rasters as frames: MP4, WebM, Matroska, AVI, IVF, YUV4MPEG2, Ogg, WAV, FLAC, MP3, AIFF and CAF; AV1, VP9 and VP8 decode and encode, Motion JPEG, Opus, Vorbis, FLAC, MP3, AC-3 and ALAC; subtitles, smart cut and scene detection Egami Video Egami.Video.H264 1.0 H.264 (AVC) decoding for Egami.Video: progressive Constrained Baseline, Main, High, High 10 and High 4:2:2 in MP4, MOV, Matroska, AVI and raw .h264 files. Opt-in because H.264 is covered by patents Egami.Video, the same version H.264 Command-line tools Package Version What it does Needs Docs Egami.Cli 1.x The egami command: convert, inspect, resize and edit images from a shell, chain steps, run workflow files and batches. A .NET tool, not a library, and the one package with a dependency outside the family: System.CommandLine Egami, Egami.Drawing, Egami.Fonts, Egami.Fonts.Substitutes, Egami.Svg, Egami.Css, Egami.Metafiles, Egami.Formats.Extended The egami command Egami.Video.Cli 1.0 The egami-video command: inspect, remux, cut, join, export frames, make clips and convert audio from a shell, with ffmpeg and ffprobe command lines and an MCP server. A .NET tool that carries Egami.Video's version Egami.Video, Egami, Egami.Drawing, Egami.Fonts, Egami.Fonts.Substitutes, Egami.Svg, Egami.Metafiles, Egami.Formats.Extended, System.CommandLine, ModelContextProtocol.Core The egami-video command Egami.Cli.Host 1.x The command host of Egami's command-line tools as source: exit codes, globs, output templates, batches and an MCP server, compiled into a tool with internal types only. For tool authors, not for apps System.CommandLine, ModelContextProtocol.Core Source on GitHub The changelog lists what each version adds.

articles/performance.html.title: Performance | Egami
articles/performance.html.summary: Performance Tips that matter Load in the type you will work in. Raster.Load<Rgba8> converts row by row while decoding; loading the natural type and converting afterwards touches every pixel twice. Use Derive for thumbnails. It reads the source once and writes only the small result; Copy then Apply copies the full image first. Decode small. ReaderOptions.MinimumSize decodes JPEG at 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 scale straight from the DCT, and averages blocks of rows as they are decoded for every other format, so a thumbnail never holds the full image. Stream large files. Raster.Transcode and RasterDecoder hold a few rows instead of the whole image; a leading crop or resize in a transcode chain becomes a decode region or reduction. Chain operations. A chain is planned as a whole: a Crop before a resize reads only the crop, adjacent color steps run as one pass, and AutoOrient before a resize turns only the result. Probe before you load when you might reject the file. Batch work on one thread per image (MaxParallelism = 1) and run images side by side; for a single large image, leave MaxParallelism at the processor count. Dispose rasters. Pixel memory is pooled; disposing returns it at once for the next image. Running the benchmarks dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/Egami.Benchmarks -- --filter "*" dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/Egami.Benchmarks -- --filter "*SimpleDecode*" The benchmarks use BenchmarkDotNet and generated test images (a 1920 × 1080 photo-like image and a screenshot-like one), so anyone can reproduce them. Egami's numbers Median times on one machine (24 cores, .NET 10, x64 with AVX2), decoding from memory into the file's natural pixel type: Scenario 1 thread All cores BMP 24-bit decode, 1920 × 1080 0.31 ms 0.37 ms BMP 8-bit palette decode 1.6 ms 1.7 ms TGA 32-bit RLE decode 3.1 ms 2.9 ms QOI decode, photo 15.3 ms 15.6 ms PPM decode 0.32 ms 0.39 ms QOI encode, photo 14.3 ms 14.4 ms TGA 32-bit RLE encode 3.6 ms 3.6 ms BMP 24-bit encode 0.46 ms 0.46 ms Steady-state decoding and encoding allocate only the result raster: under 2.5 KB of managed memory a call for these formats. Native AOT Egami is trimming- and AOT-clean: no reflection, no runtime code generation. Publish as usual: dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishAot=true Egami's own build publishes a small console app this way on every change and checks that it runs with no warnings.

articles/video-cli/assistants.html.title: egami-video for AI assistants | Egami
articles/video-cli/assistants.html.summary: egami-video for AI assistants egami-video mcp serves egami-video's commands as tools to an AI assistant (Claude, GitHub Copilot, Cursor) over the Model Context Protocol, on standard input and output. It runs on the same server code as egami mcp: one tool per command (ffmpeg and ffprobe mode aside), with the command's options as arguments. { "mcpServers": { "egami-video": { "command": "egami-video", "args": ["mcp"] } } } Tools read and write only inside the folders the assistant opened, and those given with --allow <folder>. Without either they use the working folder. Outputs never replace inputs unless a call sets in_place. Standard input and output carry the protocol, so - is refused. Every result is an object: exitCode, written (the files written), output (the command's JSON or text) and messages. info answers in its JSON. Long jobs send progress notifications as they go, with the same line the terminal shows, and stop when the call is cancelled, leaving no partial file. A call may ask for a picture of the first file it wrote (preview): an image, or a video's first frame, fit to 1024 pixels. --max-inputs (1000 by default) bounds the files one call takes; --limit sets the safety limits for decoded frames.

articles/video-cli/commands.html.summary: egami-video command reference Every egami-video command with its arguments and options, as egami-video <command> --help prints them. The options of all commands (-v, -vv, -q, --limit, --progress, --progress-format) are listed once, at the top. The egami-video command explains the conventions they share; run takes egami's steps. Description: Inspect, remux, cut, join and convert video and audio files, and export and make frames, with Egami.Video, a fully managed video library. Usage: egami-video [command] [options] Options: -v, --verbose Write information to standard error. -vv, --debug Write debugging detail to standard error. -q, --quiet Write only errors to standard error: no warnings and no progress line. --limit <name=value,...> Safety limits for decoded frames, such as pixels=100M,memory=2GB (names: pixels, width, height, frames, memory, metadata). EGAMI_LIMITS sets them too. --progress <file|-> Write progress to a file, or - for standard output: key=value lines as ffmpeg -progress writes them, or JSON with --progress-format json. --progress-format <keys|json> How --progress writes: keys (the default, ffmpeg's key=value blocks) or json (one object per line). -?, -h, --help Show help and usage information --version Show version information Commands: info <inputs> Show what media files hold: container, duration, tracks and codecs, tags, chapters and attachments; with options, packets and frames. Like ffprobe. remux <inputs> Copy tracks into another container without decoding: change AVI to Matroska, pick tracks, keep tags, chapters and attachments. trim <inputs> Cut a part out of files: every track from --from up to --to, with timestamps starting at 0; subtitle cues shown across the cut are clipped to it. Without --smart or --reencode nothing is decoded and the cut starts at the video keyframe at or before --from, like ffmpeg -ss -to -c copy. concat <inputs> Join clips with the same tracks and codecs into one file without decoding, one after another in the order given (globs sorted by name). segment <inputs> Split files into parts without decoding, at video keyframes: -o names the parts with {part} (from 1), such as out-{part:000}.mkv; a folder takes {name}-{part:000}.{ext}. timestamps <inputs> Change packet timestamps without decoding: shift tracks, re-time video to a constant frame rate, repair broken timestamps or start at 0. With --track, --shift, --rate and --fix change only those tracks; every track is written. extract <inputs> Copy a track into its own file without decoding (VP8, VP9 and AV1 to IVF, PCM to WAV, FLAC to FLAC, Opus and Vorbis to Ogg, the rest to Matroska), or write attachments and cover art as files. embed <inputs> Add tracks from other files, attachments and cover art to a file without decoding, and set track languages, names and defaults. Track numbers count the output's tracks from 1. metadata <inputs> Write tags, chapters, track names and languages and attachment names as JSON, or copy a file with them changed from such a JSON or with --set, --remove and --chapter. frames <inputs> Write video frames as images: every frame, one every few seconds, at given times, keyframes or a few evenly spaced. encode <inputs> Make a clip from images, an image sequence or a Y4M stream, with Motion JPEG, VP8 or uncompressed video, and audio from another file. run <inputs-and-steps> Run egami's steps over every frame of a video, separated by +, and encode it again: 'egami-video run in.mkv crop 0 60 1920 960 + resize 1280x + save out.mkv'. 'egami-video run --list' lists the steps; audio and subtitles are copied, and frames keep their times. thumbnail <inputs> Write a representative frame of each video as an image: a typical frame of its opening, not a black or empty one, or the frame at --at. scenes <inputs> Find the cuts between shots: list where each scene starts (frame, time and how sharp the cut is), and optionally write a frame of each. analyze <inputs> Look for black, frozen, silent, cropped, interlaced and duplicate stretches, scene cuts, signal levels and loudness in one pass, as ffmpeg's detection filters do. waveform <inputs> Draw the waveform of each file's audio as an image: the min to max outline of each column with the RMS level inside, as editors and podcast players show it. spectrum <inputs> Draw the spectrogram of each file's audio as an image: frequency up, time across, level as color. generate <source> <file> Write a test clip or sound: moving pattern with frame number and timecode, color bars, a solid color or a gradient, with or without a tone; or a sine, silence, noise or sweep on its own. sheet <inputs> Make a contact sheet: a grid of evenly spaced frames, with their times and a title if asked. animate <inputs> Make an animated GIF, WebP or PNG (APNG) from a stretch of video, at a frame rate and size of your choice. hash <inputs> Hash every decoded frame or packet of each track, in the layout of ffmpeg -f framemd5, to check that decoding matches. compare <reference> <inputs> Measure PSNR and SSIM per plane between a reference clip and others, frame by frame in presentation order, as ffmpeg's psnr and ssim filters do. audio <inputs> Decode audio to WAV, FLAC, Ogg FLAC, Opus, AIFF, CAF or ALAC in .m4a, or encode a video file's audio again while copying its video unchanged: resample, remix and change the sample format. join <inputs> Join clips of any size, frame rate and audio into one, fitted to one canvas, with an optional transition between them; everything is encoded again. For clips that already match, concat copies without decoding. fade <input> Fade a clip in from a colour and out to it, picture and sound together; like ffmpeg's fade and afade. overlay <main> <over> Draw one clip over another, such as a logo or a keyed presenter, with an opacity and a time window; like ffmpeg's overlay (with chromakey and despill for --key). pip <main> <inset> Show a second clip small in a corner of the first (picture-in-picture), with a time window and fades. stack <inputs> Show clips side by side, one above the other, or in a grid; like ffmpeg's hstack, vstack and xstack. speed <input> <factor> Play a clip faster or slower: the picture takes the nearest frames, and the sound keeps its pitch; like ffmpeg's setpts with atempo. reverse <input> Play a clip backwards, picture and sound, holding only one keyframe interval at a time; like ffmpeg's reverse and areverse, which hold the whole clip. loop <input> Play a clip several times in a row; like ffmpeg's loop and aloop. freeze <input> Hold one frame of a clip still for a while, with silence, then go on; --at end holds the last frame, like ffmpeg's tpad. slideshow <images> Make a video of images shown one after another, with transitions and an optional pan and zoom; like ffmpeg's loop=1, zoompan and xfade, but with sub-pixel motion. stabilize <input> Take the shake out of a clip in two passes: measure the camera's motion (corners tracked with Lucas-Kanade, a RANSAC fit), smooth its path with a Gaussian, and warp each frame onto it; like ffmpeg's vidstabdetect and vidstabtransform. edit <file> Render an edit file: clips on a track with transitions, layers over it and effects with time windows. Every other editing command writes one with --save-edit. formats List the containers and codecs egami-video reads and writes, like ffmpeg -formats and -codecs. ffmpeg <arguments> Run an ffmpeg command line with egami-video: 'egami-video ffmpeg -i in.avi -c copy out.mkv'. --explain prints the native command instead. articles/video-cli/ffmpeg.html.title: ffmpeg command lines | Egami
articles/video-cli/ffmpeg.html.summary: ffmpeg command lines egami-video ffmpeg and egami-video ffprobe take the command lines people already know, find in answers online or have in scripts, and run them with egami-video's own commands. They accept a documented subset of FFmpeg's options. Anything outside it stops with exit code 2 and names the option: nothing is ignored silently. egami-video ffmpeg -i in.avi -c copy out.mkv egami-video ffmpeg -ss 0.5 -i in.webm -t 1 -c copy cut.webm egami-video ffmpeg -i in.mkv -vf fps=2 shot%03d.png egami-video ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of default=noprint_wrappers=1:nokey=1 in.mkv --explain prints the native command a line stands for and stops, which is also the quickest way to learn the native syntax: egami-video ffmpeg -i in.mkv -vf scale=640:-1,hflip -c:v mjpeg out.mkv --explain prints egami-video run in.mkv resize 640 + flip horizontal -o out.mkv --codec mjpeg. What a line becomes ffmpeg line Native command -i in -c copy out (any container change, -map, -an, -sn) remux -ss, -to, -t with -c copy trim several -i with -map 0 -map 1:a embed -f concat -i list.txt -c copy concat with the files the list names -f segment -segment_time or -segment_times segment -itsoffset, or -r with -c copy timestamps -metadata key=value, -map_metadata -1 metadata an image output, %04d patterns, -vf fps=, -frames:v frames image or Y4M input (-framerate, %04d, -f yuv4mpegpipe) encode -vf with scale, crop, pad, transpose, hflip, vflip; -s; -c:v mjpeg or rawvideo run -vf thumbnail, select='gt(scene,0.4)', tile=4x4 thumbnail, scenes, sheet .gif, .apng or .webp output animate -vn, -c:a flac, -c:a alac, -c:a libopus, -b:a, -ar, -ac, -sample_fmt, an .aiff or .caf output audio -f framemd5, -f framehash hash -i distorted -i reference -lavfi psnr or ssim compare -vf blackdetect, freezedetect, cropdetect, idet, signalstats, blurdetect, blockdetect or -af silencedetect, volumedetect, astats, ebur128, with -f null - analyze --ffmpeg-log -f lavfi -i testsrc2, smptebars, smptehdbars, color, sine, anullsrc, anoisesrc generate -lavfi showwavespic or showspectrumpic (with or without -frames:v 1) waveform, spectrum Detection filters ffmpeg's detection filters write what they find to its log, and scripts read those lines back. With -f null - the filters map to analyze, and --ffmpeg-log makes it print the same lines on standard error, in the shapes ffmpeg's documentation shows: black_start:1 black_end:3.4 black_duration:2.4, silence_start: 1 then silence_end: 3.4 | silence_duration: 2.4, lavfi.freezedetect.freeze_start, cropdetect's crop=w:h:x:y, idet's field counts, volumedetect's mean_volume and max_volume and the histogram_<n>db counts, astats's per-channel block and ebur128's summary with both gate thresholds. Each line starts with [Parsed_<filter>_<n> @ egami], the filter numbered within its -vf or -af chain as ffmpeg numbers it, so the usual regular expressions still match; the ebur128 summary's later lines carry no prefix, as in ffmpeg's log. cropdetect prints its line (x1 to y2, w, h, x, y, pts, t, limit and crop=) once for each run of frames with the same rectangle where ffmpeg prints it for every frame, and rounds to 16 by default here, as ffmpeg does (analyze itself rounds to 2). egami-video ffmpeg -i in.mkv -vf blackdetect=d=0.5 -af silencedetect=noise=-50dB:d=1 -f null - egami-video ffmpeg -i in.mkv -af ebur128=peak=true -f null - The filters take their documented options by name: blackdetect d, pic_th and pix_th; freezedetect n and d; cropdetect limit, round and skip; silencedetect n, d and mono; ebur128 peak (the summary always has the sample and true peaks). signalstats, blurdetect and blockdetect have no log shape in ffmpeg's documentation, so they print the lines analyze writes. crop runs print one cropdetect line each, not one a frame. Test sources and pictures of sound -f lavfi sources become generate: testsrc and testsrc2 the moving pattern, smptebars and smptehdbars the SD and HD bars, color a solid picture, and sine, anullsrc and anoisesrc (white or pink) a sound; a picture source and a sound source together make one clip. The length comes from d= or -t, as ffmpeg's sources run until stopped. egami-video ffmpeg -f lavfi -i smptehdbars=s=1920x1080 -f lavfi -i sine=frequency=1000 -t 10 bars.mkv egami-video ffmpeg -i in.mkv -lavfi showwavespic=split_channels=1:s=1024x800 waveform.png egami-video ffmpeg -i in.mkv -lavfi showspectrumpic=s=1024x512:fscale=log spectrogram.png showwavespic takes s, split_channels, colors (the first) and scale (lin or log); showspectrumpic takes s, mode, color (magma), scale (log), fscale and legend, and draws a legend unless legend=0, as ffmpeg does. ffmpeg encodes again by default; egami-video copies streams where ffmpeg would encode with a codec it does not have, and says so in a warning. An output that exists needs -y, as in ffmpeg. Editing filters A line with an editing filter becomes one edit file, rendered by egami-video edit; --explain prints the command with edit.json for the file, then the file. -vf, -af and -filter_complex graphs take fade (in from the start, out to the end), setpts with a constant factor (0.1x to 10x), reverse, loop (whole clips), tpad (stop_mode=clone), fps, scale, xfade (with V9's transitions), concat, overlay (numbers and the W, H, w and h placement forms), hstack, vstack, xstack (grids), zoompan on an image (a constant zoom, or zoom+k with an optional cap, from the corner or the centre), chromakey, colorkey, despill, and hflip and vflip with a time window; and of the sound afade, acrossfade (where an xfade joins the same inputs), amix (of an overlay's inputs), atempo, volume, areverse and aloop. enable takes between(t,a,b), gte(t,a) and lte(t,b). -loop 1 before an image makes a still clip. egami-video ffmpeg -i in.avi -i in.mkv -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]xfade=transition=wipeleft:duration=0.5:offset=1.5[v];[0:a][1:a]acrossfade=d=0.5[a]" -map [v] -map [a] joined.mkv egami-video ffmpeg -i in.avi -i in.mkv -filter_complex "[1:v]scale=64:-1[small];[0:v][small]overlay=W-w-10:10:enable='between(t,0.5,1.5)'" pip.mkv egami-video ffmpeg -i in.avi -vf setpts=PTS/2 -af atempo=2 fast.mkv An edit changes picture and sound together, so a line that changes one and not the other stops: setpts without the same atempo, reverse without areverse and loop without aloop, unless the sound is dropped with -an. A fade fades the sound with the picture. freezeframes stops, since it replaces frames where V9's freeze adds time (tpad=stop_mode=clone or egami-video freeze hold a frame), and loudnorm stops too. deshake, vidstabdetect (to -f null, writing its result file as Egami.Video's camera motion) and vidstabtransform (its input and smoothing) become egami-video stabilize. The options ffmpeg mode takes -i, -f, -y, -n, -ss, -to, -t, -itsoffset, -framerate, -safe, -map, -c, -codec, -c:v, -c:a, -c:s, -vcodec, -acodec, -scodec, -an, -vn, -sn, -dn, -r, -s, -frames:v, -vframes, -q:v, -qscale:v, -ar, -b:a, -ab, -ac, -sample_fmt, -metadata, -map_metadata, -map_chapters, -vf, -filter:v, -lavfi and -filter_complex (psnr, ssim, showwavespic, showspectrumpic and the editing filters), -af and -filter:a (detection and editing filters), -loop 1 before an image, -segment_time, -segment_times, -update, -progress, -stats, -nostats, -stats_period, -hide_banner, -loglevel, -v and -nostdin, with pipe: and %d patterns. The filters are scale, crop, pad, transpose, hflip, vflip, fps, thumbnail, select (scene) and tile, and with -f null the detection filters above; the -f lavfi sources are testsrc, testsrc2, smptebars, smptehdbars, color, sine, anullsrc and anoisesrc. Codecs: copy, mjpeg and rawvideo for video, flac, alac, libopus (or opus) and the pcm_ codecs for audio. ffprobe mode takes -i, -show_streams, -show_format, -show_packets, -show_frames, -show_chapters, -select_streams, -show_entries, -of (also -print_format, -output_format) with the json, csv, compact, default, flat and xml writers and their nokey, noprint_wrappers, print_section and item_sep options, -v, -loglevel, -hide_banner and -pretty. Its JSON is egami-video info --format ffprobe. The tests run more than a hundred common ffmpeg and ffprobe lines: each either maps to the native command it should or stops naming its option. The subset was written from FFmpeg's published documentation only.

articles/video-cli/index.html.title: The egami-video command | Egami
articles/video-cli/index.html.summary: The egami-video command egami-video inspects, remuxes, cuts, joins and converts video and audio files from a shell or a build script, with no C# to write. It does the jobs people use ffprobe and ffmpeg for, with Egami.Video's fully managed code. It is the Egami.Video.Cli package, a .NET tool that carries Egami.Video's version. egami-video info in.mkv egami-video remux in.avi -o out.mkv egami-video trim in.webm --from 0.5 --to 1.5 -o cut.webm egami-video frames in.mkv --every 0.5 -o shots/{name}-{frame:0000}.png egami-video run in.avi resize 80x + sharpen 0.5 -o small.mkv egami-video audio in.mkv -o sound.flac The command reference lists every option. ffmpeg command lines explains egami-video ffmpeg and egami-video ffprobe, and egami-video for AI assistants the mcp server. Installing dotnet tool install --global Egami.Video.Cli With the egami tool installed too, egami video info clip.mkv runs egami-video info clip.mkv: egami runs any egami-<name> program on the PATH. The tool is free of reflection and builds with the trimming and Native AOT analyzers on. Commands Command What it does Like info Container, duration, tracks, codecs, tags, chapters, attachments; --packets, --frames, --headers ffprobe remux Copy tracks into another container ffmpeg -c copy trim Cut from the keyframe at or before --from to --to ffmpeg -ss -to -c copy concat Join clips with the same tracks and codecs the concat demuxer segment Split every --every, at --at times or at --scenes, at keyframes -f segment timestamps Shift, set a frame rate, repair timestamps -itsoffset, -r, setts extract One track, attachments or cover art to their own files -map 0:a:0 -c copy, -dump_attachment embed Add tracks, attachments and cover art; set languages and names -i a -i b -map 0 -map 1 metadata Write tags and chapters as JSON, or change them -f ffmetadata, -metadata frames Frames as images; Motion JPEG frames as JPEG without decoding ffmpeg -i in out-%04d.png encode Images, an image sequence or Y4M into a clip ffmpeg -framerate 30 -i %04d.png run egami's steps on every frame, then encode -vf scale,crop,pad,transpose thumbnail A representative frame -vf thumbnail scenes Where the scenes start, and a frame of each select='gt(scene,0.4)' analyze Black, frozen, silent, cropped, interlaced and duplicate stretches, scenes, signal levels and loudness, in one pass blackdetect, silencedetect, ebur128 … with -f null - waveform A picture of the sound's waveform -lavfi showwavespic spectrum A spectrogram picture -lavfi showspectrumpic generate Test clips and sounds: bars, a pattern, solid colors, gradients, tones, noise, sweeps -f lavfi -i testsrc2, smptebars, sine sheet A contact sheet of frames with their times -vf tile=4x4 animate Animated GIF, WebP or APNG ffmpeg -i in.mp4 out.gif hash Hashes of every frame or packet -f framemd5 compare PSNR and SSIM between clips -lavfi psnr, -lavfi ssim audio Audio to WAV, FLAC, Opus, AIFF, CAF or ALAC; audio again while copying video -vn -c:a flac, -c:a libopus -b:a, -ar, -ac join Clips of any size, rate and audio fitted to one canvas and joined, with transitions concat filter with scale, pad, fps; xfade and acrossfade fade Fade in from and out to a colour, picture and sound -vf fade -af afade overlay One clip over another, with --key for a chroma key overlay, chromakey, despill pip A second clip small in a corner scale and overlay stack Clips side by side, above each other or in a grid hstack, vstack, xstack speed Faster or slower, the sound's pitch kept setpts with atempo reverse Backwards, picture and sound reverse, areverse loop A clip several times in a row loop, aloop freeze One frame held for a while, or the last one at the end tpad, freezeframes slideshow Images one after another, with transitions and pan and zoom loop=1, zoompan, xfade stabilize Take the shake out of a clip, in two passes vidstabdetect, vidstabtransform edit Render an edit file: clips, transitions, layers and effects -filter_complex formats The containers and codecs this build reads and writes ffmpeg -formats Commands that copy packets (remux, trim, concat, segment, timestamps, extract, embed, metadata) never decode, so they work on any codec, H.264 and AAC included. Commands that decode need a codec Egami.Video decodes: Motion JPEG, VP8, VP9, AV1 and uncompressed video, and PCM, FLAC, Opus and Vorbis audio. encode and run write Motion JPEG, VP8, VP9, AV1 or uncompressed video; encode --codec vp8, vp9 or av1 takes --effort and --bitrate (see Encoding video). Inspecting info reads the headers without decoding. --all reads every packet too, for packet and keyframe counts and bit rates; --headers shows the codec headers of each track's first frame; --packets and --frames list every packet and every decoded frame. egami-video info in.mkv --all egami-video info in.webm --packets --track v egami-video info in.mkv --json egami-video info in.mp4 --format ffprobe --format picks how it writes: text (the default), json (Egami's own schema, docs/schemas/egami-video-info-1.json), csv for packet and frame lists, xml with the same fields as JSON, or ffprobe: JSON with the field names ffprobe -of json uses, so scripts written for ffprobe read it unchanged. ffprobe lists Matroska cover art as a video stream; egami-video lists it as an attachment. Tracks and times --track (-t) picks tracks by kind and position, language or number: Value Picks v, a, s, d Every video, audio, subtitle or data track a:1 The second audio track (counted from 0) s:eng Subtitle tracks in English (eng and en both match en-US) 3 Track 3, as info numbers it Repeat it, or separate values with commas, for several. --no-audio (-an) and --no-subtitles (-sn) leave those out. Times are seconds (90.5, 500ms, 2m), [HH:]MM:SS[.mmm] (1:30, 01:02:03.250) or a frame number in presentation order (#1234, counted from 0). A stream copy can only start on a keyframe. trim starts at the video keyframe at or before --from, ends exactly at --to, and says on standard error how far the start moved. segment starts each part at the first keyframe at or after its split point; segment --scenes starts each part at the keyframe at or before its scene's first frame and says on standard error how far before, with a warning when that is over a second. trim --smart starts on the exact frame: it encodes again only the frames from --from up to the next keyframe, matching the stream at its own quantizer, and copies the rest; trim --reencode encodes the whole cut again. segment --scenes --exact cuts every part that way, so each starts on its scene's first frame. egami-video trim in.webm --from 0.5 --duration 1 -o cut.webm egami-video trim in.webm --from 0.5 --duration 1 --smart -o exact.webm egami-video segment in.mkv --every 1 -o parts/{part:000}.mkv egami-video segment in.mkv --scenes -o shots/{part:000}.mkv -v egami-video concat parts/001.mkv parts/002.mkv -o joined.mkv egami-video timestamps in.mkv --shift 0.5 --track a -o later.mkv Frames and pictures frames writes decoded frames in any format egami writes; {frame} in the output is the frame's number in the video. Motion JPEG frames written as JPEG are the stored frames, byte for byte, without decoding. egami-video frames in.mkv --count 4 -o shots/{frame:000}.jpg egami-video frames in.webm --at 0.5,1.5 -o at-{frame}.png egami-video thumbnail in.webm -o thumb.jpg --size 320x egami-video scenes in.mkv --json egami-video scenes in.mkv --fades --frame middle --series scores.csv -o shots/{scene:000}.jpg egami-video sheet in.mkv --grid 3x2 --timestamps -o sheet.png egami-video animate in.webm --rate 10 --size 120x -o clip.gif scenes finds cuts with the adaptive method by default (--method content or histogram, --threshold); --min-length (once --min-gap) sets the shortest scene, --fades names scenes that start inside a fade and lists the fades, --flash suppress drops flashes instead of merging them, --frame middle or last picks the frame written for each scene, and --series writes every frame's score to a CSV file. encode goes the other way: images in name order, an image sequence (shots/{frame:000}.jpg reads frame 0, 1, 2 until one is missing), or a Y4M file or stream. egami-video encode "shots/*.jpg" --rate 2 -o slideshow.mkv Steps on every frame run takes the steps and + syntax of egami run (steps for run) and applies them to every frame. The output keeps the source codec when Egami.Video can encode it, else Motion JPEG; --codec chooses. Audio and subtitles are copied, and every frame keeps its time. egami-video run in.avi resize 80x + sharpen 0.5 -o small.mkv egami-video run in.mkv crop 0 10 160 100 + grayscale + save gray.avi --quality 90 egami-video run in.mkv --crop auto resize 80x -o cropped.mkv --crop auto reads the video once to find its black bars, as analyze -d crop does, and crops them off before the other steps. Analysis analyze reads a file once and runs the detectors --detect (-d) names, or every one with --all: scenes, black, freeze, crop, interlace, duplicates, signal, blur, blockiness, silence, levels and loudness. Each keeps the measure and defaults of the ffmpeg filter it stands for, and its settings take that filter's names: --black-min is blackdetect's d, --silence-noise -50dB silencedetect's n, --crop-limit cropdetect's limit. --start and --duration look at part of the file. The report is text, --json or --csv (one row per range or value), and --series file.csv adds per-frame and per-100 ms values: scene scores, black share, signal levels, momentary and short-term loudness. egami-video analyze in.mkv --all egami-video analyze in.mkv -d black,silence --black-min 0.5 --json egami-video analyze in.mkv -d loudness --series loudness.csv egami-video analyze in.mkv -d black --ffmpeg-log blackdetect In JSON each file has start, end and frames, and one entry per detector: scenes (scene, frame, start, end, score, kind) and fades; lists of {start, end, duration} ranges with a value for black, freeze, duplicates and silence (and silence.1, silence.2 … per channel); and objects for crop, interlace, signal, levels and loudness. Levels and loudness that do not exist (silence has no peak) are null. --ffmpeg-log prints the lines ffmpeg's filters log instead, for scripts that read them (ffmpeg command lines). waveform and spectrum draw the audio as a picture: --size, --channels mixed|stacked, a linear or dB --scale for the waveform and a linear or log frequency --scale for the spectrum, colors, and --legend for a time axis and level or frequency labels. generate makes test files: pattern, bars, solid and gradient pictures, with --tone or --audio for sound, and sine, silence, noise and sweep sounds. egami-video waveform in.mkv --legend --scale db -o wave.png egami-video spectrum in.mkv --scale log --legend --size 1200x400 -o spectrum.png egami-video generate bars --tone -t 10 bars.mkv egami-video generate sweep -t 5 sweep.flac Audio audio decodes the picked audio track to WAV, Wave64, FLAC, Ogg FLAC, Opus, AIFF or CAF, resampling with --rate, mixing with --channels and converting with --sample-format. With a video container as output it copies the video unchanged and encodes the audio again. --codec picks FLAC, PCM, Opus or ALAC (Apple Lossless); .opus and WebM outputs get Opus, WAV, Wave64, AVI, AIFF and CAF get PCM, .m4a gets ALAC, and the rest FLAC. ALAC also goes in .mov, .mka and .caf. --bitrate sets Opus's bitrate for all channels together (64k a channel by default); --level sets FLAC's compression (0 to 8) or ALAC's (0 fast, 1 the default). extract writes ALAC tracks to .m4a and AC-3 and E-AC-3 tracks to raw .ac3 and .eac3 files. egami-video audio in.mkv -o sound.flac egami-video audio in.webm --rate 44100 --channels stereo --sample-format s16 -o sound.wav egami-video audio in.mkv --codec flac -o flac-audio.mkv egami-video audio sound.flac --bitrate 96k -o sound.opus egami-video audio in.mp4 --bitrate 64k -o opus-audio.webm egami-video audio sound.flac -o sound.m4a egami-video audio sound.wav --sample-format s24 -o sound.aiff Editing join, fade, overlay, pip and stack build an edit with Egami.Video's editing library (see Video editing) and encode it again, so their clips may differ in size, frame rate, pixel format and audio: every clip is fitted to one canvas (--size, --rate and --fit, from the first clip by default) and its sound resampled. --transition joins clips with fade, fadeblack, dissolve, wipeleft, slideup, circleopen, clock, zoom, pixelize, blur and others, as kind:duration, with an equal-power crossfade of the sound. overlay --key green keys out a green screen and takes the spill out of its edges. --save-edit writes the edit as JSON, which edit renders, and which can be changed by hand: effects in it are egami run steps, such as "blur 8". egami-video join in.avi in.webm in.mkv --transition dissolve:0.5 --size 320x240 -o joined.mkv egami-video fade in.webm --in 0.5 --out 1 -o faded.webm egami-video overlay in.avi in.webm --at right-8,top-8 --scale 0.3 --opacity 0.8 --from 0.5 --to 1.5 -o overlay.mkv egami-video overlay in.avi in.mkv --key green --similarity 0.12 --despill 0.6 -o keyed.mkv egami-video pip in.avi in.webm --corner bottom-left --scale 0.25 --fade-in 0.2 -o pip.mkv egami-video stack in.avi in.mkv --gap 4 -o side-by-side.mkv --save-edit side-by-side.json egami-video edit side-by-side.json --codec raw -o again.avi egami-video speed in.webm 1.5 -o fast.webm egami-video reverse in.avi -o backwards.mkv egami-video loop in.avi --count 3 -o looped.mkv egami-video freeze in.avi --at 0.5 --for 1 -o frozen.mkv egami-video slideshow shots/*.jpg --each 2 --transition fade:0.5 --pan-zoom --size 320x240 -o show.mkv speed, reverse, loop and freeze change a clip's timing, picture and sound together; freeze --at end holds the last frame. slideshow takes images in order (globs sort by name) and moves each with a slow pan and zoom drawn at sub-pixel accuracy. A step of run can take a time window, @start-end right after it: blur 8 @0:05-0:12 blurs only that part. egami-video run in.avi grayscale @0.2-0.6 + blur 2 @0.4- + save windowed.mkv Checking hash writes a hash of every decoded frame (or every packet with --packets) in the layout of ffmpeg -f framemd5, and the hashes equal ffmpeg's for the same decoded planes. compare measures PSNR and SSIM per plane between a reference and other clips, and --min-psnr or --min-ssim turn it into a check that exits with 1. egami-video hash in.webm --total egami-video compare in.mkv small.mkv --scale --json Files, batches and pipes Inputs are files, globs (*, ?, [abc], **, expanded the same way in every shell), folders with --recursive, or - for standard input. Outputs are a file, a folder, a template with {name}, {ext}, {dir}, {index}, {format} and the command's part ({frame}, {part}, {scene}, {track}), or - for standard output with --format. Several inputs run at once (--jobs), a failed file is reported and the rest go on unless --fail-fast, and an output never replaces its input without --in-place. Standard input is read as it comes and standard output written as it goes, so egami-video sits between other programs without temporary files. Matroska, WebM, IVF, Y4M and WAV stream; AVI needs a file. egami-video remux - -o - --format mkv < in.avi > piped.mkv Progress and stopping A long job shows a line on standard error when it is a terminal: time, percent, frames, frames per second, size, speed and time left. --progress <file|-> writes the same reports as ffmpeg -progress does, as key=value blocks ending in progress=continue or progress=end, or one JSON object per line with --progress-format json. Batches report each file. --quiet turns the line off. Ctrl+C stops the job between packets: the output it was writing is deleted, and the exit code is 130. Outputs are written under a temporary name and get their own name only when complete. Exit codes Code Meaning 0 Done 1 A file failed (unreadable, corrupt, unwritable), or compare missed --min-psnr or --min-ssim 2 The command line is wrong; the message says what to change 3 An input exceeded a safety limit (--limit, EGAMI_LIMITS) 130 Stopped with Ctrl+C

index.html.title: Egami | Egami
index.html.summary: Egami Egami is an open source 2D imaging library for .NET 10 that loads, edits, draws and saves images. MIT-licensed, with no strings for commercial use. Fully managed C#: no native binaries, no P/Invoke, and no third-party dependencies. Safe on untrusted files: sizes are checked before anything is allocated, and every reader is fuzz-tested. Trimming and Native AOT clean, on every OS and CPU .NET 10 supports. Formats: PNG and APNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, TGA, QOI, the Netpbm formats, TIFF, Radiance and OpenEXR, JPEG XL, ICO, CUR and ANI read and written; AVIF, JPEG 2000, JBIG2, CCITT fax and PSD read. See Formats. Operations: resizing and geometry, color management, tone and color, filters, compositing, masks, analysis and palettes. More packages: vector drawing (Egami.Drawing), fonts and text layout (Egami.Fonts), SVG (Egami.Svg), CSS (Egami.Css), Windows metafiles (Egami.Metafiles) and barcodes (Egami.Barcodes). See Packages. using Egami; using Raster image = Raster.Load("photo.jpg"); image.Apply(ops => ops.AutoOrient().Fit(800, 800)); image.Save("photo-small.png"); Start with Getting started, read the guides for each area and its recipes, or look anything up in the API reference.
